en: The Catalogue of the Buddhist Scriptures of the Great Tang, Volume 1: A Record of the Origins of the Translation of Various Scriptures Throughout Successive Dynasties.

From the initial arrival of the teachings in the Eastern Lands, spanning successive imperial reigns, it was invariably through the patronage of the sovereigns that the Dharma was propagated and its essence made known.
Thereupon, the practitioners of the Mysterious [Daoists] and the Plain [Buddhists] followed the established prescriptions to initiate their foundations and structures.
Enlightened sovereigns valued their righteous principles and maintained a protective oversight;
obscure rulers conformed to their respective norms and followed them accordingly.
Thus, from the Later Han dynasty down to the Great Tang,
though the eras shifted between refinement and coarseness, the fundamental principles remained undivided;
all alike revered and received the supreme teachings.
It serves as the primary sign for extinguishing the fetters;
its essence comprehends the profound diagram and its mirror reflects the fundamental basis of birth and death.
Thus, it has been transmitted through the *Brahmajāla-sūtra* from generation to generation, becoming ever more manifest;
this is the continuous flow of the gift of Dharma, never ceasing at any time.
Consequently, in the Five Indias and the Western Regions, the ancestors have long revered the words of the Celestial One (the Buddha).
In the nine provinces of the Eastern Land, one follows the traces of the birds;
thus, the celestial script and the celestial language remain beyond the reach of thought in this coastal realm.
Regarding the eight styles and six literary forms,
they have rarely been seen since the time of the Great Xia; thus,
what was heard of old through successive translations is only now being witnessed here.
Now, as for national histories and the ritual classics,
their substance and form are presented alternately;
so it is with the words of the Buddha and secular texts.
How can one know [the Buddha's] natural endowment in both words and principles? Therefore,
the Buddha prioritized the dissemination of his teachings and the guidance of sentient beings through them.
To open the mind's ignorance, unravel its simplicity, resolve doubts, and remove obstructions;
this does not rely on literary elegance nor preserve scrolls and volumes,
but aims to enlighten the obscurity and clarify the principles of human emotion and reason.
It is through this that the agility of the divine mind is attained.
Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well.
"I shall analyze and explain this for you;
these are the words of the Sage.
"Excellent, excellent! We wish and desire to hear it."
I only pray that the World-Honored One will analyze and explain this Dharma of receiving [the precepts].
Since the words are repeated, I do not fear being burdened by prolixity.
One should discuss only the correct realization and not engage in textual disputation;
this is the fundamental scripture.
The translation follows local customs, as it was transmitted according to the conventions of the region.
Many have fallen into superficial errors and lost much; thus,
Dao’an’s treatise on the "Five Losses" is easy to follow,
while Yancong’s composition on the "Eight Difficulties" is hard to surpass.
This is indeed the authoritative testimony.
Other mundane customs need not be further discussed.
Now, I shall record those of the imperial era who were wise and accomplished in translation.
Furthermore, it reveals the partiality and competition between faith and slander among successive rulers;
thus, this serves as the initial record.
Now, as for the eras of the Han, Jin, Sui, Tang, and Song dynasties:
The world is one great harmony;
wherever the calendar of the sovereign reaches, the Dharma-gate is unified.

In the successive dynasties of Wei, Song, Qi, and Liang, the territory was fragmented and divided, and both Chinese and non-Chinese participated in governance, resulting in the concurrent emergence of various translations.
As for the extensive sections transmitted among the common people,
which surpass the past and precede the present,
one sees their widespread dissemination and continuous brilliance reaching far and wide.
Now, I have compiled them according to their respective eras; furthermore,
I have appended the works composed by both monastics and laypeople following them.
It is hoped that those who come after will behold these as if they were face-to-face.
In total, there are eighteen dynasties;

the various sutras produced therein comprise two thousand two hundred and thirty-two works in seven thousand two hundred fascicles, including three hundred and ten works in five hundred and thirty-eight fascicles whose translators are lost.
During the Later Han dynasty, twelve monastics and laypeople transmitted and translated scriptures and vinayas, totaling three hundred and thirty-four works in four hundred and sixteen fascicles;
one hundred and twenty-five works in one hundred and forty-eight fascicles were lost translations.
During the Former Wei dynasty, six monks transmitted and translated scriptures and vinayas, totaling thirteen works.

In twenty-four fascicles, the translations produced by four monastics and laypeople during the Southern Wu period under the Sun family comprise one hundred forty-eight works totaling one hundred eighty-five fascicles;
one hundred ten works with lost translators comprise two hundred ninety-one fascicles;
and those translated by thirteen monastics and laypeople during the Western Jin dynasty comprise [the following] scriptures and precepts.
451 works in 717 fascicles; eight works in 15 fascicles of lost translations;
scriptures and commentaries produced by twenty-seven monastics and laypeople during the Eastern Jin dynasty, totaling 263 works in 585 fascicles;
and fifty-three works in fifty-six fascicles of lost translations.
The prefaces to the volumes record that during the Fu clan’s Former Qin dynasty, eight translating monks produced forty scriptures and commentaries totaling two hundred thirty-nine fascicles;
during the Qi-fu clan’s Western Qin dynasty, one translating monk produced fourteen scriptures totaling twenty-one fascicles;
together with eight scriptures of lost translation totaling eleven fascicles, these were translated during the Yao clan’s Later Qin dynasty.
One hundred twenty-four scriptures and treatises in six hundred sixty-two fascicles produced by eight monastics;
thirty-two scriptures and treatises in two hundred twenty-four fascicles translated by eight monastics and laypeople during the Juqu regime of the Northern Liang dynasty;
and five lost translations in seventeen fascicles translated by monastics and laypeople during the Song dynasty.
The scriptures and treatises produced by twenty-three individuals total two hundred and ten works in four hundred and ninety fascicles.
Those translated during the Qi dynasty by nineteen monastics and laypersons total forty-seven works in three hundred and forty-six fascicles.
Those translated during the Liang dynasty by twenty-one monastics and laypersons total nine works comprising the sutras, vinaya, and biographies.
Ten schools totaling seven hundred and eighty fascicles were translated during the Yuan clan’s Northern Wei dynasty by thirteen monastics and laypersons;
eighty-seven works totaling three hundred and two fascicles were produced by two monastics and laypersons during the Gao clan’s Northern Qi dynasty;
and [the following] were translated during the Yuwen clan’s Northern Zhou dynasty.
Eleven monastics and laypeople produced thirty works, totaling one hundred and four fascicles, including sūtras, śāstras, and works on astronomy, translated during the Chen dynasty.
Three monastics and laypeople produced forty works, totaling three hundred and forty-seven fascicles, including sūtras, śāstras, biographies, and commentaries, translated during the Sui dynasty.
More than twenty monastics and laypeople produced nine works, including sūtras and śāstras, [translated during the same period].

Over ten dynasties spanning nine successive generations since the teachings first reached China, more than eleven monks have translated over two hundred works totaling one thousand five hundred scrolls,
including those from the preceding ten-plus dynasties comprising over five hundred and ten scrolls.
In the early days, the distinction between the authentic and the spurious was blurred, and the lands were intermingled by both the civilized and the barbarian.
Thus, there were five Liang, four Yan, three Qin, and two Zhao;
the territories of Xia and Shu were situated in narrow and confined places.
During the Jin and Song dynasties, when they held control over Jiangyin,
the translated scriptures and commentaries emerged according to the local circumstances;
these were limited to those countries that maintained both heterodox and orthodox systems.
I have recorded the origins of their transmission and translation;
the rest is not mentioned,
as there is no universal dharma [applicable to them].
I hope that future readers will understand how this was achieved.
First, the Record of the Translation of Buddhist Scriptures Transmitted during the Later Han Dynasty. The Preface states:
The source and origin of the transmission of the teachings truly dates back to the Zhou dynasty of the Ji clan;
though Qin destroyed them, their traces occasionally emerged.
When Liu Xiang collated the books at the Celestial Library, Buddhist scriptures were frequently encountered therein.
Based on this evidence, it is clear that [the tradition] did not begin merely in the era of Emperor Ming of the Han dynasty;
other details will be revealed elsewhere. For now, I shall describe the beginning of its restoration within the secular world through its radiance.
Therefore, Sengzhao lists this:
that the scripture’s emergence began during the reign of Emperor Xiaoming of the Later Han.
The emperor’s personal name was Zhuang.
His temple name was Xianzong.
He was the fourth son of Emperor Guangwu.
His spirit was profound and simple, and he took elegance as his sacred standard.
On the seventh night of the seventh year of the Eihō era, he had a dream in which a golden-bodied person, sixteen feet in height and with a sun disc upon his head, flew through the air and arrived;
its brilliant radiance shone resplendently throughout the palace courtyard.
At dawn, he assembled his ministers and ordered them to interpret his dream.
Fu Yi, a man of broad learning, stepped forward and submitted this response:
"Your servant has heard that in the past there was a deity in the West."
"He is named Buddha.
Is this not surely the one whom Your Majesty has seen?"
The Emperor considered this to be so.
Moved with joy by these auspicious omens,

he issued an edict dispatching fourteen individuals— including Qin Jing, a *yu-lin* (feathered forest) *lang* (commandant), and Wang Zun, a disciple of a *boshi* (master of classics)— to travel to India.
In the country of Yuezhi,
he encountered the śramaṇas Kāśyapa Mātanga and Dharmaratna,
from whom he obtained copies of scriptures and images.
He was carried back on a white horse and arrived safely in Luoyang.
According to the *Hanfa benneizhuan* (The Original Inner Biography of the Han Law),
at that time, various Daoist masters from the Five Sacred Peaks and eighteen mountains were assembled.
The memorial was submitted, but it was not granted.
The Emperor then established a mobile palace west of the capital and allowed them to compete in physical prowess.
The Daoist masters and others established an altar and arranged offerings;
they placed the Daoist scriptures and various treatises upon the altar and burned the scriptures with fire.
The lack of remaining ash served as proof.
Once the ritual prayers had been completed,
the sutra was cremated by fire.
The Daoist practitioners of Nanyue, Chu Shanxin and Fei Shucaī, died of their own volition;
the remaining six hundred or so Daoists all returned to the Buddha-dharma to seek ordination as monks.
The Emperor granted his permission;
consequently, he extensively ordained monks and nuns,
initially establishing ten monasteries.
He immediately established the Baima Temple on this very spot.
Various provinces vied with one another to establish temples to repay the kindness of the White Horse.
At a distance of more than two hundred paces to the left of the Qing Gate in the old city of Chang’an stands Zhongxing Temple.
The above is the remaining foundation of the White Horse Monastery (Baima Si).
It was here that Zhu Falan translated the Sutra in Forty-two Sections,
which he then sealed away in the stone chamber of the Lan Tai (Palace Library).
From that time onward, the teachings of Śākyamuni arose in succession like clouds,
and śramaṇas and lay devotees followed one after another to transmit and translate [the scriptures].
During the reign of Emperor Xiaohuan of the Han dynasty:
During the reign of Emperor Ling of the Han dynasty,
in the third year of the Guanghe era, he had images of the Buddha fashioned out of gold and silver.
He dispatched a Grand Master of the Palace to the Buddhist stupa temple in Luoyang to provide meals for the śramaṇas,
hanging silk banners, burning incense, scattering flowers, and lighting lamps.
This continued until the seventh year of the Guanghe era.
Because Zhang Jue and others plotted to eliminate his rebellious faction,
he abolished all matters concerning internal and external relatives, as well as the teachings of Laozi,
sorcery, witchcraft, medicine, and divination.
Those who uphold the Five Precepts of the Buddha must not sit [among them].
By this matter, one may verify the true and correct nature of the Buddhist teaching:
it is like something dyed black that cannot be stained.
"Though ground, it is not worn thin.
The dust of deceitful artifice is but a floating cloud upon me;
its sincerity is indeed worthy of great respect.
From the time of the Qin dynasty— beginning with the śramaṇa Śikṣānanda (Shi Lifa) and Liu Xiang of the Former Han—
although Buddhist scriptures were heard of, their titles remained unknown.
It was not until the Later Han that a definitive catalog was established.
Thus, the *Sūtra in Forty-two Sections* was the first [scripture],
and the Saṃgha began with Kāśyapa Mātanga;
this continued until the final years of Emperor Xian’s Jian’an era.
Thus, over a period of one hundred and fifty-two years,
there were eleven successive rulers; among them, twelve individuals—
both Chinese and non-Chinese, monastics and laypeople— [were involved].
Furthermore, he collected previously omitted works and supplemented earlier omissions,
including those of ancient lost translations,
totaling three hundred and thirty-four sections of sutras and vinaya.
In four hundred and sixteen fascicles,
this compendium of the Buddhist scriptures of the Later Han serves as a pivotal axis;
it is hoped that those with discerning insight will thereby recognize the dispersal and gathering of the ancient and modern classics.
Awaiting the time for his eminent promotion, the brilliant light of the Dharma-treasure shall spread throughout the world.

The *Ekottarika-āgama* (one fascicle) translated by the Śramaṇa Kāśyapamātaṅga of the Later Han; the five works totaling thirteen fascicles translated by the Śramaṇa Dharmaratna; the one hundred and seventy-six works totaling one hundred and ninety-seven fascicles translated by the Śramaṇa An Shigao (style name: Shigao); the twenty-one works totaling sixty-three fascicles translated by the Śramaṇa Lokakṣema; the two works totaling three fascicles translated by the Upāsaka Commandery Governor An Xuan; the two works totaling three fascicles translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Foshuo; the eleven works totaling twelve fascicles translated by the Śramaṇa Zhi Yao; the one work totaling one fascicle translated by the Śramaṇa Kang Ju; the seven works totaling nine fascicles translated by the Lay Practitioner Yan Fotiao; the six works totaling nine fascicles translated by the Śramaṇa Kang Mengxiang; the one work totaling two fascicles translated by the Śramaṇa Shi Tanguo; the one work totaling two fascicles translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Dalie; and various scriptures of unknown translators.
One hundred and twenty-five works, comprising one hundred and forty-eight fascicles.
Included among these are various sūtras and dhāraṇīs; the *Sūtra of Forty-two Sections* consists of one fascicle. (The above constitutes one sūtra.)
Translated during the reign of Emperor Ming of the Later Han dynasty by the Brahmin śramaṇa Kāśyapa Mātanga from the kingdom of Central India;
some say:
Regarding Zhu Shematen,
various records preserve different accounts;
it remains unclear which is accurate.
It was not translated previously;
therefore, I have recorded it in full.
In the tenth year of the Yongping era.
Following the Han envoy Cai Yin back east to Luoyang,
he translated this sutra at the Baima Monastery,
compiling it according to the original records.
This is the patriarchal scripture of the land of Han.
An old catalog states that its original text was a compilation of Indian scriptures.
Originally derived from the extensive Mahāyāna scriptures,
this is a compilation of essential passages,
resembling the eighteen chapters of the Classic of Filial Piety.
Dao’an recorded that it originated from the *Jiùlù* (Old Catalogue); subsequently,
Shi Xing’s *Hàn lù* (Han Catalogue) and Sengyou’s *Chū sān zàng jì jì* (Collection of Records on the Translation of the Tripitaka) also included it.
However, when the Great Dharma was first transmitted, those who returned with faith were few;
thus, Kāśyapa Mātanga kept his profound understanding within himself and did not translate many more texts.
Later, he passed away in Luoyang.
The details of its provenance are fully recorded in Zhu Shixing’s *Lu* (Record), as well as in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gaoseng zhuan*) and various miscellaneous records.
The *Baochang lu* states that it was translated by Dharmaratna.
This may be based on the time they arrived together. The *Buddha-benxing-jing* (Sutra of the Buddha’s Past Deeds) in five fascicles;

the *Shidi-duanjie-jing* (Sutra on the Ten Stages and Severing Bonds) in four or eight fascicles, as seen in Zhu Shixing’s catalogue; the *Erbai-liushi-jie-heyi* (Two Hundred and Sixty Precepts with Combined Variants) in two fascicles, as seen in the separate catalogue; the *Fahai-zang-jing* (Sutra of the Dharma-Ocean Treasury) in one fascicle—some versions omit the word "treasury" (*zang*)—and the *Fo-bensheng-jing* (Sutra of the Buddha’s Previous Births) in one fascicle: these five works, totaling thirteen fascicles, were brought by the śramaṇa Dharmaratna from Central India together with Kāśyapa Mātanga.
Kian arrived later and translated it during the reign of Emperor Ming.
Initially, he and Teng produced the *Sūtra in Forty-two Sections*.
The Duke of Teng passed away.
Lan translated this himself.
Formerly, when Emperor Wu of Han dredged the bottom of Kunming Lake, he encountered black ash.
He questioned Dongfang Shuo,
who replied,
"This is not within my knowledge."
"One may inquire of the Hu people from the Western Regions.
Once Dharmaratna had arrived,
he was subsequently questioned about this.
Lan said,
"This is the residual ash left from the conflagration at the end of the kalpa.
Thus, Shuo’s words were proven true.
Those who believed were very numerous.
Furthermore, when the envoy Qin Jing returned from the kingdom of Yuezhi,
he obtained a sandalwood image of King Udayana and a fourth model of a painted image, which were brought to Luoyang.
The Emperor issued an edict to have it depicted.
It was enshrined for veneration at the Xiyang City Gate and atop the Xianjie Mausoleum.
From that time on, its use of vermilion and pigments has continued to the present day.
Furthermore, as the Buddha-dharma had first arrived and heterodox paths were contending in discord,
he subsequently recounted the events of the time and composed the *Hanfa ben neizhuan* (Inner Tradition of the Origin of the Dharma in China) in five fascicles.
The author is unknown.
It currently exists in six fascicles.
It appears in Zhi Mindu’s *Lu* (Catalogue) with a preface composed by him, as well as in Baochang’s *Lu* (Catalogue) and its *Bielu* (Separate Catalogue).

One source states: *The Scripture on Walking in Accordance with the Path* (*Shun daoxing jing*) and *The Scripture on the Dignified Conduct of the Great Monks* (*Daiseng weiyi jing*), four fascicles; these appear in the *Separate Record* (*Bielu*) as newly appended and differ from other editions.

They were lost in translation according to Sengyou’s record and were divided into two parts totaling two fascicles; this [present] combined version in the *Separate Record* is the same as the *Dharmapada Scripture* (*Faju jing*) in four fascicles, which shares the same [content] as the *Dignified Conduct*.
It appears in the *Separate Record* as being divided into two parts. Also, the *Scripture on the Thirty-seven Factors of Practice for Meditation* (*Chanxing san shiqi pin jing*), one fascicle.

In the *Jian baochang lu*, it is recorded that there are two fascicles of the *Shibaofa jing* (Sūtra on the Ten Karmic Retributions); the *Yulu* states that its alternative title is the *Duozeng daozhang jing* (Sūtra on the Many Increments of the Path), while the *Jiulu* states it was extracted from the *Chang ahan jing*.
There are also two fascicles of the *Yinchi ru jing* (Sūtra on the Bases of Mindfulness and the Elements of Perception);

the *Bielu* states that Dao’an provided a commentary for this work. These are found in Zhu Shixing’s *Hanlu* and the *Yulu*. Furthermore, there are two fascicles of the *Dadian ban shouyi jing* (Sūtra on the Great Anapanasati and Mindfulness); Dao’an [provided a commentary].

It is said that the *Xiǎo ānbān* (Short Ānāpāna) was seen [in the canon] by Sengyou and Li Kuò; the *Dà ānbān jīng* (Great Ānāpān Sūtra), one fascicle, annotated by Dao’an, is recorded in Sengyou’s catalog.
There are also forty-four miscellaneous sūtras in two fascicles, or as some say, forty-four miscellaneous sūtras whose titles are not clearly manifest, so it is unknown which sūtras they are.
Dao’an stated that the *Zēngyī* (Ekottarika) is fully contained in Sengyou’s catalog. The Great Way is complete.

*Di jing* (Earth Sūtra), three fascicles; first translated by Dao’an with commentary. This is an excerpt from the *Xiuxing jing* (Sūtra on Practice); originally a Chinese abridgment, sometimes lacking large characters.

Found in the *Cháng āhán jīng* (Dīrgha Āgama) according to Sengyou’s catalogue. *Dàoyì fāxíng jīng* (Sūtra on the Practice of the Way by Daoyi), two fascicles; extracted from the *Cháng āhán jīng*. Sometimes in one fascicle.
Found in the catalogues of Dao’an and Sengyou. *Chán jīng* (Dhyāna Sūtra), two fascicles; first appeared in the *Bié lù* (Separate Catalogue). No longer extant.

*The Scripture of Immeasurable Life*, two fascicles; its initial appearance is recorded in the *Bielu*. Composed by the śramaṇa Tánluán, there is a commentary on this scripture in one fascicle consisting of one hundred and sixty sections.
An old catalog states it is the *Aṅguttara Nikāya* (Zēngyī Āhán) in one hundred and sixty chapters; it appears in Yòu’s record. *The Scripture of the Twelve Gates*, one fascicle;
the *Bielu* states it is in two fascicles. It emerged from the *Dīrgha Āgama* (Cháng Āhán), with commentary by Dào'ān; it appears in the Chàng record.
*Shōni-roku Shōjūnimon-kyō*, one fascicle; appears in the *Dīrgha Āgama*; mentioned in the *Chang*. *Shōni-roku Shichihō-kyō*, one fascicle;
the old catalogs state it is the *Abhidharma Saptadharmaprakaraṇa-sūtra*; appears in the *Dīrgha Āgama*; sometimes simply called *Saptadharmaprakaraṇa*;
mentioned in the *Shō-roku*. *Jūshichi-i-kyō*, one fascicle; the old catalogs state it is the *Bodhisattva Caturdaśamati-sūtra*.
*Jīngjiàn yùlù*: *Āpítán jiūshíbājié jīng*, one fascicle; *Míngdù wǔshí xiàojiè jīng*, two fascicles;
*Nántíkā luóyuè jīng*, one fascicle; *Jīngjiàn yùlù*:
*Dúfù zhǎngzhě jīng*, one fascicle—also known as *Dúfù zhǎngzhě cáiwù wúfù jīng* or *Wúzǐ fù*.
The *Wu wu jing* (Sutra on the Five Things) appears in the *Saṃyukta Āgama*, fascicle 46; the *Jiāzhǎng tiāonǎo èr chù jīng* (Sutra on the Householder’s Grief and Distress in Two Places),
also known as the *Jiāzhǎng ào nǎo èr chù jīng* (Sutra on the Householder’s Anguish and Distress in Two Places),

or the *Èr chù nǎo jīng* (Sutra on Distress in Two Places)— all of which are single-fascicle texts— and the *Yóuqǐ jiāzhǎng huǐguò jīng* (Sutra on the Householder’s Repentance Arising from Causes), also known as [the *Yóuqǐ jīng*].
The account of the Elder Śreṇika repenting his errors and making offerings to the Buddha; the origin of this narrative is not detailed.
One version states that the Buddha preached the *Indriyaparipāka-sūtra* for Nāku, while another states he preached the *Indriyaparipāka-sūtra* for the Elder Nākulaputra.
The account of the elder brothers visiting the Buddha; one version states it concerns the two brothers, the Elders Liśataka and [his younger brother], who went to the Buddha’s dwelling.
The *Buddha’s Supernatural Power Saving the Elder’s Son Sūtra* from the *Madhyama Āgama*; the *Ānabhiñjika Transforming His Seven Sons Sūtra* [from the same];
the *Daśaśāṭaka Gṛhapati of Aṣṭakagrāma Sūtra* from the *Ekottara Āgama*; the *Vaiśāradya Licchavi Addressing Ānanda Sūtra* from the *Madhyama Āgama*, number sixty;
and the *Sūtra on Receiving the Blessings of the Dharani* from the twenty-first fascicle of the *Saṃyukta Āgama*. One.
The Sūtra on the Elder Most Victorious Receiving the Blessing of the Recitation; the Sūtra on the Elder’s Son Zhi (also known as the Sūtra of Zhi);

the Sūtra on the Householder Ugga Seeing the Buddha, Hearing the Dharma, and Attaining Awakening; also known as the Sūtra on the Householder Sugata Attaining Awakening through the Buddha Preaching the Dharma;
extracted from the Saṃyukta Āgama as the Sūtra on Attaining Extraordinary Insight; also known as the Sūtra on the Elder Yasas.
Regarding the *Sutra on the Prince Śaṭha’s Admonition*, its initial appearance in the old catalogs states: *The Sutra of Prince Śaṭha Explaining the Twenty-eight Lunar Mansions*;

alternatively, it is called *The Sutra of Prince Mingxing (Venus) and the Twenty-eight Lunar Mansions*; or *The Sutra of the Tiger-Ear*, which is the *Sutra on the Causes and Conditions of Leaving Home*.
Some add the character "Buddha-spoken" (*bāoshuō*) and simply call it the *Sutra on Leaving Home*. It also appears as the *Sutra on the Buddha Delivering the Caṇḍāla Boy*.
*Jia jing* (Family Sutra); *Chuntuo shami jing* (Sutra of the Śrāmaṇera Cunda)—also titled *Shamen* (Śramaṇa)—appears in the twenty-fourth fascicle of the *Za ahan jing* (Saṃyukta Āgama);

*Waidao chujia jing* (Sutra on the Renunciation of Non-Buddhist Paths); *Jinqin si nianchu jing* (Sutra on Diligently Practicing the Four Foundations of Mindfulness) appears in the twenty-ninth fascicle of the *Za ahan jing*;

*Fumuen nanbao jing* (Sutra on the Difficulty of Repaying Parental Kindness)—also called *Nanbao jing*—appears in the *Zhong ahan jing* (Madhyama Āgama); *Chansi manzu jing* (Sutra on the Fulfillment of Dhyāna Contemplation).

The *Ānāpāna-sūtra* (Sūtra on the Practice of Counting the Breath) from the *Āgama*; the *Dhyāna-rahasya-sūtra* (Sūtra on the Secret Essentials of Meditation); the *Dhyāna-rahasya-vyādhi-cikitsā-sūtra* (Sūtra on the Secret Treatment of Illnesses through the Essentials of Meditation)—sometimes omitting the word "secret" (*rahasya*);

the *Loka-śubha-rūpa-sūtra* (Sūtra on the World’s Beautiful Colors); the *Sarva-saṃskāra-anitya-sthiti-sūtra* (Sūtra on All Conditioned Phenomena Not Abiding Constantly), twenty-four fascicles, from the *Saṃyukta-āgama*;

the *Puruṣa-deha-skandha-praveśa-sūtra* (Sūtra on a Person Receiving a Body and Entering the Aggregates), thirty-four fascicles, from the *Saṃyukta-āgama*; and the *Caryā-mārga-sūtra* (Sūtra on the Path of Practice).
From the *Dichu juan duojiaojian zhongsheng jing* (Sūtra on the Many Inverted Views of Sentient Beings), Volume 1; from the *Wuduozi chuxuyao jing* (Udānavarga Sūtra), Volume 16;

from the *Ren shen sibai si bing jing* (Sūtra on the Four Hundred and Four Diseases of the Human Body); from the *Chu xiuxing daodi jing* (Sūtra on the Stages of Cultivating the Path), Volume 1; from the *Renbing yi bunengzhi jing* (Sūtra on Human Illness That Physicians Cannot Cure);
from the *Fenbie shane suoqi jing* (Sūtra on the Arising of Good and Evil); and from the *Zhuo dushu fu* (Cutting Down the Poisonous Tree).
From the *Jātaka-sūtra*, the *Udānavarga*, the *Dhyāna-samādhi-upāya-anupūrva-dharma-sūtra*, the *Āraṇyaka-dhyāna-śikṣā-dharma-sūtra*, the *Bodhisattva-dhyāna-dharma-sūtra* (Chapter One:
Names of the Four Hundred Samādhis), the *Svayaṃ-pratijñā-samādhi-sūtra*—the internal title of which states "Chapter Four:
The Section on Individual Realization"—and from the *Bhikṣu-viśuddha-caryā-sūtra*. These were first extracted and compiled by Huishi.

The *Liuliwang jing* (Sūtra on King Liuli) is a slightly different version; the *Zengyi maying jing* (Sūtra on Increasing One by One: The Meaning of Abuse) was originally translated, wherein the Buddha spoke the *Xianglei jing* (Sūtra on Similar Categories) for the Brahmin Bimbisāra.

It appears in the eleventh fascicle of the *Za ahan jing* (Saṃyukta Āgama). The *Bolomen wenfo shifu defu jing* (Sūtra on the Brahmin Asking the Buddha about Receiving Merit through Giving) and the *Fowei diaoma jujuzhu shuofa jing* (Sūtra on the Buddha Preaching the Dharma for the Village Head Taming Horses) appear in the thirty-second fascicle of the *Za ahan jing*.
The *Brahmaṇa-caryā-sūtra* is found in the *Madhyama Āgama*, fascicle 39; the *Mudgalaputra-brahmaṇa-artha-vinirṇaya-pravrajyā-sūtra* is found in the *Saṃyukta Āgama*, fascicle 42;
the *Sūtra on the Buddha Preaching the Dharma for Enlightenment to the Fire-worshipping Brāhmaṇa* is found in the *Saṃyukta Āgama*;
and the *Brāhmaṇa-kuhaka-sūtra* is found in the *Saṃyukta Āgama*, fascicle 30.

The *Buddha’s Transformation and Great Flourishing of the Brahmin Who Leaves Home Sūtra*, from the *Saṃyukta Āgama* (also titled *The Buddha Speaks to Acelakāśyapa on the Suffering Created by Self and Others Sūtra*).
The *Sūtra on the Death of a Brahmin Son Whose Affection Remained Unabandoned*, from the *Ekottara Āgama*.
The *Sūtra on the Brahmin Cāṭa Leaving Home and Attaining the Way*, from the *Saṃyukta Āgama*.
The *Sūtra on the Buddha Speaking Verses for the Arrogant Brāhmaṇa* in forty-four fascicles, from the *Saṃyukta Āgama*;
the *Sūtra on the Brāhmaṇa Wearing White*, from the twenty-eighth fascicle of the *Saṃyukta Āgama*; the *Sūtra on the Brāhmaṇa Asking the Buddha about Future Buddhas*, from the *Saṃyukta Āgama*;
and the *Sūtra on the Brāhmaṇa Avoiding Death*, from the *Ekottara Āgama*. The Buddha [spoke] for the sake of the Brāhmaṇa...
The *Brāhmaṇa-kārṣaka-sūtra* (The Sūtra on the Brāhmaṇa Plowing the Field), found in the *Saṃyukta Āgama*, lacks the character "field" [in its title].

The *Saptasthavira-brāhmaṇa-upāsaka-praveśana-sūtra* (The Sūtra on the Seven Old Brāhmaṇas Requesting to Become Disciples), the *Brāhmaṇa-vyākaraṇa-śāstra-sūtra* (The Sūtra on the Brāhmaṇa’s Mastery of Treatises), both found in the twenty-fifth fascicle of the *Saṃyukta Āgama*;

the *Buddha-nagna-putra-pidhāna-sūtra* (The Sūtra on the Buddha Covering the Naked Son); the *Utpatti-sūtra* (The Birth Sūtra), also known as the *Cīrṇa-nagna-putra-sūtra* (The Sūtra on the Wandering Naked Son); and the *Brāhmaṇa-jñāna-vivaraṇa-sūtra* (The Sūtra on the Brāhmaṇa’s Understanding).

The *Fo wei nianshao boluomen shuo shan bushan jing* (Sutra on Good and Evil Spoken by the Buddha for a Young Brahmin), the *Ru huan sanmei jing* (Sutra on the Illusion-like Samādhi), the two-fascicle [text], the *Anban jing* (Ānāpāna Sūtra), and the *Neizang jing* (Inner Treasury Sūtra)—these were the second translations in the tenth month of the second year of the Yuanjia era; they are also known by a single name.

*The Inner Treasury of a Hundred Categories*, also known as *The Manifestation of a Hundred Jewels*; translated by Zhu Shixing and recorded in the Han Records; the *Sūtra on the Essential Methods of Five-Gate Dhyāna*;
the *Sūtra of the Simile of Water Emerging from a Spring*; the *Sūtra of the Simile of Floating Wood* from the *Ekottarika Āgama*; the *Sūtra of the Simile of the Turtle*;
the *Sūtra of Devadatta Entering Hell in His Own Body* from the *Ṣaṭpāramitā-samuccaya*; and the *Mānadhī Girl* from the *Udānavarga*.

*The Scripture on How a Person Who Slanders the Buddha is Born into Hell*; *The Scripture on Śikhālāvatī’s Sixfold Prostrations*, also known as *The Great Scripture on the Sixfold Prostrations*, slightly differing from the version translated by Dharmarakṣa; *The Scripture on Human Beings Desiring Birth*;

[these are] from the *Dīrgha Āgama*, with commentary by Dao’an, as recorded in the *Fajing lu*; *The Scripture on Ghosts Questioning Maudgalyāyana*; *The Scripture on the Multitude of Sufferings of Sinners in Hell*; [and] *Maudgalyāyana*.
*The Sūtra on Seeing the Body Hairs of Sentient Beings Like Arrows*, translated from the *Saṃyukta Āgama*, fascicle 19;
*The Chapter on the Retribution of Sins in the Mahāyāna Sūtra on the Perfection of Vigor*; *The Sūtra of the Venerable Bakula*, translated from the *Madhyama Āgama*, fascicle 8;

*The Sūtra of Ānanda’s Inquiry into the Auspiciousness and Inauspiciousness of Serving the Buddha* (also known as the *Sūtra of Ānanda’s Inquiry* or the *Sūtra of the Auspiciousness and Inauspiciousness of Serving the Buddha*).
The Kātyāyanāvavāda-sūtra; the Utpatti-sūtra, Volume Two; the Āyatyāṃ-vikāra-nirodha-sūtra; the Dṛḍhacitta-samyakcitta-sūtra—also known as the *Dṛḍha-sūtra* or the *Dṛḍhacitta-sūtra*;
the Vyakta-pāpapuṇya-sūtra; the Bahuvardhana-mārga-adhyāya-sūtra (the title "mārga" is absent from the old catalog);
translated from the *Dīrgha-āgama*. One source says it is a separate translation of the *Daśānuśaya-dharma* or the *Suvarṇavarṇā-sūtra*.
The Sūtra on Quarreling for a Woman in Previous Lives; the Sūtra on Birth; the Sūtra on Serving the Victorious One; the Sūtra on the Method of Repentance;
the Sūtra on Śāriputra’s Repentance; the Sūtra on the Prince’s Dream; the Sūtra on the Lesser Parinirvāṇa; the Sūtra on Seeing [the Record of] Compassion and Benevolence and Non-Killing;
the Sūtra on Ānanda’s Fellow Students—these appear in the forty-eighth fascicle of the *Ekottarika-āgama*; and the Sūtra on the Merchant Escaping the Peril of Bandits.
The *Sutra on the Man Who Went to Play the Lute* appears in the forty-eighth fascicle of the *Saṃyukta Āgama*.
The *Sutra on the Worldly Robber’s Almsgiving* appears in the *Ekottara Āgama*. The *Sutra on the Merchant’s Son Performing Buddha-Work* appears in the *Dīrgha Āgama*.

The *Sutra on Chanting a Spell When Meeting Robbers*, the *Sutra on Tying One’s Belt with a Spell*, and the *Sutra on Brahmā Visiting the Hall of the Brahmins for Discourse* appear in the fifth [fascicle] of the *Ekottara Āgama*.

*Yin cheng pei jing* (Sūtra on the Success and Failure of the Skandhas), translated from the *Xiuxing daodi jing* (Śrāvakabhūmi-sūtra). *Wubang jing* (Sūtra of the Five Radiances), translated from the *Zengyi ahan jing* (Ekottarika-āgama). *Wuzhanduren jing* (Sūtra of the Five Warriors), translated from the *Zengyi ahan jing*.

*Jian sengyou lu* (Record of Sengyou’s Catalogue) lists the *Wuxing jing* (Sūtra of the Five Practices). *Sandu jing* (Sūtra of the Three Poisons). *Liangshi nanyu jing* (Sūtra on the Difficulty of Encountering a Good Time).

*Qiuli laoyu jing* (Sūtra on Seeking Release from the Prison). *Lianhua nü jing* (Sūtra of the Lotus Woman). *Gumu sang yizi jing* (Sūtra of the Lonely Mother Mourning Her Only Son). Formerly, there were two people who loved one another.
*Jingjing chuxiaoyao jing* (Sūtra on Reverently Producing the *Udānavarga*), one fascicle; *Zhuyin chiru jing* (Sūtra on Abiding in the Aggregates, Bases, and Elements), or two fascicles;

*Jingmianwang jing* (Sūtra of King Ādarśamukha), translated from the *Ṣaṭpāramitā-saṃgraha*; *Zimingshi jing* (Sūtra of the Death of Jīvaka); *Chusheng jing* (Sūtra of Birth); *Tuan baonü jing* (Sūtra Praising the Jewel Maiden)—also known as the *Śāriputra-praśaṃsā-ratnastri-acintya-bhāṣita-sūtra*;
*Dajiaye yu nijianzi jing* (Sūtra of Mahākāśyapa Meeting the Nirgranthas). These are included in the *Dīrgha Āgama*. They are all correctly aligned [with their respective originals].
The *Sūtra on Ānanda’s Contemplation of Maudgalyāyana’s Supernatural Powers*, the *Sūtra on Śāriputra’s Questions to the Jewel Woman*,
the *Candrapradīpa Samādhi Sūtra*, the *Mahācandrapradīpa Samādhi Sūtra*, the *Sūtra on Ānanda’s Confusion*, the *Sūtra on the Arising of Human Desire*, the *Buddhamudrā Samādhi Sūtra*,
and the *Sūtra on Kāśyapa’s Rebuke of Ānanda*— also known as the *Sūtra on Kāśyapa’s Reprimand of Ānanda for the Simultaneous Ordination*.
The *Arhat-dṛṣṭānta-sūtra*, the *First Appearance of the Mahāyāna Vaipulya Essential Wisdom Sūtra*, and the *Sūtra on the Response of the Emptiness-Purity Deva to Samādhi*.
An old catalogue states:

"The *Emptiness-Purity Samādhi Sūtra* and the *Sūtra on Detaching Sentiments from Existence and Transgressions* were both annotated by the world as being of doubtful authenticity; they are [attributed to] the Bodhisattvas Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata."
*Guānjīng yìjué lǜ* (One Scroll). Also titled *Yìjué lǜ fǎxíng*. Some say it is called *Jīng* (Sūtra). Dao’an stated it was extracted from the *Āgama*;
see Sengyou’s Catalogue (*Chūsānzàng jìjí*). It is slightly different from the *Sìdì jīng* translated by Meng Xiáng. Dao’an stated it was extracted from the *Cháng āhán jīng*.
It is listed among the thirty-four works in forty scrolls mentioned in Sengyou’s Catalogue prior to this entry; the remaining miscellaneous translations are appended here.
*Jian baoji sanmei wenshu wen fashen jing* (also known as *Yiri sanmei baoji jing*, *Fashouchen jing*;
listed in the *Jiyu lu*); *Chanxing faxiang jing* (listed in the catalogs of Fajing and Sengyou);
*Ahan zhengxing jing* (also known as *Fo shuo zhengyi jing*; or *Gandhara Wang jing*, sometimes omitting the character "Wang" [King]; spoken by the Buddha).
*Chuchu jing* (Scripture on Various Places), *Shibab nili jing* (Scripture on the Eighteen Nirayas), also known as *Shibab diyu jing* (Scripture on the Eighteen Hells);

*Zuiye baoying jiaohua diyu jing* (Scripture on the Teaching and Transformation of the Hells through the Retribution of Karmic Offenses), also known as *Diyu baoying jing* (Scripture on the Retribution of the Hells); *Fanjie zuibao qingzhong jing* (Scripture on the Lightness and Heaviness of the Retribution for Violating Precepts), also known as *Fanzui jing* (Scripture on Committing Offenses);

*Wencheng shier yinyuan jing* (Scripture on Hearing the Accomplishment of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination), also known as *Shier yinyuan jing* (Scripture on the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination). Recorded in the *Jianyou lu*.

The *Benxiangyi zhijing* (Sūtra on the Mutual Dependence of Fundamental Characteristics) is found in the *Zhong ahan* (Madhyama Āgama). The *Wulu* (Record of Wu) states that the *Daxiang yi zhijing* is identical to the *Yuanben zhijing* as seen in the *Shiyou lu*.

The *Fapanyi jing* (Sūtra on the Meaning of Universal Dharma), also known as the *Jufaxing* (Complete Practice of Dharma), is found in the *Chang ahan* (Dīrgha Āgama) according to the records of Shi Xing and Shi You.
The *Modengnü jing*, also known as the *Modingnü jing*, is one [of these].

Ānanda is titled as the "Woman Practitioner of Sorcery" (*Gudao*). Regarding the *Shuojinglou Fubun Jing* (Sūtra on the Distribution of Leaks Spoken by the Woman Practitioner of Sorcery), Dao’an states it is found in the *Cháng āhán jīng* (Dīrgha Āgama) and is listed in the two catalogs by Shi Xingyu.
The *Fashi Feifa Jing* (Sūtra on Dharma and Non-Dharma) is found in the *Zhōng āhán jīng* (Madhyama Āgama) and is listed in the two catalogs by Shi Xingyu.

The *Yīqièliúshè Shǒuyīnyuán Jing* (Sūtra on the Retention of Causes and Conditions of All Streams) is in the old catalogs; the *Liúshè Jing* (Stream-Collection Sūtra) is one version, while another says it is the *Yīqièliúshè*.
The *Shoujing* (Sūtra on Guarding) is absent from the *Wulu*; it also states that the *Yinshou* was translated from the *Zhong ahan*. The *Jianxing* and *Youlu* record the *Qichu san guan jing*;
Dao’an states it was translated from the *Za ahan*, while the *Youlu* agrees with this. The *Zhuhanglu* records the *Jiu heng jing* as being from the *Za ahan*.
The *Bazhengdao jing* is from the *Za ahan*. The *Wuyin* [sūtra] appears in both the *Jianxing* and *You* records.
The *Dṛṣṭānta-sūtra* (also titled *Phenapiṇḍopama-sūtra*), found in the *Saṃyukta Āgama* according to the records of Jian and An;
the *Dharmacakra-pravartana-sūtra* (also titled *Dharmacakra-sūtra*), found in the *Saṃyukta Āgama* according to the records of Jian and An;
the *Cintā-mātraka-sūtra* (also titled *Cintā-sūtra*); the *Bimbiṣāra-dharma-āgama-mukha-vyākhyāna*; and the *Dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*.

One version is titled *The Scripture on the Severance of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination*; another is titled *The Scripture on the Oral Explanations of the Āgamas*; and yet another is titled *The Oral Explanations of Marquis An*.

Some claim it was translated by An Xuan, but according to its title, this is not the case. There is also the *Abhidharma Sūtra on the Fivefold Practice*, or simply the *Abhidharma Sūtra on the Five Dharmas*, which is included in the *Dīrgha Āgama*.
All of the above were produced during the first year of the Yuanjia era of Emperor Huan of the Later Han dynasty.

named Qing and styled Shigao.

he renounced the kingdom and entered the monastic life.
Embracing the Way, he traveled through various regions,
making the propagation of transformation his primary task.
In the second year of the Jianhe era of Emperor Huan.
Shaking his mendicant’s staff, he arrived at the capital of Luoyang.
Within a short time, he became proficient in the Chinese language through his study of it.
Lamenting that the propagation of the Dharma was still meager, he devoted himself extensively to translation work.
During the reign of Emperor Ling,
over twenty years passed,
during which a total of one hundred and seventy-odd works were translated.

its principles are clearly analyzed and its wording is authentically correct.
It is eloquent without being flowery, and plain without being rustic.
May all readers pursue this with tireless dedication.
I have extensively inquired and investigated various records and accounts concerning Lokakṣema (Shigao), noting that his presence or absence varies across different sources.
One should know that the concealment and manifestation of expedient traces mostly depend on the circumstances and the readiness of the audience for translation;
thus, there are cases where certain works were omitted and not transmitted.
Furthermore, at the end of the transmission records, it is indeed stated that these are those items recorded in the two ancient catalogs.
These were all revised and corrected by Lokakṣema from earlier translations;
it was not necessary to translate them entirely anew.
Nevertheless, Lokakṣema traveled from the Western Regions to the Central Plains.
Having traveled through Jiangnan, Lingbiao, and Dongyue, he first manifested his hidden nature and then moved throughout the world displaying his traces; thus he was a sage beyond the ordinary.
Now, I have compiled these various writings and exhaustively searched through miscellaneous records.
As for those with titles and annotations,
most are derived from the major texts based on circumstances encountered along the roads of Hexi and Jiangnan.
The catalog entries are scattered;
this alone is not sufficient to cause suspicion.
He saw that they were still there.
How could this not be continued?
I venture to compile and arrange it based on various collections;
though scattered across different sections, a detailed examination reveals it can be fully relied upon.
I hope that by broadening the flow of the Dharma, one may come to know its source.
Should you wish to discern its traces, the various *Sengzhuan* (Biographies of Eminent Monks) are available;
let them serve as your mirror.
The *Mahāsannipāta Sūtra*, twenty-seven fascicles; first appeared in Li Kuò’s catalogue. The *Dōgyō Hannya Haramitsu Kyō* (Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra), ten fascicles;
first appeared [in] the *Maka Hannya Haramitsu Kyō* (Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra), or eight fascicles;
also known as the *Hannya Dōgyō Hon Kyō*; translated by Chih Min-tu and recorded in the Yù catalogue. The *Shuryōgon Kyō* (Śūraṅgama Sūtra), two fascicles; Later Han dynasty.

On the eighth day of the second month in the third year of Zhongping, [the *Wuliangqingjing jing*] first appeared. According to the *Shixing lu*, the *Yulu*, and the *Wulu*, it consists of three fascicles.
There is also a two-fascicle *Wuliangqingjing jing* recorded in the *Wulu*, which is a different recension from the one translated by Bo Yan.
One source calls it the *Wuliangqingjing pingdengjue jing*; the *Achufoguo jing* consists of two fascicles, also known as the *Achufu*.
*Chāpúsà xuéchéng jīng* (The Scripture on the Bodhisattva Chāpúsà’s Accomplishment of Learning), also known as the *Āchù fó jīng* (Scripture of the Buddha Akṣobhya), one fascicle;

recorded in the catalog of Sūn Xiángyóu. *Bòběn jīng* (Scripture of the Original Páì), two fascicles; first appearing in the catalog of Sēng Yòu. *Dùnzhēnduólu suowèn jīng* (Scripture of the Questions of Duntadhara), two fascicles; first appearing in the old catalogs.
Also known as the *Dùnzhēnduólú níwáng jīng* (Scripture of the Nīrāja Queen Duntadhara); recorded in the catalogs of Sūn Xiángyóu and Sēng Yòu. *Āshé* (Aśvaghoṣa) [catalog entry].
*Śaiśarāja-sūtra*, two fascicles; Dao’an states at the beginning that it is extracted from the *Dīrgha Āgama*; see Sengyou’s *Collection of Records*.
*Buddhāvaśiṣṭa-maṇiratna-sūtra*, one fascicle; extracted from the Vaipulya section; also titled *Mahāyāna-ratnabhūṣaṇa-sūtra* or *Mahāratnakūṭa-sūtra*;
the "Ancient Chapter" refers to it as the *Avaśiṣṭa-prajñā-sūtra*; see Sengyou’s catalog under the *Mahāratnakūṭa*.

Dao’an called it the *Maṇiratna Sūtra* (or in two fascicles), as seen in the *Ji lu*, the *Shixing Han lu*, and the *Sengyou lu*.
The *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-vyākaraṇa Sūtra*—also known simply as the *Vyākaraṇa Sūtra*—Dao’an stated was produced from the Vaipulya section, as seen in the *Wu lu*.

The *Neizang baibao jing* (Sutra of the Inner Treasury of a Hundred Jewels), also known as the *Neizang baipin jing* (Sutra of the Inner Treasury of a Hundred Items), is the second [translation] produced;

it differs slightly from that translated by An Shigao. Dao’an states it belongs to the Vaipulya section. Since all catalogs consistently record it as "Hundred Jewels," it is known to be this very sutra.
The *Hu baniepan jing* (Turanian Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra) first appeared in two fascicles, as seen in Zhu Shixing’s *Han lu* (Catalogue of Han Translations).

The latter two are recorded in the *Wu lu* (Records of the Wu [Dynasty]) and the *An lu* (Records of An).

Additionally, the *Dhyāna-sūtra* is found in the *Bie lu* (Separate Records), and the *Saṃyukta-avadāna-sūtra* (Miscellaneous Parables Sūtra) comprises ten items. Daoxuan states that these were lost translations from the present day.

I have observed that since the arrival of sūtras in earlier generations, they were transcribed by virtuous and learned scholars.

Furthermore, the reason the nine provinces of the Eastern Land refer to the Western Regions as "Tianzhu" (India) is that this is a general name.
Some call it Shendu;
just as the Brahmans call this region Zhina,
others call it Zhendan.
Or it may be called Zhendan;
this is likely due to differences in dialect, such as Chu and Xia.
If one were to call it Han, [it would be for the same reason].
The Han dynasty was limited to two generations under the Liu clan with a single reign title;
thereafter, the systems of abdication and succession differed between the Wei and Jin dynasties.
One must therefore distinguish them according to the designations used for their emperors.
I have now corrected all of these in this record.
Furthermore, the Hu and the various Rong peoples are merely border-dwelling customs of the West;
they belong to the same category as the Di, Qiang, Man, and Yi tribes.
How can it be that the scriptures contain what are called "barbarian" (hu) words?
The Buddha was born in India;
the Brahmins there are of noble lineage.
Collectively they are called Brahmā;
"Brahmā" means purity.
They are the successors of the Ābhāsvara Heaven.
Among the Ābhāsvara devas, those in the lowest part of the Brahma-world who came here at the beginning of the kalpa and consumed the earth-fat became heavy of body and were unable to depart.
Consequently, he became a human being;
retaining his original name,
he was thus called Brahmā.
Since their language and script both imitate those of heaven,

"Now that you have left the household life, it is appropriate that you all adopt the surname Shi (Śākya).
Furthermore, regarding the translation of the four Āgamas, Fagu said:"
Those who have left the household life from the four castes are all of one Śākya lineage;
the assembly all sighed in admiration of these four castes:
first, the Kṣatriya.
This one is of the royal caste;
these two brahmins are practitioners of high conduct;
the third is named Vaiśya.
In this land, there is a fourth class called Śūdras,
who are the most lowly and base.
Thus, while serving as a mere scribe during the era of the Jin and Qin dynasties,
he compiled and finalized catalogs of scriptures and annotated the various classics,
styling himself "The Heaven-Pervading One" (Miti).
To claim that even in the later periods there were still those who translated from the Hu [language] as if they were of the Qin—
this is but a single pebble from Mount Kunlun;
it does not fully capture the excellence.
However, wherever there were fragments of foreign (Hui) speech above,
I have replaced them with Sanskrit characters,
so that future scholars who excel in discourse may attain the true and correct meaning.

*Fajing jing* (Sūtra on the Mirror of the Dharma), two fascicles, or one fascicle; annotated by Kang Senghui; recorded in the *Sengyou lu*. *Ahankoujie shier yinyuan jing* (Oral Explanation of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination from the Āgamas), also titled *Duan shier yinyuan jing* (Sūtra on Severing the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination) or *Anhou koujie jing* (Sūtra of the Oral Explanation of Lord An). These two works, totaling three fascicles, were translated by the Upāsaka Duwei Anxuan of the country of Parthia.
Later, in the fourth year of the Guanghua era of Emperor Ling of the Later Han dynasty, he traveled to Luoyang.
There he encountered the *Dharmapada-sūtra* and met Zhu Foshao,
with whom he immediately began the translation together.
The Buddha’s disciple Tiao acted as the scribe (bishou). He was also popularly known as An Hou, the Cavalry Commandant (Qiduwei).

The *Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra* in two fascicles—formerly recorded as the *Mahāpratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra* in one fascicle—is the second edition; its appearance is noted in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*. The *Daoxing Jing* was translated in the first year of the Jiaping era; it appears in Zhu Shixing’s *Han Lu* and the *Sanzang Ji*. Dao’an stated that this is an abridgment of the *Pratyutpanna* compiled by a person of high wisdom from the foreign lands, for which he [Dao’an] composed a commentary and a preface. The above two works comprise three fascicles in total.
The Indian śramaṇa Zhu Foshuo,
during the reign of Emperor Ling,
brought the *Daoxing jing* (Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra) and arrived in Luoyang.
Translating from Sanskrit into Chinese,
although the translators were occasionally hindered by the time constraints and thus missed the original intent,
they nevertheless discarded ornate phrasing in favor of preserving the substance of the meaning.
He profoundly grasped the meaning of the sutras.
During the Guanghe era, he retranslated the *Pratyutpanna-samādhi Sūtra*,
with Zhu Fashen serving as the interpreter.
Meng Fu and Zhang Yun transcribed the text by dictation.
The wording is slightly superior to previous versions; the matter is recorded in the *Chanzhuan*.

The *Xiaobenyiqing jing* (Sūtra on the Minor Account of the Original Arising) is in two fascicles; it is also called the *Xiuxing benqi* (Account of the Original Arising of Practice) or the *Suxing* (Past Deeds). Recently, the term "Minor" (*xiao*) has been added.
According to the *Jiùlù* (Old Catalogue), the *Gāosēngzhuàn* (Biographies of Eminent Monks), and the four catalogues by Zhū Shíxíng, Zhī Mǐndù, Sēngyòu, and Huìjiǎo, there are the following texts:
the *Chéngjùguānmíngdìngyìjīng* (also known as the *Chéngjùguānmíngjīng* or the *Chéngjùguānmíngsānmèijīng*);
and the *Mǎyǒubātàpìrénjīng* (also known as the *Mǎyǒubābìjīng* or the *Bātà*).
Sūtra No. 1: *The Sūtra on the Horse with Evil Manners* (*Mā-ā-yè-tài-jīng*), also known as the *Ratthapāla-sūtra*. Dao’an states that it was originally part of the *Vaipulya* section.
It begins with the fourteen questions posed to the Buddha; some versions omit the word "Buddha. *The Sūtra on Hearing the Formation of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination* (No. 2).
This version differs slightly from the *Twelve Links of Dependent Origination* translated by An Shigao. *The Sūtra on the Lay Follower Who Fell Away* (*Duòluò-yōu-pó-sè-jīng*).
The *Xiǎodàodì jīng* (Sūtra on the Stages of the Minor Path), the *Ānàlù bāniàn jīng* (Āniruddha’s Sūtra on the Eight Mindfulnesses) or simply the *Bāniàn jīng*, as seen in the old catalog;
the *Dàmójié jīng* (Mahāmāyā Sūtra)—some versions omit the character "dà" (great); and the *Mǎ yǒu sāxiàng jīng* (Sūtra on the Horse Having Three Marks). These constitute eleven works in total.
The Śramaṇa Zhi Yao from the Western Regions translated it in Luoyang during the reign of Emperor Ling.
*Wen dizhu shi jing* (Sutra on Questioning the Matters of Hell), one fascicle; recorded in Zhu Shixing’s *Han lu*.
The aforementioned one fascicle of this sutra was translated by the Chinese śramaṇa Kang Ju in the fourth year of the Zhongping era of Emperor Lingdi.
Translated in Luoyang;
the language is direct and the principles are profound,
without further embellishment.
The *Ancient Vimalakīrti Sūtra* in two fascicles, first appearing in the ancient catalogs and Zhu Shixing’s *Han Lu*;

the *Sumeru-prabha Bodhisattva Anuttara-pavitra Piṇḍapāta Sūtra* in two fascicles, also titled the *Decisive Comprehension of All Dharmas as Illusory Samādhi Sūtra*, the *Siyi Sūtra*, or the *Yiyi Sūtra*;
and the *Huishang Bodhisattva Questions on Great Skillful Means Sūtra*. Or...
There is also a two-fascicle version titled *The Sutra on the Six Pāramitās* (or *The Inner and Outer Sutra*) which lacks the word "Bodhisattva.

Regarding the term "inner and outer," An Shigao states that it was extracted from the *Vaipulya Sūtra* and the *Sutra of the Ten Wisdoms*, compiled and annotated by the Buddha himself; its preface also mentions the *Śrāmaṇera-daśajñāna-sūtra*.
This is seen in the three catalogs of Sengyou, Baochang, and the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*. [This concludes] the first section of the *Kāśyapa’s Interrogation of Ānanda Sūtra*.
The two records, the *Chujian fenghao lu* and the *Baocang lu*, and the *Shenggaoshu jiaye ze anan shuangdu luohan yujing*—
these seven works in ten fascicles are largely identical with minor differences.
Translated at Luoyang during the era of Emperor Ling by the lay devotee Yan Fotiao of Linhuai.
He simultaneously established the principles and corrected the phonology,
exhausting the subtle purport of the scriptures;
thus, the excellence of this "Master of Ying" was recorded for posterity.

The *Brahmajāla Sūtra* in two fascicles; its initial appearance is recorded in the *Wu lu*. The *Baofu jing* (Sūtra on the Retribution of Merit) in one fascicle, also known as the *Fobao jing*, appears in the *Wu lu*. The *Zhongbenqi jing* (Sūtra on the Middle Arising) in two fascicles; its initial appearance is recorded in the *Sanzang ji*. It is also known as the *Ruixiang benqi* (Auspicious Response Arising) or the *Taizi benqi* (Prince’s Arising). The *Xingqixing jing* (Sūtra on the Arising of Practice) in two fascicles, also known as the *Shiyuan* (Ten Conditions), appears in the *Wu lu*. The *Sidi jing* (Sūtra on the Four Truths) differs slightly from the version translated by An Shigao; it appears in the *Han lu* by Zhu Daozu. These comprise six works in nine fascicles.
The Śramaṇa Kang Mengxiang from the kingdom of Central India translated the *Xiuxing benqi jing* (Sūtra on the Original Acts of Practice) in two fascicles during the reign of Emperor Xian at Luoyang.
This concludes the first sūtra in two fascicles.
In the second month of the second year of the Jian’an era,
the śramaṇa Shi Tanguo, together with Zhu Dalü and Kang Mengxiang,
brought a Sanskrit manuscript from the kingdom of Kapilavastu.
Translated in Luoyang;
Meng Xiang transcribed it into the Han language.
Shi Dao’an said:
Translated by Meng Xiang;
its elegant and flowing style is sufficient to convey the profound essence.
Furthermore, the Record of Shi Dao’an states:
The Zhongbenqi jing (Sūtra on the Intermediate Origins) in two fascicles;
alternatively titled the Taizi zhongbenqi (Intermediate Origins of the Prince).
It was also translated by the śramaṇa Tanguo.
This Sanskrit manuscript was obtained in the kingdom of Kapilavastu and translated at Luoyang in the twelfth year of the Jian’an era;
Meng Xiang oversaw the oral recitation.
I have consulted the *Shixing lu* and the *Changfang lu*.
I find that what Master [Guṇabhadra] translated does not differ from the previous versions;
thus, the two accounts merely differ in their origins.
The *Hu-ben jing* (Hū-language Original Sūtra) in four fascicles appears to have emerged from within Chang’an;

it should now be called the *Fan-ben niepan hou qiansui zhong bianji jing* (Sanskrit-language Original Sūtra on Transformations During the Thousand Years After the Nirvāṇa) in four fascicles, also known as the *Qiansui bian he dao shenzu jing* (Sūtra on Transformations During the Thousand Years, Combined with the Divine Footsteps of the Way), or the *Dao shenzu wuji bianhua jing* (Sūtra on the Infinite Transformations of the Divine Footsteps of the Way).
The *Zhu jing fo ming* (Names of Buddhas in Various Sūtras) in two fascicles; the *Jiu piyu jing* (Old Sūtra of Similes) in two fascicles; the *Guanwu* [Sūtra]...
The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, one fascicle; hereafter, all are single-fascicle works:

the *Nāgagotrakulavikurvāṇa Sūtra*, the *Past World of the Fragrant Lotus Buddha Sūtra*, the *Sūtra on the Buddha Seeing a Cowherd and Showing the Way*, the *Sūtra of the Names of Three Thousand Buddhas*, the *Sūtra of the Names of Fifty-three Buddhas*, the *Sūtra of the Names of the Buddhas of the Ten Directions*, and the *Sūtra of the Thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa*—these alone exist.
The *Buddhanāma-sūtra* translated by Dharmaruci; the *Sūtra of the Names of the Thousand Buddhas*;
the *Sūtra of the Praise of the Names of One Hundred and Seventy Buddhas*, also simply titled the *Sūtra of the Names of One Hundred and Seventy Buddhas*;

the *Sūtra of the Names of the Buddhas of the Southern Quarter*, also known as the *Sūtra of the Healing City Temple*, the *Sūtra of the Names of Buddhas for Eradicating Sin and Attaining Merit*; and the *Sūtra on the Methods of Practice Spoken by Avalokiteśvara*—these are all dhāraṇī sūtras.
The *Maitreya as a Female* (*Maitreyī-bhūta*), the *Sūtra on the Questions of Śāntamati*, also known as the *Sūtra on the Purity and Subjugation Spoken by the Tathāgata*,
differs from the aforementioned sūtras. Furthermore, the *Sūtra on Sadāprarudita Bodhisattva Seeking the Image of Deep Prajñā*,

the *Sūtra on the Birthplace of the Bodhisattva*, the *Sūtra on the Place Where the Bodhisattva is Born*, and the *Sūtra on the Method for Receiving the Precepts of the Bodhisattva* differ [from one another].
The Ten Methods for the Successive Stages of Receiving the Bodhisattva Precepts; The First Method of the Bodhisattva’s Rite of Repentance.
A Bodhisattva who has first resolved upon enlightenment should constantly practice five matters during the six periods of day and night.

[This includes] the *Sutra on the Six Bodhisattvas Named Good Chanters*, the *Number of Monks*, the *Matters of Practice for Bhikṣus*, the *Various Prohibitions and Vinaya*, and the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya Bhikṣu-essentials*, also known as the *Mahā*.
*Saṃghāṭa-sūtra*; *Bhikṣu-yōjyopayoga-saṃgraha-dharma-sūtra*; *Bhikṣuṇī-daśa-śīla-sūtra*; *Daśakuśala-karma-patha-pratigraha-sūtra*;
*Caturmahārāja-sūtra* (with appended spells appearing to have been added by later persons); *Saṃyukta-āgama*;
*Dānapāramitā-caryā-sūtra* (also known as the *Sarvadānapati-dānapāramitā-caryā-sūtra*); *Puṇyavyūharāja-sūtra*.
*The Sūtra on Inviting the Buddha for Eighty-four Thousand Years*; *The Sūtra of King Māndhātṛ*, an alternative version; *The Sūtra of Admonishing Sons*;

*The Sūtra of Teaching Sons*, also known as *The Sūtra of Sudatta Teaching His Sons*; the old catalogues refer to it as *The Sūtra of Sudatta Training His Sons*, *The Sūtra of Blessing Sons*, or *The Sūtra of the Child Understanding the Dharma upon Hearing It*;
*The Sūtra of the Bodhisattva’s Practice*, also known as *The Inquiry of the Elder Vaisya*.
The *Sādhana-sūtra* (also known as the *Gṛhapati-sādhana-sūtra*, the *Bhadraśreṣṭhī-sūtra*, the *Gṛhapati-parinirvāṇa-putrābhāva-pariṇāmana-sūtra*,
the *Citta-gṛhapati-bhikṣu-yācanā-sūtra*, the *Kalyāṇabhadra-brāhmaṇa-śarīra-prārthanā-sūtra*,
the *Tīrthika-citta-gṛhapati-vinodana-sūtra*, the *Ahiṃsaka-brāhmaṇa-dhyāna-grahaṇa-sūtra*, and the *Brāhmaṇa-parihāra-sūtra*).
The Sūtra on Death; the Sūtra on the Brahmin’s Loss of His Daughter; the Sūtra on the Brahmin Attaining Liberation through Contemplating Impermanence;

the Sūtra on the Poor Son Who Went Mad upon Finding Wealth; the Sūtra on the Rhinoceros and the Dog Biting the King; the *Old Catalogue* states it is the Sūtra on the Rhinoceros and the Dog; the Sūtra on the Householder’s Body Becoming a Female Nose-Worm;
the Sūtra on the Iron City Hell; the Sūtra on the Hell of Diligent Suffering; the Sūtra on Hells; the Sūtra on Accumulated Bones; and the Sūtra on Suffering.
*Yin jing chi zhai jing ren hong fa jing hua yan ying luo jing*, one fascicle;
*Guan shi lou tan jing bo re de jing wei ri za nan jing nei shen guan zhang jing mo he cha tou jing*;
slightly different from the old *Guan ding jing*; *Qing jing fa xing jing mo he yan bao yan jing*, ten [fascicles].
The *Vibhāṣā-sūtra*, the *Buddha-avaśiṣṭa-maṇiratna-sūtra*, the *Parivartana-strībhāva-bodhisattva-sūtra*—
also known as the *Ratnāvalī-vyūha-upāya-sūtra* or the *Ratnāvalī-vyūha-strī-sūtra* (these are separate translations from the same original)—
the *Sūtra on Not Falling into Evil Destinies by Upholding the Names of Buddhas*, the *Saptaratna-sūtra*, and the *Dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda-adhyāya-sūtra*. [Recorded in the Old Catalogue.]

The *Sūtra on the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination*, the *Sūtra on the Twelve Dhūtas for Śramaṇas*, and the *Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of the Thirty-two Marks*—the latter two were translated by those who lost their source from the time of Master Dao’an; they are largely identical with minor differences to the [standard] *Sūtra on the Thirty-two Marks*.

The *Sūtra on the Thirty-seven Factors of Enlightenment*, the alternate version of the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra*, the *Buddhānusmṛti-śraddhā-bālaka-sūtra*, and the *Yogācāra-samāsa-sūtra* (translated as...).
*The Compendium of Practice*, also known as *The Dhyāna Method of Dharmatrāta*; alternatively titled *The Collection of Essential Dhyāna Methods Compiled by Bodhisattva Dharmatrāta*.

It includes: *The Sutra on the Essential Dhyāna for Rebuking Desire*, *The Parable of the Ganges*, *The Original Text of the Verses on Various Dharmas*, *The Sutra of Similes from the Dharmapada*, and *The Sutra of Similes*.

Also included are the verses in the Hu (Sogdian/Chinese) phonetic transcription, which should now be rendered in their original Sanskrit sounds: the *Verses of Praise to Amitābha Buddha* and the *Verses on the Seven Buddhas*.

The *Hengnu ni baigu wuyan yingsong* (One Hundred Quatrains in Five-Syllable Verse on the Constantly Angry Bhikṣuṇī); the *Benqi* (Origins) in one hundred and forty stanzas; the *Daoxing pin* (Chapter on the Practice of the Way);
the Sanskrit sounds of various sūtras—formerly called "Hu" (barbarian) sounds—the *Prajñāpāramitā* divine mantra in its alternative version;

the *Mantra of the Seven Buddhas*; the *Mantra of the Sesame Oil Ritual*; the *Bhūtā* Divine Mantra of the Illusionist; the *Five Dragon Mantra*; the *Poison Scripture*; and the *Spirit for Extracting Vital Energy*.
The *Zhòu* (formerly called *Xuèzhòu*), the *Zhòu qǔchǐ zhòu* (also known as the *Chǐ zhòu* or *Zhòuchǐ zhòu*),
the *Yá tòng zhòu*, the *Zhòu yǎn tòng zhòu* (from a different version), the *Zhòu zéi zhòu fǎ* (from a different version), the *Qīfó ānzhái shénzhòu* (also known as the *Ānzhái zhòu fǎ*),
and the *Bié xíng*: these constitute one hundred and twenty-five sections in total.
In total, there are one hundred and forty-eight fascicles.

These were all compiled by the Vinaya Master Sengyou from the *Chusanzangji*, the two ancient records, Dao’an’s *Shiyuan*, and the various newly acquired or lost translations of sūtras and their respective fascicles, which are extremely numerous.
In collating the various catalogues, those that were corrupt and defiled were numerous;
as entries and omissions intermingled, it was truly difficult to establish a definitive arrangement.
Having not yet seen the actual scriptures, one reads in vain through their titles alone.
There is an entry and a source, yet no entry and no translation.
Examining its origin, it is not that there was no cause;
however, as it spans many years, it is appended here at the end.
I hope that in the future, one of broad learning may encounter the original source;
I pray that it may be corrected and restored so as to provide a reliable basis,
thereby clarifying the ocean of the Dharma and stilling its turbulent waves.
Furthermore, upon examining the *Lidai sanbao ji* (Record of the Three Jewels Through the Ages), I found only twenty-five fascicles,
as detailed elsewhere in my separate account.
I have not yet been able to obtain the remaining missing volumes.
The Record of the Inner Scriptures of the Great Tang, Volume One;
The Record of the Inner Scriptures of the Great Tang, Volume Two,
compiled by Shi [Daoxuan] of Ximing Monastery in the Capital.
Part Two of the First Section of the Catalogue of the Transmission and Translation of Various Scriptures Throughout Successive Dynasties. Part Two of the First Section:

The Record of the Transmission and Translation of Buddhist Scriptures by the Cao Family of the Former Wei Dynasty. Second: The Preface to the Record of the Transmission and Translation of Buddhist Scriptures by the Cao Family of the Former Wei Dynasty. The Preface states: [text follows]
Since the Han dynasty, the empire had been unified;
at the beginning of the Jian’an era, it was divided into three contending powers.
Yuan and Cao vied for supremacy in the Central Plains.
Liu and Sun divided their horses at the gorges of the Yangtze;
the Five Peaks were choked with dust and the Nine Provinces gathered like clouds.
Some, after two sacrifices, opened the way for imperial designs.
Or they divided the realm into three parts to establish hegemonic enterprises;
thus, the founder of Wei held the Son of Heaven to command the feudal lords,
while the Liu clan relied upon Jiegate to scheme for the imperial capital at Changan.
The House of Sun possessed brilliant strategy, resting secure upon the long reaches of the Yangtze River;
with the martial prowess of a tiger’s claws and fangs and the formidable might of a Sleeping Dragon,
they established themselves as a separate domain.
With a mind intent on devouring one another,
they each occupy their borders and mutually fortify their frontiers and passes;
they widely recruit men of talent and virtue to serve as their limbs and assistants.
The state honors the worthy and capable as its treasures;
thus, the master artisan of sublime Dharma has come here once more.
Senghui arrived in Wu.
Śāriputra radiated his spiritual brilliance over the region south of the Yangtze;
Kālaya traveled to the Wei state;
and the prohibitive precepts were first inaugurated in the capital of Luoyang.
The practice of returning to the precepts spread widely from this point onward;
stupas were erected throughout the land.
Translators followed local customs and retained the original terminology of those dialects.
As the scriptures were translated, titles were assigned according to their respective periods;
thus there arose the *Wu-pin* (Five Chapters) and the *Shu-put-yao* (Shu Version of the Lalitavistara).
It was from this that the practice of re-translating works already existing began.
The loss of translations from the various schools lies precisely here.
Since the Three Kingdoms were established as separate states,
the single capital of Western Shu alone lacked a dynastic record.
Is it not the case that although the Buddha-sun adorns the heavens, those without the karmic affinity do not behold it;
and although the Dharma-thunder shakes the earth, those among the common people do not hear it?
Furthermore, although the old catalogues record that scriptures such as the *Shu Puyao* and the *Śūraṅgama* were translated, they are not included here.
Furthermore, the original sūtras, the names of the translators, and the dates of their eras were missing;
thus, even if one wished to record them, there was no basis upon which to rely.
Since they were omitted from the *Shi-fan* (Record of Lost Translations), they have perished along with that separate catalog.
Now I shall record what was transmitted in the Central Plains during the Cao Wei dynasty.
Emperor Wen, whose personal name was Pi and courtesy name Zihuan,
was a native of Qiao in Pei Commandery.
He was the eldest son of Wang Cao, the Chancellor.
On the day of his birth,
there was a blue cloud as large as a carriage canopy.
It remained verdant upon it throughout the entire day;
those who observed vapors regarded this as a sign of supreme nobility,
not the mark of a mere minister.
At the age of eight, he was skilled in composing literary works.
Initially succeeding to the position of Chancellor, he became the Prince of Wei;
upon receiving the abdication of the Later Han, the dynasty was renamed Wei.
At first, Xiang resided in Luoyang;
the Duke of Wei had his capital at Ye;
and Wang Ji was stationed at Qiao.
Furthermore, it is recorded that [the capital] was moved to Fanchang during the reign of Emperor Shouchun;
later, it was established at Luoyi.
This began from the first year of the Huangchu era of Emperor Wen, the Gengzi year.
Reaching the first year of the Xiānxī era of Emperor Xuánzōng (Jiǎshēn),
there were five sovereigns and forty-five years;
there were six monks.
The scriptures, vinayas, and karmavācanas produced therein comprise thirteen works totaling twenty-five fascicles,
which constitute the catalogue of scriptures for the Wei dynasty as a whole.
Regarding those scriptures whose translators are lost, they are all summarized at the end of the *Wu lu* (Records of Wu) and recorded therein.

The Śramaṇa Dharmakāla: one work in one fascicle, the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*. The Śramaṇa Saṃghavarman: two works in four fascicles, various sūtras. The Śramaṇa Tandi: one work in one fascicle, the *Karmavācanā*. The Śramaṇa Bo Yan: six works in eight fascicles, various sūtras. The Śramaṇa Zhi Qiangliangjie: one work in six fascicles, a sūtra. The Śramaṇa An Faxian: two works in five fascicles, various sūtras. The *Mahāsāṃghika-prātimokṣa-sūtra*, one fascicle; first appearing in the *Wei shi lu* (Records of the Wei Dynasty) by Zhu Daozu. [Total: One fascicle of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*.]
The śramaṇa Dharmakāla (translated into Wei as Fashi) from the kingdom of Central India was gifted with intelligence and wisdom from childhood,
and his physical appearance was noble and magnificent.
Upon reading a text only once, he fully mastered both its literary style and its meaning.
He was proficient in the four Vedas;
there was nothing he did not encompass, from the movements of wind, clouds, stars, and the moon to the interpretations of diagrams and prophecies.
He considered himself to have reached the ultimate limit of the world’s knowledge within his own mind and eyes.
At the age of twenty-five, he entered a monastic dwelling.
There he happened upon the *Abhidharmahṛdaya* by Dharmottara;
taking it up casually, he examined it.
He was utterly bewildered and could not understand.
As he examined the matter again with earnest persistence, his confusion increased even further, and he sighed, saying:
"The Buddha-dharma probes the profound and fully elucidates the three periods of time."
He then renounced worldly life to become a monk,
reciting the sūtras of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna as well as the various Vinaya-piṭakas;
he traveled and preached until he reached Luoyang.
At that time, although the Buddha-dharma existed within the borders of the Wei dynasty,
the spirit of the Way was corrupted and declining;
there were also members of the monastic community who had not yet received the precepts of taking refuge.
Ceasing [the practice] was merely because shaving the head is a custom of a different people.
Even if one were to establish rites of fasting and repentance, they would be identical to sacrificial offerings.
Once Kāla had arrived...
The great practitioners of the Buddha-dharma requested that the monks bring forth the Vinaya.
Kāla [responded] with the subtle regulations and the phrasing of the Vinaya-piṭaka.
As the flourishing and widespread propagation of Buddhism had not yet thrived, it was certainly not yet being adopted [by the state].
In the Jiaping era, this one fascicle of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* was translated at the Baima Monastery,
intended merely to provide for morning and evening recitation.
The precepts of the Middle Kingdom began from this point onward.

The *Ugraparipṛcchā-sūtra* in two fascicles, the second translation—also titled *Ugratāyā-paripṛcchā-bodhisattvacaryā-sūtra*—is found in Zhu Daozu’s *Wei-lu*. The *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* in two fascicles, the second translation, is found in Zhu Daozu’s *Jin-shi-zalu* (Miscellaneous Records of the Jin Dynasty) and Baochang’s records; it differs slightly from the version translated by Lokakṣema.
