*Zá āhán jīng* (Saṃyukta Āgama), one fascicle; *Yínghuǒ liùdù jīng* (Scripture on the Six Pāramitās of the Firefly); the old catalog states there was also a *Míngdù jīng* (Prajñāpāramitā Scripture), one fascicle.

*Juǎnyún yī míng yíng huǒ míngdù jīng* (The Scripture of the Bright Perfection of Wisdom, also known as the Firefly), one fascicle; *Xiǎoguān shìlóután jīng* (The Scripture of the Minor Contemplation of the Loutan), one fascicle;

*Nèi chánbōluómì jīng* (The Scripture on the Inner Perfection of Meditation), one fascicle—these are all found in the old catalogs. *Sì bèi jīng* (The Scripture of the Four Classes), one fascicle; the old catalogs call it the *Sì bèi dìzǐ jīng* (Scripture of the Disciples of the Four Classes) or the *Sì bèi xué jīng* (Scripture of the Learning of the Four Classes).
*Dà sìdì jīng* (The Scripture of the Great Four Truths), one fascicle; *Wǔ fāngbiàn jīng* (The Scripture of the Five Expedient Means), one fascicle.

1. *The Sūtra on the Five Names of Liberation* (Wéiyuèluómíng jiětuō jīng), 1 fascicle; 2. *The Sūtra on the Five Aggregates* (Wǔyīn jīng), 1 fascicle; 3. *The Sūtra on the World of Five Turbidities* (Zhōng wǔzhuóshì jīng), 1 fascicle;

4. *The Sūtra on the Six Pāramitās* (Liù bōluómì jīng), 1 fascicle; 5. *The Great Sūtra of the Seven Chariots* (Dà qīchē jīng), 1 fascicle; 6. *The Sūtra on the Eightfold Right Path and the Deviant Path* (Bā zhèngxí jīng), 1 fascicle;

7. *The Sūtra on the Eight Dhāraṇīs* (Bā zǒngchí jīng), 1 fascicle; 8. *The Sūtra on the Eight Classes of Practitioners* (Bā bèi jīng), 1 fascicle; 9. *The Sūtra on the Names of the Practices of the Eightfold Saṃgha* (Bābù sēngxíng míng jīng), 1 fascicle; 10. *The Great Ten* (Dà shí).

The *Dvayāśraya-sūtra* (Two Causes and Conditions Sūtra), one fascicle; the *Aṣṭādaśa-praśna-sūtra* (Sūtra of Eighteen Difficulties), one fascicle—both appear in the old catalogs. The *Dvācatvāriṃśat-pada-sūtra* (Sūtra of Forty-two Sections), one fascicle, appears in the old catalogs.

There is also a separate *Xiaoming Dvācatvāriṃśat-pada-sūtra*. The *Aṣṭottaraśata-tṛṣṇā-sūtra* (Sūtra of One Hundred and Eight Attachments), one fascicle, appears in the old catalogs; it seems to be an excerpt.

The *Pañcanīvaraṇa-vicikitsā-saṃyojana-sūtra* (Sūtra on the Five Hindrances and the Knots of Doubt) and the *Pratibhāna-samādhi-sūtra* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of Attaining Wisdom), one fascicle each, appear in the old catalogs.
Recorded one title: *The Scripture on Mañjuśrī Asking about the Ten Practices of Bodhisattvas* (1 fascicle);

seen in the old catalogs. *The Minor Anapāna Samādhi Scripture* (1 fascicle); seen in the old catalogs. *The Scripture on the Concentration of Mind in Dhyāna Practice* (1 fascicle); seen in the old catalogs. *The Scripture on the Enumeration of Dhyāna* (1 fascicle);

seen in the old catalogs. *The Scripture on Transformative Parables* (1 fascicle); seen in the old catalogs; also called *The Scripture on Transformative Similes*, or *The Conditions of Sentient Beings*.
One fascicle of verses; seen in the old catalog. One fascicle of the *Mahādhāraṇī-mantra-sūtra*; seen in the old catalog, also called the *Dhāraṇī-mantra-sūtra*.
One fascicle of the *Sahapa-bodhisattva-sūtra*; seen in the old catalog, also called the *King Sahapa Bodhisattva Sūtra*. One fascicle of the *Hui-ding-pu-bian-shentong-bodhisattva-sūtra*;
seen in the old catalog, also called the *Hui-ding-pu-bian-guo* (Universal Kingdom of Wisdom-Samadhi) Bodhisattva Sūtra.
One fascicle of the *Tushentong Pusa Jing* (Sutra of the Bodhisattva Earth-Spirit) and the *Pinunuren Jing* (Sutra of the Poor Woman);
these are found in the old catalogs and are also called the *Pinu Nanta Jing*. One fascicle of the *Aqiu-na Jing*; this is found in the old catalogs and is also called the *Aqiu-na Samadhi Jing*.
The above comprises one hundred and ten works.
These comprise two hundred and ninety-one fascicles;
they are all ancient scriptures whose translators were lost according to the two previous catalogs.
I have now compiled and appended them here to demonstrate the scriptural authorities relied upon in distant antiquity.
According to their titles, these were appended to the original texts and included in the current section; however,
as there were missing entries in the catalog, they were later appended upon being discovered.

4. Catalogue of Buddhist Scriptures Translated during the Western Jin Dynasty. Catalogue of Buddhist Scriptures Translated during the Western Jin Dynasty, Part Four. Regarding the gradual eastward transmission of the teachings:
although they were heard of during the Han and Wei dynasties, [the full extent of the Dharma had not yet been established].
As for the propagation of its meaning,
it was only during the Jin dynasty that it first opened up;
moreover, although the Jin was not particularly refined in its literary style.
His literary talent was truly magnificent;
thus, it was ultimately due to him that the translations were brought to light.
Consequently, it was during the Jin dynasty that the rites, music, robes, and caps first became fully established.
From this point on, the ocean of the source of faith has flourished;
could it be otherwise?
This is recorded in the Annals of the Western Jin.
Sima Yan, courtesy name Anshi,
was a native of Wen in Henei.
He served as Grand General of Wei, Palace Attendant, Director of the Secretariat, and Chancellor of the State Council.
Wang Zhao was the son of Wang Jin.
When Zhao passed away, Yan succeeded him as Prince.
Emperor Yuan knew that the mandate of destiny had returned [to his house].
He dispatched Grand Guardian Zheng Chong to present the imperial seal and confer the throne;
Yan then assumed the mandate with hands folded over his chest,
becoming Emperor Wu.
It was called Jin.
Its capitals were Luoyang and Chang’an,
which were formerly known as the Eastern and Western Capitals.
In the fifteenth year of Emperor Wu of Jin’s reign,
during the Xianning era,
he commanded Sima Zhou.
Having pacified Wu and captured Sun Hao,
he was enfeoffed as the Marquis of Submission (Guiming Hou).
This was from the twenty-fourth year of the Yongan era of the Later Han.
Reaching the Taikang era of the Jin dynasty,
beginning from the first day of the year of Gengzi,
the nine provinces were once again unified under a single rule.
Furthermore, at the beginning of the Huangwu era of the Wu dynasty, Lu Ji said:
"From now on, after another sixty years,
the chariots of the world shall follow the same ruts and its writings shall use the same characters."
By this time, it was indeed just as Zhongji had said;
from the pacification of Shu until the extinction of Wu,
nearly sixty years had passed.
Twenty years later,
at the beginning of Emperor Hui’s Yongning era,
the way of governance fell into decline.
The various warlords stood like towering peaks.
King Zhao established his foundation by initiating rebellion and usurping the throne at court;
Zhang Gui followed in his footsteps, refusing to be a subject while arrogantly governing the land of Liang.
Internally and externally, there was turmoil and seething unrest;
the order of the realm gradually fell into chaos,
which is why Liu Yuan established his power at Pingyang.
Li Xiong thereby took advantage of the celestial mandate;
Emperor Huai was reduced to wandering in the Xiang Valley,
and Emperor Min fled in disarray from Chang’an.
Since the Way relies upon its times for its rise,
yet both capitals have fallen into ruin;
and since the Dharma is manifested through persons.
Subjected to the instability of two rulers,
the myriad people were shattered and scattered;
they had no one to whom they could turn for refuge or faith.
The hundred officials lost their posts,
and the Śākya clan was left without refuge.
At that time, there were the śramaṇas Dharmarakṣa, Qiāngliánglóuzhì, and others.
Forgetting his own body to benefit all beings, he vowed to propagate the teachings extensively;
undaunted by hardship or toil,
he made the elucidation of the Dharma his primary task.
During the Jin dynasty, Dharmarakṣa produced the greatest number of translated scriptures;
it was from him that the vast protection and propagation of the Dharma-net originated.
He was followed in succession by Dharmakṣema, Nie Daoxuan, father and son, Zhu Falan, and others, who translated and expounded the teachings.
Thus, during the fifty-year period, thirteen individuals— both monastics and laypeople from China and India—
along with previously lost translations of various sūtras, precepts, and other texts, totaling four hundred and fifty-one works.
Seven hundred and seventeen fascicles were collected as the *Shilu* (Record of the World) for fifty-two years under the two capitals and four rulers of the Western Jin dynasty; it is said thus.

There are two hundred and ten works totaling three hundred and ninety-four fascicles of sutras and precepts by the śramaṇa Dharmarakṣa, and one work totaling one fascicle of a sutra by the śramaṇa Qiángliánglóuzhì.

The *Mén'ān fǎqīn* (Catalogue of Dharma-Names Established at the Gate) contains twelve fascicles of scriptures from five sections; the śramaṇa Wúluóchá has one section of twenty fascicles of scriptures; the lay believer Niè Chéngyuǎn has three sections of four fascicles of scriptures;
the śramaṇa Zhú Shūlán has two sections of five fascicles of scriptures; the lay believer Niè Dàozhēn has fifty-four sections of sixty-six fascicles of scriptures;

the catalogue by the śramaṇa Bái Fǎzǔ contains twenty-three sections of twenty-five fascicles of scriptures; the śramaṇa Shì Fǎlì has four sections of thirteen fascicles of scriptures; and the upāsaka Wèi... [text ends].

The *Shidu* (Compilation by Shi) in one section, two fascicles; the scriptures of the śramaṇa Zhimin-du in two sections, thirteen fascicles; the scriptures of the śramaṇa Shi Faju in one hundred thirty-two sections, one hundred forty-two fascicles;
the scriptures of the śramaṇa Zhifadu in four sections, five fascicles; and various scriptures of unknown translators, as well as those transcribed by Fa-xian and others, totaling seven fascicles.

These were seen in the record of Nie Daozhen. When Tan Sui recited them, he completed one passage per day; subsequently, he was moved by a divine response, and after ninety days had passed, a patronage was bestowed.

One white horse, five white sheep, and ninety rolls of silk. The *Puyao jing* (Sutra of the Universal Radiance) in eight fascicles was translated at Tianshui Temple in the second year of the Yongjia era;

this is the third translation. The śramaṇa Kangshu [Kāśyapa Mātanga] recited the text, while the lay official Bai Fa and others received it in writing. It differs slightly from the six-fascicle version produced by Zhimeng and Baoyun in Shu, as seen in the records of Nie Daozhen and ancient catalogs.

The *Batuojie sanmei jing* (Sutra on the Samādhi of Vidyutkoti) in seven fascicles and the *Xiuxing jing* (Sutra on the Practice of the Path) in seven fascicles were translated in the fifth year of the Dakang era; this is the second translation. They are similar to those produced during the Han dynasty by An Shigao.

The *Gaochu* (Exalted) in six fascicles differs slightly [from others] and is also called the *Daodi jing* (Scripture on the Stages of the Path); it is listed in Baochang’s catalog. The *Dayi jing* (Scripture of Great Compassion) in seven fascicles was translated in the first year of the Yuankang era;

it is also found in eight or six fascicles as a single chapter of the *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra*, according to Zhu Daozu’s *Jin shi zalu*. The *Xianjie jing* (Sūtra of the Worthy Kalpa) in seven fascicles was translated in the first year of the Yuankang era with Zhao Wenlong receiving the dictation;

it is also found in ten or thirteen fascicles, while older catalogs state it was translated during the Yongkang era, as seen in Nie Daozhen’s catalog. The *Xiaopin jing* (Shorter Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra) in seven fascicles was [begun] on the fourth day of the third month in the fourth year of the Taishi era.

The Japanese translation notes this as the second edition, or the eight-fascicle version, recorded by Nie Daozhen; it is largely identical with minor differences to the *Old Daoxing jing*. The *Sālendrarāja-sūtra* (Sa yun fenduoli jing) in six fascicles was translated in the first year of the Taishi era;

it is listed in Zhu Daozu’s *Miscellaneous Records of the Jin Dynasty*. The *Cittadhāraṇī-sūtra* (Chixin jing) in six fascicles appeared in the seventh year of the Taikang era, consisting of seventeen chapters.

It is also known as the *Equally Governing All Dharmas Sūtra*, the *Cittadhāraṇī-Brahmā-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, or the *Adornment of the Buddha-Dharma Sūtra*; it is also referred to as the *Cittadhāraṇī-Brahmā-sūtra*. These are found in the older records.

The Record of Nie Daozhen states that the *Du shi pin jing* (Scripture on the Chapter of Delivering the World) in six fascicles was produced on the thirteenth day of the fourth month in the first year of the Yuankang era; this is seen in the "Chapter on the World" (*Shijian pin*) of the *Huayan jing*.

The *Mi ji jin gang li shi jing* (Scripture on the Secret Trace Vajra-Powerful Hero) in five fascicles—or alternatively in eight or four fascicles—was produced on the eighth day of the tenth month in the first year of the Taikang era;

this is seen in the miscellaneous records of Zhi Mindu and Zhu Daozu from the Jin dynasty. The *Lou tan jing* (Loutan Scripture) in five fascicles—or alternatively in six or eight fascicles—is the *Chang ahan shiji* (Long Āgama: Records of the Ages); the phrasing differs slightly, as seen in the record of Nie [Daozhen].

According to the *Nie Daozhen Lu*, the *Sheng jing* (Sūtra on Birth) in five fascicles—alternatively recorded as four fascicles—was translated on the nineteenth day of the first month in the sixth year of the Taikang era; it is categorized under the Vaipulya section.
The *Rulai xingxian jing* (Sūtra on the Manifestation of the Tathāgata) in five fascicles was produced on the twenty-fifth day of the twelfth month in the first year of the Yuankang era;

this is the "Tathāgatagotra-parivarta" chapter of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, also known as the *Xingxian ruyuan jing*. It is recorded in the *Nie Daozhen Lu*. The *Achamo jing* (Akṣayamati Sūtra) in four fascicles was translated on the first day of the twelfth month in the first year of the Yongjia era; this is the second [work].

It was translated in five or seven fascicles; it appears in the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra* (or is called the *Akṣayamati-bodhisattva-sūtra*), as seen in the records of Nie Daozhen and the *Bielu*. The *Akṣayamati-sūtra* in four fascicles was the second translation produced during the Taishi era;
it shares the same original text as the *Akṣayamati* but is a separate translation, appearing in the *Mahāsaṃnipāta* according to the records of Nie Daozhen, in either five fascicles.

The *Ratnāvalī-sūtra* in four fascicles was translated on the twenty-seventh day of the fourth month in the eighth year of the Taikang era, or in three fascicles; it is also called the *Ratnāvalī-samādhi-sūtra* or the *Ratnāvalī-paripṛcchā-prajñā-sūtra*, appearing in the *Mahāsaṃnipāta*.

The *Ji jian nie dao zhen lu* (Record of the Collection Compiled by Nie Daozhen) lists the *Puchao jing* (Sūtra of Universal Transcendence), four fascicles, translated in the seventh year of the Taikang era; this second translation is identical in substance to the *Ajātaśatru-rāja-sūtra* by Lokakṣema of the Han dynasty, though it is a separate translation.

It is also called the *Puchao sanmei* (Samādhi of Universal Transcendence) or the *Wenshu puchao sanmei jing* (Mañjuśrī Sūtra on the Samādhi of Universal Transcendence), as noted in Zhu Daozu’s *Za lu* (Miscellaneous Records).

The *Hai longwang jing* (Sūtra of the Sea Dragon King), four fascicles, was translated in the seventh month of the sixth year of the Taikang era; it is also recorded as being in three fascicles, according to the *Nie dao zhen lu*. The *Awei yue zhi jing* (Sūtra of Non-retrogression), four fascicles, is also referred to as the *Awei yue zhi che jing*.

Some call it the *Avaivartika-dharmacakra-sūtra* in four fascicles, while others call it the *Vaipulya-pariśuddhi-sūtra* in six fascicles; these four sūtras are translations of the same original text, as recorded in the *Nie Daozhen Lu*.

The *Dharanidhara-bodhisattva-paripṛcchā-sūtra* in three fascicles—or perhaps two fascicles—is also a translation of the same original text, according to the *Nie Daozhen Lu*. The *Sarvaguṇasamudgata-samādhi-sūtra* in three fascicles is also called the *Sarvapuṇyasamuccaya-samādhi-sūtra*, or it may be in two fascicles, as seen in the *Nie Daozhen Lu*.
The *Sūryavairocana-samādhi-sūtra* in three fascicles was translated in the first month of the seventh year of the Taishi era; this was its initial appearance.

Either in two fascicles or simply titled *Chāorìmíng jīng* (Sūtra of Transcending the Sun’s Radiance), it appears in the record of Niè Dàozhēn. *Púsàzàng jīng* (Bodhisattva-piṭaka Sūtra) in three fascicles; *Zhūshénzhòu jīng* (Sūtra of Various Divine Spells) in three fascicles; *Bǎojì púsà suowèn jīng* (Sūtra of the Questions of Bodhisattva Ratnaśikhin) in two fascicles.

On the fourteenth day of the seventh month of the first year of the Tàixī era, the *Dàjí* (Great Assembly) was produced—also known as the *Púsà jìngxíng jīng* (Sūtra of the Pure Conduct of Bodhisattvas). An old catalog calls it the *Bǎojié jīng* (Jewel-Knot Sūtra).

*Xūzhēntiānzǐ jīng* (Sūtra of the Son of Heaven Susiddhi) in two fascicles was produced at the Bǎimǎ Temple in Qīngmén, Cháng'ān, during the second year of the Tàiśǐ era. Ān Wénhuì translated the text and Bái Yuānxìn acted as the oral interpreter for Niè.
Chengyuan and Zhang Xuanbo, with Sun Xiuda taking dictation, also state that it is the *Sūtra on the Four Questions*. It is found in Zhu Daozu’s *Miscellaneous Records of the Jin Dynasty*.

The *Mañjuśrī-buddhakṣetra-vyūha-pariśuddhi-sūtra* in two fascicles was translated during the Tai-xi era; it is also called the *Sūtra on the Adornment and Purity of the Buddha-field* or the *Sūtra on the Pure Buddha-field*, and is found in Zhu Daozu’s *Miscellaneous Records of the Jin Dynasty*.

The *Hongdao-guangxian-sanmei-jing* (Sūtra of the Samādhi for Widely Manifesting the Propagation of the Way) in two fascicles was translated in the third month of the second year of the Yongjia era; it is also called the *Anouda*, the *Anouda-invites-the-Buddha*, or the *Jin*.

The *Gangdingyi* (剛定意) or the version without the character for *samādhi* has four titles in total and consists of ten fascicles; one manuscript contains only seven fascicles, lacking the middle three. Another manuscript contains only the first five fascicles. This is recorded in the catalog of Nie Daozhen.

The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* (大般泥洹經) in two fascicles was translated on the third day of the seventh month in the fifth year of the Taishi era; it is also called the *Vaipulya-parinirvāṇa-sūtra* (方等泥洹經), as recorded in the catalog of Nie Daozhen.

The *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* (無量壽經) in two fascicles was translated on the twenty-first day of the first month in the second year of the Yongjia era; this is the fourth translation, following that by Zhi Qian of the Wu dynasty.

During the Wei dynasty, Kang Sengkai, Bai Yan, and others produced a version with identical text but different titles, also known as the *Wuliang qingjing pingdengjue jing* (Sūtra of the Immeasurable Pure Equal Enlightenment), as recorded in Zhu Daozu’s *Jin shi zalu* (Miscellaneous Records of the Jin Dynasty).

There is also a separate translation of the two-fascicle *Shoulengyan jing* (Śūraṅgama Sūtra); the *Shoulengyan* states that Ānanda spoke it. There is also the two-fascicle *Baocang jing* (Ratnakaraṇḍa Sūtra), translated in the sixth year of the Taishi era.

There is also the two-fascicle *Yaoji jing* (Essential Collection Sūtra), also called the *Zhufu yaoji jing* (Essential Collection of All Buddhas Sūtra). Regarding the two-fascicle *Banzhou sanmei jing* (Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra), Dao’an stated it was produced from the *Banzhou sanmei jing*. There is also the *Dashanquan jing* (Sūtra of Great Skillful Means).

Two fascicles; translated in the sixth month of the sixth year of the Taikang era. Its initial appearance was also titled *The Sūtra on the Bodhisattva Hui-shang’s Inquiry into Great Skillful Means*, or *The Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Hui-shang*, or *Skillful Means*, or *The Infinite [Virtue] of Deliverance through Skillful Means*—thus there were five titles recorded in the *Nie Daozhen Lu*.

The *Sūtra on Accordance with Skillful Means*, two fascicles, is also called *The Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Transforming the Female Body*, or *The Sūtra on Accordance with Skillful Means*; the old catalogs call it *The Sūtra on Accordance with Skillful Means for Women*, as seen in the *Nie Zhen Lu*. The *Sūtra on Following Skillful Means for Women*, two fascicles, is found in a separate record.

The *Ruru-anlu-ru-wu-ruchan-sanmei-jing* (Lalitavistara-sūtra) in two fascicles, or three fascicles; the *Jiemopusa-jing* (Gaganagañja-bodhisattva-sūtra) in two fascicles, or three fascicles; and the *Yongfu-ding-jing* (Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra) in two fascicles.

These were translated on the ninth day of the fourth month in the first year of the Yuankang era. This is the fourth translation, which corresponds to the versions produced by Zhi Chen, Zhi Qian, Bai Yan, and others. Their similarities and differences appear in the *Nie Daozhen Lu*.

Furthermore, there is the *Ajase-wang-jing* (Ajātaśatru-kumāra-sūtra) in two fascicles, the second translation of the *Jiake-jing* (Sārthavāha-sūtra) in two fascicles, and the *Wenshushili-xian-baozang-jing* (Mañjuśrī-ābhāsa-ratnagarbha-sūtra).

*The Sūtra in Two Fascicles*, also known as *The Sūtra on Mañjuśrī’s Adornment and Purification of the Buddha-field* or *The Sūtra on the Buddha Ascending to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to Preach the Dharma for His Mother*;

two fascicles, translated during the Taishi era; also known as *The Chapter on the Buddha’s Ascent to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven*; recorded in the *Nie Daozhen Catalogue*. *The Benevolent Kings Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, one fascicle; recorded in the *Miscellaneous Catalogues of the Jin Dynasty*.

Subsequently, there is the standalone scripture: *The Sūtra on the Universal Gate Chapter*, one fascicle; translated in the first month of the eighth year of Taikang; recorded in the *Nie Daozhen Catalogue*. *The Sūtra of the Youth Candraprabha*, one fascicle; also known as... [text ends].
The *Candraprabha-kumāra-sūtra* (Moonlight Youth Sutra) is a different translation of the same original text as the *Śunyata-śunyata-dauṣṭhulya-sūtra* and two other sūtras.

The *Vajragarbha-bodhisattva-caryā-sūtra* (One Scroll), translated at the West Temple in Chang’an during the seventh year of the Yuanjia era. The *Mahāviśuddhi-dharmamukha-sūtra* (One Scroll), the twenty-second fascicle of the *Avataṃsaka*, translated on the twenty-sixth day of the twelfth month of the first year of the Jianxing era;
recorded in the *Daozhen lu*. The *Vimaladatta-dārikā-sūtra* (One Scroll), translated on the second day of the second month of the tenth year of the Taikang era; recorded in the *Nie* [catalogue].
*Daozhen lu*: *Sumati Bodhisattva Sūtra*, one fascicle; also called *Sumati Sūtra* or *Suma Sūtra*; found in the catalogs of Nie Daozhen, Zhu Daozu, and others. *Longshi nü jing*, one fascicle;
old catalogs state it is the second part of the *Longshi ben jing*. *Dafangdeng dingwang jing*, one fascicle;
its first appearance was also titled *Dingwang jing*, also called *Weimojie ziwen jing*, and also called *Shansi tongzi jing*; found in the catalog of Zhi Min-du. *Wusuoxiwang jing*, one fascicle.

Also called the *Elephant-Step Sūtra* (*Xiàngbù jīng*) and the *Elephant-Axilla Sūtra* (*Xiàngyè jīng*); recorded in the *Nì Dàozhēn Lù*. One fascicle of the *Mó Nì Jīng* (Sūtra on Demons and Rebellions); appeared on the second day of the twelfth month of the tenth year of the Tàikāng era; recorded in the *Nì Dàozhēn Lù*.

One fascicle of the *Jì Zhū Fāngděng Xué Jīng* (Sūtra on Saving Those Who Study the Vaipulya); sometimes the character "student" (*xué*) is omitted; recorded in the *Zhú Dàozǔ Jìnshì Zá Lù*. One fascicle of the *Púsà xíng wǔshí yuánshēn jīng* (Sūtra on the Fifty Circumstances of the Bodhisattva’s Body);

also called the *Wǔshí yuánshēn xíng jīng* (Sūtra on the Practice of the Fifty Circumstances of the Body) or the *Púsà yuánshēn wǔshí shì jīng* (Sūtra on the Fifty Matters of the Bodhisattva’s Circumstances of the Body); recorded in the *Zhú Dàozǔ Jìnshì zá Lù*.

*Recorded by Maitreya Bodhisattva’s Inquiry on His Original Vows*, one fascicle. Translated on the seventeenth day of the fifth month in the second year of the Dà'ān era. Also known as the *Maitreya’s Original Vows Sūtra* and the *Maitreya’s Questions Sūtra*.
Seen in the records of Niè Dàozhēn and Zhú Dàozǔ. *Mañjuśrī’s Pure Discipline Sūtra*, one fascicle.

On the eighth day of the fourth month in the tenth year of the Tàikāng era, [the translator] Hù was at the Bǎimǎ Temple in Luóyáng when he encountered the Western Region śramaṇa Jízhì, who recited this sūtra for him. There were originally several more chapters, but he forgot them entirely; he has only propagated what he remembered.

According to the record of Zhu Daozu as transcribed by Nie Daozhen: one scroll titled *Jinglü jīng* (Scripture on Pure Discipline); one scroll titled *Wúsì háotóng púsà jīng* (Scripture of the Inconceivable Child Bodhisattva), also known as *Wúsìyì guāng suowèn jīng* (Scripture of the Questions of Inconceivable Light) or simply *Wúsìyì guāng jīng* (Scripture of Inconceivable Light);

one scroll titled *Mílè chéngfó jīng* (Scripture of Maitreya’s Attainment of Buddhahood), translated in the second year of the Tà'ān era, also named *Mílè dānglái xiàshēng jīng* (Scripture of Maitreya’s Future Descent and Birth), as seen in the record of Nie Daozhen;
and one scroll titled *Shèlìfú mùlián yóuzhūguó jīng* (Scripture of Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana Traveling Through Various Kingdoms), also called *Shèlìfú móhémùqiánlián yóuzhū*.

*Siqiu jing* (Sutra on the Four Crossroads), one fascicle; *Liuliewang jing* (Sutra of King Vairāṭya), one fascicle; *Baoshi nü jing* (Sutra of the Girl Ratnadattā)—also titled *Sumati fǎlǜ sānmèi jīng* (Sutra of the Samādhi of the Dharma-Rules of Sumati)—seen in the *Niè Dàozhēn lù* (Record of Niè Dàozhēn);

*Fó wéi púsà wǔmèng jīng* (Sutra of the Five Dreams of the Buddha as a Bodhisattva), one fascicle, translated in the fifth month of the second year of the Tà'ān era—also titled *Fó wǔmèng* (The Buddha’s Five Dreams), *Tàizǐ wǔmèng* (The Prince’s Five Dreams), or *Xiānrén wǔmèng* (The Immortal’s Five Dreams)—seen in the old records and the *Niè Dàozhēn lù*;
*Mó mùqiánlián běnjīng* (Original Sutra of Mahāmaudgalyāyana), one fascicle—one version lacks the character "jiàn" (ma); *Tàizǐ mùmò jīng* (Sutra of the Prince’s Tomb), one fascicle.

Scroll Two: *The Scripture on the Four Unobtainables*, one fascicle; listed in the *Nie Daozhen* and *Zhengdu* catalogs. *The Scripture on the Bodhisattva’s Method for Repenting Transgressions*, one fascicle;

alternatively, the character "scripture" (*jing*) is omitted, with a note below stating it is extracted from Nāgārjuna’s *Daśabhūmivibhāṣā-śāstra*. *The Scripture on the Milk-Radiance*, one fascicle; identical in translation to the *Vatsa-sūtra*.

*The Scripture on the Brahmin Woman Cittā Giving a Portion of Rice-Wash as Alms*, one fascicle; also simply titled *Cittā-sūtra*. *The Scripture on the Six Great Prostrations*, one fascicle; translated in the first year of the Taian era (303 CE); alternatively, it is called *The Six [Prostrations] of Cīvaraka*.

Regarding the *Jingxiang baijing* (Sutra of Homage and Recitation), it is also simply called the *Liuxiang baijing*. It is seen in the catalogs of Zhi Mindu and Baochang. The *Aṅgulimāla Sūtra*, one fascicle, also known as the *Zhizhan jing* or the *Aṅgulimāla Sūtra*, is seen in the Daozhen lu.

The *Bodhisattva Dashuzhu jing* (Sūtra on the Ten Stages of Bodhisattvas), one fascicle, is largely the same with minor differences from the *Bodhisattva Shidi jing* (Sūtra on the Ten Grounds of Bodhisattvas).

The *Modiao wang jing* (Sūtra of King Māndhātṛ), one fascicle, is the second edition, which is largely the same with minor differences from the version translated by Zhi Qian during the Wu dynasty. The *Zhao ming sanmei jing* (Sūtra of the Illuminating Samādhi), one fascicle, is that which is sought after.

*Huàn jīng* (Sūtra on Sickness), one fascicle; translated in the first month of the third year of the Tà'ān era. Recorded in the catalogs of Niè Dào zhēn and Wáng Zōng. *Fǎ mò jìn jīng* (Sūtra on the Extinction of the Dharma), one fascicle; sometimes written with the character "miè" (extinguish).

One source states it is the *Kōngjì púsà suowèn jīng* (Sūtra of the Questions of the Bodhisattva Śūnyatāśānti), a second translation identical to that produced by Zhīqián during the Wù dynasty. *Bōsà zhāifǎ jīng* (Sūtra on the Ritual for Bodhisattva Fasting), one fascicle;

sometimes the word "jīng" (sūtra) is omitted. Also known as the *Zhèngzhāi*, *Chízhāi*, or *Xiánshǒu púsà zhāifǎ jīng*. *Dúzèng zìshì sānmèi jīng* (Sūtra of the Self-Vowed Samādhi of Direct Realization), one fascicle; also known as the *Rúlái* [Sūtra].

*Self-Vow Samādhi Sūtra*, one fascicle; *Past Buddhas’ Almsround Sūtra*, one fascicle (also known as *Seeing the Past World Sūtra*; according to the old catalog, *Five Hindrances and Doubtful Knots Causing Loss of Practice Sūtra*, one fascicle);

*Dharanī Sūtra*, one fascicle, issued on the twelfth day of the fourth month in the second year of the Yongning era (seen in the record of Nie Daozhen); *Birth Sūtra* (also known as *Buddha-Mind Dharanī Sūtra*);

*Five Blessings Bestowed Sūtra*, one fascicle (also known as *Pure Vinaya Vaipulya Sūtra*; seen in the Tang catalog); *Sorrowless Bestowal Sūtra*, one fascicle; *The Daughter of King Ajātaśatru Named No-* [fascicle].

*Jībǎo sānmèijīng* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of Ultimate Jewels), one fascicle; translated on the third day of the third month in the first year of the Yongjia era. Found in the records of Niè Dàozhēn and the *Bièlù*. *Bǎowǎng tóngzǐ jīng* (Sūtra of the Jewel-Net Youth), one fascicle;

also called *Bǎowǎng jīng*. Found in the records of Niè Dàozhēn. *Ménwúshīlì huìguò jīng* (Sūtra of Mañjuśrī’s Repentance), one fascicle; its initial appearance was also titled *Wénshūshīlì wǔtǐ huìguò jīng*.

*Pǔfǎyì jīng* (Sūtra on the Meaning of the Universal Dharma), one fascicle; also called *Pǔyì jīng*. This second translation is largely identical with minor differences to that produced by Shènggāo during the Han dynasty. Found in the records of Niè [Dàozhēn].

*Daozhen lu mie shifang ming jing* (The Scripture on the Extinction of the Ten Directions’ Obscurity Recorded by Daozhen), one fascicle. Produced on the fourteenth day of the eighth month of the first year of the Guangxi era; one copy lacks the character "mie" (extinction). *Pusa shidi jing* (The Scripture on the Ten Stages of the Bodhisattva), one fascicle.
Also called *Shidi jing*; also called *Dafangguang jing*. Extracted from the "Ten Stages Chapter" (*Daśabhūmika-parivarta*) of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.

*Wenshi xiyu zhong seng jing* (The Scripture on Bathing the Assembly of Monks in a Warm Chamber), one fascicle. Also known as the *Wenshi jing*. Recorded in the *Daozhen lu*. *Laita heluo suo wen guangde taizi jing* (The Scripture on the Questions of Rāṣṭrapāla Regarding Prince Guǎngdé), one fascicle. [Produced] in the sixth year of the Taishi era.

On the thirtieth day of the ninth month, one scroll of the *Guangde Taizi Jing* (Sūtra of Prince Guangde) was produced; it appears in Zhu Daozu’s *Jin Shi Zalu* (Miscellaneous Records of the Jin Dynasty). One scroll of the *Danglai Bian Jing* (Sūtra of Future Transformations), in one fascicle, appears in Nie Daozhen’s records.

One scroll of the *Wubai Dizizi Zishuo Benqi Jing* (Sūtra of the Five Hundred Disciples’ Own Accounts of Their Past Deeds), translated in the fifth month of the second year of the Tai’an era; the old records call it the *Wubai Dizizi Shuo Benmo Jing* (Sūtra of the Five Hundred Disciples’ Account of the Origins and Ends), and it appears in Nie Daozhen’s records.

One scroll of the *Shiziyue Fosheng Jing* (Sūtra of the Birth of the Buddha Simha-candra), translated during the Tai’an era, appears in Nie Daozhen’s records. One scroll of the *Jiaye Jiejichuan Jing* (Sūtra on Kāśyapa’s Compilation of the Teachings).

One fascicle; alternatively called the *Jie jing* (Vinaya Sūtra). Seen in the record of Nie Daozhen. The *Nai nü qi yu jing* (Sūtra of the Maiden Nai and Qi Yu), one fascicle. Translated during the Taian era. Also titled the *Nai nü jing*.

Seen in the record of Nie Daozhen. The *Po tai jing* (Sūtra of the Womb), one fascicle. Translated on the first day of the eighth month of the second year of the Taian era. Alternatively called the *Po tai shou shen jing*. Seen in the record of Nie Daozhen.

The *Weimojie suoshuo famen jing* (Sūtra of the Dharma Gates Spoken by Vimalakīrti), one fascicle. Translated on the first day of the fourth month of the second year of the Taian era. This is the third translation, following those by Yan Fotiao of the Han dynasty and Zhi [Qian] of the Wu dynasty.

The third translation, produced by Zhi Qian, is largely similar with minor differences; it is recorded in the *Nie Daozhen Lu* as the *Yugayuewen pusa xing jing* (一卷) or the *Yujia zhangzhe jing* (一卷), which is the same as the *Dayuqia jing* (大郁伽經) or the two-fascicle version.
This third translation is identical in content to the versions translated during the Wei dynasty by Kang Sengkai and during the Wu dynasty by Zhi Qian, though the texts differ in length.

It is recorded in the catalogs of Dao’an and Zhi Mindu. There is also the *Huanshi renxian jing* (一卷), recorded in the *Nie Daozhen Lu*. There is further the *Juetongchi jing* (一卷), also known as the *Jueding tongchi*.

*Chí jīngshǒuyì nǚ jīng* (Sūtra on the Maiden Śirīmatī Who Upholds the Sūtra), one fascicle; also known as *Fànnǚ shǒuyì jīng* (Sūtra on the Brahmin Maiden Śirīmatī). *Shètóu jiàn jīng* (The Sūtra of Śāṭhā’s Admonition), one fascicle;

also known as *Tàizǐ èrshíbā xiù jīng* (Sūtra of the Prince and the Twenty-eight Lunar Mansions) or *Hǔ’ěr yì jīng* (Sūtra of the Tiger-Ear Maiden). This is a different translation from the same source as the *Móténgjiā jīng* (Mātṛkā-sūtra); it is slightly different from the version translated during the Han dynasty by An Shigao, as recorded in Shi Dao’an’s catalogue. *Shíèr yīnyuán jīng* (Sūtra of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination), one fascicle;
the third translation, identical to that produced during the Han dynasty by An Shigao; also known as *Jùduō shùxià sīwéi shí* (Ten Contemplations Under the Jujube Tree).
*The Sūtra on the Sixty-two Views Based on the Two Conditions* (Er-yuan jing-jian), one fascicle; also called *The Sūtra on the Sixty-two Views of the Brahmajāla* (Fanwang liu-shier-jian jing);

listed in the *Zhu Daozu Lu*. *The Sūtra on Self-Inflicted Harm* (Si-qin jing), one fascicle. *The Sūtra of the Silent Youth* (Wu-yen tongzi jing), one fascicle or two; also called *The Sūtra of the Silent Bodhisattva*; found in the *Mahāsaṃnipāta*; listed in the *Nie Daozhen Lu*.

*The Sūtra of the Holy Dharma Seal* (Sheng-fa-yin jing), one fascicle; translated on the fifth day of the twelfth month of the fourth year of the Yuankang era at Jiuquan Commandery; transcribed by Zhu Fashou. It is also simply called the *Sūtra of the Holy Seal*. It is also... [text fragment].

Regarding the *Yunhuiyin jing* (Cloud-Wisdom-Seal Sūtra), Dao’an stated it was extracted from the *Saṃyuktāgama*; it is also found in the records of Nie Daozhen and Baochang. The *Yishan jing* (Sūtra on Moving Mountains) in one fascicle; the old records call it the *Lishi yishan jing* (Sūtra on the Strongman Moving Mountains). The *Yanjingding jing* (Sūtra on the Pure Samādhi) in one fascicle;

it is also titled the *Xushi jing* (Sūtra on the Introduction to the World). The *Hui ming jing* (Sūtra of Wisdom-Brightness) in one fascicle. The *Daka’eben jing* (Sūtra of the Original Account of Mahākāśyapa) in one fascicle. The *Guangshiyin Dashizhi shoujue jing* (Sūtra on the Prophecy of Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta) in one fascicle;

it appeared during the Yuankang era and is also simply called the *Guanshiyin shouji jing* (Sūtra on the Prophecy of Avalokiteśvara); it is found in the record of Nie Daozhen. The *Zhufang fo ming gongde jing* (Sūtra on the Merits of the Names of Buddhas in All Directions).
*The Sūtra on Maudgalyāyana Ascending to the Śuddhāvāsa Heaven*, one fascicle; one version lacks the character "heaven" (*tiān*). Excerpted from the *Saṃyukta-buddha-carita-sūtra*.

*The Sūtra of the Youth Viśiṣṭacāritra*, one fascicle; recorded in the catalog of Nie Daozhen. *The Sūtra of the Names of the Buddhas of the Ten Directions*, one fascicle. *The Sūtra on the Three Grades of Practice*, one fascicle; also called the *Sūtra on the Repentance of the Three Grades*.

Dao’an stated that this was a compilation by people of recent times. *The Sūtra of the Great Practitioner*, one fascicle. *The Sūtra of the Elder’s Son Jin-yi*, one fascicle. *The Sūtra of the Multitude of Blessings*, one fascicle. *The Sūtra on the Four Matters of Unwavering Contemplative Practice*, one fascicle.

*The Sūtra on the Extinction of the Lesser Dharma*, one fascicle; *The Parable of the Four Women*, one fascicle; *The Sūtra of Lu-yi-hsien*, one fascicle; *The Sūtra of King Hala*, one fascicle; *The Sūtra of Dan-jo*, one fascicle; *The Sūtra of Nāga-dāna*, one fascicle;

*The Sūtra of the Horse-King*, one fascicle; *The Sūtra of the Deer-Mother*; *The Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Vimaladatta’s Analytical Eloquence* (identical to the *Sūtra of the Woman Vimaladatta*, as seen in the T’ang Record);

*The Sūtra of the Virtue of Anāthapiṇḍada*, one fascicle (also called the *Sūtra of the Anāthapiṇḍada Clan*); *The Sūtra of the Brothers Dragon Kings Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Virūḍhaka*, one fascicle; *The Exhortation*.

*Huawang jing* (Sūtra on the Transformation King), one fascicle; *Bai fo ming jing* (Sūtra of the Names of One Hundred Buddhas), one fascicle; *Chu chu zhong de ben jing* (Sūtra on Initially Planting the Roots of All Virtues), one fascicle; *Shamen guo zheng jing* (Sūtra on the Fruits of Realization for Śramaṇas), one fascicle; *Shen guan jing* (Sūtra on Contemplation of the Body), one fascicle;

*Yiwang jing* (Sūtra of the Medicine King), one fascicle; *Faguan jing* (Sūtra on Contemplation of the Dharma), one fascicle; *Yi jing* (Sūtra on the Mind), one fascicle; *Jianglong jing* (Sūtra on Subduing the Dragon), one fascicle; *Yingfa jing* (Sūtra on Corresponding to the Dharma), one fascicle; *Xiejian jing* (Sūtra on False Views), one fascicle;

*Shousui jing* (Sūtra on Observing the Uposatha), one fascicle; *Pinqiong jing* (Sūtra on Poverty), one fascicle; *Guannal jing* (Sūtra on the Waxing and Waning [of the Moon]), one fascicle—also known as the *Baninihuan hou si bei guannal jing* (Sūtra on the Four Classes of Disciples Observing the Uposatha after the Parinirvāṇa); *Miju jing* (Sūtra on the Honey-Preparation).

One fascicle: *Chusheng jing* (Sūtra on Birth); one fascicle: *Huiguo jing* (Sūtra on Repentance), also known as *Śāriputra Huiguo jing* (Sūtra on Śāriputra’s Repentance) or *Zuifan jing* (Sūtra on Transgressions); one fascicle: *Fashu jing* (Sūtra on the Dharma-Community); one fascicle: *Shizhu weiyiza zan jing* (Sūtra of Miscellaneous Praises with Explanatory Notes), traditionally considered doubtful;

one fascicle: *Yulan jing* (Ullambana Sūtra); one fascicle: *Fenbie jing* (Sūtra on Discrimination); one fascicle: *Fushi jing* (Sūtra on the Stomach Messenger); one fascicle: *Chusheng jing kuying jing* (Sūtra on Birth and the Sūtra on the Response to Suffering);

one fascicle: *Xianju jing* (Sūtra on Dwelling in Solitude); one fascicle: *Chusheng jing sishongren jing* (Sūtra on the Four Types of People from the Chusheng Sūtra); one fascicle: *Qibao jing* (Sūtra on the Seven Jewels); one fascicle: *Si weizengyou jing* (Sūtra of the Four Unprecedented Events), also known as *Si wei*.

There is one fascicle of the *Bazhang jing* (Sūtra of the Eight Yangs); one fascicle of the *Sanʼershierxiang yin jing* (Sūtra on the Causes of the Thirty-two Marks), also known as the *Pusa sanʼershierxiang jing* (Sūtra of the Bodhisattva’s Thirty-two Marks) according to Dao’an’s catalogue;

one fascicle of the *Sizai shentong jing* (Sūtra of the Four Sovereign Superknowledges); one fascicle of the *Fo huiguo jing* (Sūtra of the Buddha’s Repentance); one fascicle of the *Sanzhuan yueming jing* (Sūtra of the Three Turnings of the Moonlight); one fascicle of the *Jie wuchang jing* (Sūtra Explaining Impermanence);

one fascicle of the *Taizang jing* (Womb Treasury Sūtra); one fascicle of the *Li gou gai jing* (Sūtra of the Stainless Canopy); one fascicle of the *Xiao yuqia jing* (Shorter Sūtra of Ugga), which is distinct from the *Yuqia changzhe jing* (Sūtra of the Elder Ugga); one fascicle of the *Ajieshi wangnü jing* (Sūtra of King Aśoka’s Daughter); and [one fascicle of] the *Jianwu*.

In the first year [of the reign], he produced the second translation, which differs slightly from that translated by Zhi Qian during the Wu dynasty. It is also titled the *Aśokadatta-sūtra*, the *Sūtra of the Daughter of King Ajātaśatru*, and the *Aśokadatta-bodhisattva-sūtra*.
These are recorded in the catalogs of Nie Daozhen and Zhi Mindu. [The following works were also produced:

one fascicle of the *Sūtra on the Origin of Beings*, one fascicle of the *Sūtra Admonishing Rāhula*, one fascicle of the *Sūtra of the Goose King*, one fascicle of the *Sūtra of the Tenfold Treasury*, one fascicle of the *Sūtra of the Goose King and Five Hundred Geese*, one fascicle of the *Sūtra Admonishing the Fully Equipped*, and one fascicle of the *Sūtra Resolving the Worldly and the Sacred*.

*The Scripture on Fierce Giving* (1 fascicle), also known as *The Scripture on the Stage of Fierce Giving*; seen in the Old Catalogues. *The Scripture of the City Parable* (1 fascicle). *The Scripture of Admonishing the King* (1 fascicle).

*The Scripture on the Bodhisattva’s Fast*, also known as *The Scripture on the Fast of the Bodhisattva Śrī-mukha* (1 fascicle). The above 161 works in 335 fascicles are all found in the Old Catalogues and the *Records of the Tripitaka*. *The Scripture of Much Hearing* (1 fascicle).
The following 48 works in 48 fascicles are all found in the *Wu Record*, the *Separate Record*, and the various records from the Jin Dynasty. *Maitreya*...

*The Bodhisattva as a Female Body*, one fascicle; one version lacks the word "Bodhisattva. *The Sutra on Leaving Sleep*, one fascicle. *The Mañjuśrī-bodhisattva-sūtra*, one fascicle. *The Sutra on Awakening the Mind*, one fascicle. *The Ratnacandraprabha-bodhisattva-sūtra*, one fascicle;
also titled *The Sutra on the Appearance of the Lotus Land as Asked by the Bodhisattva Ratnārcis*. *The Sukhasaṃjñā-sūtra*, one fascicle. *The Uttara-sūtra*, one fascicle.
*The Sutra on the Eighty Minor Marks as Asked by Maitreya*, or simply titled *The Sutra on the Eighty Minor Marks*; recorded in Dao’an’s catalogue. *The Pūrṇa-sūtra*, one fascicle.

*Jùtuólánběn jīng* (The Sūtra on the Original Account of Jūtalā), one fascicle; the *Bièlù* (Separate Record) notes that this is a different recension of the *Wéilán pīnnǚ wèi guówáng fūrén jīng* (Sūtra on the Poor Woman of Vairaṇyā Becoming the King’s Consort), one fascicle;

*Bǎonǚ wèn huì jīng* (Sūtra on the Inquiry of the Jewel Woman into Wisdom), one fascicle; the second translation is identical to that produced by Zhi Qian during the Wu dynasty; *Sìjuǎn bǎonǚ jīng* (Four-Fascicle Sūtra of the Jewel Woman), seven fascicles;

the second translation is identical to that produced by Zhi Qian during the Wu dynasty; *Nǚrén yùchì huāngmí jīng* (Sūtra on Women’s Lust Burning and Their Confusion), one fascicle; *Chūchuyào xībīlí tiānzǐ yì fó shuōgē jīng* (Sūtra on the Emergence from the *Udānavarga*: The Son of Heaven Xībīlí Visits the Buddha and Speaks Verses), one fascicle.
*Zhā'àhán fànwáng biànhuán jīng* (Sūtra on the Transformation of the Brahma King from the Saṃyukta Āgama), one fascicle; *Guānshìyīn jīng* (Sūtra of Avalokiteśvara), one fascicle;

*Chū zhèngfǎhuá jīng wéimíng èrshí shǒu* (Twenty Verses on the Clarification of the Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra), one fascicle—these second editions are identical to those translated by Zhīqiān of the Wù dynasty. *Sānpǐn huìguò jīng* (Sūtra on Repentance in Three Sections), one fascicle; *Qíshéjuéshān jiè jīng* (Sūtra on the Explanation at Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain), one fascicle;

*Bǐqiūní jiè* (Precepts for Bhikṣuṇīs), one fascicle, recorded in the Jiàn Yòu catalogue. *Shísòng běn* (The Ten Recitation Texts), which may contain slight differences from the version produced by Dharmagupta. *Zòngxīng mùlù* (Catalogue of All Scriptures), one fascicle. Total: two hundred and one [items].
Ten sections,
totaling three hundred and ninety-four fascicles.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi kingdom.
Known in the Jin language as Dharmarakṣa,
his original surname was Zhi.
He traveled extensively throughout the Western Regions.
He understood the languages and scripts of thirty-six countries.
From the kingdom of India,
he brought back with him a great quantity of Sanskrit manuscripts of the Brahmanical scriptures.
He arrived at Yumen and settled in Dunhuang,
subsequently adopting the surname Zhu.
Later, he arrived in Luoyang and subsequently traveled to the region south of the Yangtze River.
This period spanned from the first year of the Dashi era during the reign of Emperor Wu to the second year of the Yongjia era during the reign of Emperor Huai.
During that time, he translated as he encountered various conditions.
The lay devotee Nie Chengyuan held the brush to assist in the translation.
The resulting volumes were most numerous.
However, the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (Gaoseng zhuan) states only that Saṃghavarman translated one hundred and sixty-five works,
while Sengyou’s *Collection of Records on the Tripitaka* (Sanzang jiji) records [a different number].
The Zhilu (Catalogue of Stopping) contains one hundred and fifty-four works in three hundred and nine fascicles;
among these, four works are further missing from Shi Dao’an’s catalogue.
Yuzuo said: "Having encountered an era of chaos,
the recorded catalogs have been scattered like stars."
They intersect and overlap with one another; it is indeed so.
This is why there are miscellaneous records and various separate chronicles.
Many commentaries were produced by Zhu Fahu;
therefore, we know that what has been obtained today is certainly the translation of Master Hu, without any doubt.
Thus, [it was written by] Nie Chengyuan’s son, Daozhen.
Zhu Fashou, Chen Shilun, Sun Baihu, Yu Shi,
and others were all the scribes who recorded the teachings at various times;
they have already been mentioned in their respective biographies.
I shall not record them in further detail.
Furthermore, both Li Kuò’s catalogue and the Miscellaneous Separate Catalogue state:
The Bodhisattva Zhi translated six works comprising sixteen fascicles.
Sengyou’s Record states that the number of sūtras translated by this Indian Bodhisattva is consistent with other catalogs.
The names alone differ;
however, the commentary by Sengyou below notes that [this text] was translated jointly by Zhi Qian and Zhu Fahu.
Upon examining the translations of the titles above, [the discrepancy is clarified].
Dharmarakṣa— translated into the Jin language as Fǎhù (Dharma-protected)—
is listed among the six sections of scriptures by the Bodhisattva Zhi [Qian].

*Ekottarika Āgama: The Sūtra on the Individual Aspirations of the Bhikṣus*, one fascicle; *The Sūtra on the Birth [of the Bhikṣu]*, one fascicle; *The Sūtra on the Bhikṣu’s Illness*, one fascicle;

*Chu ahan xin ren zhe sheng wu zhong guohuan jing* (Sūtra from the Āgama on the Five Kinds of Calamities that Befall Those Who Believe), one fascicle;
