The *Yilu* (Records of Doubtful Works) to the right comprises one hundred and thirty-two works,
totaling one hundred and forty-two fascicles,
from the era of Emperor Hui.
Translated by the śramaṇa Shi Fa ju.
Initially, Ju and Fa li co-translated it;
after Li passed away, [Ju] continued alone.
The Torch also appeared spontaneously;
it frequently produced large sections that corresponded with and were interspersed throughout those produced by Li.
The difference lies merely in the extent of the text.
Sengyou’s catalogue does not record it at all;
however, having consulted various older catalogues, [it is found there].
I have relied upon these to continue [the work],
hoping that there may be a basis for examining and correcting the spurious.

*Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā-ratnakaraṇḍa-sūtra*, two fascicles; the second edition, which is largely identical with minor differences to the three-fascicle version translated by An Fagin, is recorded in Zhu Daozu’s *Zalu*. *Sūtra on the Ten Wholesome and Ten Unwholesome Deeds*, one fascicle; recorded in Zhu Daozu’s *Jinshi zalu*. *Sūtra of the Departing Youth*, one fascicle; the third edition, also titled *Sūtra of the Elder’s Regulation*, also simply called *Sūtra of Regulation*, also called *Sūtra of the Bodhisattva’s Departure*, and also simply called *Sūtra of Departure*. These five versions differ only in their translations and titles. *Sūtra of the Son of Good Birth*, one fascicle; the third edition, which is largely identical with minor differences to the *Sūtra of Śikṣānanda’s Sixfold Prostrations* translated by Dharmarakṣa and Zhu Nanti, is recorded in the catalogs of Min Du and Zhu Daozu. The above four sūtras comprise five fascicles in total. They were translated by the śramaṇa Zhi Fadu during the Yongning era of Emperor Hui. This is recorded in Baochang’s catalog.

*The Scripture on the Chapter of Delivering the World*, six fascicles; *The Scripture on the Secret Treasury of the Tathāgata*, two fascicles—also titled *The Great Vaipulya Scripture on the Subtle Secret Treasury of the Arising of the Nature of the Tathāgata*, or simply *The Scripture on the Arising of the Nature of the Tathāgata*; *The Scripture of the Dragon King Anavatapta*, two fascicles; *The Vaipulya Dhāraṇī Scripture*, one fascicle; *The Scripture on the Jewel Adornment*, one fascicle; *The Scripture on the Five Meritorious Virtues*, one fascicle—also simply called *The Scripture on the Five Blessings*; *The Scripture on the Perfection of the Ground of Continuous Liberation*, one fascicle; *The Scripture on the Three Grades of Disciples in Training*, one fascicle—also called *The Scripture on the Three Grades of Disciples*. These are the eight scriptures above.
In total there are fifteen fascicles.
Both the separate catalogs from the Wu period list them as having been translated during the Yuankang era, with direct annotations.
The translator is not specified;
having examined various catalogs in detail, no definitive identification has been found.
Consequently, this separate item remains distinct from those works of lost translation.

*The Catalogue of the Buddhist Scriptures of the Great Tang*, Volume II, Part 4: A Record of the Translation of Buddhist Scriptures during the Western Jin Dynasty. Part IV: The Transmission and Gradual Spread of the Teachings. Although the teachings were heard in the Han and Wei dynasties, it was only during the Jin that their broad meaning was fully opened up.
Furthermore, although the Jin was not renowned for its literary refinement, its talent for literature was truly abundant;
thus, it was through the translations of [Dharmakṣema] that the work ultimately became manifest through human agency.
Consequently, it was during the Jin dynasty that the rites, music, robes, and caps were first fully established.
Is it not so that the source of faith and the ocean of wisdom arose together?
This is recorded in the Western Jin Annals.
Sima Yan, courtesy name Anshi,
was a native of Wen in Henei.
The Prince of Jin, Zhao, was the son of the Grand General of Wei, the Palace Attendant, and Director of the Secretariat,
the Chancellor. When Zhao passed away,
Yan succeeded him as Prince.
Emperor Yuan knew that the mandate of the calendar had returned;
he thus commissioned the Grand Guardian Zheng Chong to present the imperial seal and offer the throne.
Yan [Wang] folded his arms and graciously yielded the succession.
This refers to Emperor Wu,
who styled the cities of Luoyang and Chang'an as the old Eastern and Western Capitals of Jin.
Emperor Wu reigned for fifteen years.
During the Xianning era,
he commanded Sima Zhao to pacify Wu, capturing Sun Hao and bestowing upon him the title of Marquis Who Surrenders His Life.
This was from the twenty-fourth year of the Yongan era of the Later Han onwards.
Reaching the beginning of the first year of the Taikang era of the Jin dynasty, the year of Gengzi,
the nine provinces were once again unified under one rule.
Furthermore, this was during the early Huangwu era of the Wu dynasty.
Lu Ji once said:
"From this day forward, after another sixty years,
the chariots of the empire shall follow the same ruts and its writings shall share the same characters."
By this time, it was indeed just as Zhi Ji had said.
From the pacification of Shu until the destruction of Wu,
nearly sixty years had passed.
Twenty years later,
reaching the beginning of Emperor Hui’s Yongning era,
the True Way declined and fell into ruin while the various factions rose up like mountain peaks.

King Zhao established his foundation by plotting rebellion and usurping the throne at court; Zhang Gui followed in his footsteps but refused to serve as a subject, instead monopolizing the governance of the Liang territories.
Both internally and externally, affairs were in turmoil, gradually providing the basis for further disorder.
This is why Liu Yuan established his capital at Pingyang,
why Li Xiong took advantage of the Jingluo region,
and why Emperor Huai was driven into exile beyond the Hangu Pass.
The Emperor was piteously displaced from Chang’an;
though the Way relies on timely flourishing, both capitals had fallen into ruin.
Since the Dharma is manifested through persons, [the Master] took up residence there.
The two sovereigns were left in a state of frantic distress;
the myriad subjects were scattered and disunited, finding no one to whom they could entrust their faith.
The hundred officials lost their posts, and the Śākya clan was left without refuge.
At that time, there were the śramaṇas Dharmarakṣa, Jiāngliánglóuzhì, and others,
who disregarded their own persons for the benefit of sentient beings and vowed to propagate the teachings.
They did not shrink from hardship or toil, making the elucidation of the Dharma their primary task.
During the Jin dynasty, Dharmarakṣa produced the greatest number of translated scriptures;
it was from him that the broad protection of the Dharma’s principles originated.
His disciples included Dharmakṣema, Nie Daoxuan, father and son, and Zhu Foshou and Zhu Shulan.
Successively, he translated [these works].
Thus, within fifty years, thirteen individuals— both Chinese and non-Chinese, monastics and laypeople—
along with previously lost translations of various sutras and precepts, were brought forth.
In total, there are four hundred and fifty-one works comprising seven hundred and seventeen fascicles;
these were compiled as the "Record of the World" for the fifty-two years of the two capitals and five emperors of the Western Jin dynasty. Thus it is said.
The Śramaṇa Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin translated 210 works in 394 fascicles, including sūtras and precepts;
the Śramaṇa Kanglengqiuji translated 1 work in 1 fascicle; the Śramaṇa Anfaqin translated 5 works in 12 fascicles;
and the Upāsaka Nie Chengyuan [translated] 1 work in 20 fascicles.
Four fascicles of sutras by the śramaṇa Zhu Shulan; two fascicles of sutras by the lay devotee (upāsaka) Nie Daozhen;
a catalogue of fifty-four works totaling sixty-six fascicles by the śramaṇa Bai Fazhu;
twenty-three works totaling twenty-five fascicles by the śramaṇa Shi Fali; and four works totaling twenty-two fascicles by the upāsaka.
The *Weishi du yibu* (One Section of the *Du* [Collection]) in two fascicles; the scriptures of the śramaṇa Zhimidu in two sections totaling thirteen fascicles;
the scriptures of the śramaṇa Shi Faju in one hundred thirty-two works totaling one hundred forty-two fascicles;

the scriptures of the śramaṇa Zhifadu in four works totaling five fascicles; and the scriptures of unknown translators in eight works totaling fifteen fascicles. [Compiled during] the Western Jin dynasty.

*Zapiyu sanbai wushi shou jing* (Sūtra of Three Hundred and Fifty Miscellaneous Parables), twenty-five fascicles; listed in the *Bielu*. *Guangzan banruo jing* (Sūtra of the Radiant Prajñāpāramitā), ten fascicles;
listed in Dao’an’s catalogue. *Xin daoxing jing* (New Sūtra of the Practice of the Way), ten fascicles; also known as the *Xiaopin* (Shorter Version);
produced from the *Guangzan banruo jing*; ten fascicles; listed in Dao’an’s catalogue, or alternatively said to have been translated by Nie Daozhen.

The *Lù xiánjū jīng* (Record of the Scripture on Leisurely Dwelling), ten fascicles; the *Zhèngfǎhuá jīng* (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra), ten fascicles, recorded in the *Jiàndào zhēn lù* (Record of the True Path);
the *Pǔyào jīng* (Lalitavistara-sūtra), eight fascicles, recorded in the *Jiàndào zhēn* and ancient catalogs; the *Bàtuójié sānmèi jīng* (Bhadrapāla-samādhi-sūtra), seven fascicles;

and the *Xiūxíng jīng* (Pratimokṣa-sūtra), seven fascicles, recorded in the *Bǎochàng lù* (Catalogue of Bǎochàng). Translated in the fifth year of the Tàikāng era, this second translation differs slightly from that by An Shìgāo, and it is also so called.

The *Dàodì jīng* (Sūtra on the Stages of the Path) and the *Dà'āi jīng* (Sūtra of Great Compassion), seven fascicles each, are listed in the *Jiàn dào zǔ* (Record of the Ancestral Masters of the Way) and the *Jìn shì zá lù* (Miscellaneous Records of the Jin Dynasty).

The *Xiánjié jīng* (Sūtra of the Auspicious Aeon), seven fascicles—or thirteen fascicles according to some accounts—is listed in the *Jiàn dào zhēn lù* (Record of the True Masters of the Way). The *Xiǎopǐn jīng* (Shorter Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra), seven fascicles, was translated on the fourth day of the third month in the fourth year of the Tàishǐ era;

it is listed in both the *Jiù lù* (Old Record) and the *Zhēn lù* (True Record), or in eight fascicles, being identical in substance to the earlier *Dàoxíng jīng* (Prakrit Pañcaviṃśati-sāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā Sūtra).
The *Wen* (Text) differs slightly from the six-fascicle *Sāyúnfēnduólì jīng* (Saṃpuṇḍarīka-sūtra), which is recorded in the *Jīnshì zálù* (Miscellaneous Records of the Jin Dynasty) by Dào zǔ;

it was translated in the first year of the Tàishǐ era. The six-fascicle *Chíxīn jīng* (Cittadhara-sūtra) is found in the *Jiùlù* (Old Record) and the *Dàozhēnlù* (Record of Dàozhēn); it has four alternative titles, including the six-fascicle *Dùshìpǐn jīng* (Sūtra on the Chapter of Transcending the World), which is recorded in the *Zhēnlù*.
The five-fascicle *Lóutàn jīng* (Lokānuvartana-sūtra)—or, as some say, eight fascicles—is the *Cháng āhán jīng* (Dīrgha Āgama).

The *Shishuo* contains slightly different textual divisions; the *Jian Dao Zhen Lu* states that An [Shigao] says it was translated from the Vaipulya section as the *Miji Jingang Lishi Jing* (Sūtra of the Secret Trace Vajra-wielding Malla) in five fascicles, produced in the first year of the Taikang era.
The *Zhi Mindu and Zhu Daozu Jin Shi Za Lu* lists the *Sheng Jing* (Sūtra of Birth) in five fascicles, found in the *Zhen Lu*.
The *Rulai Xingxian Jing* (Sūtra of the Manifestation of the Tathāgata) in four fascicles is found in the *Zhen Lu*. The *Achashu*... [text fragment].

The *Mojing* (末經) in four fascicles appears in the *Zhen* and *Bie* catalogs, or in seven fascicles according to the *Tang* catalog. The *Wujinyi jing* (無盡意經) in four fascicles appears in the *Zhen* catalog.

The *Baonü jing* (寶女經) in four fascicles, or alternatively in three fascicles—also called the *Baonü sanmei jing* (寶女三昧經) or the *Baonü wenhui jing* (寶女問慧經)—is found in the *Daji* [collection] and appears in the *Nie Daozhen* catalog. The *Puchao jing* (普超經) in four fascicles appears in the [same].

*Daozu zálu* (Miscellaneous Records of the Patriarch Daozu), fascicle 1; *Samādhi Zihǎi* (Ocean of Samādhi Characters); *Lóngwáng jīng* (Sūtra of the Dragon King), four fascicles—translated in the seventh month of the sixth year of the Taikang era, or three fascicles according to the *Jiēnzhen lù* (Record of Verified Authenticity);
*Āwéiyuèzhì jīng* (Sūtra of the Non-retrogressive), four fascicles—seen in the *Jiēnzhen lù*, or three fascicles;

*Chí rén púsà suowèn jīng* (Sūtra of the Questions of the Bodhisattva Dhāraṇīdhara), three fascicles, or four fascicles—this is a separate version of the same text as the *Chíshì jīng* (Sūtra of Holding the World).
*Yi deng ji zhong de san mei jing* (Translated Compendium of All Merits Samādhi Sūtra), three fascicles;

also known as *Ju yi qie fu de san mei jing* (Sūtra on the Samādhi that Gathers All Merits and Virtues), or in two fascicles (*Jian dao zhen lu*). *Chao ri ming san mei jing* (Sūtra on the Sunlight Samādhi), three fascicles (*Jian dao zhen lu*).

*Pusa zang jing* (Bodhisattva-piṭaka Sūtra), three fascicles. *Zhu shen zhou jing* (Sūtra of Various Divine Spells), three fascicles. *Bao ji pusa suo wen jing* (Sūtra of the Questions of Ratnaśikhin Bodhisattva), two fascicles.

The *Jiùzhēn èlù* (Old Catalogue of the Two Records) lists one work titled the *Jìngxíng jīng* (Sūtra on Pure Conduct); the *Ānòudá Lóngwáng jīng* (Sūtra of the Dragon King Anavatapta), two fascicles;
the *Wénshūshī Fótǔ Yánjìng jīng* (Sūtra on the Adornment and Purity of Mañjuśrī’s Buddha-field), two fascicles—these are found in the *Táng lù* (Tang Record);

and the *Xūzhēn Tiānzǐ jīng* (Sūtra of the Devaputra Susīma), two fascicles (or four fascicles)—these are found in the *Dàozǔ Jìn lù* (Daozu’s Jin Record). Also listed is the *Hóngdào Guǎngxiǎn Sānmèi jīng* (Sūtra on the Broad Manifestation of the Samādhi of Spreading the Way).
*Jianzhen lu*: *Daban niepan jing*, two fascicles; one source in the *Jianzhen lu* states it is the *Fo ban niepan jing*.
*Jiandao zu zalu*: *Wuliangshou jing*, two fascicles. *Soutang lu*: *Shoulengyan jing*, two fascicles;
there is a separate variant edition of the *Shoulengyan* which states that Ānanda spoke it. *Soutang lu*: *Baocang jing*, two fascicles; translated in the sixth year of the Taishi era. Essential.
*Jijing* (Collection of Sūtras), two fascicles; also known as *Zhufu yaoji* (Essential Collection of All Buddhas) or *Banzhou sanmei jing* (Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra), two fascicles.

Dao’an states it was translated from the *Banzhou sanmei jing*. *Dashaquan jing* (Sūtra of Great Skillful Means), two fascicles; it has five titles in total as seen in the *Daozhen lu* (Record of the True Path): 1.

*Jiahuishang pusa zishunquan fangbian jing* (Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Jiahuishang’s Accordance with Skillful Means); 2. *Shunquan anjing* (Sūtra of Accordance with Skillful Means and Peace), according to the old records.

The *Jiandao zhenlu* (Record of the True Catalogue of the Path of Seeing) lists the *Suiquan nüren jing* (Scripture on Following the Power of Women) in two fascicles; it is absent from the *Bielu* (Separate Record) and the *Anlu* (An’s Record).

The *Ruhuan sanmei jing* (Scripture on the Samādhi Like an Illusion) is in two or three fascicles; the *Dumuk pusa jing* (Scripture of the Bodhisattva Dumuk) is in two or three fascicles, or includes the title *Suowen jing* (Scripture of the Questions);
and the *Yongfu ding jing* (Scripture on the Heroic Subduing Samādhi) in two fascicles was translated on the ninth day of the fourth month of the first year of the Yuankang era. (4th)

Translated by Zhi Chen, Zhi Qian, Bai Yan, and others; the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra* is of the same original text as those previously produced, differing only slightly (as seen in the *Jiandao zhenlu*).
Furthermore, he produced the two-fascicle *Ajātaśatru-rāja-sūtra*.
Second, he produced the two-fascicle *Vaṇij-sūtra*, the two-fascicle *Mañjuśrī-prabhāsa-ratnagarbha-sūtra*—also known as the *Mañjuśrī-buddhakṣetra-vyūha-śuddhi-sūtra*—and the *Buddha-...*.

*The Scripture on Ascending to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to Preach the Dharma for His Mother*, two fascicles; translated during the Taishi era. One source says it is titled *The Scripture on the Buddha’s Ascent to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven*;
it appears in the *Nie Daozhen Record*. *The Benevolent Kings Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, one fascicle; appears in the *Miscellaneous Records of the Jin Dynasty*.

Subsequently, the single scripture *The Universal Gate Chapter Sūtra* (*Pumenpin Jing*) was translated in the first month of the seventh year of the Taikang era; it appears in the *Nie Daozhen Record*.
The *Record of the Candraprabhakumāra Sūtra* is the same text as the three *Śunyata* sūtras, differing only slightly.
The *Vajragarbhabodhisattvacaryā Sūtra* was translated at the West Temple in Chang’an in the seventh year of Yuankang. It is the twenty-second fascicle of the *Avataṃsaka*.
The *Mahāviśuddhidharmamukha Sūtra* appeared on the twenty-sixth day of the twelfth month of the first year of Jianxing. [Verified as authentic.]
The *Record of the Sūtra on the Girl Vimaladattā* was first seen in the catalog of Daozhen on the second day of the second month of the tenth year of Taikang.
The *Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Sumati*, also known as the *Sumati Sūtra*, was also seen in the catalog of Daozhen. The *Record of Daozu* and others lists the *Sūtra of the Girl Nāgadattā*;
the old catalogs state that this is the second appearance of the original *Nāgadattā Sūtra*. The *Mahāvaipulya Śikhin-rāja Sūtra* appeared for the first time [in this record].
1. *Ekottarāgra-rāja-sūtra* (also known as the *Vimalakīrti-putra-paripṛcchā-sūtra* or the *Susīma-kumāra-sūtra*; fourth name: *Dṛṣṭi-anāśaṃsa-sūtra* according to Zhi Mindu’s catalogue;
also known as the *Hastipada* or the *Hastivāha* according to the Jianzhen catalogue; also known as the *Māravidhvaṃsana-sūtra* according to the Jizhen catalogue).
Translated on the first day of the twelfth month in the tenth year of Taikang. Recorded in the Daozhen catalogue.
*Ji zhū fāngděng xué jīng* (Sutra on the Study of Various Vaipulya Teachings), or *Wú xué zì jiàn* (Seeing Without Learning Characters); listed in the catalog of Zhù Dàozǔ.
*Púsà xíng wǔshí yuán shēn jīng* (Sutra on the Fifty Causes and Conditions of the Bodhisattva’s Deeds); these two titles appear in the catalog of Zhù Dàozǔ.

*Mílè púsà suǒwèn běnyuàn jīng* (Sutra on the Original Vows Asked by Maitreya Bodhisattva), translated on the seventeenth day of the fifth month in the second year of the Tàikāng era; these three titles appear in the catalog of Dào Zhēnzǔ. *Wénshū*... [text fragment].
The *Mañjuśrī-viśuddha-śīla-sūtra* appeared in the tenth year of the Taikang era; it is listed in the *Daozhen daozu lu*.
The *Wuji bao sanmei jing* appeared on the third day of the third month in the first year of the Yongjia era; it is listed in the *Daozhen lu* and the *Bielu*.
The *Baowang tongzi jing*—also known as the *Baowang jing*—is listed in the *Daozhen lu*. The *Wenshushili hui guo jing* appears at the beginning [of the list].

The *Wénshū wǔtǐ huìguò jīng* (Mañjuśrī’s Sutra on Repentance with the Five Limbs), also known as the *Pǔfǎ yì jīng* (Sutra on the Meaning of the Universal Dharma) or the *Pǔyì jīng* (Sutra on Universal Meaning);
a second translation, slightly different from that produced by Hào Chū during the Han dynasty, is recorded in the *Jiàndào zhēnlù* (Record of the True Record of the Path).

The *Miè shífāng míng jīng* (Sutra on the Extinction of Darkness in the Ten Directions) was translated on the fourteenth day of the eighth month of the Guangxi year; one copy lacks the character "miè" (extinction) and is recorded in the *Niè dàozhēn lù* (Record of Niè Dàozhēn). The *Pú...* [text fragment].

The *Sāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (also known as the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* or the *Mahāvaipulya-sūtra*), translated from the "Ten Stages Chapter" of the *Avataṃsaka*, and the *Jentaka-snāna-bhikṣu-saṃgha-sūtra*, recorded in the catalog of Nie Daozhen;

the *Rāṣṭrapāla-paripṛcchā-jyotirguṇa-kumāra-sūtra*, translated on the thirtieth day of the ninth month in the sixth year of the Taishi era, recorded in the catalog of Zhu Daozu. These [texts] should be [included].

*The Scripture on the Transformation of Coming* (Lái biàn jīng), translated in the fifth month of the second year of the Tà'ān era; recorded in the *Jiàn dào zhēn lù* (Record of Daozhen’s Verification) as the *Scripture of the Five Hundred Disciples’ Own Account of Their Original Arisings*.
*The Scripture on the Birth of the Buddha Siṃhacandra* (Shīzǐyuè fó shēng jīng), translated during the Tà'ān era; recorded in the *Jiàn dào zhēn lù*.

*The Tradition of Kāśyapa’s Compilation of the Scriptures* (Jiāshè jiéjí chuán jīng), also known as the *Compilation of the Precepts Scripture* (jiéjí jiè jīng); recorded in the *Jiàn dào zhēn lù*. *The Story of the Maiden Āmrapālī* (Nài nǚ).
The *Ji-yü jīng* (Sūtra of Jīvaka) was translated during the Taian era; it is also titled the *Nai-nü jīng* (Sūtra of the Woman Nai), as recorded in the *Jiandō zhēn-lù*.

The *Pāo-tāi jīng* (Sūtra of the Womb) was translated on the first day of the eighth month of the second year of the Taian era; it is also called the *Pāo-tāi shòu-shēn jīng* (Sūtra of Receiving a Body in the Womb), as recorded in the *Jiandō zhēn-lù*.

The *Weimoji suǒshuō fǎmén jīng* (Sūtra of the Dharma-gate Expounded by Vimalakīrti) was translated on the first day of the fourth month of the second year of the Taian era; this is the third translation.

The *Yugārarāja-paripṛcchā-bodhisattvacaryā-sūtra* (or *Yugāra-jātakasūtra*), translated during the Han by Dharmakṣema and during the Wu dynasty by Zhi Qian, is largely the same with minor differences;
it is recorded in the *Zhēnlù*. It is also called the *Yugā-jātakasūtra*, which is the same as the *Mahāyugā-sūtra* in two fascicles.
This second translation differs slightly from those by Saṃghavarman and Zhi Qian, as noted in the records of Dao’an and Zhi Min-du. It is also known as the *Māyāvin-sūtra*.

The *Renxian jing* (Sūtra of Benevolence and Wisdom), also known as the *Jiandao zhenlu jue zongchi jing* (Sūtra of the True Record and Decision of the Path of Seeing, Compendium of Dharanis), is also called the *Jueding zongchi jing* (Sūtra of the Determinate Dharani).
The *Shouyi nü jing* (Sūtra of the Maiden Shouyi), also called the *Fannü shouyi jing* (Sūtra of the Brahmin Maiden Shouyi).

The *Shetoujian jing* (Sūtra of the Admonition of Śatrujit), also called the *Taizi ershiba xiu jing* (Sūtra of the Prince and the Twenty-eight Lunar Mansions) or the *Hueryi jing* (Sūtra of the Tiger-Ear Maiden); this is the same as the second translation of the *Madengqie jing* (Mātṛkā Sūtra) by An Shigao.
The *Dvādaśāṅgapratītyasamutpādasūtra* (Sūtra on the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination), the third translation produced by Shi Huchu, which differs slightly from that of Dao’an’s record;
one version says it is the *Sūtra on Contemplating the Twelve Links under the Pei-tuo Tree*, seen in the Tang Record as the sixty-second;

the *Īśvaradeva-sūtra* (or *Brahmajāla-sūtra*), seen in Daozu’s record as the fourth; the *Svātmanupaghāta-sūtra* (Sūtra on Self-Inflicted Harm); and the *Anabhilāpya-kumāra-sūtra* (Sūtra of the Silent Youth).

Alternatively, it consists of two fascicles. One version is titled the *Avyākṛta-bodhisattva-sūtra*; it appears in the *Daji jian dao zhen lu* (Record of the True Path Seen in the Mahāsaṃnipāta) and the *Sheng fayan jing* (Sūtra of the Holy Dharma Seal).
It was produced on the fifth day of the eleventh month of the fourth year of Yuankang (284 CE) at Jiuquan Commandery, with Zhu Fashou serving as the scribe.

Another version is called the *Shengyin jing* (Sūtra of the Holy Seal), and another is called the *Huiyin jing* (Sūtra of the Wisdom Seal). Dao’an stated that it appears in the *Za ahan* (Saṃyuktāgama) and is seen in the *Zhenshi* (True Reality).
The *Catalogue of Equal Records* (*Denglu*) lists the following:

the *Sūtra on Moving Mountains by the Mallas*, the *Sūtra on the Child Bodhisattva of Inconceivable [Power]*—also called the *Sūtra on the Questions of Inconceivable Light* or the *Sūtra of Inconceivable Light*—and the *Sūtra on Maitreya’s Attainment of Buddhahood*, which was translated in the second year of the Tai’an era;
it is also known as the *Sūtra on Maitreya’s Descent to Be Born*, and is seen in the *Daozhen*.
*Record of the Journey of Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana Through Various Kingdoms*, also known as *The Sūtra of Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana Traveling the Four Crossroads*;
*The Sūtra of King Virūḍhaka*; *The Sūtra of the Girl Ratnadattā*, also known as *The Sūtra of Sumati on the Dharma and Vinaya Samādhi*;
*The Record of the True Realization of the Path*; and *The Sūtra of the Five Dreams of the Buddha as a Bodhisattva*. Translated in the fifth month of the second year of the Tai’an era.
One title is *The Five Dreams of the Buddha*, another is *The Five Dreams of the Crown Prince*, and another is *The Five Dreams of the Immortal*.

These are seen in the *Jiulù* (Record of Old) and the *Dàozhēnlù* (Record of Daozhen). There is one copy of the *Mahāmaudgalyāyana-ben-jīng* (Original Sūtra of Mahāmaudgalyāyana), though some versions lack the character "jiàn" (犍).

The *Tàizǐmùpòjīng* (Sūtra of the Crown Prince’s Death and Rebirth), fascicle one, is found in the *Sìbùkědéjīng* (Sūtra on the Four Unobtainables) and is recorded in the *Dàozhēn* and *Zhèngdù* catalogs. [This concludes] the *Bodhisattva-huǐ* (Repentance of the Bodhisattva).

The *Guòfǎ jīng* (Sūtra on the Dharma of Transcendence), or sometimes without the word "sūtra," has a note below it stating that the *Lóngshù shízhù lùn* (Nāgārjuna’s *Daśabhūmika-bhāṣya*) identifies the *Rúlǎng jīng* (Kṣīranirghoṣa Sūtra) as a different translation of the same text as the *Dúzi jīng* (Vatsiputriya Sūtra).

The *Xīnmíng nǚ fànlì fù fànzhī fū fànzhī shī jīng* (Sūtra of the Brahmin Woman Xīnmíng Offering Rice Water to Her Husband), also known as the *Xīnmíng jīng*, is the *Dà liù xiàng bài jīng* (Sūtra of the Sixfold Prostrations), translated in the first year of the Tà'ān era; some say it is the *Shījia liù xiàng bài*. Or it is said: [text continues].
In the *Liùxiàngbài jīng* (Sutra of the Sixfold Prostrations), one sees the records of Zhi Mindu and Baochang;

the *Aṅgulimāla-sūtra* is also known as the *Zhǐmàn jīng* or the *Yāngjuémóluó jīng*, as seen in the *Dàozhēn lù*. The *Púsà shízhù jīng* (Bodhisattva Ten Dwellings Sutra) is largely the same as the *Púsà shídì jīng* (Bodhisattva Ten Grounds Sutra), differing only slightly.
The second translation of the *Módiào wáng jīng* (King Māndhātṛ Sutra) differs slightly from that translated by Zhi Qian.

*Chūliùdù jí zhàomíng sānmèijīng* (The Scripture on the Illumination Samādhi Collected from the Six Pāramitās); *Suǒyù zhìhuàn jīng* (The Scripture on the Sufferings Resulting from Desires), translated in the first month of the third year of the Tà'ān era;

recorded by Jìndào Zhēn and Wáng Zōng; *Fǎmòjìn jīng* (The Scripture on the Exhaustion of the Dharma)—also written as *Miè* (Extinction) or titled *Kōngjì púsà suowèn jīng* (The Scripture on the Questions of the Bodhisattva Śūnyatā-śānti)—the second translation, identical to that produced by Zhī Qiān; *Púsà zhāifǎ jīng* (The Scripture on the Rituals for the Bodhisattva Fast), or...

There is no sūtra text; it is known by several names: *Zhengzhai* (Correct Fasting), *Chizhai* (Maintaining Fasting), and *Xianshou Pusa Zhai Fa Jing* (Sūtra on the Ritual for the Fasting of the Bodhisattva Worthy Head).

It is also titled *Duzheng Zishì Samādhi Jing* (Sūtra on Self-Vowing Samādhi) or *Rulai Zishì Samādhi Jing* (Sūtra on the Tathāgata’s Self-Vowing Samādhi), as well as *Guoqufo Fenwei Jing* (Sūtra on the Almsround of Past Buddhas).

Some say it is called *Guoshi Jianjiu Lu Wugai Yijie Shixing Jing* (Sūtra on Seeing the Old Records of the Past World Regarding the Five Coverings, Doubtful Knots, and Lost Practice). It was [translated] in the second year of the Yongning era.

On the twelfth day of the fourth month, the following were seen: the *Daozhen lu* (Record of the True Path), the *Zongchi jing* (Sūtra of Total Retention), the *Chusheng jing* (Sūtra of Birth), also called the *Foxin zongchi jing* (Sūtra of the Buddha-Mind Total Retention), the *Wuyushi jing* (Sūtra of the Giver of No Sorrow), the *Ajātaśatru-rājñī-dhītā-pañcamaṅgala-dāna jing* (Sūtra of the Five Blessings Given by the Daughter of King Ajātaśatru), also called the *Qingjing pinifangdeng jing* (Sūtra of the Pure Vinaya Vaipulya), the *Yanjingding jing* (Sūtra of the Pure and Adorned Samādhi), the *Hui ming jing* (Sūtra of Wisdom and Clarity), and the *Mahākāśyapa-pūrva-yoga* (The Former Deeds of Mahākāśyapa). These are recorded in the Tang catalogue.

*The Sūtra on the Prophecy Bestowed upon Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta*, translated during the Yuankang era; also known as *The Sūtra on the Prediction for Avalokiteśvara*, recorded in the *Zhēnlù*.

*The Sūtra on the Merits of the Names of Buddhas in All Directions*. *The Sūtra on Maudgalyāyana Ascending to the Śuddhāvāsa Heavens*, one fascicle (the character "heaven" [天] is absent in some editions).
*The Sūtra on the Original Deeds of the Buddha*, recorded in the *Dàozhēnlù*. *The Sūtra on the Youthful Puṣya*, containing the names of the Buddhas of the ten directions.
The *Sūtra on the Practice of the Three Categories*, the *Sūtra on Repentance of the Three Categories*, what Dao’an called the *Sūtra Compiled by Recent Generations*,
the *Sūtra on Great Practice*, the *Sūtra of the Elder’s Son Jin-yi*, the *Sūtra of the Multitude of Blessings*, the *Sūtra on the Four Matters of Unwavering Contemplative Practice*,
the *Sūtra on the Extinction of the Lesser Dharma*, the *Sūtra of the Parable of the Four Women*, the *Sūtra of Lu-yi-xun*, the *Sūtra of King Harṣa*, and the *Sūtra of Dānyè*.
The *Nāgadatta-sūtra*, the *Aśvaparivarta-sūtra*, the *Mṛgajā-sūtra*,
the *Vimaladattā-bodhisattva-vibhaṅga-pratibhāna-sūtra* (identical to the *Vimaladattā-dārikā-sūtra* as seen in the Tang records), the *Anāthapiṇḍada-mingde-jing* (or the *Anāthapiṇḍada-śrī-sūtra*),
the *Nāgarāja-bhrātṛ-dauḍa-jie-wang-jing*, the *Quanhua-wang-jing*, and the beginning of the *Śata-buddhanāma-sūtra*.

The *Sutra on the Emergence and Cultivation of the Roots of All Virtues*, the *Sutra on the Fruits of the Śramaṇa’s Realization*, the *Sutra on the Buddha’s Repentance*, the *Sutra of the Three Turnings and the Moonlight*,
the *Sutra on the Explanation of Impermanence*, the *Womb Treasury Sutra*, the *Sutra of the Stainless Canopy*, the *Minor Ugra Sutra*, and the *Sutra on the Gift to the Householder Ugra*—
these differ from the *Sutra of the Daughter of King Ajātaśatru*. This second translation was made in the first year of the Jianwu era, alongside the version translated by Zhi Qian.
There are slight variations: some call her Āśuddhā, others call her the daughter of King Ajātaśatru, and others call her the Bodhisattva Āśuddhā.

She is seen in the *Zhendu* (Jianduo) and other catalogs. Regarding the scriptures concerning her origins, there are also the *Socunlaijie* (Śrāmaṇera-śīla), the *Lóuyún jīng* (Rāhula-sūtra), the *Yàn wáng jīng* (Hamsarāja-sūtra), the *Shíděng zàng jīng* (Daśottara-sūtra), the *Yàn wáng wǔbǎi yàn jù jīng* (Hamsarāja-pañcaśata-haṃsa-sahita-sūtra), the *Jièjù jīng* (Śikṣāsamuccaya-sūtra), and the *Jué dào* (Mārgaviniścaya).
The *Sujātā-sūtra* (also known as the *Sujātā-mārga-bhūmi-sūtra*), seen in the old catalogs;
the *Nagara-upama-sūtra*, the *Śīlarāja-sūtra*, and the *Bodhisattva-poṣadha-sūtra* (or the *Bhadramukha-bodhisattva-poṣadha-sūtra*).

The above one hundred and sixty-one works in three hundred and forty-five fascicles are all found in the old catalogs and the *San-zang-ji*. Below these are four [works], beginning with the *Bahusruta-sūtra*.
The eighteen sections comprising forty-eight fascicles are all found in the *Wu lu*, the *Bie lu*, and the miscellaneous records of the Jin dynasty. These include:

one fascicle of the *Mile pusa wei nü shen jing* (Sūtra on Maitreya Bodhisattva as a Female Body)—which lacks the word "bodhisattva"—the *Li shui mian jing* (Sūtra on Leaving Sleep), the *Wenshushili pusa jing* (Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva Sūtra), the *Wuyi jing* (Sūtra on Awakening the Mind), and the *Baoyue guangming pusa jing* (Sūtra on the Bodhisattva Jewel Moon Radiance), or alternatively, the *Baoyue guangming pusa*.

Question: The *Sūtra on the Appearance of the Lotus Land*, the *Sūtra on the Perception of Joy*, the *Sūtra on the Most Honorable*, the *Sūtra on Contemplation of the Body*, the *Sūtra on the King of Physicians*,

the *Sūtra on Contemplation of the Dharma*, the *Sūtra on the Mind*, the *Sūtra on Subduing Dragons*, the *Sūtra on Correspondence with the Dharma*, the *Sūtra on Erroneous Dharmas*, the *Sūtra on What is Suffering*,

the *Sūtra on Observing the Year*, the *Sūtra on Poverty*, the *Sūtra on the Wax Offering*, or the *Sūtra on the Four Classes of Disciples Offering Wax after the Parinirvāṇa*, the *Sūtra on the Fullness of Honey*, and the *Sūtra on Birth*.
The *Sūtra on Repentance*, or the *Śāriputra Repentance Sūtra*; the *Sūtra on Transgressions*; the *Dharmasaṃgha Sūtra*;
the *Worldly Commentary on the Doubtful and Miscellaneous Prajñapti Sūtra*; the *Ullambana Sūtra*; the *Vibhaṅga Sūtra*; the *Kukṣisena Sūtra*; the *Jātaka Sūtra*; the *Duḥkhasatyasūtra*;
the *Praviveka Sūtra*; the *Jātaka Sūtra*; the *Catuṣpuruṣayoga Sūtra*; the *Saptaratna Sūtra*; the *Catur-āścarya Sūtra*, or the *Catur-anutpāda Sūtra*.

There are the *Jing* (Sūtra), the *Bā-yáng jīng* (Eight Yang Sūtra), the *Sì-zìzài shéntōng jīng* (Sūtra on the Four Sovereign Supernatural Powers), the *Sānshí'èr xiàng yīnyuán jīng* (Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of the Thirty-two Marks) or the *Púsà sānshí'èr xiàng jīng* (Sūtra on the Thirty-two Marks of a Bodhisattva)—these are recorded in the catalog of Dao’an;
the *Círén wèn bāshí zhǒnghǎo jīng* (Sūtra on the Eighty Minor Marks Asked by Círén) or the *Bāshí zhǒnghǎo jīng* (Sūtra on the Eighty Minor Marks)—these are recorded in the catalog of Dao’an;
furthermore, the *Fú nàluó jīng* (Naraka Sūtra) and the *Suílán běn jīng* (Sūtra on the Original Account of Sūlana) are noted as being found in a separate catalog.

This is a different version of the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, the *Sūtra of the Poor Woman Who Became a King’s Consort*, and the second translation of the *Sūtra of the Jewel Woman Asking about Wisdom*, which is identical to that produced by Zhi Qian;
it consists of four fascicles. It is also the second translation of the *Sūtra of the Seven Women’s Origins*, which is identical to the translation by Zhi Qian of the Wu period.
Furthermore, it includes the *Sūtra of Women’s Lustuous Infatuation* and the *Udānavarga* (The Verses of the Buddha) translated by Xuanzang.

The *Sūtra on the Devaputra Visiting the Buddha and Speaking in Verse* appears in the *Saṃyukta Āgama*; the *Sūtra on the Transformation of the Brahma King* and the *Sūtra on Avalokiteśvara* appear in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*;
the twenty verses of the *Vimalaprabhā* (or *Weiming*) are the second [recension] appearing alongside those translated by Zhi Qian;

the three chapters of the *Sūtra on Repenting of Transgressions* and the *Sūtra on the Explanation at Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain* are recorded in the *Jiyou Lu*; and the *Bhikṣuṇī Vinaya* is found in the *Daśādhyāya-vinaya*. Or...
There is a scripture whose title differs slightly from that produced by Dharmadatta; one fascicle of the *Zhongjing mulu* (Catalogue of Scriptures).
The above comprises two hundred and ten works, totaling three hundred and ninety-four fascicles.
The śramaṇa Dharmarakṣa from the country of the Yuezhi—
“Dharmarakṣa” meaning “Fa-hu” (Dharma-protector) in the Jin language—
was originally surnamed Zhi.
Having traveled extensively through the Western Regions, he mastered the languages and scripts of thirty-six kingdoms.
From the kingdom of India, he brought back a great quantity of Sanskrit manuscripts of the Brahmanical scriptures and arrived at the royal court.
Because he resided in Dunhuang,
he subsequently adopted the surname Zhu.
Later, he arrived in Luoyang.
Furthermore, from the time he went to Jiangzuo during the first year of the Taishi era of Emperor Wu,
until the second year of the Yongjia era of Emperor Huai,
he translated whatever teachings he encountered along the way as circumstances arose.
The lay devotee Nie Chengyuan held the brush to assist in the translation.
Although the scrolls were most numerous,
the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (Gaoseng zhuan) states only that Dharmarakṣa produced one hundred and sixty-five works.
Sengyou compiled the *Collection of Records on the Tripitaka*,
recording a total of one hundred and fifty-four works in three hundred and nine fascicles;
among these, Sengyou supplemented four works that were missing from Shi Dao’an’s catalog.
An said: "To have encountered an age of turmoil, with catalogs scattered like stars and further intermingled with one another—
this is indeed the case."
Therefore, since the *Zalu* (Miscellaneous Records) and various other separate records frequently annotate that [these works] were translated by Zhu Fahu,
we know that what has now been obtained is certainly the translation of Master Hu; of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, Nie Chengyuan’s son Daozhen, Zhu Fashou, Chen Shilun, Sun Bohu, Yu Shi,
and others were all the scribes who recorded [the teachings] at various times.
This has already been seen in the separate biographies (*biezhuan*), so it will not be recorded here in detail.
Furthermore, there are the records by Li Kuò and the various miscellaneous registers of the assembly.
Siyun states that the Bodhisattva Zhi translated six scriptures in sixteen fascicles.
Sengyou’s Catalogue states:
The number of sutras translated by the Bodhisattvas from India is the same as in the various catalogs;
only their titles differ.
This is noted in the sub-commentary by Sengyou.
Translated by the Bodhisattva Zhi together with Zhu Fahu.
Upon examination, the name previously translated as Tanwuluoche (Dharmaraksita) corresponds in the Jin language to Fahu (Dharmarakṣa).
However, the titles of the six works by Dharmarakṣa are all included in the catalog of Dharmarakṣa;
the difference lies only in the fact that their surnames differ— Dharmarakṣa being of the Zhi clan— and that their biographies vary from beginning to end.
Regarding the term "Bodhisattva," it is merely a laudatory title; yet,
upon a thorough examination of the various records, one finds...
The Bodhisattva Qizhi was none other than Zhu Fahu;
they were not two different people.
This entry in the *Chusanzang jiji* (Record of the Tripitaka Translated) results in a double listing, which is an error resulting from an unverified translation.
*The Scripture on the Twelve Wanderings*, one fascicle.
The aforementioned scripture was [translated] during the reign of Emperor Wu by the foreign śramaṇa Qiāngliánglóuzhì (Jìn: Zhēnxǐ).
Translated at Guangzhou in the second year of the Taishi era,
as seen in the Shixing and Baochang catalogs.

The *Mahā-Aśoka-rāja-sūtra* in five fascicles, translated during the Guangxi era; listed in the *Daozu lu*. The *Dao shenzu wuji bianhua jing* (Sūtra on the Infinite Transformations of the Divine Footsteps of the Path) in two fascicles, a second translation; or in three fascicles. This is the same text as the *Buddha Ascends to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to Preach the Dharma for His Mother* translated by Dharmarakṣa, though the wording differs slightly; listed in the *Zhu Zu lu*. The *Mañjuśrī-prabhāsa-ratnagarbha-sūtra* in two fascicles, translated in the second year of the Tai’an era; or in three fascicles. Also called the *Shixian baozang jing*; listed in the *Daozu lu*. The *Ajātaśatru-rāja-sūtra* in two fascicles, translated during the Taikang era; listed in the *Daozu lu*. Record of Buddhist Scriptures Translated During the Eastern Jin Dynasty, Part Five. Preface: [The following is the preface to] the Record of Buddhist Scriptures Translated During the Eastern Jin Dynasty. Fifth. It states:
The Sūtra says:
"The three realms are impermanent; conditioned things do not endure long.
Such was the foundation of the Jin dynasty.
The Wei house possessed a distant lineage and lofty standards;
they executed Cao Shuang and severed his clan.
When the imperial decree was established and his achievements were set forth,
the Jin dynasty succeeded the earthly mandate as the destiny of the calendar fell upon him;
he pacified Shu and brought the Great Wu into submission.
During the Shengping era, it was called the Kuānzhèng period;
when civil culture was fully established, military arms were likewise sheathed.
Yet suddenly, the calamity of the "one hundred and six" arrived, and the royal officials lost their posts.
The world was in great chaos, with nothing but this [suffering].
At that time, both monastics and laypeople were scattered and separated; they could not plan for even the next morning.
Governance was entrusted to the region south of the Yangtze River, where the Dharma flourished in accordance with the administration. Thus, śramaṇas and lay believers gathered there.
Therefore, I have recorded it here.
As for the "Record of the Eastern Jin," [the author] was the son of Prince Gong, a descendant of Emperor Xuan’s great-grandson, King Wu of Langya.
His name was Rui and his courtesy name was Jingwen.
On the day of his birth,
a divine light appeared within the room, illuminating it entirely.
A white hair grew from the left side of his brow at the "sun-peak" (ri-corner).
His eyes possessed a brilliant luster, and his gaze was radiant and majestic.

He held successive offices, serving as the Commandant-in-Chief with Investiture of Authority (Shichijie), General Who Guards the East (Andong Jiangjun), Inspector-General of the Military Affairs of Yangzhou, and Left Chancellor (Zuo Xianghuang).
After the defeat of Emperor Hui and Emperor Min, the hundred officials were scattered;
some fled to the south of the Yangtze River,
while others were slaughtered by Liu Yao.
Chang’an lost its stronghold and the Emperor was held captive in Pingyang.
At that time, five suns suddenly appeared in the sky over Jiangdong.
The subordinates urged Yao Rui that he should assume the title of Prince of Jin.
Governing the myriad affairs of state and presiding over a billion subjects,
he ascended the throne following the demise of Emperor Min, established the Jianwu era,
and subsequently made Jianye his capital.
It was changed to Jiankang to avoid the taboo name of Emperor Min.
Previously, in the second year of Taikang,
Guan Gong, a former general of Wu, had raised a rebellion.
At that time, Wu Zhen performed a divination in Jianye and said,
"Gong has already perished."
"However, after thirty-eight years,
there shall be an Emperor in Yangzhou. At this point,
it indeed came to pass exactly as he had said.
Furthermore, during the era of the First Emperor of Qin,
a diviner of vapors declared that the Jinling Mountains of Wu possessed [auspicious] qi.
Five hundred years hence, a Son of Heaven shall emerge.
Fearing this, the First Emperor dispatched troops and excavated Mount Jinling, altering its name to Moling.
Hoping to sever his rule,
[the dynasty] was rectified by the wisdom of the Emperor for five hundred and twenty-six years,
until the Jin of the Metal Phase suddenly became the lord of the four seas.
"The auspicious omen of Jinling lies herein.
At that time, there was also a popular song which said:
"Five horses float across the river."
One horse was transformed into a dragon.
During the chaos and upheaval of the Yongjia era, when the empire fell into ruin,
only the five princes of Langya, Xiyang, Runan, Nandong, and Pengcheng managed to find refuge beyond the Yangtze River.
Yet it was Rui who first laid the foundation for Emperor Yuan.
One can thus know that his reception of the Mandate was an upward resonance with celestial spirits,
while his desire to span the realm’s cartographic expanse was supported by the downward influence of terrestrial topography.
The earth bore its momentum;
even when the First Emperor excavated it, it did not perish.
Heaven bestowed its spiritual power; though Liu Yao destroyed it, it was not exhausted.

Compiled by the śramaṇa Shi Tanshen of Donglin Monastery on Mount Lu.
Tanshen was a disciple of Huiyuan and possessed great talent and learning.

The *Weishi lumu* (Catalogue of the Wei Dynasty), the *Wushi lumu* (Catalogue of the Wu Dynasty), the *Jinsi zalu* (Miscellaneous Catalogues of the Jin Dynasty), and the *Hexi lumu* (Catalogue of the Hexi Region).
These four catalogues of scriptures comprise four fascicles in total.
They were first compiled by the monk Shi Daoliu, a disciple of Master Huiyuan of Donglin Monastery on Mount Lu.
He passed away before his work was completed;
his fellow student Zhu Daozu completed it for circulation in the world.
The *General Catalogue of Sūtras and Śāstras* (Jīnglùn dūlù) consists of one fascicle.
During the reign of Emperor Cheng,
the śramaṇa Zhi Mindu of Mount Yuzhang collated the various scriptures,
combined the catalogs of ancient and modern times, and compiled this comprehensive record.
Regarding the "Discourse on the Initial Meaning of Human Figures" mentioned above:
during the reign of Emperor Cheng,
the śramaṇa Kang Fachang would always carry a fly-whisk whenever he encountered renowned guests.
He would invariably engage in pure conversation (*qingtan*) throughout the day.
The rest is as recorded in his biography.
This concludes the "Biographies of Eminent and Recluse Śramaṇas."
Compiled by the śramaṇa Zhu Faji of Mount Yang in East Shan during the reign of Emperor Xiaowu.

It consists of the *Liben lun* (Treatise on Establishing the Foundation) in nine chapters and the *Lishi zhigui* (Pointing to the Return of the Six Consciousnesses) in twelve sections; these two works comprise two fascicles.
During the reign of Emperor Xiaowu,
the śramaṇa Shi Tanyuei of Shangming Monastery in Jingzhou composed [this work].
Tanyuei was originally a disciple of Master Dao’an.
His occupation was to perform prostrations using diagrams and preach for profit.
Consequently, the men and women of Jiangling all faced westward to pay their respects to the Bodhisattva Yinsou (Yinshou).

There are two fascicles of the *Yijiao sanmei jing* (Sutra on the Samādhi of the Bequeathed Teaching), also known as the *Yijiao sanmei falü jing* (Sutra on the Samādhi of the Bequeathed Teaching and the Vinaya) or the *Weichengyou yinyuan* (Unprecedented Causes and Conditions).
*Jing* (Sūtra) in two fascicles; *Weicengyou jing* (Sūtra of Marvels); *Anagāmi jing* (Sūtra on Non-returners) in two fascicles; *Naxian jing* (Nāgasena Sūtra) in two or three fascicles;

*Guān wuliangshoufo jing* (Sūtra on the Visualization of Amitāyus Buddha); *Sanshi sanqian fo ming jing* (Sūtra of the Names of Three Thousand Buddhas of the Three Times); *Yu li yijuan* (Miscellaneous Examples, one fascicle); *Qianfo yinyuan jing* (Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of the Thousand Buddhas);

*Wushisan fo ming jing* (Sūtra of the Names of Fifty-three Buddhas); *Babu fo ming jing* (Sūtra of the Names of Eight Classes of Buddhas); *Shifang fo ming jing* (Sūtra of the Names of the Buddhas of the Ten Directions).

The *Sūtra of the Names of the Thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa* contains only the names of the Buddhas, which differ from those in the *Sūtra of the Four Truths* (Catuḥsatya-sūtra) produced by Dharmaruci;
the *Sūtra of the Praise of the Names of One Hundred and Seventy Buddhas*, or simply the *Sūtra of the Names of One Hundred and Seventy Buddhas*; the *Sūtra of the Names of the Southern Buddhas*;

*Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya-bhikṣu-āvaśyaka-saṃgraha* (also known as *Sāṃghika-paryāya-āvaśyaka-saṃgraha-dharma*),
*Upāli-paripṛcchā-buddha-sūtra*, *Śrāmaṇera-īryāpatha* in one fascicle, *Bhikṣuṇī-daśa-śīla-sūtra*, *Daśakuśala-karma-patha-pratigraha-dharma*,
*Śrāmaṇerī-śīla-sūtra*, *Āyuṣmat-pañca-maṅgala-sūtra*, *Āyuṣmat-pañca-śīla-sūtra*, or alternatively titled...
The Sūtra on the Dignified Conduct of the Wise; the Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra (Sūtra on the Five Precepts for Lay Followers); the Upāsaka-vinaya-sūtra (Sūtra on the Dignified Conduct of Lay Followers);
the Prajñāprāpti-sūtra; the Avalokita-loka-sthiti-sūtra; the Mūlapravṛtti-ṣaṭpāramitā-sūtra; the Samādhi-manaḥ-samādhi-sūtra;
the Pratyutpanna-samādhi-buddhānusmṛti-parivarta-sūtra; and the Yogācāra-sūtra (translated into Chinese as *Xiuxing lü* [Brief Account of Practice], also known as the *Dacheng yuqie jing*).
The *Matara-dharma* (also known as the *Matara Bodhisattva’s Compendium of Essential Methods for Dhyāna*), the *Sūtra on the Sequential Methods for the Expedients of Dhyāna-Samādhi*,
the *Sūtra on the Essentials of Dhyāna: Rebuking Desire*, the *Dharani Sūtra of the Seven Myriad Three Thousand Divine Kings Protecting Bhikṣus*,
the *Dharani Sūtra of the Twelve Myriad Divine Kings Protecting Bhikṣus*, and the *Dharani Sūtra for Wearing and Carrying for Body Protection via the Three Refuges and Five Precepts*.
The Scripture of the Hundred-Knot Spirit King’s Body-Protection Dhāraṇī; the Scripture of the Palace-Residence Spirit Kings’ Guarding and Pacifying Spells for Left and Right;

the Scripture of the Four-Directional Spirit Dhāraṇīs on the Causes and Conditions of Tombs; the Scripture of the Great Spirit Dhāraṇī of the Demon-Subduing Sealing Seal; the Scripture of the Great Spirit Dhāraṇī of Maṇirohaṇa;
the Scripture of the Spirit Dhāraṇī for Summoning the Dragon Kings of the Five Directions and Controlling Pestilence and Toxicity—from these seven thousand three hundred spirits.

From the "King" [section] down to this point, all contain consecration (*abhiṣeka*) characters; these are now collectively titled the *Mahābhiṣeka Sūtra*, the *Brahmadeva-daivajña Sūtra*, and the *Puguang Sūtra*.
These two fascicles, together with the *Bhaiṣajyaguru-saṃghāta*, constitute one collection. Combined with the preceding works, they form the *Abhiṣeka Sūtra* in twelve fascicles.
The *Seven Buddhas’ Consecrated Oil Ritual Mantras* is a different version, extracted from the *Seven Buddhas’ Divine Mantras*.

There are the *Jielü fa* (Method of Knotting Thread), the *Yichu benduolu nizhangju jing* (Sutra of Additional Chapters and Verses of the Original Dhāraṇī), the *Maniluandan shenshou anmo jing* (Sutra of the Mani-ratna King Deity’s Incantation for Massage)—

also known as the *Wuwang* (Without the Word "King")— the *Wulong zhudujing* (Sutra of the Five Dragon Incantations Against Poison), the *Quchi zhuojing* (Sutra of the Tooth Decay Incantation)— also called the *Zhouchuchi* (Incantation for Tooth Decay) or the *Zhouchi* (Incantation for Teeth)—

and the *Qifo anzhai shenzhujing* (Sutra of the Seven Buddhas’ Divine Incantation for Pacifying Dwellings), the *Anzhai jing* (Sutra on Pacifying Dwellings), and the *Sanguiwujie shen* (Divine Incantation of the Three Refuges and Five Precepts).
The *Wangming* (Names of Kings) in one fascicle; the *Da'an Fahu Jingmu You Shenzhou* (Dao’an’s Catalogue of Dharmarakṣa’s Scriptures with Divine Spells) in three fascicles.
Since these names of divine kings are already included within the [previous] collection, they are not considered lost translations. The above fifty-three scriptures [are thus accounted for].
In total, there are fifty-seven fascicles.
These are all works collected and recorded by the Tripiṭaka Master Sengyou in his new catalog as translations of unknown origin for which extant manuscript copies currently exist:
eight hundred and forty-six works.
In total, there are eight hundred and ninety-five fascicles.
Those outside of this have been scattered into various dynastic catalogs;
the remainder are appended here as lost sources from the Jin period and below.

6. Records of the Translation of Buddhist Scriptures by the Two Qin Dynasties, Former and Latter. Section Six. Since the Jin dynasty lost its governance and the empire fell into fragmentation, [the records follow].
The Xiongnu burned Luoyang, Yi, Chan, Jing, and Wei; it was not that they intended to make these their permanent capitals.
As the Master said: [the location of the capital is determined by the circumstances of the time].
The four barbarian tribes invade from all sides and the Central Kingdom is in decline;
is it not here that we see this?
Thus, Heaven has no second sun.
If one possesses the Way, one may be a ruler.
Among the sixteen states, the two Qin were the most powerful and attained success.
The Fu clan possessed the wealth of eight provinces.
The Emperor Yao’s intent lay in unifying the realm;
his heart was set upon the Triple Gem,
and his resolve was to propagate and protect the citadel of the Dharma.
Thus, he was sent ten thousand *li* to pursue the wind [of the Dharma], appearing as a peerless man among men;
he translated the great scriptures, which have flourished and gathered to this day.
In this way, the main pillars [of the Dharma] were thereby further strengthened and elevated.
His rectifying and saving efforts were never faltering;
his lofty reputation preceded him.
As for the records of the Qin Fu clan:
His ancestors were of the Pu-kan-di (Kun-mi) people of Wudu.
Taking advantage of the chaos caused by the two Zhao dynasties, they seized control of Guansi.
His descendants, seizing the opportunity, established themselves in succession and proclaimed themselves emperors.
The capital was named Chang'an in the state of Qin.
Reaching the third ruler, whose name was Jian and courtesy name Yonggu,
he was born with a divine light extending from heaven to earth.
The inscription on the back of the seal read "Cao Fu Chen" (Cao Fu, the subject).
Consequently, he changed the surname Pu to Fu.
Sixteen years after Fu Jian established his reign, [the dynasty fell].
At that time, the Grand Astrologer reported:
"A star of virtue has appeared in the celestial division corresponding to foreign lands;
there shall surely be a sage who will assist the Middle Kingdom."
One who obtains them shall become a king.
Fu Jian then dispatched General Lü Guang to seek Kumārajīva from the kingdom of Kucha,
and further sent General Fu Pi to attack and capture Xiangyang, where he captured the "Heaven-Filling" monk Shi Dao’an, Xi Zuochi, and others.
Once Jian had captured him,
he was delighted and said to the Vice President of the Secretariat,
Quan Yi: "I do not consider pearls and jade to be treasures."
"Rather, one should treasure the worthy and wise.
Now, with an army of one hundred thousand, we have captured but one person and a half at Xiangyang.
Yu Yi asked, "Who is he?"
Jian said,
"Master Dao'an alone is like a whole tooth;
Master Zaochi is but half."
Whenever he shared the same carriage with Fu Jian,
whenever the subject of the eastern expedition was raised,
Fu Jian would earnestly remonstrate, saying:
The land to the southeast is low-lying and its climate is miasmic;
it is not what is called the Central Kingdom.
Moreover, even the Sage Emperor Shun traveled there and did not return.
The First Emperor of Qin perished while on his expedition and did not return.
Now, to seek out land of the lowest grade with an army of a million men—
this I dare not even mention.
The rest is not recorded here.
From that time on, he inquired after [Kumārajīva’s] well-being and engaged in both governance and the exposition of Buddhist scriptures.
Thus, the General of the West obtained Kumārajīva.
Fajian had already passed away.
Six rulers held power for forty-four years.
Calculating by the sexagenary cycle, the first year of Fu Jian’s Huangshi era corresponds to the gengxu year, the sixth year of the Yonghe era of Emperor Mu of the Jin dynasty.
In the twenty-first year of the Jianyuan era,
which corresponded to the year of Yiyou, the tenth year of the Taiyuan era of Emperor Xiaowu of the Jin dynasty,
there were eight practitioners from both the Chinese and the non-Chinese peoples.
The collected records of the sūtras, precepts, treatises, catalogs, commentaries,
and biographies produced [therein] comprise forty works totaling two hundred and thirty-nine fascicles.
It was compiled as the record of Former Qin.

The *Dvibhāṣā-dvigrantha-śīla-sūtra-vinaya-maṇḍala-pāṭha* by the Fú-Qín śramaṇa Dharmatrata, two fascicles; the *Śīla-sūtra* by the śramaṇa Śrī Hui-cháng, one fascicle; the [text] by the śramaṇa Dharmapriya, one fascicle, five volumes; the [text] by the śramaṇa Kumārabodhi, one fascicle, two volumes; the *Sūtra-saṃgraha-śāstra* by the śramaṇa Dharmaratna, five works totaling one hundred fourteen fascicles; the [text] by the śramaṇa Saṃghabhūti, three works totaling twenty-seven fascicles; the *Abhidharma* by the śramaṇa Saṃghadeva, three works totaling sixty fascicles; and the annotated records of twenty-four works totaling twenty-eight fascicles by the śramaṇa Shi Dao-an, including the *Jiǔsòng-bhikṣu-śīla-sūtra*, the *Bhikṣuṇī-śikṣamāṇā-vidhi*, and the *Vinaya-maṇḍala-pāṭha*. These were obtained from the kingdom of Kucha by Seng-chún; Fo-nian held the original text while translating the language, and Hui-xiang acted as the scribe. This is recorded in the *Bǎochàng-lù*; the above comprises two groups of works.
Combined in two fascicles.
During the reign of Emperor Jianwen of the Jin dynasty,
the Tripitaka Master and Vinaya Master Dharmamitra from the Western Regions [translated this].
The Qin term for this is *Fahui*.
It was translated at Chang’an by Zhu Fonian and others,
with Huixiang receiving the dictation.
The Bhikṣuṇī Mahā-śīla-sūtra, one fascicle.
Translated in Chang’an during the reign of Emperor Jianwen of the Jin dynasty by the Vinaya Master Śramaṇa Huichang, together with Dharmatrata, Zhu Fonian, and others.
The catalog does not record the name of the school from which it was translated;
it should likely be the *Śāriputra-abhidharma-śāstra* (or *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya-mātṛkā*).

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* was translated in the eighteenth year of the Jianyuan era, or perhaps in seven fascicles as seen in Sengrui’s *Sanqin lu*. Thus, this single scripture consists of five fascicles.
During the reign of Emperor Xiaowu of the Jin dynasty,
there was the Tripiṭaka Master from India,
the śramaṇa Dharmapriya (translated into Chinese as Fà'ài).
The *Dapin* (Large Chapter) Sanskrit manuscript was translated into the Qin language by Zhu Fonian.
It is also called the *Chang'an Pin* (Chapter on Chang’an), named after its place of origin;
it is an excerpt from a foreign scripture.
The *Sūtra on Extracts from the Four Āgamas*, translated in the fourteenth year of the Jianyuan era. This one sūtra, in two fascicles,
was produced during the reign of Emperor Xiaowu of the Jin dynasty by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārabuddhi, a śramaṇa from the Western Regions.
The Qin term for "child-enlightenment" (tóngjué) was translated at a monastery in Ye.
Buddhabhadra held the Sanskrit manuscript.
Translated into the Qin language by Zhu Fonian, Fo Nian, Hu, and others;
received in writing by the śramaṇas Sengdao, Tanjiu, Sengrui, and others.
The *Madhyama Āgama* in fifty-nine fascicles was produced in the twenty-first year of the Jianyuan era; this is the first translation by Zhu [Fonian].
Hui-nian served as the scribe for the *Ekottarika Āgama* in fifty fascicles, which was transcribed from the *Miscellaneous Records of the Jin Dynasty* by Zhu Daozu.

On the first day of the fourth month in the twentieth year of the Jianyuan era, it was translated for Zhao Ye, the Protector of Wuwei of the Qin, with Hui-song serving as the oral reciter and Hui-nian as the scribe.
This is recorded in Seng Rui’s *Biographies of the Two Qin* and Yu’s *Chang Record*, both of which include the *Aśoka-avadāna*.

The *Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of the Crown Prince’s Blinding of His Eyes* (also known as the *Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of Prince Dharmavardhana’s Blinding of His Eyes*) was translated by Yao Min, the Grand Chancellor, at the city of Anding on the eighth day of the sixth month in the second year of the Jianchu era.

One copy [of the catalog] lacks the character "sūtra" (*jing*). This should be included among the later works; following the majority, it is appended here. It is part of the collection of Saṃgharakṣa. II.
Compiled seven hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa by Saṃgharakṣa; recorded in the Jianchang lu (Record of Manifested Chants).
The *Sanfadu* (Three Dharma Degrees) in two fascicles differs slightly from the version translated during the Jin dynasty by Saṃghadeva. The above comprises five works.
In one hundred and fourteen fascicles.
During the reign of Emperor Xiaowu of the Jin dynasty,
the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmalan-di from the country of Tukhāra [translated this].
In the language of Qin, this means "Dharma-joy.
Arriving in Chang'an at the beginning of the Jianyuan era,
he recited the Sanskrit original of the *Caturāgama* and orally transmitted it.
Zhu Fonian transcribed it into Sanskrit.
In the twentieth year [of the reign], during the rule of Fu Jian,
it was translated and produced in fifty-nine fascicles.
At that time, it fell during the era of慕容冲 (Murong Chong).
When Yao Chang rebelled, the Guanzhong region was in perilous turmoil;
the full details have not yet been related.
Nandiśa departed to the west and was never heard of again;
his propagation of the Dharma encountered many hardships,
yet he applied himself with diligence whenever the opportunity arose.

Worthy of reverence and yet pitiable. The *Vasumitra-sūtra* in ten fascicles was translated in the twentieth year of the Jianyuan era; some say it is the *Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra*. The *Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra* in fourteen fascicles (or eleven fascicles) was translated in the nineteenth year of the Jianyuan era. The *Saṃgharakṣa-saṃgraha-sūtra* in three fascicles was translated on the thirtieth day of the eleventh month in the twentieth year of the Jianyuan era. These are the three works mentioned above.
In twenty-seven fascicles.
During the reign of Emperor Xiaowu of the Jin dynasty,
the Tripiṭaka Master Saṃghabhūti from Kaśmīra [translated this].
In the language of Qin, it is called Zhongxian (Manifestation of the Multitude).
The old recitation of the Brahmanic original was extremely proficient and fluent;
Nanti previously transcribed it into Sanskrit script.

Translated by the Buddhist monk Fotu-luocha (Buddharakṣa), with the scribes Śramaṇa Huīsōng, Zhìmǐn, and the Court Secretary Váo Wényè recording it into the language of Qín. The *Abhidharma-aṣṭagrantha* in thirty fascicles was produced in the nineteenth year of the Jiànyuán era;

it is also titled the *Kātyāyanīya-abhidharma*. Translated by the Śramaṇa Fóniàn, with the scribes Śramaṇa Huílì and Sēngmào recording it. More than three hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the Arhat Kātyāyana [compiled this work]. It consists of either twenty fascicles or sixteen fascicles of the *Abhidharmahṛdaya*. It was produced in Luoyang at the end of the Jiànyuán era; see the *Sēngruì Record* and the *Two Qín Records*. The *Vibhāṣā-abhidharma* in fourteen fascicles is also called the *Guǎngshuō* (Extensive Explanation); it likewise appeared in Luoyang; see the *Two Qín Records*. The above three sections comprise sixty fascicles.
The Tripiṭaka Master Saṃghadeva from Kaśmīra—
also called T’i-ho—
this is likely merely a difference between the "Spring" and "Autumn" dialects of the Sanskrit language.
In the language of Qin, he was called Zhòngtiān (Zhongtian).
During the Jianyuan era of Emperor Jianwen of the Jin dynasty, specifically within the Jianyuan reign of the Fu clan,
he entered Chang’an to propagate and spread the Dharma teachings.
Initially, Saṃghabhūti brought forth [the texts],
which were translated by Vasumitra and Dharmanandin; in the interim,
two *śāstras* and the *Tri-dharmaka-śāstra*, etc., were added.
At that time, as the region was beset by military turmoil,
the translation was not yet complete or detailed.
Dao’an passed away.
He did not have the opportunity to correct this.
Later, when the Shandong region was pacified,
Deva, together with Dao’an’s fellow student Shi Fahe, both traveled to Luoyang.
For four or five years, he studied and lectured on the aforementioned scriptures.
Having resided in China for some time,
he became thoroughly proficient in the language of Qin.
Only then did he realize that the earlier translations contained many errors and omissions.
Depressed by the fact that this rarely encountered Dharma had been published without being perfected,
Fǎhé then further entreated Guṇabhadra to retranslate the previous scriptures.
After such a short time,
the Buddhist affairs under Yao Xing became very flourishing,
and Faho returned to the West.
Because Deva crossed southward [to India],
there are minor discrepancies between the earlier and later versions of the original text.

The *Prajñāpāramitā-saṃśaya-vibhaṅga* (Brief Analysis of Doubts regarding Prajñā), two fascicles; the *Mahādvādaśamukha-śāstra-ṭīkā* (Commentary on the Great Twelve Gates), two fascicles; the *Skandhadhātvāyatana-ṭīkā* (Commentary on the Aggregates, Elements, and Bases), two fascicles; the *Dharmarakṣa-dūṣaṇa-pratyuttara* (Response to Dharmarakṣa’s Difficulties), one fascicle; the *Siyu-zhi* (Record of the Western Regions), one fascicle; and the *Zongli-zhongjing-mulu* (Comprehensive Catalogue of All Sutras). These constitute twenty-four items in total.
It consists of twenty-eight fascicles and was compiled by the former Qin śramaṇa Shi Dao’an during the Taiyuan era of Emperor Xiaowu of the Jin dynasty.
Anben was a native of Fuliou in Changshan.
His secular surname was Wei;
his family had been distinguished scholars for generations.
Having lost his protective shelter at an early age,
he was raised by his maternal uncle, Mr. Kong.
At the age of seven,
he was able to recite from memory after reading a text only once;
his neighbors marveled at this extraordinary talent.
At the age of twelve, he left home to become a monk.
Although his spiritual nature was sharp and quick-witted,
his physical appearance was so extremely coarse that he was not held in high regard by his teacher.
He performed manual labor and service without ever showing a trace of resentment.
Possessing a sincere nature and diligent in his practice, he never failed in his observance of the fasts and precepts.
Only after several years did he finally request the scriptures from his teacher.
The Master possessed one fascicle of the *Bianyi jing*,
comprising approximately five thousand words.
Dao’an took this scripture with him when he entered the fields.
Taking advantage of a break from his breath-counting meditation,
he went to read it; at dusk, he returned the scripture to his teacher and sought for others.
The Master said,
"Yesterday you had not yet read the sutra;
why do you seek it again today?"
Ananda replied,
"I have finished reciting it.
Although the Master marveled at this, he did not yet believe him.
He further brought with him one fascicle of the Chengju guangming jing (Sūtra of the Perfectly Endowed Radiance),
comprising slightly less than ten thousand words,
carrying it just as he had done previously.
In the evening, he returned to his teacher.
The teacher held up the scripture and reviewed it with him;
there was not a single character that did not match.
The Master was greatly astonished and marveled at this extraordinary feat.
Later, he conferred the full precepts upon him and allowed him to travel freely to study.
This occurred during the reigns of Emperors Huai and Min of the Jin dynasty.
