the sūtras produced and those of unknown translators are as indicated in the separate sections.
I shall not list them exhaustively here.
First is the *Vaipulya Ākāśagarbha-sūtra* in eight fascicles—also known as the *Ākāśagarbha-paripṛcchā-sūtra*—or in five fascicles;
this second edition is the same text as the *Rāmaka* translated by Fa-xian, as noted in the *Jin zalu*. It is excerpted from the *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra*.
The second translation of the *Dàosú Yèjīng* (Sutra on the Layman Daoxu) differs slightly from that translated by Zhi Qian; one fascicle follows this later example.

The second translation of the *Bàijīng* (Sutra of Paiśunya) differs from the translation by Zhi Qian of the Wu kingdom. The *Tàizǐ Xū dà ná jīng* (Sutra of Prince Viśvantara) was produced at Jiangling Temple with the brush of Yu Shuang, as seen in the *Shìxīng Bǎochàng Lù*;
it should be classified under the Jin period, though it is appended here according to the person [Yu Shuang] who belonged to the Qin. The *Shǎn zǐ jīng* (Sutra of Śyāma). One fascicle.

The *Xiàoshǎn jīng* (1), the *Púsà shǎn jīng* (1), the *Fóshuō shǎn jīng* (1), the *Shǎnběn jīng* (1), and the *Xiàozǐ yīn jīng* (1)—these six titles constitute the second edition, which differs slightly from the version translated by Kumārajīva;
it is recorded in the *Shìxīng lù*. The *Wúyájì chífǎmén jīng* (1) is also called the *Wújì jīng*;
it is recorded in the *Shìxīng lù*. It is also known as the *Jīnguāngshǒu*.
The *Sūtra on the Questions of the Woman* (*Nüsuowen jing*), also known as the *Sūtra on the Elimination of Fearful Calamities* (*Chukong zaihuang jing*), second;
translated during the Wei dynasty by Bai Yan, differing slightly from other versions, as seen in the *Shixing baochang lu* and the *Erlu*. The *Furen yugu jing*, as seen in the *Shixing lu*.
The *Ānwen shifo jixiong jing*, also titled the *Ānwen fenhui jing*; one fascicle, the *Fenhui jing*, together with the disciple Mandā.

Jīvyaka’s *Account of the Sūtras* records that these nine sūtras share the same origin as seen in the *Shixing Lu* (Record of Shixing). The *Fashang Lu* (Record of Fashang) states they were produced from the *Bie lu* (Separate Record):

1. *The Sūtra on the Place of Birth of Bodhisattvas*; 2. *The Sūtra on the Questions of Mahākāśyapa*, seen in the *Zhao Lu* (Record of Zhao), though its chronological relation to the preceding [text] is unknown;

3. *The Sūtra on the Expulsion of People by Zhao*, appended to the Western Qin period as seen in the *Shixing Lu*; 4. *The Sūtra of the Virtuous Head*, also known as the *Sūtra of the Lady Virtuous Head*, seen in the [same record].

The *Shixing lu* (Record of Shixing) contains the second excerpt of the *Jiannanjing* (Sūtra on Resolving Difficulties) translated by Dharma-kṣema (Tong Kashyapa), which is identical to the *Kāśyapa-sūtra* translated by Kumārajīva;
it was recorded by Yu Shuang and appears in the *Zongbao* of Prince Shixing. It is also included in the four records compiled by Zhi Min-du.

Furthermore, the *Guanfojing* (Sūtra on Contemplating the Buddha) is largely the same as, though slightly different from, the separately translated *Mahākātyāyanasūtra*; this is seen in the *Shixing lu*. Also included is the *Benjing of the Seven Daughters*.
The second, translated by Zhi Qian, is largely the same as the previous with slight differences;

it is also titled the *Nüben Xinming Jing* (Sūtra on the Woman’s Fundamental Mind) or the *Luojiamojing* (Sūtra of Rāgamati), in three fascicles, and is seen in the Tang Records. Thus, there are fifteen sūtras in total.
In twenty-two fascicles.
During the reign of Emperor Xiaowu of the Jin dynasty,
the śramaṇa Shengjian [translated it] in the kingdom of Henan.
Translated by Qifu Qiangui;
some call him Master Jian,
others call him Fajian.
It is not clear which of these is correct;
therefore, I have listed them all for reference.
I have verified this by consulting various catalogs.
One scripture was found at Jiangling;
one scripture appeared in the Zhao lu;
ten scriptures appear in the Shixing lu.
The *Shixing jian nan lu* (Record of Southern Dynasties Compiled by Shixing) or the *Zhu Daozu jin shi za lu* (Miscellaneous Record of the Jin Dynasty by Zhu Daozu).
Either the *Dulu* (General Catalog) by Zhi Mindu,
or that of Wang Zong,
or that of Baochang.
Examining various catalogs,
it appears that this person traveled to many places and produced scriptures wherever he went.
Since there is no fixed location for this entry and it is unknown to which dynastic record it should be appended for verification,
I have now followed the previous general inclusion and recorded it in the *Shi-qi-fu Xi-Qin Shilu* (Record of the Western Qin of the Qifu clan).

The Hu-ben (Hu-language) scriptures consist of four fascicles, appearing to have been produced in Chang’an. These include the *Śarvasena-rāja-sūtra*, the *Ādarśa-samādhi-sūtra* (also rendered as the *Ādatta-xianwang-jing*), the *Bhadra-pratideśanā-sūtra*, the *Śrāmaṇera-sūtra*, the *Vaipulya-viniścaya-sūtra*, and the *Dvāvastu-bhikṣu-sūtra*. Altogether, there are eight works.
In eleven volumes in total,
these are all from the *Chusanzangjilu* (Collection of Records for the Tripitaka) compiled by the śramaṇa Sengyou,
based on the records of Shi Dao’an.
The *Guanzhong yijing* (Various Scriptures from Guanzhong) is now appended to the *Sanqin lu* (Record of the Three Qin),
and is collectively categorized as being of unknown translation period.

9. Catalogue of Buddhist Scriptures Translated during the Northern Liang under the Juqu Clan. Preface to the Ninth Catalogue of Buddhist Scriptures Translated during the Northern Liang under the Juqu Clan:
Juqu Mengxun was a Hu from Lushui in Linong.
He served as the Left Grand Official (*zuo da*) for the Northern Xiongnu;
the Juché were his clan name.
He relied upon the foundation established by his former occupation under Former Liang.
In the fifth year of Long’an during the reign of Emperor An of the Jin dynasty, the year being Xinchou,
he styled himself Northern Liang and changed the era name to Chengqian.
In the twelfth year,
he changed the era name from Guzang to Xuanshi and encountered the Dharma Master Dharmakṣema.
The translation of the great scriptures spread widely the Buddha-dharma;
this was precisely during the early reign of Emperor Wu of the Song dynasty.
At first, Sengxun offered repentance with a reverence that was peerless and difficult to equal.
When the Northern Wei heard that Sengxian’s spiritual arts were about to spread, they sent an envoy to invite him to the east.
Sengxun feared that Sengxian might devise a scheme for the Wei or,
conversely, plot against them from the west.
He remained obstinate and refused permission.
Fǎzhì, realizing he must yield to his master's feelings, took his leave and headed west to seek out the scriptures.
Furthermore, he knew that the time for his karmic retribution was approaching.
Feigning the practice of mediation, he repeatedly used this as a pretext to conclude his affairs.
Once these actions were completed,
Daoxun, out of resentment, ordered an assassin to kill Sengxian on the road.
An ancient proverb says:
"When those who know one meet, misfortune follows if it was not auspicious.
These words are worthy of being recorded.
Later, Xun’s conduct became tyrannical, and his own heart felt remorse for his deeds.
During the day, he saw a ghost who stabbed him with a sword, and he subsequently perished.
These two rulers [reigned] for forty-three years.
He was conquered by the Wei dynasty.
In total, nine monastics and laypeople translated scriptures;
the works produced numbered thirty-two fascicles.
Two hundred and sixty-six fascicles;
these are scriptures of lost translators,
recorded as belonging to the Northern Liang period.
The *Jūqú Bèiliáng Shāmén Shì Dàogōng* [translation of] twelve fascicles of sūtras; the *Shāmén Shì Fǎzhòng* [translation of] one work in four fascicles of sūtras;
the *Shāmén Sēngqiátuó* [translation of] one work in two fascicles of sūtras;
the *Shāmén Tánwǔchèn* [translation of] twenty-four works totaling one hundred and fifty-one fascicles of sūtras; and the *Jiètán Wén* (Text on the Precept Platform) by Jūqú Ānyáng Hóu.
One work by Jing-sheng: two fascicles. One work by the śramaṇa Buddhabhadra on the Dharma of Chan:
sixty fascicles. One work by the śramaṇa Shi Zhimeng on Abhidharma: twenty fascicles. One work by the śramaṇa Shi Tanyue on Sūtras:
fifteen fascicles. One work by the śramaṇa Shi Daotai on Sūtras: two fascicles. Five works of various Sūtras translated by unknown translators: one [set].

The *Buddhanāmasūtra* in seventeen fascicles; the *Karunāpuṇḍarīkasūtra* in ten fascicles, which appears in ancient catalogs and seems to have been translated earlier, though Gong subsequently revised it;
and the *Ratnarāśisūtra* in two fascicles, as recorded in Zhu Daozu’s *Hexi lu*. These comprise the two aforementioned works.
Combined into twelve fascicles.
During the reign of Emperor An of the Jin dynasty,
the śramaṇa Shi Daogong [compiled this].
In Zhangye, he appeared for the Hexi Wang (King of the West) family of Juqu.
He produced the *Mahāvaipulya-dāntra-dhāraṇī-sūtra* in four fascicles, also known as the *Vaipulya-dhāraṇī-sūtra*. This was during the reign of Emperor An of the Jin dynasty.
The śramaṇa Shi Fazhong of Gaochang County translated [this work] at Zhangye for Juqu, the King of Hexi.
This is recorded in Zhu Daozu’s *Miscellaneous Records of the Jin Dynasty*.

The *Huishang pusa wen dashanquan jing* (Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Huishang’s Inquiry on Great Skillful Means), two fascicles; the second edition, identical to the translation by Dharmarakṣa known as the *Shanquan fangbian jing*. It is recorded in the *Shixing lu*; it has five titles in total: *Dashanquan jing*, *Dacheng fangbian jing*, and *Huishang pusa jing*. All these versions are identical to the one above, produced during the reign of Emperor An of the Jin dynasty.
The śramaṇa Saṃghadatta from the Western Regions—
*liang* (Guanzhong) language:
"Abounding in Virtue"— translated for the Hechi King Juqu [Mendangxun] at Zhangye.
Record of the Vision of Dharmottara.
The Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra consists of forty fascicles; it was translated at Guzang beginning in the third year of Xuanshi and completed in the tenth year.
This sūtra originally contained thirty-five thousand gāthās, amounting to one million words in the Liang region; now only ten thousand or so gāthās remain. (3)
Regarding the initial appearance of the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra* in one fascicle during the Western Jin dynasty, the Liang dynasty catalog records it as having been produced twice:

once in twenty-seven fascicles by the Han translators, and once in thirty fascicles by Kumārajīva. These versions differ slightly in their breadth and brevity, appearing sometimes as twenty-nine or thirty-two fascicles.
Because the original was not yet finalized when it was first transcribed, the resulting manuscripts differed; now, upon re-examining the translations, [the discrepancies] are verified.
The *Jianduzu lu* (Record of the Patriarchs of the Path) states that the ten-fascicle *Beihua jing* (Sutra of the Compassionate Flower) was the second appearance [of this text].

Furthermore, the *Hexilu* (Record of Hexi) and ancient records state that this [translation] by Dao-gong had already appeared, though the dates differ; these were both produced during the Liang period.

It is suspected that because the earlier translation was not yet refined, there were two different versions, which appear to be a re-translation. This is actually the ten-fascicle *Pusa dizhi jing* (Bodhisattva-bhūmi-saṃgraha-sūtra), also known as...
The *Lun* (Treatise) in eight fascicles; the *Jian Dao Zu He Xi Lu* (Record of the Ancestors of the Path Compiled at Hexi);

the *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra* in ten fascicles, transcribed by the śramaṇa Daotai on the twenty-second day of the second month of the first year of the Yongxuan era, when over five hundred monastics and laypeople gathered within the city of Liang to hear it together;
the *Bodhisattva-śīla Sūtra* in six fascicles, the number of fascicles varying between six and eight; and the *Mahāvaipulya Mahāmegha Sūtra* in eight fascicles.
The *Sūtra in Six Volumes* (one fascicle), the *Vaipulya Mahāmegha Asaṃjñika*, the *Mahāmegha Asaṃjñika*, and the *Mahāmegha Guhyagarbha* were produced at the Neiyuan Temple in Liang.
They appear in the two Qi Records and the Li Kuò Record.

Furthermore, the Wu Record also contains the *Ākāśagarbha Bodhisattva Sūtra* in five fascicles, the second production of which was translated by Śrīghoṣa during the Later Qin as the *Vaipulyarāja Ākāśagarbha*.
The *Kongzang jing* (Sūtra of the Treasury of Emptiness) was translated together with the five-fascicle *Daji fo benxing jing* (Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra on the Original Acts of the Buddha);

this is the second appearance. The *Jinguangming jing* (Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra) in four fascicles was the first appearance; it consists of eighteen chapters. The *Hai longwang jing* (Sūtra of the Dragon King Sāgara) in four fascicles was translated in the seventh year of the Xuanshi era;
this is the second translation, which is the same text as that produced by Dharmarakṣa. These are recorded in the *Hexilu* (Record of the West River) by Jian Daozu.
The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* in four fascicles; the *Śraddhābalādhānāvatāramudrā Sūtra* (also known as the *Sujātā Sūtra*) in two fascicles;
the *Yi wéidào jīng* (Sūtra on Doubting the Unconditioned Path) in two fascicles—Sengyou states this is suspected to be the *Śrīmālādevī Sūtra*;
the *Śrīmālādevī Siṃhanāda Eka-yāna Mahā-upāya Sūtra* in one fascicle; and the *Rāmāgrasūtra* in one fascicle, which is a second edition produced during the Wei dynasty by An Faxian.
The *Sūtra of the Son of Heaven Susīma* exists in three fascicles with varying degrees of detail; it is recorded in the *Wu Lu*. It is also said that Master Kumārajīva translated it twice.
The *Sūtra on a Layman Inviting Monks as a Field of Merit* is found in the *Bie Lu*.

Sengyou states that the *Sūtra of King Mandhātṛ*, the *Sūtra of the Jewel of Merit*, the *Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Single-Ray*, the *Sūtra of the Woman in the Womb Listening to the Dharma*, and the *Sūtra of the Unadorned Woman Determining Sin and Merit* are all one and the same text.
The second section from the *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra-mūla* (Bodhisattvabhūmi-śīlaparivarta), containing the text for the Bodhisattva Precept Platform and the text for the Upāsaka Platform,
as seen in the *Changlu*. The above twenty-four works comprise one hundred and fifty-one fascicles in total.
During the reign of Emperor An of the Jin dynasty,
there was the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmakṣema from the kingdom of Central India;
he was also called Wu-chan.
Liangyan Fa-feng brought the first ten fascicles of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* along with the Bodhisattva Precepts and other texts.
Upon arriving at Guzang, he stayed at the guest house.
Fearing he might lose the original manuscript of the sutra, he tucked it under his pillow and went to sleep.
During the night, someone pulled the *Chen* (the manuscript) down to the ground.
Startled awake, he thought it was a thief.
After three such nights had passed,
a voice was heard from the air, saying:
"This is the treasury of liberation of the Tathāgata."
"What is this for? The seer then felt ashamed and enlightened;
he moved to a high, secluded place, and indeed, a thief arrived.
Throughout the night, he repeatedly attempted to lift it but could not succeed.
At dawn, when Baoyu held it up, he did not consider it heavy.
The thief said, "The Sage has come," and they all came forward to prostrate themselves and offer their thanks.
Juqu Mengxun, who had usurped the territory of Liang and styled himself King of Hexi,
heard of the name of Chen De and summoned him for an audience. Upon meeting him face-to-face,
they conversed, and he treated him with great courtesy and generosity.
He further requested that [the text] be proclaimed and translated.
The eminent śramaṇa Huìsōng from the territory of Liáng personally received the oral transmission and acted as scribe.
Several hundred monastics and laypeople from Xīzhōu were also present.
Delightedly beholding Ming’s ability to pose questions and challenges with ease and mastery,
Śīkṣānanda resolved doubts and cleared away obstructions with a clarity of discernment like flowing water;
he subsequently produced various sūtras and other texts from the Jewel Monastery (Ratnavihāra).
It comprises more than six hundred thousand words,
constituting one-third of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*. From beginning to end,
throughout its various sections and transitions, it has been traced and sought out in its entirety.
Over the course of eight years,
it was translated on three occasions before finally reaching completion.
Although it consists of forty fascicles,
much is still lacking;
I hope that the Dharma King will cause it all to be complete.
Upon a single glance, the Perfect Teaching flourished once more! The translation of the scriptures was completed by Liang [Dharmakṣema].

During the second year of the Yongchu era of Emperor Wu of the Song dynasty, there were two fascicles of the *Essential Explanation of the Methods of Dhyāna* (Chánfǎ yàojiě), translated during the reign of Emperor An of the Jin dynasty.
Mengsun’s younger cousin, Jingsheng, Marquis of Anyang,
was a man of broad learning who had perused both the secular histories and the classics.
Because he propagated the scriptures through the medium of prophetic texts (*chan*), he subsequently applied his mind to the Buddhist canon (*neidian*).
He upheld the five precepts and restrained the six sense faculties.
He requested Dharmakṣema to translate the scriptures, which he was then able to recite fluently.
He traveled westward as far as Khotan.
He consulted on the meaning of the Way with the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhasena from India—
“Buddha-jiang” (佛將) in the Liang language.
This man of genius was so intelligent that he could recite fifty million verses of sutras and was thoroughly proficient in the methods of dhyāna; therefore,
the various kingdoms of the Western Regions hailed him as a "Lion among Men."
An-yang studied the essentials of Chan and various techniques;
he recited the Sanskrit texts orally and,
upon returning to Liangzhou, translated them for circulation and dissemination.
Later, he crossed the Yangtze River to the south;
the details of this are found in his separate biography.
*Abhidharma-vibhāṣā*, sixty fascicles. This was compiled more than six hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
Compiled by five hundred disciples of the Arhat Kātyāyana;
recorded in the *Baocang lu* (Record of the Precious Song) during the reign of Emperor Wen of the Song dynasty.
The śramaṇa from the Western Regions,
Buddhabhadra— also called Buddha;
in the language of Liang, this means "Awakening Armor."
In the Xianyu Palace Temple within Liangcheng,
during the fifth year of the Chenghe era, it was translated by Sunzi Qian,
with the śramaṇa Daotai acting as the scribe.
Huìsōng and Dàolǎng, together with more than three hundred monks of renowned virtue,
examined and corrected the textual meanings for two full cycles before finally completing the work;
it comprised one hundred fascicles in total.
The śramaṇa Daotíng composed this preface during the period when the Wei dynasty destroyed Liang;
at that time, the scriptures and Dharma were burned, resulting in the loss of thirty scrolls.
To this day, there should be sixty scrolls in total.
However, the *Wangzong lu* (Record of the Royal Lineage) states it is one hundred;
this is based on the original text itself.
Today, there are one hundred and nine fascicles currently in circulation;
these must have been divided by later people in recent times.
The *Parinirvāṇa Sūtra* in twenty fascicles [was translated] during the reign of Emperor Wen of the Song dynasty.
The śramaṇa Shi Zhimeng of Yongzhou traveled through the Western Regions in search of rare scriptures,
bringing back Sanskrit manuscripts from the kingdom of India.
The *Dàojīng* was translated at Yumen in Liangzhou.
In the fourteenth year of the Yuanjia era, it circulated to the capital of Yangdu.
This is recorded in the *Song Qi Lu* (Records of the Song and Qi Dynasties) alongside the account of Faxian.
The *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish*, fifteen fascicles. During the era of Emperor Wen of the Song dynasty,
the śramaṇa from Liangzhou, Shi Tanjue— also known as Huijue— [translated this].
Sengwei obtained the Sanskrit original of this sūtra in Khotan.
It was translated at Tian’an Temple in the kingdom of Gaochang during the twenty-second year of the Yuanjia era.
According to the *Records of the Song and Qi Dynasties* (*Song Qi Lu*), there are five works:

the *Great Sūtra on Forbearance* in ten fascicles; the *Sūtra of Non-retrogression* in four fascicles—also known as the *Sūtra of the Vajra-samādhi of the Non-retrogressive Dharma-wheel* or the *Sūtra of the Golden Wheel King*; and the *Names of the Five Hundred Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa*. These constitute the right-hand group of five works.
In seventeen fascicles in total,
this is the new compilation by the śramaṇa Sengyou of the various scriptures from the Liang region by Shi Daoan.
I have now appended these to the catalog of the Liang dynasty as works of unknown translators,
so that one may know whether they were translated during that era, and identify where the extant versions differ in terms of the number of fascicles or other details.
*The Treatise on Entering the Mahāyāna*, two fascicles, composed by Bodhisattva Sthiramati.
This single work was translated during the Northern Liang period by Shi Daotai;
it is recorded in the Old Tang Catalogue.
The Great Tang Catalogue of Buddhist Scriptures, Volume Three;
The Great Tang Catalogue of Buddhist Scriptures, Volume Four,
compiled by Shi [Daoxuan] of Ximing Monastery in the Capital.

The *Xiànzài Fómíng Jīng* (Sūtra of the Names of Buddhas Present Now) in three fascicles was translated at Jingzhou for Liu Yixuan, Prince of Nanqiao, on the twenty-seventh day of the first month in the twenty-ninth year of the Yuanjia era;
it is also titled *Huafu Xiànzài Fómíng*. It is recorded in the Shixing and Gao [records].
The *Sengzhuan pusa xing fangbian shentong bianhua jing* (Biographies of Monks: Sūtra on the Bodhisattva’s Practice of Expedient Means and Supernatural Transformations), three fascicles;

recorded in Li Kuò’s catalogue. The *Jingdu sanmei jing* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of Pure Deliverance), three fascicles; recorded in Li Kuò’s catalogue. The *Xiangxu jietuo liao yi jing* (Sūtra on the Definitive Meaning of Continuous Liberation), two fascicles;
produced at Dong’an Temple; recorded in the catalogues of Daohui, Sengyou, Li Kuò, and Fashang. The *Dafagujing* (Great Dharma Drum Sūtra), two fascicles.
The *Āraṇyaka-śamatha-vipaśyanā-sūtra* in two fascicles, translated at Dong’an Temple by Daohui; recorded in the catalogs of Sengyou, Li Kuò, and other supplementary records.
The *Śrīmālā-siṃhanāda-ekayāna-mahā-upāya-sūtra* in one fascicle, produced at Danyang Commandery;
the transmission of Baoyun was seen by Daohui, Sengyou, Li Kuò, and others in their records. The *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra*.
Translated during the Xiaojian era; the eighth translation is seen in Daohui’s *Song Qi Lu*. Translated by Saṃghavarman, Zhi Qian, Bo Yan, Dharmarakṣa, Kumārajīva, Dharmapāla, Ratnamegha, and others.
It is largely the same [as the previous versions], though with differences in brevity and detail.
The *Sūtra on Piṇḍola-Bharadvāja Preaching the Dharma to King Udayana* and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* were produced at Xin Temple in the first year of the Xiaojian era.

The second translation, which either lacks the character "ban" (般) or is nearly identical to the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* produced by Dharmarakṣa, is found in the *Jiandouhui* (見道惠) catalog of the Song and Qi dynasties.
It states that the *Sūtra of the Eight Auspicious Ones* was translated at Jingzhou for the Minister of Works, Prince Nanqiao, in the twenty-ninth year of the Yuanjia era.
This second production differs slightly from the version produced by Zhi Qian of Wu. According to the catalogs of Sengyou and Daochang, it is the *Aśoka-sūtra*.
*Wangjing houli* (One fascicle), translated at Xin Temple in Jingzhou; recorded in the *Wulu*. *Wuliang chimen jing* (Recorded in the *Wulu*).
*Sanjie jing* (Recorded in the *Bielu*). *Shisi jing* (Recorded in the *Bielu*). *Diyier shiyou jing* (Second fascicle);
its publication differs slightly from the version translated by Kālodaka of the Jin dynasty; recorded in the *Jiulu*. *Dishier toutuo* (Twelve Dhūtas).
The *Sūtra on the Three Causes and Conditions*, the *Sūtra on the Seven Places and Three Contemplations in Different Locations* (the second edition of the *Saṃyukta Āgama*,
or perhaps lacking the words "in different locations"), the *Sūtra on Eleven Perceptions and Mindfulness of the Tathāgata* (or the *Twelve Chapters on Contemplating Birth and Death*),

the *Sūtra on the Ten Retributions*, the *Sūtra on the Three Compendiums in Brief*, the *Sūtra on the Retribution of Sin and Merit*, the *Sūtra on the Six Fasts and Eight Precepts*, and the *Sūtra on the Ten [Precepts]*.
The *Dhūta-sūtra*; the *Caturmahāpuruṣa-prādurbhāva-sūtra* (from the fourth chapter of the *Saṃyukta Āgama*); the *Śikṣāpada-sūtra*;

the *Śreṇika-bhrātṛ-sūtra* (also known as the *Śreṇika-mātula-pautra-sūtra*); the *Jātaka-sūtra*; the *Nāgasena-sūtra* (an alternative version appearing as the *Sūryodana-sūtra*, also called the *Vatsarāja-amātya-sūtra*);
the *Jātaka-sūtra*; the *Vimāla-sūtra*; the *Śuka-sūtra*; and [texts] from the *Madhyama Āgama*.
The Sūtra on Debt as an Ox; the Sūtra on Birth; the Nālada Sūtra; the Sūtra on Birth (second); the Sūtra on the Two Brahmins; the Sūtra on the Arising of the Udānavarga; the Sūtra on Śreṇika;
the Sūtra on the Original Account of Śrona; the Sūtra on Araṇa; the Sūtra on the Old Mother; the Sūtra on Jyotiṣka; the Sūtra on Aśvajit; the Sūtra on the Great Meaning;
the Sūtra on Maudgalyāyana Subduing the Dragon King; and the Sūtra on Ānanda Seeing a Performer Weep for Impermanence.
The *Śāriputra-ādi-bhikṣu-kāyasaṃsākṣāt-kriyā-sūtra*, the *Buddha-gamana-cāṣpa-glāna-pariṣvāsa-sūtra*,
the *Panthaka-bhikṣu-adhyeṣaṇā-sūtra* (also known as the *Buddha-ājñā-ananda-yāti-jyeṣṭha-seṭṭhi-sūtra*),
the *Maudgalyāyana-bhrātṛ-dāna-tatkṣaṇa-pratyupakāra-ākāṅkṣā-sūtra*, the *Śāriputra-parinirvāṇa-sūtra*, the *Jātaka-sūtra*, and the *Mahākāśyapa-sūtra*.
The Sūtra on Saving the Poor Mother; The Sūtra on Aniruddha’s Seven Recollections; The Sūtra of the Miscellaneous Collection; The Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha;
The Sūtra of the Bodhisattva’s Rebuke of Desire; The Second Edition of the Amitābha Sūtra; The Sūtra on the Non-Activity of All Dharmas;
The Sūtra of the Poor Son Sudāna; [These titles] appear in Li Kuò’s Catalogue; The Sūtra of the Immeasurable Meanings appears in Li Kuò’s Catalogue; The Sūtra on Killing a Dragon to Save a Nation.
The Sūtra on the Collection of the Six Perfections Without Limit; the Sūtra on Holding the Dharma Gate; the Sūtra on the Lost Jewel Returned from the Sea; the Sūtra on Birth;
the Sūtra on the Selection of All Evil Worlds in the Future; the Ānandamukha-nihārita-sūtra; the Sūtra on the Buddha Entering the Ambrosia to Harmonize and Rectify the Mind;
the Sūtra on the Emergence of the Great Twelve Gates; and the Sūtra on Past Practice of the Dāna-pāramitā.
The aforementioned *Benxing liuboluomi jing* (Sūtra on the Original Practice of the Six Pāramitās), those works not annotated in various catalogs, the *Bie lu* (Separate Catalog),
the *Diyi yi wuxiang lueji* (Brief Collection of the Five Characteristics of the First Principle) in one fascicle translated at Dong’an Temple,
and the *Zangfa shi zishu yu* (Metaphor Self-Described by the Tripiṭaka Master) in one fascicle seen in the *Zalu* (Miscellaneous Catalog)— these constitute the seventy-seven works listed above.
In one hundred and sixty-one fascicles.
During the reign of Emperor Wen,
the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra from the kingdom of Central India [translated this].
In the Song language, his name was Guṇabhadra.
He was well-versed in Mahāyāna studies;
his contemporaries also referred to him as Mahāyāna.
He was also called Yan.
In the twelfth year of the Yuanjia era,
he arrived at the capital city of Yangdu.
The Emperor held him in deep reverence and honor.
So too did Liu Yikang, Prince of Pengcheng,
and Liu Yixuan, Prince of Nanqiao.
He served both masters as his teachers.
By imperial decree, he was stationed at Jetavana Monastery,
where he was further requested to translate the *Saṃyukta Āgama* and other texts.
Baoyun transmitted the words,
and Huiguan recorded them in writing.
Later, he followed Prince Xiao as he went to govern Jingzhou.
Furthermore, from the Xin Monastery, he again brought forth over one hundred fascicles of scriptures, such as those concerning King Aśoka;
most of these were oral translations transmitted by his disciple Fáyǒng.
The Prince of Qiao requested that he lecture on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra.
Guṇabhadra reflected to himself that he was not yet proficient in the Song language.
Every morning and evening he prayed to Avalokiteśvara;
consequently, he dreamed that his head was replaced.
The following morning, he proceeded to the lecture hall.
His eloquent commentaries flowed like a stream;
his further spiritual awakenings and profound realizations over the course of one year are fully recorded in the *Monastic Biographies* (*Sengzhuan*).
The *Yùlù* (Record of the Catalogue) merely states:
"Xian translated seventy-three fascicles.
Now, examining various catalogues:

All are listed in full. *The Sūtra on the Secret Essentials of Dhyāna*, three fascicles (also known as *The Essential Source of Dhyāna Methods*); translated at Qihuan Temple in the eighteenth year of the Yuanjia era; recorded in Sengyou’s catalog. *The Essential Methods for the Five-Gate Dhyāna Sūtra*; recorded in Sengyou’s Chang Catalog. *The Sūtra on the Method of Contemplating the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra*; derived from the *Sūtra of Profound Merit*; one copy titled *Samantabhadra-Contemplation Sūtra*; recorded in Sengyou’s catalog. *The Sūtra on the Contemplation of Ākāśagarbha Bodhisattva*; one copy lacks the character "contemplation" (*guan*); recorded in the catalogs of Daohui, Sengyou, and others. *The Sūtra of the King of Valiantness of All Dharmas*; recorded in Li Kuò’s catalog. The following six sūtras are all found in Li Kuò’s Wei-era catalog: *The Sūtra of the Buddha Ascending to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to Preach the Dharma for His Mother*, *The Sūtra on Transforming the Female Body*, *The Elephant-Armpit Sūtra*, *The Sūtra of the Questions of the Householder Ugga*, and *The Sūtra of the Divine Incantations of Ākāśagarbha Bodhisattva*. Thus, there are ten works in total.
In twelve fascicles.
During the reign of Emperor Wen,
the Tripiṭaka Master from Kaśmīra, Dhamamitra, [translated this].
In the Song language, his name was Fashou.
He was born with joined eyebrows and was by nature profound and introspective.
He possessed profound wisdom and discernment.
Good spirits constantly protected him in secret, concealing their forms,
whenever he traveled to the borders of kingdoms.
The deity will surely manifest in a dream to inform the king;
when he departs, it shall be the same.
He vowed that his life's purpose would be to travel abroad to teach and transform others;
by nature he was pure and ascetic, unconcerned with fame or profit.
When he first arrived in Dunhuang, he...
He immediately established a meditation pavilion on a secluded and spacious site,
planted a thousand *nai* trees, and opened a garden of one hundred mu;
the assembly of meditators gathered in great numbers, arriving like clouds.
At the beginning of the Yuanjia era, he arrived at Jianye and stayed at Zhongsi Temple.
Later, while resting at Qihuan Temple,
he translated the *Dhyāna-sūtra* and various *dhāraṇī* spells.
Furthermore, he also transmitted the painted image of the Kāpila Spirit-King;
its style remains the standard to this day.

As for the *Sūtra of the Two Bodhisattvas Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata* and the *Sūtra on the Contemplation of Amitāyus*, both are recorded in Daohui’s *Song Qi Lu* (Records of the Song and Qi Dynasties) and the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (Gaoseng zhuan), dating from the era of Emperor Wen.
The śramaṇa from the Western Regions,
Qiāngliángyèshē (in the Song language,
Shíchēng), was by nature upright and had few desires.
He was well-versed in the study of the Tripiṭaka and possessed extensive hidden knowledge;
he was particularly adept at meditative contemplation.
At the beginning of the Yuanjia era, he arrived at the capital of the Middle Kingdom.
The Emperor highly esteemed him and issued an edict for him to reside at Daolin Monastery on Mount Zhong.
The two sutras above are secret arts for transforming obstacles and causes for making offerings to the Pure Land.
One should constantly uphold, recite, and chant them.
Therefore, the śramaṇa Senghan requested its translation;
Han personally transcribed it by hand.

This second translation of the *Avalokiteśvara-bodhisattva-vyākaraṇa-sūtra* differs slightly from that produced by Hu. Furthermore, there is the *Foguo zhuan* (Account of Travels to Foreign Lands) in five fascicles, which Jie himself described as his travels to the Western Regions. These two works comprise six fascicles in total.
In the first year of the Yongchu era of Emperor Wu,
the śramaṇa Dharmodgata— translated into Chinese as Fayong— from the country of Huanglong arrived [in China].
A group of twenty-five fellow practitioners, including the monk Sengmeng,
gathered together and traveled westward to the regions beyond the Western Regions.
For more than twenty years, he had been abroad converting others;
now, having exhausted his efforts and returned alone to the kingdom of Kaśmīra,
he has transcribed the aforementioned Sanskrit manuscripts of the sutras and brought them here.
It reached the region south of the Yangtze River at the end of the Yuanjia era.
He translated it himself while in the capital of Yangzhou.
This is recorded in the catalogs of Wang Zong, Sengyou, Huijiao, Li Kuò, Fashang, and others.
*Treatise on the Secret Essential Methods for Healing the Diseases of Dhyāna*, two fascicles; produced at Zhuyuan Temple in the second year of the Xiaojian era (455 CE);

some versions omit the word "jing" (sūtra). Seen in Zu You’s *Changlu*. *The Sūtra of King Śuddhodana’s Parinirvāṇa*, second production. *A Different Version of the Sūtra on the Eight Precepts of the Fast*.
*The Sūtra of King Puming* (Universal Radiance). *The Great Sūtra of the Buddha and the Great Saṃgha*. Seen as titled *The Sūtra on the Transformation of Consciousness in Birth and Death*.
The *Bhārgava-rāja-sūtra*, the *Gṛhapati-svarānanda-sūtra*, the *Āyuṣmat-vinaya-sūtra*, the *Ekācāra-śikṣā-sūtra*,
the *Upāsaka-pañcaśīla-sūtra*, the *Pañcalakṣaṇa-sūtra*, the *Khaṭvāṅga-sūtra*, the *Mādhuka-sūtra*, the *Pañca-brāhmaṇa-śata-sūtra*, the *Candrayaśas-sūtra*,
the *Pañca-parivarta-mahārtha-sūtra*, the *Kāśyapa-śīla-sūtra*, and the *Śiṣya-maraṇa-sūtra*.

*Fusheng jing* (Sūtra on Rebirth), *Dizi shifo jixiong jing* (Sūtra on the Auspiciousness and Inauspiciousness of Disciples Serving the Buddha), *Wuku zhangju jing* (Sūtra on the Verses of the Five Sufferings), *Shizhong wen upasai jing* (Sūtra on the Śākya Clan Asking the Upāsaka), *Chu za ahan* (Extracts from the Saṃyukta Āgama),
*Bosiniwang sangmu jing* (Sūtra on King Prasenajit’s Mourning for His Mother), *Pusa shi jing* (Sūtra on the Bodhisattva’s Vow), *Zhongyin jing* (Sūtra on the Intermediate State),

*Zhouyi biqiu jing* (Sūtra on the Bhikṣu Zhōuyī), and *Fomu ban niepan jing* (Sūtra on the Parinirvāṇa of the Buddha’s Mother). [Copied] at Dinglin Temple on Mount Zhong in the second year of the Xiaojian era.

The *Chujian you lu* (Record of What Was Seen and Heard) also mentions the *Mahāprajāpatī Sūtra*, the *Brahmadatta Sūtra*, the *Upāsaka-pañcadharma Sūtra*, the *Pañcabhaya-loka Sūtra*, the *Malla-rāja Sūtra*, and the *Sudarśana-maitreya-bodhisattva-ūrdhvasaṃbhava-tuṣita-svarga-sūtra*.

These are recorded in the *Jian dao hui Song Qi lu* (Record of Dao Hui of the Song and Qi Dynasties) and the *San zang ji* (Records of the Tripitaka). Furthermore, there are the *Avalokiteśvara-dhyāna Sūtra*, the *Rājan-paripṛcchā Sūtra*, and the *Śraddhā-viśuddha Sūtra*.
The *Śrāmaṇera-ayan-vījan Sūtra* (1); the *Ayan-vījana-holding Father-and-Son Sūtra*; the *Disciple’s Arrogance Told to Jīvaka Sūtra* (1);
the *Disciple Telling Jīvaka of His Arrogance*, or the *Disciple’s Playful Exaggeration Sūtra*.
The locations for the above have not been annotated, as they all appear in the *Bie lu* (Separate Catalog). These constitute thirty-five works.
It consists of thirty-six fascicles.
During the era of Emperor Xiaowu,
Juqu Mengxun, the Prince of Hexi of Northern Liang, [commissioned its translation].
His younger cousin, Jingsheng, the Marquis of Anyang,
fell when the fortunes of the Liang dynasty ended and he was extinguished by the Northern Wei.
The court officials fled in secret toward Jiankang in the south.
Hui kept his ambitions humble and withdrew from worldly society;
he frequently stayed in pagodas and monasteries, styling himself a lay practitioner (*upāsaka*) to remain lowly.
He severed ties with his wife and family and renounced worldly honors and profit.
He gave full support to his fellow practitioners so that they might propagate the True Teaching.
Consequently, both monastics and laypeople alike showed him the highest respect.
Since he had long been familiar with reciting and practicing the aforementioned miscellaneous essential scriptures,
he was never hindered when transcribing them for the assembly.
Meng Yi, the Governor of Danyang, praised him for this.
The rewards and provisions were most generous and abundant;
this is recorded in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gaoseng zhuan*).

The *Bodhisattva Nianfo Sanmei Jing* (Sutra on the Bodhisattva’s Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha) in six fascicles, also known as the *Nianfo Sanmei Jing*, is listed in the *Records of Daohui* (Song and Qi Dynasties). The *Wuliangmen Poemo Duren Jing* (Sutra of the Immeasurable Gate Dhāraṇī for Dispelling Māras), also known as the *Wuliangmen*, is listed in the *Record of Sengyou*. These two works comprise seven fascicles in total.
During the reign of Emperor Xiaowu,
the śramaṇa Guṇadatta from the Western Regions arrived in the sixth year of the Daming era.
In Jingzhou, it was translated by the śramaṇa Shi Xuanchang.
Xuanchang edited and standardized the textual meanings and terminology, making them elegant and profound;
yet, as he stretched out his hand, incense issued forth and flowing water emerged from his palm.
No one could fathom him.
Later, he traveled to Chengdu and stayed at Dashi Temple,
which was the site of King Aśoka’s stūpa.
He then personally fashioned images of the sixteen deities, such as Vajrapāṇi and Guhyapada, which have been handed down to the present day.

The *Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabhā-sūtra* was translated in the first year of the Daming era; it removes transgressions and sins, and enables one to attain liberation from the cycle of birth and death.
One title is *The Sūtra on the Emergence of Empowerment* (*Guǎngdìng chūguǎngdìng jīng*). It was included in the *Yùlù* (Record of the Doubtful). Chángfáng examined it against a Brahmin manuscript;
there is currently a Sanskrit original, with minor differences from the divine words [of the Chinese version]. The *Sūtra on the Merchant Seeking the Dharma* was translated by the Saṃgharāja.

The *Sūtra of the Five Divine Messengers* contains the word "Saṃgha" (*sēng*), which is suspected of being an error. The *Sūtra of Prince Śubhavyūha* is also a different translation. The *Sūtra of the Sixfold Prostrations*, the *Sūtra of the Lazy Plowman*, and others were recorded in the old catalogs.
*The Sutra on Seeing through Sloth*, *The Sutra on Śākyamuni Exhausting His Karmic Debt*, one fascicle;

*The Sutra on the Birth of the Characters of a Master Craftsman*, *The Sutra of the Poor Old Man*, or *The Sutra of the Poor Old Man Who Sacrificed Himself to Save a Merchant*; [these] appear in the *Collection of the Six Pāramitās*.

*The Sutra of the Person in Śrāvastī Going Mad after Losing a Son*; appears in the *Sutra of Parables from the Āgamas*. *The Sutra on the Method for Inviting Piṇḍola*; [the account of] Ānanda’s Vision.

The *Shuiguang Ruijing* (also known as the *Shuiguang Jing*, the *Zhouyuan Jing*, the *Jiumotimi Jiguo Jing*, the *Xueren Luanyi Jing*, or the *Yimuzi Zuo Biqiu Biquni Luanyi Jing*) appears in the *Ekottarika Āgama*.
The *Qiewei Shamen Jing* and the *Fomu Baninihan Jing* differ slightly from those translated by An Yanghou; they are for the Elder [Dharmarakṣa].
The *Sutra on the Six Faults of Leaving Home* (from the *Udānavarga*). The *Sutra on the Hunter Who Abandoned His Home to Study the Path* (from the *Udānavarga*). The *Sutra of Gautamī*.
The *Sutra on the Matter of Candraśrī’s Malicious Slander of the Buddha* (from the *Udānavarga*).

The *Sutra on Two Old Men Seeing the Buddha, Leaving Home, and Attaining the Way*. The *Sutra on Genuine and Spurious Śramaṇas*, also known as the *Genuine or Spurious Sutra*. The *Sutra of the Buddha*.

The *Nirvāṇa-parinirvṛta-bhikṣu-sūtra* (one version); the *Mahānagna-Bhadra-sūtra*, which appears in the *Saṃyukta Āgama* and its own separate record as the *Lokavikāra-mahānagna-pravrajya-mārgalābha-sūtra*;
and the *Mahānagna-Bhadra-sūtra*, which also appears in the *Saṃyukta Āgama* and its own separate record as the *Svaparābhāva-sūtra*. These constitute twenty-five works in total.
It comprises twenty-five fascicles.
During the reign of Emperor Xiaowu,
the śramaṇa Shi Huijian [compiled it].
Extracted from the Rurujing Monastery.
*The Essential Karmavācanas for Bhikṣus and Bhikṣuṇīs of the Ten Recitation Vinaya*, two fascicles. During the reign of the deposed Emperor, the seventh year of the Daming era.

The Vinaya Master Shi Sengqu compiled this work based on the Vinaya at Zhongxing Temple in the capital of Yangdu; it is also titled *Lüeyào Jiemó Fǎ* (Abridged Essential Karmavācanā). This is recorded in Sengyou’s *Sanzàng Jì*.

The *Śāriputra-dharmaguptaka-vinaya-bhikṣu-prātimokṣa-sūtra*, translated in the Daming era; the *Śāriputra-dharmaguptaka-vinaya-bhikṣuṇī-prātimokṣa-sūtra*, translated in the Taishi era; and the *Śāriputra-dharmaguptaka-vinaya-karman* (Miscellaneous Matters on Ritual Procedures), both essential texts, translated in the Taishi era. These three scriptures comprise three fascicles.
During the reign of Emperor Ming,
the Vinaya Master Shi Faying compiled this work based on the Vinaya at Changgan Temple in the capital of Yangdu.
According to Sengyou’s *Chusanzang jiji* and Baochang’s *Lülu*, there are six works totaling twenty-nine fascicles:

the *Wujinyi jing* (Ten Fascicles), the *Haiyi jing* (Seven Fascicles), the *Rulai enzhi bushiyi jing* (Five Fascicles), the *Baoding jing* (Five Fascicles), the *Ashudabosha jing* translated in Guangzhou during the Taishi era—the third translation, which is largely identical to the second translation by Dharmarakṣa of the Jin—and the *Sanmi diye jing*, also known as the *Xianren yonglü jing*. These constitute the six works.
During the reign of Emperor Ming,
the Indian śramaṇa Zhu Fajian translated [this work] in Guangzhou.
I have examined Sengyou’s *Chū-sanzō-ki* (Record of the Tripitaka) from Shixing, as well as the three catalogs by Baochang and others.

The *Liu-shou pusa wushang qingjing fenwei jing* (The Sutra on the Peerless Pure Alms-Gathering of Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī), two fascicles, and the *Yi jue liao zhu fa ru huan sanmei jing* (The Sutra on the Samādhi of Resolving All Dharmas as Illusions)—the latter was not clearly dated during the Song dynasty.
It is not known which emperor's reign this was translated during.
Various catalogs simply state:
"The śramaṇa Master Xiang produced it in Nanhai Commandery."
The *Jian Dao'an Shixing You Lu* (Record of Dao’an’s Works from the Shixing Era),

the two-fascicle *Yingluo Benye Jing* (Sūtra on the Original Acts of the Diadem), the *Fozang Dafangdeng Jing* (Buddha-treasury Mahāvaipulya Sūtra), and the *Hewen Mingxian Jing* (Sūtra of Questions and Manifestation) were not clearly dated during the Song dynasty.
It is not known which emperor's reign this was translated during;
various catalogs simply state that it was produced by the śramaṇa Śākya Daoyan.
These are recorded in both the *Shixing lu* and the *Fashang lu*.

The *Kongjing sanmei jing* (also titled *Kongjing da ganying sanmei jing*), the *Che’i jing* (or *Che’i benmo jing*), the *Quanjin xue dao jing* (translated together with the official Li of the Liang dynasty, also titled *Quanjin jing*), and the *Fannü shouyi jing* (also titled *Shouyi nü jing*)—these four works are listed above.
It was translated during the Song dynasty by the Emperor of the Unmanifest Year;
the various catalogs simply state that it was produced by the śramaṇa Śramaṇa Shi Yong.
I have consulted the *Zhao lu* of Shixing;
the *Fashang lu* also records this.

The *Lüe yingluo zhuangyan fangbian jing*—also titled *Dacheng yingluo zhuangyan* and *Zhuan nüshen pusa jing*—is identical to the *Shunquan fangbian jing* translated by Dharmarakṣa. The *Jiaotiao yin suo wen jing*—also titled *Rulai suoshuo qingjing diaofu jing*—is the same original text as the *Wenshushili xinglü jing* translated by Dharmarakṣa. These two volumes [are thus verified].
Translated during the Song dynasty, though the imperial year is not specified.
The collective catalogs note that it was produced by the śramaṇa Shi Fahaha.
I have consulted the *Fashang lu* (Catalogue of Fashang) from Shixing.
The *Candrapradīpa-samādhi-sūtra* is also titled the *Mañjuśrī-bodhisattva-daśa-kriyā-sūtra* and the *Jianhui-samādhi-sūtra*; the above details are the same as previously stated.

produced at Yíngzhōu Temple in Yechéng in the second year of the Tiānpíng era. Also known as the *Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā-bodhicitta-sūtra-śāstra*;
recorded by pen by Sēngbiàn and Dàozhàn. The *Tri-samaya-sūtra-śāstra*, five fascicles; [produced] in the first year of Zhèngshǐ.
In the year [X], under the supervision of Cui Guang, Court Attendant (Zhongzhong), the *Commentary on the Sūtra of the Upadeśa of the Immeasurable Life* was transcribed by Wusheng.
In the first year of the Putai era, the *Sūtra on the Four Dharmas of the Ratnaśikhin Bodhisattva* was transcribed by Sengbian; the *Sūtra on Turning the Wheel of Dharma*, by Tanlin;

and the *Treatise on the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination*, the *Treatise on the Hundred Syllables*, the *Treatise Refuting the Four Tenets of the Tīrthikas*, and the *Treatise Refuting the Nirvāṇa of the Tīrthikas*.
Catalogue of Translated Sūtras and Śāstras: The thirty-nine works listed above comprise one hundred and twenty-seven fascicles.
[Compiled] during the reign of Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty.
The Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci from Northern India—
translated as "Daoxi" (Path-Wish) in the Wei dynasty—
was present from the second year of the Yongping era to the Tianping era of the Wei dynasty.
In the interval, he spent a total of over twenty years translating in Luoyang and Ye;
this was recorded by Li Kuò.
Within the chamber of the Tripiṭaka Master,
there were approximately ten thousand fascicles of the original texts of Brahmanical sūtras and śāstras,
as well as the manuscript copies of the sūtras and śāstras translated by him that had been taken down by scribes.
He filled an entire room;
however, his wisdom and understanding were nearly equal to those of Ratnamati.
He possessed divine intuition and keen intelligence, was thoroughly proficient in local dialects, and was skilled in various arts.
Once, while sitting at the edge of a well, the interior of his *kamaṇḍalu* was empty;
as his disciples had not yet arrived and there was no one to draw water,
the Tripitaka Master took a willow branch and lightly swept the mouth of the well.
As soon as he had recited the mantra silently in his mind for only a few times,
the spring surged upward until it reached the rim of the well.
The Tripitaka Master then immediately drew water from it using his alms bowl.
The monks who saw this all sighed in admiration and praised him as a sage.
The Dharma Master said, "This is merely a magical art; it is practiced by everyone in foreign lands."
In this region, because people do not practice [these teachings], they claim them to be sacred;
fearing they might delude the world,
he subsequently concealed the miscellaneous dharmas, saying:
The *Vyāsaparipṛcchā-sūtra*, two fascicles; the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, twelve fascicles.

When this treatise was first translated, the translator was not yet proficient in the Wei language and rendered "bhājana-loka" (the receptacle world) as "the world of cups. Later, while entering the hall for a vegetarian feast, he observed the assembly of virtuous monks requesting their vessels;

they collectively received large jars (*aṅga*) and cloth bags (*po*). Thereupon, he realized that "vessel" (*qi*) was a general term and subsequently revised "the world of vessels" to "the world of receptacles" (*jiu*).

The *Jing yicheng baoxing lun* (Treatise on the Ultimate One Vehicle and the Jewel Nature) in four fascicles, consisting of the *Baoxing fenbie* (Discrimination of the Jewel Nature) and the *Qicheng zengshang lun* (Treatise on the Superiority of the Seven Vehicles), was produced by Zhao Xinzhai;

this is recorded in the *Baochang lu*. The *Baoji jing lun* (Treatise on the Ratnakūṭa Sūtra) in four fascicles was translated alongside the *Shidi jing lun* (Treatise on the Ten Stages) by Bodhiruci;
however, as these two masters were at odds and did not consult one another, there are omissions and discrepancies between them.
There are also differences in the compilation of the phrasing; it was only later that these were combined.

As recorded in Baochang’s *Lu* (Catalog), there are six works in total, including the *Fahua jing lun* (Treatise on the Lotus Sutra) with its text transcribed by Cui Guang, Palace Attendant, and the *Longshu pusa hexiang fang* (Incense Recipe of Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna) consisting of fifty methods.
In twenty-four fascicles.
During the era of Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty,
the Tripiṭaka Master Ratnamati from Central India [translated this].
Some call him Bodhi; in the Wei language, this means "Precious Intention" (Baoyi).
He arrived in the fifth year of the Zhengshi era and translated [this work] within the palace halls in Luoyang.
Initially, Bodhiruci assisted in the transmission;
later, they disputed and translated separately.
The śramaṇas Senglang and Jueyi, along with the Palace Attendant Cui Guang and others, acted as scribes for the *Vajrarasadhāraṇīsūtra*.

The *Tathāgata-siṃhanāda-sūtra* (upper volume); these two sūtras were translated in the sixth year of the Zhengguang era. Furthermore, there are the *Daśadharma-sūtra*, the *Rūpyamālā-dārikā-sūtra*, and the *Saddharmagaurava-sūtra*—the latter also known as the *Vīrya-dhāraṇī-sūtra* or the *Abhayamati-dārikā-sūtra*. These are different translations from the same original text as the *Āśutara-bodhisattva-sūtra*, with Tanlin acting as the scribe. Also, the *Anakṣara-ratnakaraṇḍaka-sūtra*. These six sūtras above were translated in the second year of the Yuanxiang era. Additionally, the *Ānanda-mukha-nirhāra-dhāraṇī-sūtra* is a separate translation of the same original text as five other sūtras: Zhi Qian’s *Aparimitāyur-jñāna-guhya-dhāraṇī*, the *Bhadra-aparimitāyur-mukha-dhāraṇī*, the *Śāriputra-dhāraṇī*, the *Guṇaratna-aparimitāyur-mukha-māra-bhañjana-dhāraṇī*, and others; they differ only in name. Finally, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-śāstra* in two fascicles was translated in the first year of the Putai era. Thus, there are ten works in total.
In eleven volumes combined.
During the era of Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty,
the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas from North India [translated this].
The Wei term for this is *Jueding* (Awakening and Concentration).
It was translated from the sixth year of the Zhengguang era to the second year of the Yuanxiang era at Baima Monastery in Luoyang and Jinhuasi Monastery in the capital of Ye.

The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* in seventy fascicles was translated at the capital of Ye by Gao Cheng, the Grand Chancellor of the Northern Wei, and his younger brother in the first year of the Xinghe era;
Tanlin, Sengfang, and others acted as scribes.

The *Āryasuvikrāntavikrami-paripṛcchā-sūtra* in three fascicles appeared at Jinhua Temple in the city of Ye in the third year of the Xinghe era, translated by Hu with the assistance of Ruyanhansanmei.

The *Sūtra of the Eight Buddhas’ Names* and the *Sūtra of the Golden-Colored King*—two sūtras of the same root but different titles—were both produced at Jinhua Temple in the fourth year of the Xinghe era, with Tanlin serving as the scribe.
The *Sūtra of the Stainless Woman* was produced in the third year of the Xinghe era;
the *Sūtra of the Inquiry of the Stainless Upāsikā* was produced in the fourth year of the Xinghe era; and the *Sūtra of Precious Intent and the Cat* was produced [in the same year].

At Jinhua Monastery, for Gao Zhongmi, he produced the *Bodhisattva-caturdharma-sūtra*; at Jinhua Monastery, he produced the *Vinaya-mātṛkā-vimukti-śīla-sūtra*, with Tanlin and Li Xiyi serving as scribes;
in the third year of the Xinghe era, he produced [the same], with Sengfang serving as the scribe;
and at Jinhua Monastery, for Gao Zhongmi, he produced the *Kāśyapīya-vinaya-vatsīputrīya-praśna-śāstra*, with Li [Xi]yi serving as the scribe.
The *Vigrahavyāvartanī* was transcribed by Xi Yi during the first year of the Yuangxiang era;

the *Karmasiddhiprakaraṇa* was transcribed by Tanlin during the third year of the Xinghe era at Jinhua Temple; the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-viṣayapratiṣedha-śāstra*—also known as the *Vijñaptimātratā-śāstra*—was likewise transcribed by Tanlin at Jinhua Temple;
and the *Ekāṣṭaka-śloka-śāstra*. These latter two treatises were both produced at Jinhua Temple. (One item above.)
Fourteen sections,
totaling eighty-five fascicles,
translated during the reign of Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty.
The Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci— *Prajñāruci* meaning "Wisdom-Longing" in the Wei language— of the city of Vārāṇasī in the South Indian kingdom of East Wei,
arrived from the beginning of the Yuánxiàng era until the end of the Xīnghé era.
Translated at Ye City.
At that time, there was Bodhiruci, who,
although he had previously and subsequently produced similar translations of the scriptures, [was distinct from this master].
However, in various catalogues and records transmitted through successive copying, the characters "Bodhi" and "Prajñā" have been omitted;
it merely states that it was translated by Liu Zhi,
without specifying which Liu Zhi it refers to.
To this day, various records have been intermingled with one another;
errors and redundancies have overlapped such that a definitive determination is difficult to achieve.
I hope that future scholars of broad learning will investigate and rectify this.

The *Saṃghāṭa-sūtra* in four fascicles was translated in the first year of the Yuansiang era at the residence of the Minister of Education, Sun Teng. The *Mahākāśyapa-sūtra* in two fascicles (one lacking the character "da") and the *Bimbisāra-rāja-prcchā-buddha-pūjā-sūtra*, upper fascicle—these two sutras were both produced in the third year of the Xinghe era. The above three sections comprise seven fascicles.
During the reign of Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty,
there was Prince Śubhakarasiṃha from the kingdom of Ujjayinī in Central India;
in the Wei language, his name means "High Void."
Translated at Ye City;
Fang received the dictation.
*A Record of Buddhist Monasteries in Luoyang*, five fascicles (or seven fascicles), compiled by Yang Xuanzhi, Prefect of Qi City Commandery.
Its preface states:
"The doctrines of the Three Mounds and Five Canons;
the words of the Nine Schools and the Hundred Masters."
Furthermore, the principles reside within the human realm and their significance does not lie beyond the mundane world.
This extends to the source of the One Vehicle and the Two Truths,
as well as the purport of the Six Supernatural Powers and the Threefold Penetration.
The Western Regions are described in exhaustive detail, yet the Eastern Land has no such record.
Since the time when King [Aśoka] was moved by a dream of the full moon’s radiance,
the gates of Yang have been adorned with images of the white-eyebrowed one.
In the Liangtai (Cool Terrace) [inscription], the form of the dark hair [of the Buddha] was depicted;
since then, people have vied with one another to emulate it, and this trend has spread widely.
By the time of the Yongjia era of the Jin dynasty, there were only forty-two monasteries remaining.
The Imperial Wei dynasty has received the Mandate of Heaven and brought glory to Mount Song and the Luo River.
Faith has become increasingly profound, and the teachings of the Dharma have flourished even more;
thus, it is the kings, princes, and noble ministers [who uphold them].
They cast aside elephants and horses as if discarding worn-out sandals;
the common officials and wealthy families relinquish their wealth and possessions as if they were discarded traces.
Thereupon, pagodas were erected in every direction, standing in dense rows, and so forth.
Within the capital city, there were approximately one thousand monasteries;
all were selected for their auspicious and extraordinary features and recorded in this account.
Catalog of Various Scriptures: The above was compiled by the lay devotee Li Kuo of Luoyang during the reign of Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty,
under imperial decree in the Yongping era of the Wei.
He mastered both internal and external studies and composed commentaries and catalogs of scriptures that were highly systematic and well-ordered.
*Mahāparinirvāṇa-śāstra*, one fascicle. According to the catalog prior to the Tang dynasty, this was translated by Dharmabodhi;
the imperial reign period is not specified.
Appended here due to doubt. 14.

Record of the Translation of Buddhist Scriptures by the Gao Clan of the Later Qi. Record of the Translation of Buddhist Scriptures by the Gao Clan of the Later Qi, Number Fourteen. During the reign of Emperor Yuan of the Northern Wei, the mandate of his dynasty fragmented and collapsed.
During the reign of Emperor Xiaoming of the Song dynasty, Buddhist principles were held in high esteem.
Empress Dowager Hu personally oversaw the affairs of state,
and within a single decade, the empire enjoyed peace and tranquility.
Upon the Emperor's demise,
Xiao Jing succeeded him; subsequently,
Er Zhu Rong died in the inner palace.
Tu Wanren captured Emperor Jin in Yangzhou;
Gao欢 (Gao Huan) took advantage of this vulnerability and defeated the Erzhu clan at Ye.
When Yuwen Jie caused the chaos,
Helian Yi pacified Pingyang within the Guannei region.
Thereupon, Helian欢 (Huan) burned the palaces of Luoyang and utterly destroyed the imperial designs.
He established the reign title Tianping and moved the capital to Northern Ye.
For seventeen years, he supported and protected the Wei dynasty.
In the third year of the Taicheng era of the Liang dynasty,
after Emperor Wu had passed away,
Gao Huan died first.
The heir apparent Cheng succeeded him,
but the Chancellor passed away as well.
Thereupon, the Emperor Jing of Wei abdicated the throne to Gao Yang.
He was the third son of King Xiang.
His family lineage was of the Wuchuan clan, whose divine influence was preeminent and extraordinary;
therein, the foolish and the wise mingled their tracks, and the worthy and the sagely were intermingled in their ranks.
He established his reign title as Tianbao and continued to reside in Ye;
he ruled over three of the four great rivers.
He unified five of the nine provinces and executed Li Er.
As for the rebellious Daoist practitioners who had left the household life, he suppressed them.
The Emperor issued an edict ordering Shen to shave his head;
he subsequently executed him.
Thereupon, they all returned to the Buddha-dharma.
Within ten years, the Buddha-dharma flourished greatly;
there were over two million monks and forty thousand monasteries.
Together they propagated, protected, and revitalized the Great Dharma;
six successive patriarchs held the lineage for twenty-eight years.
He was destroyed by the Zhou dynasty.
Among his translations were two works for both the clergy and the laity,
totaling eight scriptures and treatises.
Fifty-three fascicles. According to the Gaodi Record: The śramaṇa Narendrayaśas translated seven works totaling fifty-two fascicles of sūtras and śāstras.

Upāsaka Wàntiānyì translated one work, one fascicle: the *Bodhisattvadarśanabhūtasaṃādhi-sūtra* (14 fascicles). The *Candragarbha-sūtra*, twelve fascicles, was produced at Tiānpíng Temple in the fourth year of the Tiāntóng era. The *Candrapradīpa-samādhi-sūtra*, ten fascicles, was produced at Tiānpíng Temple in the second year of the Tiāntóng era. The *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra*, five fascicles, was produced at Tiānpíng Temple in the eighth year of the Tiānbão era. The *Sumerugarbha-sūtra*, also known as the *Dīpadāna-puṇya-sūtra*, two fascicles, was produced at Tiānpíng Temple in the ninth year of the Tiānbão era. Both of these latter two sūtras were produced at Tiānpíng Temple in the ninth year of the Tiānbão era. The *Abhidharma-dharmatrāta-śāstra*, seven fascicles, was produced at Tiānpíng Temple in the second year of the Héqīng era. These constitute the aforementioned seven works.
Fifty-two fascicles.
During the reign of Emperor Ming of the Northern Zhou dynasty,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Narendrayaśas, a monk-general from the kingdom of Udyāna in North India under the Gao Qi.
The title "Qi" (齊) refers to a mark of honor.
It was translated at the city of Ye (鄴城).
The chief śramaṇa of the Office of Buddhist Affairs (Zhāoxuán), Gautama Prajñāruci, was the elder son [of the King].
Dharmajñāna; in the Qi language, this means "Dharma-knowledge.
This is the transmitted term.
The Sūtra of the Questions of the Bodhisattva Uṣṇīṣavijayā, also known as the Dhāraṇī of Entering the Gate of Immeasurability.
Translated during the reign of Emperor Wu of the Zhou dynasty by the lay devotee Wan Tianyi of the Northern Qi at Ye City.
Yiyuan was a Xianbei of the Wan-mi clan.
Having left home at a young age, he took a Brahman as his teacher.
He was exceptionally intelligent and wise, proficient in Sanskrit scripts and languages,
and skilled in incantations and medical arts;
therefore, he was included among the translators.
The Catalogue of the Inner Scriptures of the Great Tang, Volume Four;
The Catalogue of the Inner Scriptures of the Great Tang, Volume Five.
Compiled by Shi [Daoxuan] of Ximing Monastery in the Capital.
The Fifth Part of the First Section of the Catalogue of the Translation of Various Scriptures Throughout Successive Dynasties:

The Later Zhou, Chen, Sui, and Imperial (Tang) Dynasties. Part Fifteen: A Record of the Translation of Buddhist Scriptures by the Yuwen Clan of the Later Zhou. The world was inherited through generations of turmoil and separation; the Wei and Jin dynasties underwent further upheaval.
Each proclaims its own calendar while mutually denouncing the other as a false dynasty;
benevolence and righteousness can thus be exhausted day by day,
and virtue and conduct are said to be withering away.
Yet, throughout successive dynasties, the national histories have consistently proclaimed "I am right and they are wrong.
This results in one being right and the other wrong,
one being benevolent and the other tyrannical.
It is difficult for anyone to find a satisfactory resolution;
who would dare to deliberate upon it?
Thus, the Northern Wei dynasty regarded those south of the Yangtze River as "island barbarians."
The Southern Jin dynasty regarded Henei as the domain of the Xiongnu.
The Zhou inherited the mandate from Wei, and Wei in turn succeeded the foundation of Jin;
all others were merely regional kings with no stable basis for authority.
As for the periods of the Song, Qi, Liang, and Chen dynasties, they naturally have their own official archives;
now that the kingdoms have perished and the emperors have fallen,
these records must consequently follow the same process of editorial revision as all other historical documents.
Could it not be so? Zhou’s progenitor, Yuwen Jue,
was the eldest son of Hei Tai, the Grand Chancellor of Western Wei.
Tai enthroned Gao Yang as Emperor of Wei and moved westward to Chang’an.
He changed the color of ceremonial robes and banners to black and designated the first year of the Datong era.
After eighteen years had passed since the change of the era name,
the deposed emperor was enthroned.
He died in the fourth year of Emperor Qi’s reign of the Wei dynasty.
Jue succeeded to the Wei throne;
however, he was deposed that same year,
and his younger brother Yu was established as emperor.
He passed away after four years of reign.
His younger brother Yong was established as Emperor;
he was the third son of Taizu.
Magnanimous and broad-minded, he brought the petty factions under his command.

Having held power for twelve years, he executed his uncle, the Grand Steward of the Great Tomb, Kuni no Oki no Mikoto, along with ten members of his family, as well as the leaders of six great ministerial houses.
The era name was changed to Jiande.
In the third year, the Daoist Zhang Bin presented himself at court with sycophantic and heterodox claims,
asserting that Buddhism was inauspicious for the state.
He subsequently abolished them.
By the sixth year of the Jiande era,
the Eastern Wei state of Qi further destroyed the public and private temples and pagodas that had existed for several hundred years since previous dynasties.
The ground was swept clean;
[Hui]rong scraped away sacred images and burned the scriptures.
From the Buddhist temples across the eight provinces, forty thousand [images and texts] were removed.
He bestowed all the lands upon the princes and dukes, releasing three hundred thousand people from bondage to return them to the common registers.
The Emperor considered that the Great Zhou was unified and the world was at peace.
His aspirations were lofty and his foresight far-reaching.
He changed the era name to Xuānzhèng.
Five months later, he passed away.
The Crown Prince Yǔnlì ascended the throne.
He executed eight members of the Qi royal family, including the King and his sons,
and changed the era name to Dàchéng.
In the second month, he established his son Yan as the Crown Prince and abdicated the throne to him.
He changed the era name to Daxiang.
He styled himself Emperor Tianyuan.
He established four empresses,
whose ceremonial deportment and attire were twice as grand as those of antiquity.
In the fifth month of the second year of the Daxiang era,
the Heavenly Sovereign passed away.
His son, Yan, ascended the throne.
On the first day of the first month, he changed the era name to Dading.
In the second month, he abdicated the throne to the Sui dynasty;
thus, there were five emperors in total.
In the twenty-fifth year,
he resided in Chang’an,
where eleven śramaṇas served as translators.
The scriptures, treatises, astronomical essentials,
and so forth produced therein comprise thirty-two works totaling one hundred and four fascicles;
this is according to the *Beishi Zhongjing Lu* (Beiqi Zhongjing Mulü).
The Śramaṇa Shi Tanyǎn produced one collection of twenty fascicles of sūtras; the Śramaṇa Rāṇabhadra produced one collection of one fascicle of śāstras;
the Śramaṇa Dharmaruci produced one collection of twenty fascicles of Sanskrit texts;
the Śramaṇa Tanyayasha produced six collections totaling seventeen fascicles of sūtras; and the Śramaṇa Yaśogupta produced three collections totaling eight fascicles.
The *Fourfold Sūtra in Five Volumes* translated by the śramaṇa Jñānagupta; the *Two Treatises in Two Volumes* transmitted by the śramaṇa Shi Sengmin;
the *One Collection in Eight Volumes* by the śramaṇa Shi Huishan; the *Eleven Treatises in Eleven Volumes* by the śramaṇa Shi Wangming;
the *One Collection in Eleven Volumes* consisting of epigraphs and biographies by the śramaṇa Shi Jing’ai; and the *Compendium of the Three Jewels*.
One work in one fascicle by the śramaṇa Shi Dao’an: *Sanjiao lun* (Treatise on the Three Teachings). Twenty-two fascicles on the essentials of the various scriptures:
*Yibai ershi famen* (One Hundred and Twenty Dharma Gates). These two works comprise twenty-three fascicles in total.
Wang, the Chancellor of Wei,
and Yuwen Helai (Yuehuai) caused the Buddhist scriptures to flourish and held the Mahāyāna in high esteem;
although they oversaw the myriad affairs of state, they constantly propagated the Triple Gem.
Within his inner quarters, he constantly provided for a hundred Dharma masters to seek out and study the sūtras and śāstras, lecturing on the Mahāyāna;
he subsequently commissioned the śramaṇa Shi Tanxian and others [to do so].
Based on Mahāyāna sūtras, he compiled the essential passages from the various scriptures of the Bodhisattvapiṭaka and one hundred and twenty dharma-gates,
beginning with the Buddha-nature and ending with the Gate of Integration;
these he constantly expounded whenever he gave lectures.
It was established as a permanent standard to replace the five-period teaching traces of former masters;
it has circulated until the present day throughout Shandong and Jiangnan.
Although it is called the ocean of learning, its rules and regulations are such that nothing surpasses them;
even the incense and lamps, the chanting of the *brahman* voice, the prostrations,
and the praises of the Buddha are all contained within them.
In every matter, he verified the facts and established his principles with evidence.

His *Pañcavidyā-śāstra* (Treatise on the Five Sciences) consists of: first, the science of sound; second, the science of medicine; third, the science of arts and crafts; fourth, the science of incantations; and fifth, the science of seals and talismans. It was completed over two years during the reign of Emperor Ming of the Later Han.
Translated at Póqié Monastery in the Old City of Cháng'ān by the Tripiṭaka Master Saṃghavarman of the country of Pāṭaliputra—
whose name means "Wise and Virtuous" (Zhìxián) in the language of Zhōu— together with Jñānayaśas.
Translated by Yaśagupta, Jñānagupta, and others;
received in writing by the śramaṇa Zhi Qian.
The *Brahmaṇa-jyotiṣa* in twenty fascicles was brought out during the Tianhe era [of the Northern Qi], in the reign of Emperor Wu.
In the country of Moli,
there was the śramaṇa Dharmaruci,
whose name in the language of Zhou means "Dharma-Desire."
Translated by Yuwen Hu, Duke of Tang and Grand Chancellor of Jin.

*The Scripture on the Questions of the Devaputra Samāhita-mati*, five fascicles; translated during the sixth year of the Tianhe era, with the śramaṇa Yuánmíng acting as scribe. *The Ratnakūṭa-sūtra*, three fascicles; translated during the sixth year of the Tianhe era, with the śramaṇa Dàoshēng acting as scribe. *The Tathāgata-jñānācintya-sūtra*, three fascicles. *The Mahāyāna-samatā-nirdeśa-sūtra*, four fascicles—also titled *The Buddha-daśabhūmi-sūtra* or *The Sarvabuddha-caryā-praveśa-jñāna-vairocana-kośa-sūtra*; translated during the fifth year of the Tianhe era, with the Duke of Tóngyáng, Xiāo Jí, acting as scribe for the official protocol. *The Buddhoṣṇīṣa-dhāraṇī-sūtra and its Efficacy*, translated during the fourth year of the Bǎodìng era, with the Academician Bào Yǒng acting as scribe. *The Mahāmegha-cakra-sūtra: Chapter on Entreaty for Rain*, fascicle one hundred; translated during the fifth year of the Tianhe era, with the śramaṇa Yuánmíng acting as scribe. The above six works, totaling seventeen fascicles, were first brought out.
During the reign of Emperor Wu,
there was the Tripiṭaka Master Jayayasa from the kingdom of Magadha; in the language of Zhou,
his name is translated as Zangcheng (Treasure-Call).
Together with his two disciples, Yaśogupta and Jñānagupta,
he translated [the text] for the great minister and Protector of the State, Yuwen Hu (styled Dànggōng),
at the Siṃhala Caturdevī Temple in the Old City of Cháng'ān.
The Pillar of State, Duke of Pingyang, Hou Fu-shou, served as the General Supervisor and Inspector.

The *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, further expanding upon the Great Life-Span and Great Eloquence Dhāraṇī, in five fascicles, was translated at Guisheng Monastery; Zhi-xian acted as the scribe. The *Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of Subhadra*, in two fascicles, was translated at Si-tianwang Monastery; the śramaṇa Yuan-ming acted as the scribe. The *Eleven-Faced Avalokiteśvara Dhāraṇī* together with the *Sūtra on its Efficacy*, translated at Si-tianwang Monastery, had Shang-yi, Duke of Tongyang, Xiao Ji, acting as the scribe. These three sections comprise eight fascicles in total.
During the reign of Emperor Wu,
