The *Duliushijian jing* (Sūtra on Leaving the World) in six fascicles and one hundred nineteen sheets is the "Leaving the World" chapter (*Lokottara-parivarta*) of this very sūtra, translated by Dharmarakṣa during the Yuankang era of the Western Jin dynasty.

The *Bieyi zhanbei yiqiezhide jing* (Separate Translation of the Sutra on the Gradual Preparation of All-Wise Virtue) in five fascicles and one hundred five sheets is a separate translation by Zhu Fahu of the Zhi-jin Yuan-kang era; it is the "Ten Grounds" (*Daśabhūmi*) chapter.

The *Xinli ruyin famen jing* (Sutra on the Dharma-Gate of Entering the Seal through the Power of Faith) in five fascicles and ninety-three sheets is a separate translation by Dharmaruci of the Zheng-shi era of the Northern Wei; it is the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* in four fascicles and ninety [sheets].
The "Ten Stages Chapter" (Daśabhūmika-parivarta), 7 sheets, translated by Kumārajīva together with Buddhayaśas during the Hongshi era of the Later Qin;

the *Tathāgatotpattisambhava-sūtra* in four fascicles, 67 sheets, translated by Dharmarakṣa during the Yuankang era of the Western Jin; the "Nature-Arising Chapter" (Gzhi-byung-gi le'u), and the *Rāmāyaṇa-sūtra* [variant:
*Lokottara-parivarta*] in three fascicles, 77 sheets, translated during the Xiqin period; the "Entering the Dharma Realm Chapter" (Dharmadhātupraveśa-parivarta).
The *Qunlu* (Collection of Records) compiled by Master Jian also states: "The *Bodhisattva-daśabhūmika-sūtra*, one fascicle, five sheets, translated by An Faxian;
the *Bodhisattva-mūla-karma-sūtra*, one fascicle, thirteen sheets, translated by Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin;

and the *Sarvabodhisattva-buddha-mūla-karma-sūtra*, one fascicle, ten [sheets], translated by Zhi Qian during the Huangwu era of the Wu dynasty—this latter work contains no verses from the 'Chapter on Pure Conduct' (*Śīla-viśuddhi-parivarta*)."
One sheet: *The Sutra on the Tuṣita Heaven Spoken by the Buddha*, Chapter on Pure Conduct, one fascicle, five sheets; translated separately by Zhi Chen of the Later Han.
Excerpts from the *Mahāvaipulya Daśabhūmika Sūtra*, Chapter on the Ten Abodes (previously seen as a separate translation).
The above eleven sutras are all distinct translations of individual chapters from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* consists of forty fascicles, or thirty fascicles, or twenty-seven fascicles, totaling six hundred and nineteen sheets.
It was translated by Kumārajīva at the Xiaoyao Garden in Chang’an during the Hongshi era of the Later Qin dynasty.
The *Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* consists of thirty fascicles, or twenty fascicles, totaling four hundred and sixty [sheets].
Ten sheets; translated by Dharmarakṣa and others at Chenliu during the Yuankang era of the Western Jin dynasty:

*Guangzan Banruo Boluomi Jing* (The Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra of Radiant Praise), ten fascicles, or fifteen fascicles, totaling two hundred and fifteen sheets. Translated by Zhu Fahu at Chang’an during the Taikang era of the Western Jin dynasty:
*Dapin Shangzhi Xinsmallpin Jing* (The First Volume of the Large Version and the New Small Version Sūtra), seven fascicles, totaling one hundred and five sheets.
14 sheets. The *Xiaopin jing* (Shorter Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra), translated by Kumārajīva of the Later Qin, in seven fascicles, totaling 154 sheets;

also known as the *Xin daoxing*. The *Daoxing banruoboluomi jing* (Aṣṭasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra), translated by Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin, in ten fascicles or eight fascicles, totaling 165 sheets;
translated by Zhi Chen of the Later Han. This is the *Daming* (Great Illumination) version of the *Xiaopin jing*.
*Du jing* (Sutra on Crossing Over), six fascicles or four fascicles, ninety-one sheets; translated by Zhi Qian during the Huangwu era of the Wu dynasty.
*Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, five fascicles; some say it was translated at Chang’an by Dharmapriya during the Jianyuan era of the Former Qin.
*Mahāprajñāpāramitā-uttara-sūtra*, four fascicles; a separate translation. The above nine sutras are all... [text continues].

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (Large Sutra on Perfect Wisdom) has several partial translations from the same original text recorded in earlier and later periods; furthermore, there are other separate translations that are missing because their originals were not extant.

The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* in forty fascicles and seven hundred and twenty sheets was translated by Dharmakṣema at Guzang, the capital of Liang, during the Xuanshi era of the Juqu clan of Northern Liang. The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* in thirty-six fascicles and twenty-five chapters was embellished with literary prose by Shi Huiguan and Xie Lingyun during the Yuanjia era of Emperor Wen of the Song dynasty and circulated in the region south of the Yangtze River. The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* in twenty fascicles was translated by Shi Zhimeng in Xiliangzhou during the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty. The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* in six fascicles and one hundred and thirty sheets consists of the first ten fascicles of the aforementioned [thirty-six-fascicle] scripture; it was translated by Shi Faxian at Yangdu during the Yixi era of the Eastern Jin dynasty. These four scriptures share the same original source.
The earlier and later separate translations were still incomplete;
therefore, the original version from the Juqu kingdom consists of this *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* in its entirety, totaling one hundred thousand verses.
Currently, four bundles have been produced, totaling thirty thousand verses;
more than two parts remain to be completed.
If the original text were fully translated into the language of Tang, it would amount to [the following].

Thus, there are more than one hundred scrolls. The *Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra* in thirty fascicles (604 sheets) was translated by Dharmakṣema at the capital of Liang during the Northern Liang dynasty. The *Mahāvaipulya Sūryagarbha Sūtra* in ten (or fifteen) fascicles (204 sheets) was translated by Jñānayaśas at Daxingshan Temple in the capital during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty. The *Mahāvaipulya Candragarbha Sūtra* in ten fascicles (214 sheets) was translated by Jñānayaśas at Ye-du (Yecheng) during the Northern Qi dynasty. The *Mahāvaipulya Mahāsannipāta Sūtra* in eight fascicles (128 sheets) [was also translated by him]. These four aforementioned sūtras are all of the essential purport of the *Sannipāta*; together they comprise 1,150 sheets. Although these were translated separately at different times, when combined they constitute sixty (or fifty-eight) fascicles, as recorded in Fei Changfang’s *Kaihuang Sanbao Ji*.
The *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra* in eight fascicles, also known as the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva Dhāraṇī-īśvara-rāja" from the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra*, consists of one hundred and nineteen pages;
it was translated by Zhu Fahu in Chang’an during the Yuankang era of the Western Jin dynasty.
The *Ākāśagarbha-paripṛcchā-sūtra* in eight fascicles (or six fascicles) is the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha"; [it consists of] one hundred [pages].
The *Bodhisattva-viśuddha-caryā-sūtra* (菩薩淨行經) in two fascicles, translated by Shi Shengjian (世聖堅) of the Xiqifu clan of Western Qin at Henan;
it consists of forty sheets and is the "Ratna-śikhara-bodhisattva-parivarta" (寶髻菩薩品), also known as the *Ratna-śikhara-bodhisattva-sūtra* (寶髻菩薩經).
The *Akṣayamati-nirdeśa-sūtra* (無盡意經) in six fascicles—or alternatively four fascicles—translated by Zhu Fahu (竺法護) in Chang’an during the Yongxi era of the Western Jin.
The *Akṣayamati-sūtra* consists of eighty-six scrolls; it was translated by Zhu Fahu in Chang’an during the Taishi era of the Western Jin dynasty.
The *Akṣayamati-sūtra* in ten scrolls was translated by Fajian during the reign of Emperor Ming of the Song dynasty at Guangzhou.
The *Akṣayamati-sūtra* in seven or four scrolls is the *Akṣayamati-parivarta*, consisting of ninety-two scrolls; it was [translated] by Zhu Fahu during the Yongjia era of the Western Jin dynasty.
Dharmarakṣa translated at Chang’an the *Sūtra of the Minor Aśokasena* in two fascicles and the *Sūtra of the Silent Youth* in two fascicles;
this latter work consists of forty-one pages and belongs to the "Chapter on Silence," also titled the *Sūtra of the Silent Bodhisattva*.

Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin dynasty also translated at Chang’an the *Sūtra of the Precious Woman* in either two or four fascicles; this work consists of sixty-three pages and belongs to the "Chapter on the Precious Woman. (1)
*The Scripture of the Inquiry of the Jewel-Woman on Wisdom*, translated by Dharmarakṣa in Chang’an during the Taikang era of the Western Jin dynasty;
ten fascicles, one hundred twenty-five sheets. *The Ratnolkā Sūtra*, translated by Paramārtha at Daxingshan Temple during the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty; ten fascicles.
*The Scripture of the Bodhisattva Ratnakūṭa*, one fascicle, an excerpt from the "Ratnakūṭa" chapter, forty-eight sheets; also known as the *Bodhisattva [Sūtra]*.
*The Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Sovereign King*, translated by Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin during the Jingxing period; two fascicles.

This is a partial transcription of the *Dhāraṇī Chapter*, with some minor differences. *The Sūtra of the Questions of the Bodhisattva Vigorous King*, translated by Kumārajīva at Chang’an during the Later Qin;
two fascicles, forty-two pages. The first two [fascicles] are the same text separately issued. *The Sūtra of Māra*, translated by Bodhiruci at the capital of Luoyang during the Later Wei.

*The Scripture on the Woman Asking How to Attain a Male Body*, one fascicle; this is a separate translation of the "Ancient Accounts" section of the *Ratnaketu-dhāraṇī Sūtra*, as recorded in the *Baochang lu*.
*The Sumeru-garbha Sūtra*, three fascicles, thirty-eight sheets; translated by Yaśas of the Northern Qi dynasty at Tianping Temple.
These are the fifteen scriptures mentioned above.
This is a separate chapter from the *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra* translated independently;
it is not included in the main text and circulated as a distinct section.
*Mahātejas-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, twenty fascicles, two hundred and sixty-five sheets;
translated at Xingshan Monastery in the capital during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty by Jñānagupta and others.
*Mahādharmolkā-tejas-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, twenty fascicles, three hundred sheets; translated at Shanglin Park in the Eastern Capital during the Daye era of the Sui dynasty by Dharmagupta.
The *Mahābodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra* in twenty fascicles and four hundred ten sheets,
translated at the Yüan Fanjing Guan by Xuanzang at Hongfu Monastery in the capital during the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty;
and the *Bodhisattvamaṇyāvalī-sūtra* in twelve (or fourteen) fascicles and three hundred thirty-seven sheets, translated by Zhu Fonian in Chang’an during the Jianyuan era of the Former Qin.
*The Bodhisattva’s Samādhi of Seeing Reality*, translated by Ye She of the Northern Qi dynasty at the capital of Ye, in fourteen fascicles and two hundred thirty-eight sheets.
*The Sūtra of the Names of Buddhas*, translated by Bodhiruci of the Northern Wei dynasty at the capital of Ye, in twelve fascicles and two hundred forty-seven sheets.
*The Moon Lamp Samādhi Sūtra*, translated [by Dharmakṣema] in eleven fascicles (or ten), totaling two hundred... [sheets].
Two sheets later: During the Tiāntóng era at Yèdū, Yeshé translated the *Bhadrakalpika-sūtra* in thirteen fascicles, totaling one hundred and ninety-five sheets.
During the Yuánkāng era of the Western Jìn dynasty at Cháng'ān, Zhú Fǎhù translated the *Puṣpakūṭa-sūtra* in thirteen fascicles, totaling two hundred and twenty-five sheets.
During the Hóngshǐ era of the Later Qīn dynasty at Cháng'ān, Kumārajīva translated [the same].

*The Scripture on the Ten Abodes and the Severing of Bonds* (Shízhù duànjié jīng), ten fascicles, three hundred fifty-four sheets; translated by Zhu Fonian in Cháng'ān during the Jiànyuàn era of the Former Qín dynasty. *The Great Consecration Scripture* (Dà guǎndìng jīng), twelve fascicles (or nine fascicles), one hundred twelve sheets;

translated by Śrīmitra in Yángdū during the first year of the Eastern Jìn dynasty, under the reign of the Emperor. *The Scripture on the Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha* (Guānfó sānmèi jīng), ten fascicles (or eight fascicles), one hundred fifty-nine sheets; translated by Buddhabhadra in Yángdū during the Yongchūi era of the Song dynasty. *The Scripture of the Compassionate Flower* (Bēihuá jīng), ten fascicles, one hundred ninety-four sheets; translated by Dharmakṣema in Liángdū during the Xuánsī era of the Northern Liáng dynasty. *The Scripture of the White Lotus of Great Compassion* (Dàbēi fēntuólì jīng), eight fascicles, one hundred sixty-five sheets. The two scriptures above are the same original text with different translations.

The *Nianfo Sanmei Jing* (Sutra on the Samādhi of Buddha-Recollection), six fascicles (or five fascicles), ninety-two sheets; translated by Gongdezhí at Yangdu during the Daming era of the Song dynasty. The *Dafangdeng Daji Pusa Nianfo Sanmei Jing* (The Great Vaipulya Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra on the Bodhisattva’s Samādhi of Buddha-Recollection), ten fascicles, one hundred and thirty-two sheets; translated by Jñānagupta at the Translation Hall in the Shanglin Garden at the Eastern Capital during the Daye era of the Sui dynasty. These two sutras are translations of the same original text.

The *Mahāvaipulya Daśacakrakṣitigarbha Sūtra*, eight fascicles, one hundred and ten sheets; the *Mahāyāna Mahāsannipāta Kṣitigarbha Daśacakrakṣitigarbha Sūtra*, ten fascicles, one hundred and seventy-one sheets. Translated by Xuanzang at the Great Ci’en Monastery in the capital during the Yonghui era of the Tang dynasty by imperial decree. These two sūtras are translations of the same original text.

The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* (Correct Dharma Lotus Sutra) in ten fascicles, totaling one hundred and eighty-nine sheets, was translated by Dharmarakṣa in Chang’an during the Taikang era of the Western Jin dynasty. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* in seven or eight fascicles, totaling one hundred and forty-eight sheets, was translated by Kumārajīva in Chang’an during the Hongshi era of the Later Qin dynasty. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* in eight fascicles, totaling one hundred and fifty-five sheets, has the "Entrusting Chapter" (*Parīndanā-parivarta*) moved to the end and adds the "Herbs Chapter" (*Oṣadhi-parivarta*) for five sheets; the dharanis differ. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* in eight fascicles, totaling one hundred and fifty-five sheets, was translated by Jñānagupta at Xingshan Monastery in the second year of the Renshou era of the Sui dynasty. These three sutras are the same original work with different translations.

The *Laṅkāvatāra-ratna-sūtra* in four fascicles and ninety-two pages was translated by Guṇabhadra at the capital of Yang during the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty. The *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* in ten fascicles and one hundred seventy-five pages was translated by Bodhiruci at the capital of Luo during the Later Wei dynasty. These two sutras are translations of the same original text.

*The Sūtra of the Names of Five Thousand Five Hundred Buddhas*, eight fascicles, one hundred twenty-six sheets; translated at Xingshan Monastery in the capital during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty by Jñānagupta. *The Mahā-upāya-kauśalya-buddha-pratyupakāra-sūtra*, seven fascicles, one hundred twenty-four sheets; translator lost, appearing in the *Baochang lu*. *The Bodhisattvacaryā-upāya-viṣaya-ṛddhi-vikurvaṇa-sūtra*, three fascicles, forty-seven sheets. *The Mahāsāṃghika-nirgrantha-putra-sūtra*, seven fascicles (or eight), one hundred thirty-one sheets; translated at the residence of the Prince of Runan in the capital Luoyang during the Yanchang era of the Later Wei by Bodhiruci. The above two sūtras are different translations of the same original text.

The *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra* (Sheng Tianwang Banruo Jing), seven fascicles, one hundred and twenty-one sheets; translated during the Chen dynasty by Vasurendra, Prince of the Yuezhi kingdom, at Jiangzhou. The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* (Jin Guangming Jing), six fascicles—or sometimes seven or eight—totaling one hundred and fifteen sheets; translated by Dharmakṣema of the Northern Liang dynasty. The first four fascicles were translated by Paramārtha of the Chen dynasty for the latter three. The *Ratnamegha-sūtra* (Baoyun Jing), seven fascicles, one hundred sheets; translated at Yangdu by Mandaraka during the Liang dynasty. The *Dharmasaṃgīti-sūtra* (Faji Jing), six fascicles—or sometimes seven—totaling one hundred and twenty-two sheets; translated at Luoyang by Bodhiruci of the Later Wei dynasty. The *Bodhisattvagarbha-sūtra* (Pusa Chutai Jing), five fascicles, one hundred and thirteen sheets; translated at Chang’an by Zhu Fonian of the Former Qin dynasty.
*Mahākaruṇā-sūtra*, five fascicles, eighty-eight sheets; translated at Ye-du (Yecheng) by Yaśas during the Tiāntǒng era of the Northern Qi dynasty.
*Mahāsannipāta-Bhadrapāla-bodhisattva-sūtra*, five or six fascicles, ninety-three sheets;
translated at Dàxīngshàn Temple during the Kāihuáng era of the Sui dynasty by Yaśas. *Mahāmegha-sūtra*, six fascicles, also titled *Mahāvaipulya-nirnimitta*.
In ninety-two sheets, translated in Chang’an by Zhu Fonian of the Former Qin;

the Record of Baochang states that Dharmakṣema translated the *Vajrapāṇi-mañjuśrī-sūtra* (Miji jinganglishi jing) in five fascicles and one hundred twelve sheets at the Neiyuan Monastery in the capital of Liang;
translated by Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin, appearing in the Record of Zhi Mindu; the *Mahāvaipulya-dhāraṇī*.
*Sāgaranāgarājaparipṛcchā-sūtra*, four fascicles, sixty-two sheets; translated by the Northern Liang monk Shi Fazhong at Gaochang Commandery.
*Sāgaranāgarājaparipṛcchā-sūtra*, four fascicles, seventy-three sheets; translated by Dharmakṣema of the Northern Liang at Liangcheng.
*Aṅgulimālīya-sūtra*, four fascicles, seventy-eight sheets; translated during the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty by Guṇabhadra at Yangdu.
*The Sutra of the Bodhisattva Anupalipta* (Wúsuǒyǒu púsà jīng), four fascicles, sixty sheets; translated by Dharmagupta and others at Daxingshan Monastery during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty.
*The Saṃghāṭa Sūtra* (Sēngqiézhà jīng), four fascicles, fifty-one sheets; translated by Prince Moksagupta at the capital of Ye during the Later Wei dynasty.
*The Sutra on Contemplating All Dharmas* (Guānchá zhūfǎ jīng), four fascicles, sixty sheets; translated during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty.
Kumārajīva and others translated the *Saptabuddha-mantra-sūtra* in four fascicles (70 sheets) at Daxingshan Temple;
the *Mahādruma-kinnara-rāja-paripṛcchā-sūtra* in four fascicles (65 sheets);
and during the Hongshi era of the Later Qin, Kumārajīva translated the *Cundarāja-paripṛcchā-sūtra* in two or three fascicles (57 sheets) in Chang’an.
Paper manuscript: translated by Zhi Chen at the capital Luò during the Jiànníng era of the Later Hàn dynasty. The above two sūtras are different translations of the same original text.

*The Sūtra of the Questions of the Bodhisattva Dhāraṇīdhara*, four fascicles, fifty-three sheets; translated by Zhú Fǎhù in Cháng'ān during the Western Jìn dynasty. *The Sūtra of Holding the World* (also titled *The Sūtra of the Dharma Seal*), four fascicles, seventy-five sheets; translated by Kumārajīva in Cháng'ān during the Hóngshǐ era of the Later Qín dynasty. The above two sūtras are different translations of the same original text.

*Hongdao guangxian sanmei jing* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of Extensively Manifesting the Broad Way), four fascicles, fifty-three sheets; translated by Zhu Fahu in Chang’an during the Yongjia era of the Western Jin dynasty. *Anouda longwang jing* (Sūtra of the Dragon King Anavatapta), two fascicles (or three), fifty-two sheets; also titled *Anou qingfo jing* (Sūtra of the Invitation of the Buddha by Anavatapta); translated by Zhu Fahu in Chang’an during the Western Jin dynasty. These two sūtras are different translations of the same original text.
*Bodhisattvapūrvacaryā-sūtra*, three fascicles, fifty-two sheets; translated by Kumārajīva at Cháng'ān during the Hongshǐ era of the Later Qin dynasty.
*Sarvabuddhaguṇavyūha-sūtra*, three fascicles, fifty-five sheets; translated by Kumārajīva at Cháng'ān during the Hongshǐ era of the Later Qin dynasty.
*Bodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra*, three fascicles, sixty-one sheets; translated by Kumārajīva of the Later Qin dynasty. *Balavyūha-samādhi-sūtra*, three fascicles, forty [sheets].
Six sheets: Translated by Jñānayaśas at Xingshan Monastery during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty, *Sūdhana-devaputra-sūtra*, three fascicles (or four fascicles), forty-six sheets.

Translated by Dharmarakṣa in Chang’an during the Taishi era of the Western Jin dynasty, *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra*, three fascicles (or two fascicles), forty-one sheets. Translated by [Kumārajīva] during the Hongshi era of the Later Qin dynasty... [Luo]... (Note:

The source text appears to be a fragment of a bibliographic catalog, likely the *Kaiyuan Shijiao Lu* or a similar work. The final character "羅" (Luo) likely refers to the beginning of the name of the translator for the next entry, such as Kumārajīva.)
The *Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra* (Banzhou sanmei jing), three fascicles (or two fascicles), forty-seven sheets; translated by Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin.
The *Samādhi of Universal Transcendence Sūtra* (Puchao sanmei jing), three fascicles, sixty-seven sheets; translated by Dharmarakṣa in Chang’an during the Taikang era of the Western Jin.
The *Ajātaśatru-rāja Sūtra* (Ajiashi wang jing), two fascicles, fifty-four sheets; translated by Zhi Chen of the Later Han.
The two sutras translated above are different translations of the same original text.

*The Sutra on the Samādhi of the Equal Collection of All Virtues*, three fascicles (or two fascicles), forty-nine sheets, translated by Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin; *The Sutra on the Samādhi of the Collection of All Merits*, three fascicles, forty-eight sheets. These two sutras are different translations of the same original text.

The *Ārya-Suvikrāntavikrami-paripṛcchā-sūtra* in three fascicles and fifty-five pages, translated by Dharmaruci of the Later Wei dynasty at the capital of Luoyang; the *Māyopama-samādhi-sūtra* in three fascicles (or alternatively four) and fifty-six pages, translated by Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin dynasty; and the *Mahāvaipulya-Suvikrāntavikrami-paripṛcchā-sūtra* in four fascicles and sixty-eight pages, translated by Jñānagupta at the Translation Hall in the Eastern Capital during the Daye era of the Sui dynasty—these three sūtras are the same text with different translations.

*The Sutra of the Vast, Majestic, Pure, and Non-retrogressive Wheel of Dharma*, four fascicles (or six fascicles), seventy-eight sheets; translated at the capital of Yangdu by Zhiyan and others during the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty. *The Sutra of the Non-retrogressive Wheel of Dharma*, four fascicles, seventy-seven sheets; *The Sutra of the Avivartiya*, three fascicles (or four fascicles), sixty-one sheets; translated by Dharmarakṣa during the Taikang era of the Western Jin dynasty. These three sutras are different translations of the same original text.

The *Suyāmasaṃcodana-sūtra* (思益梵天問經), four fascicles, eighty-two sheets; translated by Kumārajīva at Cháng'ān during the Hongshǐ era of the Later Qín dynasty. The *Cittadhārā-suyāmasaṃcodana-sūtra* (持心梵天所問經), either four or six fascicles, ninety-four sheets; also titled *Samatā-sarvadharmādhipati* (等御諸法) or *Buddhadharmālaṃkāra* (莊嚴佛法); translated by Dharmarakṣa during the Tàikāng era of the Western Jìn dynasty. The *Suvikrāntavikrāmī-suyāmasaṃcodana-sūtra* (勝思惟梵天所問經), six fascicles, one hundred sheets; translated by Bodhiruci at Luòyáng during the Northern Wèi dynasty. These three sūtras are the same original text with different translations.

*The Sūtra on the Buddha Ascending to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven to Preach the Dharma for His Mother*, in two fascicles (or three fascicles), thirty-six sheets; translated by Dharmarakṣa in Chang’an during the Taikang era of the Western Jin dynasty. *The Sūtra on the Infinite Transformations of the Divine Footsteps of the Way*, in four fascicles (or two fascicles), fifty-one sheets; translated by An Fagin in Luoyang during the Taikang era of the Western Jin dynasty. The above two sūtras are the same original work with different translations.

The *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* in five fascicles and seventy-two sheets was translated by Bodhiruci of the Northern Wei at the capital of Luoyang. The *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* in five fascicles and seventy-three sheets was translated by Xuanzang at Ci'en Monastery in the capital during the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty. The *Anupūrvasamudgata-parivarta-sūtra* in eighteen sheets was translated by Guṇabhadra during the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty. The *Vibhaṅga-sūtra* in ten sheets was translated by Paramārtha during the Chen dynasty. These four sūtras are different translations of the same original text.

The *Vimalakīrti-sūtra* in two fascicles and fifty-two pages was translated by Zhi Qian at Wuchang during the Huangwu era of the Wu dynasty. The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* in three fascicles and sixty-one pages was translated by Kumārajīva at the Xiaoyao Garden during the Hongshi era of the Later Qin. The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* in six fascicles and ninety-seven pages was translated by Xuanzang at the Great Ci'en Monastery during the Zhenguan era of the Tang. These three sūtras are the same text with different translations.

*The Sutra on the Non-Activity of All Dharmas*, two fascicles, thirty-one pages; translated by Kumārajīva during the Hongshi era of the Later Qin dynasty. *The Sutra on the Fundamental Activity of All Dharmas*, three fascicles, forty-eight pages; translated by Jñānagupta and others at Daxingshan Monastery during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty. The above two sutras constitute a single work with different translations.

*Wújí Bǎo Sānmèijīng* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of the Ultimate Treasure), one fascicle, thirty sheets; translated by Dharmarakṣa during the Yongjia era of the Western Jin dynasty. *Bǎo Rúlái Sānmèijīng* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of the Treasure Tathāgata), two fascicles, thirty sheets. The above two sūtras are different translations of the same original text.

*The Vaipulya Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, two fascicles, thirty-five sheets; translated at the capital of Yangdu by Buddhabhadra together with Faxian during the Eastern Jin dynasty. *The Sūtra of Lamentation and Weeping*, two fascicles, thirty sheets. *The Sūtra of the Four Boys*, three fascicles, forty-two sheets; translated at Daxingshan Temple by Jñānagupta and others during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty. The above three sūtras are different translations of the same original text.

*The Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Prajñottara on Great Skillful Means*, two fascicles, thirty sheets; translated by Dharmarakṣa during the Taikang era of the Western Jin dynasty. *The Mahāyāna Sūtra of Skillful Means*, three fascicles (or two), forty-one sheets; translated by the Indian layman Zhu Nanti at the capital of Luoyang during the Yuanxi era of the Western Jin dynasty. These two sūtras are the same text with different translations.

The *Mañjuśrī-buddhakṣetraguṇavyūha-sūtra* (文殊師利現寶藏經), three fascicles, thirty-three pages, translated by Dharmarakṣa during the Taishi era of the Western Jin dynasty; and the *Mahāvaipulya-ratnakaraṇḍa-sūtra* (大方廣寶篋經), three fascicles, thirty pages. These two sūtras are the same text with different translations.

*The Scripture on the Bodhisattva Samantacakṣus Asking about Samādhi*, two fascicles (or three fascicles), fifty-one sheets; translated by Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin. *The Scripture on the Fifty Calculations of the Prajñāpāramitā*, two fascicles, forty sheets; translated by An Shigao of the Later Han. *The Scripture on the Original Vocation and Adornments of the Bodhisattvas*, two fascicles, thirty-eight sheets; translated by Zhu Fonian at Chang’an during the Former Qin.

*The Scripture on the Bodhisattva Guardian of the State*, two fascicles, forty-two pages; translated at Daxingshan Monastery by Ratnamati and others during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty. *The Scripture on the Samādhi of Transcending Solar Radiance*, two fascicles, forty-six pages; translated by Dharmarakṣa during the Taishi era of the Western Jin dynasty. *The Scripture on the Daughter of the Moon*, two fascicles, twenty-seven pages; translated by Ratnamati during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty. *The Scripture on the Intermediate State*, two fascicles, twenty-seven pages; translated by Zhu Fonian in Chang’an during the Former Qin dynasty.
*The Sūtra on the Storehouse of Mount Sumeru*, two fascicles, thirty-eight sheets; translated by Yeśa at the capital of Ye during the Later Qi dynasty.

*The Buddha’s Flower Adornment Entering the Inconceivable Realm of the Tathāgata*, two fascicles, twenty-one sheets; translated by Jñānagupta at Daxingshan Temple during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty.
*The Great Dharma Drum Sūtra*, two fascicles, thirty-one sheets; translated by Guṇabhadra of the Song dynasty.
Bodhirmarṣa translated at Yangdu the *Sūtra of the Essential Collection of All Buddhas* in two fascicles, thirty-one pages; translated by Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin.
He also translated the *Sūtra on the Adorned Purity of Mañjuśrī’s Buddha-field* in two fascicles, thirty-four pages;
translated by Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin during the Yongxi era at Luoyang. Furthermore, he translated the *Anuttara-pāramitā-bhikṣā-caryā of the Bodhisattva Ruciraketu*.

A sūtra in two fascicles and twenty-seven sheets, also titled *The Sūtra on the Samādhi of Resolving that All Dharmas are Like Illusions*, translated during the Song dynasty by Master Yue at Nanhai Commandery;

*The Mahāyāna-samatā-nirdeśa-sūtra* in two fascicles and thirty-nine sheets, translated during the Tianhe era of the Later Zhou by Ratnamati together with Seng’an at Chang’an; and *The Mahāsannipāta-dṛṣṭāntarāja-sūtra* in two fascicles.
Thirty-two pages; translated at Xingshan Monastery during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty by Dharmagupta and others:
*The Scripture on the Buddha-land of Akṣobhya*, two fascicles, thirty-eight pages; also titled *The Scripture on the Bodhisattva Training in the Buddha-field*.

Translated at Luoyang during the Jianhe era of the Later Han by Zhi Chen: *The Scripture on the Lotus Face*, two fascicles, twenty-three pages; [translated] during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty.
The *Kāśyapa Sūtra* in two fascicles and twenty-nine sheets, translated by Yanjie;
the *Mahāmāyūrī Vidyārājñī Dhāraṇī Sūtra* in two fascicles and thirty-two sheets, translated by Prince Moposhouna of the Later Wei at the capital Luoyang;
and the *Sūtra on the Awakening of Pure Mind* in two fascicles and twenty-seven sheets, translated by Saṃghavarman at the Zhanyun Hall in the capital Yangdu during the Liang dynasty.

During the Kaihuang era of the Chen dynasty, Dharmagupta and others translated the *Anuttarāśrayasūtra* (The Sutra on the Supreme Basis) in two fascicles and thirty-one sheets at Daxingshan Monastery.
During the Chen dynasty, Paramārtha translated the *Vijñānasaṃkrāntisūtra* (The Sutra on the Transmigration of Consciousness) in two fascicles and thirty-three sheets in Guangzhou.

During the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty, Dharmagupta and others translated the *Adbhutadharmaparyāyasūtra* (The Sutra on the Unprecedented Causes and Conditions) in two fascicles and four [sheets] at Xingshan Monastery.
Ten sheets: The *Tathāgatagarbha-sūtra* (translated as *Dafangguang rulai xing jing*) in two fascicles, or three, by Tanying of the Southern Qi dynasty at Yangdu;
fifty-one sheets. The *Acintya-guṇa-sūtra* (translated as *Bukeshiyi gongde jing*) in two fascicles, or four, thirty-eight sheets.
The *Mahā-maṅgala-mantra-sūtra* (translated as *Daji yi zhou jing*) in two fascicles, or four, thirty-eight sheets. The *Bodhisattva-svapna-sūtra* in two [fascicles].
Scroll 34: *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra*, 2 fascicles, 39 sheets;
*Bhadrakalpikā-rājaprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, 2 fascicles, 28 sheets; *Dharmadhātuprakṛtyasambhedanirdeśa-sūtra*, 2 fascicles, 24 sheets;
*Guhyakapārṣadyavajrapāṇi-sūtra*, 2 fascicles, 36 sheets; *Mahāvaipulyatathāgata-...* [text truncated]
The *Guhyagarbha Sūtra*, two fascicles, twenty-four sheets; the *Sūtra of the Questions of Bodhisattva Subāhu*, two fascicles, twenty-six sheets;
the *Sūtra of the Great Pure Dharma Gate*, one fascicle, twenty-four sheets, translated by Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin;
the *Sūtra of the Dharma Gate of Great Adornment*, two fascicles, twenty-six sheets, translated by Yaśas during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty. The above.
These two sūtras are translations of the same original text.

*The Sūtra on Accordance with Expedient Means* (Shunquan fangbian jing), in two fascicles—or one fascicle, twenty-seven pages—also titled *The Sūtra on the Bodhisattva’s Transformation of Female Form* (Zhuan nüshen pusa jing), was translated by Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin. *The Sūtra on the Joyful Adornment of Necklaces and Expedient Means* (Yue yingluo zhuangyan fangbian jing), in one fascicle, twenty-five pages, was translated by Faha of the Song dynasty. The above two sūtras are different translations of the same original text.

*Mahāmegha-ādhyeṣaṇa-varṣa-sūtra*, one fascicle, twenty-two pages; translated by Jñānagupta in Chang’an during the Later Zhou dynasty. *Mahāmegha-cakra-ādhyeṣaṇa-varṣa-sūtra*, two fascicles, twenty-eight pages; translated by Jñāya during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty. *Mahāvaipulya-mahāmegha-ādhyeṣaṇa-varṣa-sūtra*, one fascicle, nine pages; translated by Jñānagupta at Xingshan Monastery during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty. The above three sūtras are translations of the same original text.

*The Sūtra on the Adornment of the Realm and Wisdom of All Buddhas*, one fascicle, eleven pages; translated by Saṃghavarman at the capital of Yang during the Tianjian era of the Liang dynasty. *The Sūtra on the Entrance into the Buddha’s Realm through the Light of the Tathāgata’s Adorned Wisdom*, one fascicle, thirty-four pages; translated by Bodhiruci at the capital of Luo during the Later Wei dynasty. *The Sūtra on the Adornment of the Light of the Realm and Wisdom of All Buddhas*, one fascicle, seventeen pages. The above three sūtras are translations of the same original text with different translations.

*The Scripture of the Youth Candraprabha*, one fascicle, eight sheets; there is also another fascicle of the same name that is incomplete. Translated by Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin. *The Scripture of Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa*, one fascicle. *The Scripture of the Elder Guhagupta*, two fascicles, twenty-six sheets. Translated by Jñānayaśas at Chang’an during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty. These three scriptures are different translations of the same original text.

*Mahāvaipulya-śikhara-rāja-sūtra*, one fascicle, twenty sheets; also known as *Vimalakīrti-putra-paripṛcchā-sūtra*. *Mahāyāna-śikhara-rāja-sūtra*, one fascicle, sixteen sheets. *Susīma-kumāra-sūtra*, two fascicles, twenty sheets. Translated by Jñānagupta during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty. The three sūtras above are of the same original text.

*The Sūtra of the Questions of the Householder Ugga*, one fascicle, twenty-four sheets; translated by the Wei dynasty monk Kang Sengkai in Luoyang. *The Sūtra of the Questions of Sudatta on the Bodhisattva Practice*, one fascicle, twenty-five sheets; translated by Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin dynasty. *The Dharmādarśa-sūtra*, two fascicles, twenty-three sheets; translated by An Xuan and Buddhasmṛti of the Later Han dynasty. The above three sūtras are the same original text.

The *Wúliàng qīngjìng děngjué jīng* (Sūtra on the Immeasurable Pure Equal Enlightenment), two fascicles, sixty sheets; translated by Bóyán at Luòyáng Temple during the Wèi dynasty. The *Āmítuó jīng* (Amitābha Sūtra), two fascicles, fifty-three sheets; translated by Zhīqián at Wǔchāng during the Huángwǔ era of the Wú dynasty. The *Wúliàngshòu jīng* (Immeasurable Life Sūtra), two fascicles, forty-nine sheets; translated by Zhú Fáhù during the Yǒngjiā era of the Western Jìn dynasty. The three sūtras above share the same original text.

The *Ākāśagarbha-bodhisattva-sūtra* in two fascicles, translated by Dharmamitra at the capital of Yangdu during the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty; the *Ākāśagarbha-bodhisattva-sūtra* in one fascicle and twenty-seven pages, translated by Buddhayaśas of the Later Qin at Kapiśī and brought to this land; and the *Ākāśagarbha-bodhisattva-dhāraṇī-sūtra* in seventeen pages, translated by Jñānagupta during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty—these four sūtras are of the same original text. The *Ākāśagarbha-bodhisattva-sūtra* in two fascicles and thirty pages was translated by Jñānagupta during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty. These aforementioned four sūtras share the same source.

*Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*, two fascicles, twenty-two sheets; translated by Dharmagupta at the Translation Hall in the Shanglin Garden of the Eastern Capital during the Daye era of the Sui dynasty. *Vibhaṅga-pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*, two fascicles, twenty-two sheets; translated by Xuanzang at the Great Ci'en Monastery during the Yonghui era of the Tang dynasty. These two sūtras are translations of the same original text.
*The Sūtra of the Tathāgata Supreme Lamp King of the East*, thirteen sheets; translated at Daxingshan Temple by Jñānagupta during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty.
*The Sūtra of the Supreme King of All Dharmas*, twenty-two sheets; translated at Daxingshan Temple by Jñānagupta during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty.
*The Sūtra of the Samādhi of Perfect Radiance*, twenty-two sheets; [translated] during the Later Han dynasty by An Shigao.
At that time, Zhi Yao translated the *Sudāna-jātaka-sūtra* (The Sutra of Prince Sudāna) in sixteen sheets at the capital of Luoyang;
during the era of Fa Jian of the Western Qin under Qifu Guoren, [it was also] translated in Henan; Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin translated the *Sūrata-sūtra* (The Sutra of Sūrata) in nineteen sheets;
and during the Huangwu era of the Wu dynasty, Zhi Qian translated the *Suvarṇavarṇa-rāja-sūtra* (The Sutra of King Suvarṇavarṇa).
*The Scripture on the Samādhi of Self-Vow and Sole Testimony*, eight sheets; translated by Bodhiruci of the Later Wei dynasty at the capital of Luoyang;
also titled *The Scripture on the Tathāgata’s Self-Vow Samādhi*, translated by Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin dynasty.
*The Mahāmāyā Sūtra*, twenty-five sheets; translated by Tanjing of the Southern Qi dynasty at the capital of Yangdu. *The Mahāvaipulya Tathāgatagarbha Sūtra*.
Nine sheets: translated at the capital of Yangdu by Buddhabhadra during the Yixi era of the Eastern Jin dynasty;
*Tathāgata-upāyakauśalya-mantra-sūtra*, eleven sheets: translated during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty by Jñānagupta;
*Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-ekayāna-mahopāya-sūtra*, nineteen sheets: [translated] at the capital of Yangdu by Guṇabhadra during the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty.
*The Sūtra of Sumati*, translated by Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin Dynasty, eight sheets; also known as *The Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Sumati*.
*The Sūtra on the Rare and Meritorious Comparison*, translated by Jñānagupta during the Kaihuang era of the Sui Dynasty, six sheets.
*The Sūtra of the Brahmin Girl Śrīmatī*, translated by Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin Dynasty, five sheets. *The Sūtra of the Prediction for Kṣemapati*, four sheets.
The *Candraprabha-bodhisattva-sūtra* in three sheets was translated by Dharmaruci at the capital of Luoyang during the Later Wei dynasty;

the *Samantamukha-parivarta-nirdeśa* (also known as the *Mie shifang ming jing*) in six sheets was translated by Zhi Qian during the Huangwu era of the Wu dynasty; the *Bodhicittotpāda-sūtra* in eleven sheets was translated by Dharmarakṣa during the Yuanxi era of the Western Jin dynasty;
and the *Pǔ...* [text fragment] was translated by Jñānagupta at Daxingshan Temple during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty.
*The Scripture on the Chapter of the Gates*, twelve sheets; translated by Dharmarakṣa during the Taikang era of the Western Jin dynasty.
*The Scripture of the Devaputra Śreṣṭhī*, sixteen sheets; translated by Ratnabhadra and others at Daxingshan Temple during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty.

*The Scripture of the Sun-Brightness*, three sheets; translated by Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin dynasty. *The Scripture of the Moon-Lamp Samādhi*, ten sheets; also known as *The [Scripture of] Mañjuśrī*.
*The Scripture on the Samādhi of Establishing Wisdom through the Practice of Ten Matters*, translated during the Song dynasty by the former Lord [Kumārajīva];
*The Scripture Spoken by the Bodhisattva Acintyaprabha*, twelve sheets, also known as *The Scripture of the Childlike Bodhisattva Acintyaprabha*, translated by Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin;
*The Scripture on Mañjuśrī’s Inquiry into the Bodhisattva Stations*, twenty sheets, also known as *Inquiry into the Stations*.
The *Sūtra of Prince Virtuous Light* (*De-guang taizi jing*), nineteen sheets, translated during the reign of Emperor Ling of the Later Han by Zhi Chen;

also known as the *Sūtra of Sulābha Questioning Prince Virtuous Light*. The *Sūtra on the Merit of Offering Lamps* (*Shi deng gongde jing*), fourteen sheets, translated at Chang’an during the Taishi era of the Western Jin by Zhu Fahu.
The *Bodhisattva’s Rebuke of Lust and Desire* (*Pusa he seyu jing*), translated at Ye by Yashas during the Northern Qi dynasty.
Two sheets; translated by Kumārajīva at Cháng'ān during the Hóngshǐ era of the Later Qín dynasty. *Puruṣotpatti-sūtra*, fourteen sheets;
translated by Ān Shìgāo during the reign of Emperor Huán of the Later Hàn dynasty. *Puruṣaparamparā-sūtra*; original text lost, translated by Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jìn dynasty.
*Anutvaviśeṣa-sūtra*, six sheets; translated by Dharmaruci of the Northern Wèi dynasty. *Buddhabhāṣita-sūtra*, three [sheets].

*The Sutra of the Jewel Casket of Wordlessness*, six sheets, translated by Dharmaruci of the Later Wei; *The Sutra of the Tathāgata’s Lion’s Roar*, five sheets, translated by Dharmaruci of the Later Wei;
*The Sutra of the Ten Dharmas*, twenty sheets, translated by Bodhisattva Dharmaruci together with Buddhasanta of the Later Wei;
[The above] include the character "Mahāyāna" [in their titles]. Translated by Saṃghavarman at the capital of Yang during the Putong era of the Liang dynasty.
*The Sutra on the Seal of Entering the Unconditioned*, twenty-one fascicles, translated by Dharmaruci of the Northern Wei;

*The Sutra of the Divine Mantra of the Names of the Twelve Buddhas*, six fascicles, translated by Jñānagupta during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty; *The Sutra of the Reversal of Māra*, eighteen fascicles, translated by Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin during the Taikang era;
and *The Sutra for Saving Those Who Study the Vaipulya*, fourteen fascicles, translated by Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin.
*The Sūtra on the Fifty Conditions of the Bodhisattva’s Practice*, translated by Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin Dynasty, six sheets;
*The Sūtra of the Inner Treasury of a Hundred Jewels*, translated by Zhi Chen during the reign of Emperor Ling of the Later Han Dynasty, eight sheets;
*The Mahāvaipulya Dhāraṇī Sūtra*, translated by Vinītāruci during the Kaihuang era of the Sui Dynasty, thirteen sheets; *The Sūtra of the Original Vows Asked by Maitreya Bodhisattva*.
The *Mañjuśrī-bhāṣita-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, eight sheets, translated by Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin;

the *Sthira-mātṛkā-sūtra*, twenty sheets, translated by Mandaraka at the capital of Yangdu during the Tianjian era of the Liang dynasty; the *Dṛḍha-mātṛkā-sūtra*, six sheets, translated by Yaśas during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty;
the *Sādhana-kuśala-karma-nirdeśa-sūtra*, nine sheets, translated by Faqian of the Later Qin; and the *Bodhisattva-janma-bhūmi-sūtra*.
The *Cāmarakṣa Sūtra*, three sheets; translated by Zhi Qian during the Huangwu era of the Wu dynasty. Also known as the *Sihāsana Samādhi Sūtra*. Eleven sheets.
Also known as the *Bodhisattva-mārga-vṛkṣa Sūtra* or the *Mārga-vṛkṣa Samādhi Sūtra*. Translated by Zhi Qian during the Huangwu era of the Wu dynasty.
The *Ratnajāla Sūtra*, twenty-three sheets; also known as the *Ratnajāla-kumāra Sūtra*. Western Jin dynasty.

*The Sutra of the Names of One Hundred Buddhas*, translated by Dharmarakṣa, six sheets; *The Sutra of Immeasurable Meanings*, translated by Jñānayaśas during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty, seventeen sheets;
*The Sutra of the Visualization of Maitreya’s Ascent to Tuṣita Heaven*, translated by Dharmakṣema at Guangzhou in the Jianyuan era of the Southern Qi dynasty, eight sheets;
*The Sutra of the Visualization of Immeasurable...*, translated by Juqu Ananghou of Northern Liang.
The *Āyuṣparyanta-sūtra*, sixteen sheets; translated at the capital of Yangdu during the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty by Jñānayaśas.

The *Bhadracaryā-praṇidhāna-sūtra* (Sūtra on Contemplating the Practices of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva), sixteen sheets; translated at the capital of Yangdu during the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty by Dharmamitra.

The *Bhaiṣajyarāja-bhaiṣajyasamudgata-bodhisattva-sūtra* (Sūtra on Contemplating the Two Bodhisattvas Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata), nineteen sheets; translated at the capital of Yangdu during the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty by Jñānayaśas.
*The Sutra on the Invocation of Avalokiteśvara to Eliminate and Subdue Poisonous Harm*, eleven sheets; translated during the Song dynasty by the foreign maritime merchant Zhu Nanti.
*The Sutra on the Prediction of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara*, fourteen sheets; translated during the Song dynasty by Dharmakṣema at the capital of Yangdu.
*The Sutra of the Mother of Deer*, four sheets; translated during the Western Jin dynasty by Zhu Fahu. *The Sutra of the Child of the Deer*, three sheets; translated during the Wu dynasty.

*Jianxing nian Zhi Qian yanyi Chukong zaihuang jing* (The Scripture on Eliminating Fear and Calamity), 15 sheets; translated during the Wei dynasty by Bo Yan. *Wenshi xiyu zhongseng jing* (The Scripture on Bathing the Assembly of Monks in the Warm Chamber), 3 sheets;
translated during the Western Jin dynasty by Zhu Fahu. *Sibuke de jing* (The Scripture on the Four Unobtainables), 4 sheets;

translated during the Western Jin dynasty by Zhu Fahu. *Futian jing* (The Scripture on the Field of Merit), 6 sheets—also known as the *Zhude futian jing* (The Scripture on the Field of Merit for All Virtuous Ones). West.
*The Sutra on the Merit of Leaving Home*, translated by Dharmakṣema and Dharmasthiti et al. of the Jin dynasty, four sheets.

*The Sutra on Entering the Essential Nature of the Dharma-realm*, translated by Zhi Qian during the Wu period, ten sheets. *The Sutra on Maitreya Attaining Buddhahood*, one scroll, seventeen sheets; translated by Jñānagupta et al. at Daxingshan Temple during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty.
*The Sutra on Maitreya’s Descent*, translated by Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin dynasty.
*The Sūtra on Birth*, six sheets; also known as *The Sūtra on Maitreya Receiving the Prediction*, translated by Kumārajīva during the Hongshi era of the Later Qin dynasty.
*The Sūtra on Maitreya’s Coming*, three sheets; a search for the original manuscript. These three sūtras above share the same source but are different translations.
*Amoghapāśakalparāja Sūtra*, ten sheets; translated by Jñānagupta during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty. *Amoghapāśavidyāmantra Sūtra*, twelve sheets;
translated by Xuanzang during the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty. *Sūtra of the Shorter Amitāyus*, four sheets;
translated by Guṇabhadra at the capital of Yangdu during the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty. *Amitāyurbuddha Sūtra*, five sheets; translated during the Later Qin dynasty.
The *Sūtra on the Buddha’s Acceptance of the Praise of the Pure Land*, translated by Kumārajīva during the Hongshi era, consists of ten sheets. The three aforementioned sūtras share the same source;

they were translated by Xuanzang at Ci’en Monastery during the Yonghui era of the Tang dynasty, comprising thirteen sheets. The *Sūtra of the Medicine Master Lapis Lazuli Light* is annotated by the world as being of doubtful authenticity;
it was translated by Huìjiǎn of Lùnyè Monastery in the Fǎngdū capital of the Song dynasty, based on the original vows of the Medicine Master Tathāgata.
Twelve sheets; translated by Jinamitra at the Shōrin-en Garden in the Eastern Capital during the Daye era of the Sui dynasty:
*The Scripture on the Merit of the Original Vows of Bhaisajyaguru Tathāgata*, twelve sheets. The three scriptures above are the same text with different translations.
Translated by Xuanzang at Ci’en Monastery in the Capital during the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty: *The Scripture of the Old Mother*, two sheets, also known as *The Scripture of the Old Woman*.
The *Lǎomǔ liùyīng jīng* (Sūtra of the Six Heroines of Old Age), translated during the Wu dynasty by Zhi Qian; two sheets. The above two sūtras are different translations of the same original text.

The *Wénshūshìlì xúnxíng jīng* (Sūtra of Mañjuśrī’s Perambulation), translated during the Later Wei dynasty by Dharmaruci; five sheets. The *Wénshūshīlí xíngjīng* (Sūtra of Mañjuśrī’s Practice), translated during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty by Jñānagupta;
seven sheets. The above two sūtras are different translations of the same original text. The *Jīngāng shàngwèi tuóluóní jīng* (Sūtra of the Vajra-Supreme-Taste Dhāraṇī).
The *Roni Sūtra*, fourteen sheets, translated by Buddhayaśas during the Northern Wei dynasty;
the *Vajramaṇḍala Dhāraṇī Sūtra*, fourteen sheets, upper volume—these two sūtras are the same text translated separately. Translated by Jñānagupta during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty;
the *Samyakgaurava Sūtra*, five sheets, translated by Buddhayaśas during the Northern Wei dynasty; the *Kalyāṇagaurava Sūtra*, seven sheets—these two sūtras above are the same.
The *Vimaladattā-dārikā-sūtra* (24 sheets), translated by Dharmagupta during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty;
the *Vimaladattā-bodhisattvā-pratibhāna-sūtra* (22 sheets), translated by Dharmarakṣa during the Taikang era of the Western Jin dynasty;
and the *Vimalāprāptā-dārikā-sūtra* (25 sheets), also translated by Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin dynasty—these three sūtras are the same original text.
I recently obtained the following: the *Sūtra on the Girl Bhīṣmottarā*, fifteen sheets, translated at the capital of Ye by Gautama Ruci in the third year of the Xinghe era of the Later Wei;
and the *Sūtra on the Bodhisattva Aśokadattā, Daughter of King Ajātaśatru*, seventeen sheets, translated in the Yuanxiang era of the Later Wei by Buddhayaśas.
These two aforementioned sūtras share the same original text as that translated by Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin.
*The Scripture on the Dharma-Gate of Holding the Boundless*, fifteen sheets; translated by Fa-jian of the Western Jin dynasty.

*The Scripture on the Dhāraṇī of the Bodhisattva Uṣṇīṣavijayā Entering the Immeasurable Gates*, seventeen sheets; these two preceding scriptures are the same original, translated by the layman Wan Tian-yi of the Northern Qi dynasty at the capital of Ye.
*The Scripture on the Supreme Dharma of the First Principle*, fourteen sheets; translated during the Xinghe era of the Northern Wei dynasty.
The *Mahātejo-raśmi-ṛṣi-paripṛcchā-sūtra* translated by Dharmaruci, fourteen sheets;
the above two sūtras are the same text, translated during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty by Jñānagupta as the *Aṣṭamaṅgalaka-sūtra*, two sheets.
The *Aṣṭabuddhanāman-sūtra* translated by Guṇabhadra at the capital of Yangdu during the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty, three sheets; the above two sūtras are the same text, translated separately.
The *Sūtra of the Daughter Nāgadattā*, translated by Jñānagupta during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty, in two sheets;

and the *Sūtra on the Previous Life of the Bodhisattva Nāgadatta*, translated by Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin dynasty, in four sheets. These two aforementioned sūtras are different translations of the same original text.

The *Śyāmaka-putra Sūtra*, translated by Dharmanandi of the Later Qin dynasty, in five sheets; and the *Bodhisattva Śyāmaka-putra Sūtra*, in five sheets. These two aforementioned sūtras are different translations of the same original text. [End.]
*The Sūtra on Fundamental Birth and Death*, four sheets; translated by Zhi Qian during the Huangwu era of the Wu dynasty. *The Sūtra of the Rice Seedling*, six sheets;

the above two sūtras are different translations of the same original text. *The Vaipulya Bodhisattva Daśabhūmika Sūtra*, seven sheets; translated by Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin dynasty. *The Sūtra on Adorning the Bodhicitta*, seven sheets;
the above two sūtras are different translations of the same original text. [Translated] during the Hongshi era of the Later Qin.

The *Wúsuǒxīwàng jīng* (Sūtra on Having No Expectations), translated by Kumārajīva during the Yao Qin period, consists of nineteen sheets; it is also known as the *Xiàngbù jīng* (Elephant-Step Sūtra) or the *Xiàngyè jīng* (Elephant-Axle Sūtra) in fifteen sheets.
These two aforementioned sūtras are translations of the same original text by Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin.

The *Dàfāngděng xiūdúlówáng jīng* (Sūtra King of the Great Vaipulya), consisting of two sheets, was translated by Bodhiruci of the Later Wei. The *Zhuǎnyǒu jīng* (Sūtra on the Transformation of Existence), consisting of two sheets, is identical to the two aforementioned sūtras.
*The Mahāyāna Vaipulya Essential Wisdom Sūtra*, one fascicle (separate translation); *The Sūtra on the Questions of Maitreya Bodhisattva*, four fascicles (upper volume).
These two sūtras are the same original text translated separately by Dharmaruci of the Later Wei. *The Sūtra of the Samādhi of the Seal of Wisdom*, twenty fascicles;
translated during the Wu dynasty by Zhi Qian. *The Tathāgata-jñāna-mudrā Sūtra*, nineteen fascicles. These two [latter] sūtras are the same original text with different translations.
*The Sūtra on the High King of All Dharmas*, translated by Dharmaruci during the Xinghe era of the Northern Wei, twenty sheets;
*The Sūtra on the Heroic King of All Dharmas*, seventeen sheets. These two aforementioned sūtras are different translations of the same original text.

*The Sūtra of the Decisive Dhāraṇī*, eight sheets, also titled *The Sūtra of the Decisive Dhāraṇī*, translated by Dharmarakṣa during the Western Jin dynasty. *The Sūtra on Slandering the Buddha*, seven sheets. The two aforementioned [sūtras]...

The *Mahāyāna-ratnālaṃkāra-sūtra*, twenty-one sheets; the above three sūtras are separate translations from the same original text.

The *Śreṣṭhidāraka-paripṛcchā Sūtra*, six sheets; also known as the *Śreṣṭhi Sūtra* or the *Sudatta-kumāra Sūtra*. Two [versions].
*The Sūtra on the Departure of the Bodhisattva*, translated by Zhi Fadu of the Western Jin Dynasty, four sheets; also known as the *Sūtra on Departure*.

*The Sūtra on the Elephant Head Monastery*, translated by Dharmaruci, nine sheets; the above three sūtras are different translations from the same original, translated during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty by Vinītaruci.

The *Garbhakośa-sūtra* (Womb Treasury Sūtra), three sheets. The *Vimaladatta-bhikṣuṇī-sūtra* (Sūtra of the Immaculate Virtuous Woman), three sheets. The above four sūtras are identical [in origin].
*The Sūtra on the Profound Secrets of the Immeasurable Gate*, five sheets; translated by Zhi Qian during the Huangwu era of the Wu dynasty.

*The Sūtra of the Dhāraṇī for Destroying Māra through Immeasurable Gateways*, eleven sheets; translated by Guṇabhadra during the Daming era of the Song dynasty at Jingzhou.
*The Śāriputra Dhāraṇī Sūtra*, eight sheets. *The Sūtra on the Sole Birth of Bodhisattvas*, eleven sheets.

The *Sūtra of the Silver-Colored Woman*, six sheets; the *Sūtra of the Silver-Colored Woman*, six sheets—these two sūtras above are different recensions of the same original text.
The *Sūtra of Prince Huixiu*, three sheets; the *Sūtra of Prince Shuhu*, four sheets—these two sūtras above are different translations of the same original text.
The *Sūtra of the Dhāraṇī of Skillful Means of the Good Dharma*, six sheets; the *Dhāraṇī of the Secret Gate of the Vajra*, five sheets—above.
These two sūtras are separate translations from the same original text.
*The Sūtra on King Ajātaśatru Receiving the Prediction*, four pages; *The Sūtra on Plucking Flowers against the King’s Command and Ascending to the Buddha to Receive the Prediction*, two pages.

These two aforementioned sūtras are separate translations from the same original text. *The Sūtra on the Questions of the Bodhisattva Siṃhavikrīḍita*, two pages; *The Flower Accumulation Dhāraṇī*... [text ends].
The *Rāṇī Sūtra*, two sheets; the *Huājù Dhāraṇī Sūtra*, three sheets—these three sūtras above are separate translations from the same original text.

*The Eleven-Faced Avalokiteśvara Divine Mantra Sūtra*, eleven folios, translated during the Later Zhou period by Jñānagupta; the above two sūtras are the same text translated separately.

*The Sūtra on the Questions of Ākāśagarbha Bodhisattva Concerning the Retention [of Mantras]*, translated by Śrīmitra during the Xiankang era of the Eastern Jin dynasty.

The *Dhāraṇī Sūtra*, two sheets; the *Pumimittā Dhāraṇī Sūtra*, two sheets; the *Lokadhara Dhāraṇī Sūtra*, seven sheets;

and the *Devaparipṛcchā Sūtra*, three sheets—these are the Mahāyāna Vinaya texts, including both single and multiple translations, along with their commentaries.

The *Catalogue of What Exists and Does Not Exist* records the single and multiple translations of Mahāyāna Vinaya texts, totaling thirty-four works in one hundred and eleven fascicles and two thousand twenty-two sheets.
Among them, the *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra* consists of six or seven fascicles;
it contains the bodhisattva precepts for laypeople and comprises eighty-two sheets. It was translated by Dharmakṣema of the Northern Liang during his stay at Liangcheng.
*Xiányù gōngnèi yì fózàng jīng* (The Scripture on the Translation of the Buddha’s Treasury within the Leisurely Palace), four fascicles, sixty-nine sheets;

translated by Kumārajīva at Cháng'ān during the Hóngshǐ era of the Later Qín dynasty. *Dàfāngguǎng sānjiè jīng* (The Mahāvaipulya Scripture on the Three Precepts), three fascicles, thirty-four sheets.

*Bǎoliáng jīng* (The Ratnarāśi Sūtra), two fascicles, thirty sheets; translated by Dàogōng during the Northern Liáng dynasty. *Fànwǎng jīng* (The Brahmajāla Sūtra), two fascicles, thirty-four sheets; translated during the Later... [period].

The *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra*, nine sheets, translated by Kumārajīva of the Qin; the *Vinayaviniścaya-sūtra*, nineteen sheets, translated by Saṃghavarman at the capital of Yang during the Tianjian era of the Liang dynasty.
All catalogs state that these were translated in Dunhuang, though the specific period and the names [of the scribes] are not made clear.
The *Mañjuśrī-paṭinissagga-sūtra*, twenty-one sheets, also known as the *Mañjuśrī-pañca*... [text fragment].

translator lost. *The Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra*, six sheets. *The Sūtra on the Bodhisattva’s Observance of the Fast*, two sheets. *The Sūtra on Purifying Karmic Obstructions*, fourteen [sheets].
*Śīlaparivarta-sūtra* (The Sūtra on the Good Precepts for Bodhisattvas), 15 sheets; *Bodhisattva-pañcadharma-pratikramaṇa-vibhāṣā* (The Text on the Fivefold Repentance for Bodhisattvas), 2 sheets;

the single and multiple translations of Mahāyāna treatises along with a record of their presence or absence—totaling seventy-two works in five hundred fascicles and nine thousand two hundred and twenty sheets, including the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.

alternatively, ten fascicles. Composed by the Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa, translated by Kumārajīva of the Later Qin.
*The Commentary on the Ten Stages* (*Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*), fourteen fascicles, two hundred [sheets], compiled by the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna.

and the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* [translated] by Ratnamati and others at Luoyang during the Yongming era of the Northern Wei.

The *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra-vyākhyā* (Commentary on the Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra), fifteen fascicles, three hundred and thirty sheets; translated by Paramārtha at Zhizhi Temple in Guangzhou during the Chen dynasty.
The *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra-vyākhyā*, fifteen fascicles, three hundred and forty-five sheets; translated by Paramārtha at Guangzhou during the Chen dynasty.

Record of the Presence or Absence of Single and Multiple Translations of the Hinayana Tripitaka Through Successive Dynasties. Part Three:
Preface. The Preface states: [The text continues with the preface.]
What is called the Hīnayāna Piṭaka refers to the gradual teachings by which the Buddhas respond to conditions and adapt to the capacities of sentient beings.
This is truly because their wisdom and understanding are narrow and limited, and they are stubbornly and rigidly attached [to their views].
The void and existence are divided by boundaries, and the mind and its objects are distinguished by their respective spheres;
they are confined within realms and fetters, established through sequential causes and conditions,
thereby overturning the fundamental basis of the self.
They severed the fetters of saṃsāra;
weary of the long journey of the Buddha-way, they halted at the City of Transformation.
Ashamed that their śrāvaka disciples followed their teachers and dwelt in the empty lands, [they resolved to proceed].
These scriptures are named the Path of the Two Vehicles.
In discussing their Teacher, they circuitously cite Śākyamuni,
who manifested his radiance by relying upon the eight phases of enlightenment.
He borrows the names of the three realms;
born from the right side of his mother’s womb,
he draws in those of similar kind to guide sentient beings.
If one abandons this state and dismisses it,
one will encounter the deluded guest of defiled craving for forty-nine years.
The Three Wheels appeared among humans and devas for eighty years;
the Four Truths were proclaimed throughout the realms of rebirth.
This Way has been spread among the common people, and its methods of guidance are truly manifold.
Yet these were not the Buddha’s original intent; they were established through skillful means in response to specific opportunities.
Thus, a sutra says:
Throughout the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, there is but a single vehicle;
however, because of expedient means suited to circumstances, three teachings are expounded.
Those whose capacities are awakened rely upon these teachings to exert themselves in cultivation.
Severing the entanglements of precepts and views,
and overturning the cycle of birth and death in its segmented form—
those of dull faculties may realize this.
This means that having exhausted the source of the veils and canopies,
one whose sharp wisdom clarifies the mind remains immersed in doubt regarding emptiness.

Therefore, although the five schools hold differing attachments and engage in speculative calculations, by investigating their delusions one finds them all rooted in the eighteen [original schools]; and by tracing back to the two [fundamental principles], one knows that the ultimate truth is one.
Thus we know that it is like rabbits and horses crossing a stream.
The capacity of the fragrant elephant remains unexhausted;
how could the sheep, the deer,
or the camel compare to the strength of the great bull?
Therefore, the fundamental principle of the Mahāyāna is that the emptiness of intrinsic nature reaches the ultimate limit of its doctrinal system;
the reasoning of the Hīnayāna, by contrast, is shallow.
Arising and ceasing are realized as identical to true understanding.
Thus, the *Buddhadhātu-śāstra* states:
"Those of the Two Vehicles perceive arising and ceasing as identical to True Suchness."
Judging by this statement,
it clarifies the divergent paths and methods of the Lesser and Greater Vehicles.
As for those works subsumed under the Sūtra-piṭaka, they must all ultimately derive from the four Āgamas.
The *Samyuktāgama* was expounded at random to further open up the *Kṣudrakapiṭaka*.
The Vinaya regulations spread throughout [the teachings] but are not subsumed within the Sūtras;
their exegesis and analysis are the most extensive and detailed.
Furthermore, the Great Sage’s dispensation of transformation is fundamentally intended to dispel the entanglements of delusion.
In administering medicine to eliminate illness, he does not restrict himself to fixed names or forms;
thus, he first taught the Four Noble Truths.
Eighty thousand devas gave rise to the great resolve.
Subsequently, he preached the six perfections,
and hundreds of millions of bhikṣus realized the four fruits of the path.
As for the rest, those of vulgar and shallow caliber who cling to their teachings like woodcutters to a stump and mutually denounce one another completely miss the original intent.
This concludes the account of the two physicians from the past.
Being well-versed in the ultimate teachings,
he disparaged the two-legged Teacher;
this is recorded in the Miscellaneous Writings.
The small lacks the capacity to describe the great;
it merely confines itself to narrow calculations.
The great possesses the quality of encompassing the small.
The pervasive clarity dispels the obscurations;
thus we know that Kāśyapa gave rise to compassion for the withered seeds and urged his fellow disciples forward.
Śāriputra regrets his hesitation regarding the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*);
awakening and delusion are thus opposites.
As for all other habitual tendencies, their transformation and cessation are ultimately difficult to achieve.
In the end, he awaits the convergence of capacities to employ various names and methods to transform beings through his teachings.
The collection of sutras now assembled begins at the Immortal Garden (Lumbinī) and concludes at the Golden River (Hiraṇyavatī).
The teachings described as the "Half-Teachings" are designated as the Śrāvaka Piṭaka;
the dates of their transmission and gradual eastward spread are well known.
In total, there are two hundred and seventy-two sections.
One thousand four hundred and ninety-four fascicles are used as the catalogue for the Hīnayāna Piṭaka;
the remainder consists of the *Collection of Biographies of Worthies and Sages*.
There are two hundred fascicles of texts concerning both minor and major principles, as well as miscellaneous matters pertaining to the sacred and the mundane;
these are not included within the Two Baskets (the Sūtra and Vinaya Piṭakas),
but are instead manifested according to their own separate catalogues.
As for the single or multiple translations, their transmissions, and their preservation or loss,
there is no need for separate accounts; rather, one should enter thoroughly into the Tripiṭaka,
so that those who peruse it may gain understanding.
Since things of a similar kind follow one another, I have used the "Great Overview" (Da guan) to provide a clear and easy explanation.

The Śrāvaka scriptures comprise 544 fascicles; the Śrāvaka Vinaya, 274 fascicles; and the Śrāvaka Śāstras, 676 fascicles. These were collected and transmitted by the worthy sages of the Western Regions. Including those that pertain to the Mahāyāna, they total 184 fascicles. Altogether, these four categories comprise 319 works in 1,678 fascicles and 20,042 sheets of paper.

The four Āgamas constitute the foundation of the Mahāyāna’s Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) tradition;
as its branches have dispersed, many schools have arisen.
Herein, the fundamental sūtras are collectively cited as above.
The remaining distinct sections have been translated separately;
