*Zhong ben qi jing* (Sūtra of the Middle Account of the Arising), translated by Kang Mengxiang during the Jian’an era of the Later Han; two fascicles, twenty-seven sheets.
*Qǐxìng xíng jīng* (Sūtra on the Arising of Practice), two fascicles, twenty-eight pages; translated by Zhù Dàlì.
*Dámíduōluó chán jīng* (Dharmatrāta’s Sūtra on Meditation), two fascicles, fifty pages; translated by Kāṅ Mèngxiáng of the Later Han.
*Yìzú jīng* (Sūtra on the Fulfillment of Meaning), two fascicles, forty-four pages; translated by Zhī Qián during the Huangwu era of the Wu dynasty. *Píyeshā wèn* (The Questions of Vaiśravaṇa).

*Sūtra* in two fascicles, thirty-one sheets; translated by Bodhiruci of the Later Wei. *Dà ānbān shǒuyì jīng* (The Scripture on Guarding the Mind through Great Ānāpāna) in two fascicles, or one fascicle, thirty sheets;
translated by An Shigao of the Later Han. *Upāsikā-śīla-saṃvara-sūtra* (The Scripture on the Pure Conduct of Laywomen) in two fascicles, or one fascicle, thirty sheets.
*Nāgasena-bhikṣu-sūtra* (The Scripture of the Bhikṣu Nāgasena) in two fascicles, or one fascicle, thirty sheets.
*Da'anban jing* (Sutra on Anapanasati), two fascicles or one fascicle, twenty sheets; a later manuscript discovered, translated by An Shigao of the Later Han.
*Baninihuan jing* (Parinirvana Sutra), one fascicle, twenty-two sheets; translated by Gunabhadra at Yangdu during the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty.
*Danglai bian jing* (Sutra on Future Transformations), two sheets; translated by Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin. *Guoqu fo fen* (Portion of the Past Buddhas).
The *Wei jing* (Scripture on the [Five] Precepts), two sheets, translated as before; the *Nai nü qi yu jing* (Sutra of the Maiden Jīvaka), seventeen sheets, translated by the same;
the *Jing fan wang ban nie pan jing* (Sutra on the Parinirvāṇa of King Śuddhodana), six sheets, translated by Juqu Jingsheng, Marquis of Anyang during the Northern Liang;

the *Ba shi jing* (Sutra of the Eight Teachers), three sheets, translated by Zhi Qian during the Wu dynasty; and the *Da jiaye ben jing* (Sutra of the Original Account of Mahākāśyapa), five sheets, translated by Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin.
*The Sūtra of the Four Vows*, two sheets; translated by Zhi Qian during the Huangwu era of the Wu dynasty. *The Sūtra of Women Encountering Calamity*, two sheets;
also titled *The Sūtra of Women Encountering Retribution*; translated by Fa Jian during the Western Qin dynasty. *The Sūtra of the Elder’s Son Bianyi’s Questions*, nine sheets;
also titled *The Sūtra of the Elder’s Questions on Intent*; translated by Fachang during the Later Wei dynasty. *The Sūtra of the Womb*, fifteen sheets; also titled *The [Sūtra of] the Womb*.

*The Sūtra on Receiving a Body in the Womb*, translated by Dharmarakṣa during the Taian era of the Western Jin dynasty; four sheets. *The Sūtra on the Four Self-Inflicted Injuries*, translated by Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin dynasty;
four sheets. *The Sūtra on the Original Conditions Narrated by Five Hundred Disciples*, twenty sheets; translated by Dharmarakṣa during the Taikang era of the Western Jin dynasty.
*The Sūtra of the Seven Daughters*, six sheets; translated by Zhi Qian during the Huangwu era of the Wu dynasty. *The Ānanda [Sūtra]*.

*The Sūtra on the Four Matters*, three sheets; translated by Zhi Qian during the Huangwu era of the Wu dynasty. *The Sūtra on the Troubles One Desires to Encountered*, two sheets; translated by Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin dynasty.
*The Sūtra on Dharmas Receiving Dust*, two sheets; translated by An Shigao of the Later Han dynasty. *The Sūtra on the Dharma-Contemplation of Dhyāna Practice*, two sheets;
translated by An Shigao of the Later Han dynasty. *The Sūtra of the Four Heavenly Kings*, two sheets; translated during the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty.

*The Sūtra on the Brief Teaching and Admonition Given by the Buddha at the Time of His Parinirvāṇa* (six sheets), also known as the *Sūtra on the Bequeathed Teaching*, translated by Zhiyan Baoyun in the capital of Yang during the Liu Song dynasty;
*The Sūtra on Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana Wandering through the Four Crossroads*, translated by Kumārajīva of the Later Qin in Chang’an;
*The Sūtra on Nandiśa*, translated by Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin (four sheets); and those following, for which the translators have been lost.
The *Upāsikā Vimalā-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, three sheets; the *Pratimā-karaṇa-puṇya-vipāka-sūtra*, two sheets;
the *Dharmasthiti-sūtra*, two sheets; the *Kusīda-kārṣaka-sūtra*, two sheets; the *Udayana-rāja-sūtra* (also known as the *Udayana-rāja-buddhapratimā-karaṇa-sūtra*), five sheets;
the *Ānanda-sapta-svapna-sūtra* (also known as the *Ānanda-aṣṭama-svapna-sūtra*), two sheets.
The *Svapna-sūtra* (or perhaps the *Aṣṭākṣara-bhrānti-sūtra*); the *Guhya-pāda-vajra-mahābala-anuśocana-sūtra*;
the *Kāśyapa-gamana-buddha-parinirvāṇa-sūtra*, two sheets; also titled *Nirvāṇa-kāla-kāśyapa-gamana-buddha-sūtra*;
the *Buddha-parinirvāṇa-śarīra-saṃskāra-urdhvadeha-sūtra*, three sheets; also titled *Bhikṣu-śāstṛ-sūtra* or *Bhikṣu-sūtra*. *Ma*... [fragmentary].

The *Hachātòu jīng* (Sūtra on the Destruction of the Realm), four sheets; also known as the *Guǎnxǐ fó jīng* (Sūtra on Washing the Buddha). The *Luóyún rěnrù jīng* (Sūtra on Rāhula’s Patience), three sheets;

also known as the *Rěnrù jīng* (Sūtra on Patience) or the *Chūjiā yuán jīng* (Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of Leaving Home). The *Chūzǐ jīng* (Sūtra on Disciples), two sheets, in three chapters. The *Dìzǐ xué sānbèi jīng* (Sūtra on Disciples Learning the Three Grades), three sheets;
also known as the *Sìbèi jīng* (Sūtra on the Four Grades). The *Jiànzhèng jīng* (Sūtra on Seeing the Correct), seven sheets; also known as the *Shēngsǐ biàn* (Transformation of Birth and Death).

1. *Śikṣā-sūtra* (The Scripture on Training), titled *Kauṇḍinya-anāgāmin-sūtra*, two sheets; also known as *Kauṇḍinya-anāgāmin-sūtra*. 2. *Pañca-āvartana-sūtra* (The Scripture on the Five Returns), three sheets; also known as *Pañca-āvartana-sūtra*. 3.
*Āgama-samyak-pratipatti-sūtra* (The Scripture on Right Practice in the Āgamas), four sheets; also known as *Buddhabhāṣita-samyak-mati-sūtra* (The Scripture Spoken by the Buddha on Right Intention).
4. *Trāsa-sūtra* (The Scripture on Fear), one sheet. 5. *Mahāmatsya-vastu-sūtra* (The Scripture on the Matter of the Great Fish), two sheets. 6. *Aṭṭhaka-sūtra* (The Scripture on Aṭṭhaka).

The *Dhānañjāni-sutta* (The Sūtra of Dhanañjāni), two sheets; the *Brahmadatta-rāja-sūtra* (The Sūtra of King Brahmadatta), two sheets; the *Mahākāśyapa-daridra-mātṛ-paritrāṇa-sūtra* (The Sūtra of Mahākāśyapa Saving the Poor Mother), four sheets;
the *Madhyama-hṛdaya-sūtra* (The Sūtra of the Central Heart), five sheets;

the *Nāgarāja-bhrātṛ-sūtra* (The Sūtra of the Two Dragon Kings), three sheets—also known as the *Nāgarāja-vinaya-sūtra* or the *Śaṅkha-bhikṣu-puṇya-sūtra*, two sheets; the *Jyotiṣka-śreṣṭhin-sūtra* (The Sūtra of the Merchant Jyotiṣka).

The *Zhèzhě jīng* (Sūtra of the Elder Zhèzhě) in five sheets; the *Lúzhì zhǎngzhě jīng* (Sūtra of the Elder Lúzhì) in nine sheets; the *Xūmóti zhǎngzhě jīng* (Sūtra of the Elder Xūmóti) in eight sheets;

the *Dēngzhǐ yīnyuán jīng* (Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of the Lamp-Finger) in eight sheets; the *Shí'èr pǐn shēngsǐ jīng* (Sūtra of Twelve Chapters on Birth and Death) in two sheets; the *Wǔwáng jīng* (Sūtra of the Five Kings) in four sheets;

the *Mólówáng jīng* (Sūtra of King Mōluó) in two sheets; the *Módáguówáng jīng* (Sūtra of King Módá) in two sheets; the *Pǔdáwáng jīng* (Sūtra of King Pǔdá) in three sheets; and the *Qiánduō* [Sūtra]...
The *Rājan-sūtra*, two sheets; the *Dṛḍhādhyāśaya-sūtra*, two sheets—also known as the *Dṛḍhacitta-sūtra*;
the *Buddhamahāsangha-sūtra*, six sheets; the *Cīya-sūtra*, two sheets; the *Dvādaśadhūta-sūtra*, five sheets—also known as the *Śramaṇadhūta-sūtra*;
the *Śucirakṣaṇa-sūtra*, two sheets; the *Karañja-phala-sūtra*, one sheet; the *Kālakāla-sūtra*, two sheets—number one.
*The Sūtra on the Names of Time*, three sheets; *The Sūtra on the Ladder for Attaining the Way*, three sheets; *The Sūtra on the Sandalwood Tree*, three sheets;
*The Sūtra on the New Year*, five sheets—also known as the *Bhāra-sūtra*; *The Sūtra of the Poor Old Man*, three sheets—also known as the *Sūtra of the Poor Elder*;
*The Sūtra of the Householder’s Son Mourning in Three Places*, four sheets; *The Buddha-spoken Sūtra of Overcoming Difficulties*, two sheets—also known as the *Sūtra of the Day of Difficulty*.
The *Candana-vyūha-rāja-sūtra*, three sheets; the *Svātmavatsala-sūtra* (also known as the *Svātmavatsalānavatsala-sūtra*), four sheets;
the *Buddhabhāṣita-sthānasthāna-sūtra*, fifteen sheets; the *Anuttara-sthāna-sūtra*, one sheet; the *Pañcagati-cakra-puṇyapāpa-vipāka-sūtra*, four sheets;
the *Ajātaśatru-sūtra*, three sheets; the *Aṣṭādaśa-niraya-sūtra*, five sheets; the *Niraya... [fragmentary]*.

The *Lì jīng* (Plow Sūtra), thirteen sheets; also known as the *Qínkǔ nílí jīng* (Sūtra on the Hardships of Hell) or the *Zuìyè bàoyìng jiàohuà dìyù jīng* (Sūtra on the Retribution of Karmic Offenses and the Teaching of the Hells), six sheets;

the *Sēnghù jīng* (Saṅgharakṣita Sūtra), twenty sheets; the *Wèicéngyǒu jīng* (Sūtra of Unprecedented Events), three sheets; the *Jiāqiányán shuōfǎ mòjìn jīng* (Kātyāyanāvavāda Sūtra on the Extinction of Phenomena), five sheets;
and the *Fó wèi niánshào bǐqiū shuō zhèngshì jīng* (Sūtra on the True Matter Spoken by the Buddha for Young Bhikṣus), three sheets—these four sections comprise the study.

The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (one fascicle): A record of whether or not the Small Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*) Vinaya texts were translated, totaling thirty-five works in two hundred and seventy-four fascicles and five thousand eight hundred and thirteen sheets.
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* (sixty-one fascicles): One thousand sheets. Translated during the Hongshi era of the Later Qin by Puṇyatāra together with [Kumārajīva].

The first two divisions were translated by Kumārajīva; the latter division was translated by Vimalākṣa at Shijian Temple in Shouchun during the Eastern Jin dynasty, comprising sixty fascicles and 1,001 sheets.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* in forty fascicles was translated by Buddhayaśas in Chang’an during the Hongshi era of the Later Qin dynasty.
The [Dharmaguptaka-vinaya] was translated by Buddhabhadra together with Faxian during the Eastern Jin dynasty.

The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* (Five-Part Vinaya) in thirty fascicles was translated at the capital of Yangdu during the Jingping era of the Song dynasty by Buddhayaśas, together with Daosheng and Zhisheng.
The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* in eighteen fascicles was translated at Yangdu during the Southern Qi dynasty by Saṃghavarman.

The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* (Bi-nai-ye) in ten fascicles was translated at Guangzhou during the Yongming era of the Southern Qi dynasty by Saṃghabhadra. [The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-mātṛkā*] in ten fascicles was translated by Zhu Fonian during the Former Qin dynasty.
Dao’an and others translated [the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-mātṛkā*] in Chang’an;

it consists of ten fascicles. During the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty, Saṃghavarman translated [the *Mahāsāṃghika-prātimokṣa-sūtra*] in Yangdu; it comprises twenty sheets. During the Former Wei, Dharmakāla translated [the *Mahāsāṃghika-bhikṣuṇī-prātimokṣa-sūtra*] in Xuchang.

The *Sifen jieben* (Four-Part Prātimokṣa), twenty-three sheets, translated by Buddhayaśas of the Later Qin at Chang’an; the *Jietuojieben* (Prātimokṣa Sūtra), twenty-one sheets, translated by Gautama Dharmaruci of the Northern Wei; the *Shami weiyi* (Śrāmaṇera-Ācāra), nine sheets, translated by Guṇavarman at Yangdu during the Song dynasty; and the *Tanwude jiemolü* (Dharmaguptaka Karmavācanā), thirty-one sheets, translated by Tanyao in Luoyang in the first year of the Zhengguang era of the Northern Wei.
*The Four-Part Vinaya for Nuns* (15 sheets), translated by Guṇavarman during the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty.
*The Characteristics of the Five Precepts for Upāsakas* (15 sheets), translated by Guṇavarman of the Song dynasty.

*Mahīśāsaka Prātimokṣa Sūtra* (19 sheets), also known as the *Five-Part Prātimokṣa*, translated by Buddhayaśas at the capital of Yangdu during the Jingping era of the Song dynasty. *Sarvāstivāda [Prātimokṣa]*...
*Vinayavibhāṣā*, nine fascicles; *Mahābhikṣu-trisahasra-vaipulya-vidhi-sūtra*, two fascicles;
*Vinayamātṛkā-śāstra*, eight fascicles; *Mahāprajāpatī-bhikṣuṇī-sūtra*, two fascicles; *Śāriputra-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, eleven pages and below—these were all lost translations;
*Sandeha-saṃgha-sūtra*, three pages, also known as the *Mahābhikṣu-sūtra*; *Śīla-sūtra*.
*Xiāozāi jīng* (Sūtra on the Elimination of Calamities), four sheets; *Jiāshè jìnjiè jīng* (Kāśyapa’s Sūtra on the Prohibitions), three sheets;

*Fànjiè zuìbào qīngzhòng jīng* (Sūtra on the Lightness and Heaviness of the Retribution for Violating Precepts), two sheets—also titled *Fànzuì jīng* (Sūtra on Offenses); *Shēngqí bǐqū nìjièběn* (Mahāsāṃghika Bhikṣuṇī Prātimokṣa), twenty-four sheets;

*Shísòng bǐqū jièběn* (Sarvāstivāda Bhikṣu Prātimokṣa), twenty sheets; *Shísòng bǐqū nìjièběn* (Sarvāstivāda Bhikṣuṇī Prātimokṣa), twenty-six sheets; *Sìfèn bǐqū jièběn* (Dharmaguptaka Bhikṣu Prātimokṣa) [incomplete].
The Bhikṣuṇī Prātimokṣa Sūtra, thirty-one sheets; the Upāsaka Pañcaśīla Vinaya-vidhi, twenty-three sheets;
the Upāli-paripṛcchā Vinaya, twenty-three sheets; the Mahāśramaṇa Ekottara-karman, twenty-two sheets;
the Sarvāstivāda Karman, twenty-three sheets; the Śrāmaṇera Daśaśīla with its Vinaya-vidhi, twenty-one sheets; and the Śrāmaṇera [Sūtra].
The Ten Precepts for Bhikṣuṇīs: 4 sheets; the Precepts on Abandonment for Śrāmaṇerikās: 4 sheets;

the Single and Double Editions of the Hīnayāna Treatises, including the records of what was translated and what was not, totaling thirty-three works in six hundred and seventy-six fascicles and twelve thousand one hundred and seventy-seven sheets; the Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra: 200 [fascicles].
Volume 3,109, pages 1–278. Translated by Xuanzang at the Capital during the Yonghui era of the Tang dynasty by imperial decree:
*Abhidharma-aṣṭagrantha-vibhāṣā*, sixty fascicles, 1,278 pages. The above two treatises are the same original work translated separately.
Translated during the Juqu reign of the Northern Liang by Daoting and others at Guzang in the Northern Liang. Concordance.
*Nyāyānusāra-śāstra*, eighty fascicles, one thousand four hundred and twenty sheets; translated by Xuanzang at the Great Ci’en Monastery during the Yonghui era of the Tang dynasty.
*Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya-ṭīkā-tattvārthā-śāstra*, forty fascicles, six hundred and forty-four sheets;
translated by Xuanzang at the Great Ci’en Monastery during the Yonghui era of the Tang dynasty. *Abhidharma-aṣṭagrantha-śāstra*, thirty fascicles, four hundred [sheets].

The *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* (Fazhi lun) consists of twenty fascicles totaling five hundred scrolls (500 sheets). The aforementioned two treatises are translations of the same original text but produced separately;
they were translated by Xuanzang within the Imperial Palace during the Yonghui era of the Tang dynasty.

The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* (Jushelun) consists of twenty-two fascicles totaling four hundred fifty-eight scrolls (458 sheets), translated by Paramārtha of the Chen dynasty at Guangzhou. The *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* consists of thirty fascicles totaling four hundred [scrolls].
The two treatises on the first one hundred and seventy pages are separate translations from the same original text.
The *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra* in twenty-two fascicles and five hundred and ninety-nine sheets was translated by Xuanzang within the palace during the Xianqing era of the Tang dynasty.
The *Abhidharmadīpa-śāstra* (or *Chuyao lun*) in twenty fascicles and four hundred and eight sheets was translated by Dharmagupta in Chang’an during the Hongshi era of the Later Qin dynasty.
*Satyasiddhi-śāstra*, twenty fascicles (or fourteen fascicles), four hundred sheets; translated by Zhu Fonian in Chang’an during the Former Qin dynasty.
*Vijñānakāya-pāda-śāstra*, sixteen fascicles, two hundred seventy-one sheets; translated by Kumārajīva during the Later Qin dynasty.
*Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, eighty fascicles, three thousand eight hundred and thirty-four sheets; translated by Xuanzang in the palace during the Xianqing era of the Tang dynasty.
*Vibhāṣā-Abhidharma*, fourteen fascicles, three hundred and forty-seven sheets; also known as the *Vyākhyā-śāstra*.
Translated in Luoyang by Saṃghadeva during the Jianyuan era of the Former Qin dynasty. *Dharma-skandha-pāda-śāstra*, twelve fascicles, one hundred and ninety-two sheets.
Translated within the palace by Xuanzang during the Xianqing era of the Tang dynasty. *Vimukti-mārga-śāstra*.
The *Saṃyukta-abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* in twelve fascicles and two hundred and ninety-nine sheets was translated by Saṃgharākṣa at the Zhanyun Hall in the capital of Yang during the Liang dynasty.
The *Abhidharma-prakaraṇapāda-śāstra* in twelve fascicles and two hundred and nine sheets [was also translated there].
The *Saṃyukta-abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* in eleven fascicles and two hundred and eighty sheets was translated by Guṇavarman together with [Dharmatrāta] during the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty.
*The Treatise on the Abhidharma of the Establishment of the World* (Lishi apitan lun), ten fascicles, one hundred and seventy-three sheets;
translated by Nāgabodhi during the Chen dynasty at Shixing Commandery. *The Compendium of Venerable Vasumitra* (Zunposumi suoji lun), ten fascicles, two hundred and seventy-five sheets;
translated by Saṃghabhūti together with Buddhasmṛti during the Jianyuan era of the Former Qin. *The Abhidharma of Dharmottara* (Fasheng apitan).
*Śāstra* (Treatise), six fascicles, one hundred and three pages; translated during the Tiāntǒng era of the Northern Qi by Yaśas together with Fǎzhì.

*Catuḥsatya-śāstra* (Treatise on the Four Truths), four fascicles, seventy-four pages; translated at Nánkāng Commandery by Paramārtha of the Chen dynasty. *Abhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* (Treatise on the Heart of Abhidharma), four fascicles, sixty-seven pages;
translated at Lúshān during the Tàiyuán era of the Eastern Jin by Āryadeva together with Huìyuǎn.

*Vibhaṅga-śāstra* (Treatise on the Analysis of Merit), four fascicles or five fascicles, seventy-three sheets; translator lost. *Tri-midhi-śāstra* (Three-fold Basis Treatise), three fascicles, thirty-five sheets;
included in the Abhidharma. *Abhidharma-śāstra*, two fascicles, twenty sheets; translated by Xuanzang at the palace during the Xianqing era of the Tang dynasty.
*Abhidharma-amṛta-rasa-śāstra* (Taste of the Nectar of Abhidharma), two fascicles, forty-five sheets. Pratyekabuddha [section].

*Foyinyuan lun* (Treatise on the Causes and Conditions of the Buddha), two fascicles, twenty sheets; translated by Saṃghadeva at Mount Lu during the Taiyuan era of the Eastern Jin dynasty. *Sanfadu lun* (Treatise on the Three Dharma Categories), three fascicles, forty-four sheets;
translated by Saṃghadeva at Mount Lu during the Taiyuan era of the Eastern Jin dynasty. *Abhidharmakośa-kārikā* (Verses of the Abhidharmakośa), four sheets;

translated by Xuanzang of the Tang dynasty. *Bashibu lun* (Treatise on the Eighteen Schools), seven sheets; translated by Paramārtha of the Chen dynasty. *Bushiexi lun* (Treatise on the Different Tenets of the Schools), nine sheets; translated by Paramārtha of the Chen dynasty.

The *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra-vyākhyā* (Treatise on the Elucidation of the Abhidharma), twenty-four sheets, also known as the *Vinaya-vibhāṣā-prakaraṇa-śāstra*, translated by Paramārtha of the Chen dynasty;
the *Anu-lakṣaṇa-śāstra* (Treatise on Following Characteristics), thirty-four sheets; and the *Record of the Collection of the Worthy and Holy* (*Kṣānti-ārya-saṃgraha*).
These comprise forty-seven works totaling one hundred eighty-four fascicles and two thousand seven hundred and sixty sheets. [From] the *Buddha-ben* (Fundamentals of the Buddha).
*Gongxing ji* (Collection of Practices), sixty fascicles, eight hundred and sixty-two pages; translated by Jñānagupta at the capital during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty.
*Shi bai yuan jing* (Sutra of One Hundred Narratives), ten fascicles, one hundred and thirty-five pages; translated by Zhi Qian of the Wu dynasty at Jianye.
*Daluoni ji* (Collection of Dhāraṇīs), ten fascicles, one hundred and eighty-seven pages; also known as *Zazhou* (Miscellaneous Spells).

*Ji jing* (Collection of Sūtras), nine fascicles; *Liudu ji jing* (Collection of the Six Pāramitās), eight fascicles, totaling one hundred thirty-five sheets, translated by Kang Senghui at Wuchang during the Wu dynasty;
*Fobenxing jing* (Sūtra on the Original Deeds of the Buddha), seven fascicles, totaling one hundred fourteen sheets, translated by Baoyun at Yangdu during the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty;
*Ayuwang zhuan* (Biography of King Aśoka), seven fascicles (or five fascicles), totaling one hundred one sheets, translated during the Liang dynasty.
The monk Sanghabhara, under imperial supervision, translated the *Dharmatāraśāstra* (付法藏傳) in six fascicles—or four fascicles—comprising seventy-five sheets, at the capital of Yangdu.
Later, during the Northern Wei, Jikaya, together with Tanyao, translated the *Buddhacarita* (佛所行讚傳) in five fascicles comprising ninety sheets at Beitaishan.
The *Mātr̥ceṭastotra* (馬鳴菩薩讚) was translated by Baoyun of the Eastern Jin at Yangdu. The *Dhyānarahasya* (禪祕) [was also translated there].

The *Yao* (Essentials) in five fascicles or three fascicles, totaling seventy-one sheets; also known as the *Chanfa Yao* (Essentials of the Dhyāna Method), translated by Dharmamitra in the Jiangbiao region during the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty.

3. Catalogue of All Scriptures Seen Entering the Canon Throughout Successive Dynasties, Part Three:
Preface. The Preface states:
From the time of the first catalogue until now...
The Emperor’s age was advanced,
and as for the regulations and statutes, they were so diverse and entangled that it was truly difficult to discern and simplify them.
This is primarily because the treatises, sūtras, commentaries, and compositions produced by various translators throughout successive generations do not follow a fixed chronological order;
consequently, when compiling them based on this [principle], one cannot distinguish their respective paths.
At present, however, following the principle of the Great or Small Vehicles and according to whether the translations are single or multiple,
the Sūtras, Vinayas, Śāstras, and biographies are categorized separately.
Yet, as we still follow established precedent, I have not yet dared to make a major distinction between them.
This is undertaken to reveal what has not yet been heard, knowing that this is not done intentionally.
Relying on the separate entry into the canon, the volumes are supported by bookshelves;
their cases, rolls, labels, and slips clearly display their titles and names.
One must immediately investigate and examine [the situation] to bring an end to confusion.

As for the fact that ordinary consciousness is muddled and deluded while the subtle [truth] relies upon the opening of wisdom—there is no class of beings excluded from this teaching; this is a common proverbial saying.
Yet, those of brilliant acumen and extraordinary spiritual insight in recent times have been deficient in their studies and negligent in their reading;
though they enter the Tripitaka and see more than three thousand scrolls of scripture, [they fail to comprehend them].
Having never traversed the path of clear wisdom, from where could it arise?
In vain one wastes a lifetime, falsely proliferating the six consciousnesses;
unable to distinguish the heterodox from the orthodox, the true and the false remain muddled together.
Flowing along with worldly customs, there is no way to return to the source.
Alas! How can one understand the essential path of the Tripiṭaka?
He mastered the essential principles of the Three Studies;
internally, he remained true to his initial resolve,
and externally, he maintained control over his subsequent thoughts.
Now, [the practitioner] practices none of these at all;
instead, they claim that the five sensory objects are the root of the Way,
indulging in and clinging to them without relinquishing them as if they were the true sages.
The metaphor of "stealing clothes" has already been made manifest in the *Daśacakrakṣitigarbha-sūtra*,
and the censure of "birds and mice" is further revealed in the *Buddhapiṭaka*.
One cannot help but acknowledge the burden of this physical form.
The toil of mouth and belly cannot be dispensed with;
since the means for liberation have been severed,
the schemes of the net of delusion grow ever deeper.
A single cup of water was long withheld by the Sage;
a garment of a single fold caused the sacred texts to be interrupted and his robes discarded.
Thus, he underwent the amputation of his feet for both the hidden and the manifest realms.
Furthermore, suffering will be retributed in the future;
as long as the spirit has not transcended to rebirth, how can one escape its traces?
I have heard that in the past there was Xiao Li, a man of secular standing.
He read more than thirty thousand scrolls.
Hui-fei was a monk left behind in the Dharma-ending age;
he transcribed by hand more than two thousand fascicles.
Who is that person who is so superior?
Who is this person who is so inferior?
The decadent customs of these degenerate times are not even worth mentioning.
One may look up to those on high mountains as a model for admonition;
when has there not been a virtuous friend who embodies the entirety of the holy life?
Following this standard of flowing conformity,
which has been practiced throughout successive generations,
one should certainly always take the mind as one's teacher to govern the states of emotion and circumstance.
One must personally restrain one's course; how can one allow others to act as they please?
One should peruse the sacred scriptures of the three regions and seek out the laws and regulations of the three thousand [precepts].
Having traversed the distant journey of three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* and reached the site of enlightenment of the Three Buddhas,
how could one turn one's back on this Way that has not perished?
I have thus repeatedly employed these analogies;
may the reader examine them closely.
Now, based on the previously translated old scriptures, I shall provide a summary.
It is fully as set forth in the separate exposition.
There are other [versions] translated later at Yuhua;
I have not yet seen the new edition.

The Mahāyāna sūtras consist of seven hundred and ninety fascicles and thirteen thousand seven hundred and ninety sheets; the Mahāyāna vinaya consists of thirty-two fascicles and four hundred and thirty sheets; and the Mahāyāna śāstras consist of four hundred and forty-five fascicles and eight thousand one hundred and fifteen sheets. In total, the Mahāyāna sūtras, vinaya, and śāstras comprise three hundred and thirty-seven works, totaling one thousand two hundred and sixty-seven fascicles and twenty-one thousand six hundred and twenty-five sheets.

Mahāyāna Sūtras: Original Texts, two hundred and fifty-four works in total. *The Mahāvaipulya Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra*, sixty fascicles (or fifty fascicles), one thousand eighty-seven sheets, twenty-eight lines per sheet. comprising the *Fàngguāng* (Prabhāsa), *Guāngzàn* (Ratnaguṇasaṃcayagāthā), *Dàoxíng* (Aṣṭasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā), and *Xiǎopǐn* (Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā),
each of which exists in both earlier and later versions.
