First, during the Song dynasty, Guṇabhadra produced the *Sutra on the Liberation through Understanding Phenomena* (*Mingxiang jietuo jing*).
During the Chen dynasty, Paramārtha produced [another version].
It is titled the *Jiejing* (Sūtra on the Unraveling of the Knots). The text is abbreviated and incomplete;
it is identical to the *Samdhinirmocana-sūtra* translated by Dharmaruci during the Later Wei dynasty.
Therefore, the later version is retained as the definitive text.

The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*, three fascicles and sixty-one pages, translated by Kumārajīva of the Later Qin at the Xiāoyáo Garden in Cháng'ān, on the western bank of the Wèi River. This concludes the aforementioned scripture.
There are three translations.
That translated during the Wu period by Zhi Qian is titled the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*.
Two fascicles.
Translated by Xuanzang of the Tang dynasty.
It is the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*.
In six fascicles;
as a middle way between the prolix and the concise, it is difficult to surpass the Qin translation.
Ultimately, it is as can be known from the principle that the Zhou dynasty adopted the rites of Yin, modifying them by subtraction and addition.
The *Sarvadharmāpravṛttinirdeśa-sūtra*, two fascicles, thirty-one pages; translated by Kumārajīva of the Later Qin.
This aforementioned sūtra was translated a second time during the Sui dynasty by Jñānagupta as the *Sarvadharmābhāvasvabhāvanirdeśa-sūtra*.
Three fascicles.
Because its literary power was insufficient compared to the same source text, it has been abbreviated.
*The Sutra on the Immeasurable Jewel Samādhi*, one fascicle, thirty sheets; translated by Dharmarakṣa during the Yongjia era of the Western Jin dynasty. The above is one sutra.
Re-translated.
An alternative translation, one volume of which is titled *The Sūtra on the Samādhi of the Tathāgata Ratna*,
consists of two fascicles.
The translator is lost;
as the text is identical [to the previous entry], it is omitted here.

*Fangdeng niepan jing* (Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra), two fascicles, thirty-five sheets, translated at the capital of Yangdu by Buddhabhadra together with Faxian during the Eastern Jin dynasty. The above is one scripture.
Translated three times;
an alternative translation is titled the *Aiqi jing* (Sutra on Lamentation) in two fascicles.
Translated during the Sui dynasty by Jñānagupta.
Entitled the *Sūtra of the Four Boys*,
in three fascicles.
The text is no different [from other versions];
therefore, the Jin edition is preserved.
*The Sūtra on the Bodhisattva Hui Shang Asking about Great Skillful Means*, two fascicles, thirty sheets; translated by Dharmarakṣa during the Taikang era of the Western Jin. The above is one sūtra.
Two fascicles.
Translated by the Indian lay practitioner Zhu Nanti during the Western Jin dynasty.
Titled *Mahāyānopāya-sūtra*.
It consists of three fascicles.
As it is identical to the previous edition,
it is omitted here for brevity.

The *Mañjuśrī-buddhakṣetraguṇavyūha-sūtra* (The Scripture on Mañjuśrī Manifesting the Treasure Treasury), three fascicles, forty-three pages, translated by Dharmarakṣa during the Taishi era of the Western Jin dynasty.
This aforementioned scripture is also translated as the *Mahāvaipulya-ratnakaraṇḍa-sūtra*.
Three fascicles.
The era and author are not specified;
as the text is identical [to the previous entry], it is abbreviated here.
*Samādhi-sūtra of the Bodhisattva Samantacakṣus*, two fascicles (or three fascicles), fifty-one sheets; translated by Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin.
*Prajñāpāramitā-śata-vyākhyāna-sūtra*, two fascicles, forty sheets; translated by An Shigao of the Later Han.
*Bodhisattva-avaivartika-karma-alaṃkāra-sūtra*, two fascicles, eighteen sheets; [translated] by Zhu Fonian of the Former Qin at Chang’an.

*An-yi Huo-guo Pusa Jing* (The Sutra on the Bodhisattva Who Protects the State), two fascicles, forty-two sheets; translated at Daxingshan Monastery by Jñānagupta and others during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty.
*Chao-riming Sanmei Jing* (The Sutra on the Samādhi of Transcending the Sun’s Radiance), two fascicles, forty-six sheets; translated by Dharmarakṣa during the Taishi era of the Western Jin dynasty.
*Yue-shang-nü Jing* (The Sutra of the Girl Candrottarā), two fascicles, twenty-seven sheets; [translated] during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty.
*Madhyamāgama-sūtra* (Zhongyin jing), two fascicles, twenty-seven sheets; translated by Dharmagupta during the Northern Liang dynasty.

*Sumerugarbha-sūtra* (Xumi zang jing), two fascicles, forty-eight sheets; translated by Zhu Fonian of the Former Qin dynasty. *Buddhāvataṃsaka-praveśa-tathāgatācintyaviṣaya-sūtra* (Fohuayan ruru lai busi jing), two fascicles, twenty-one sheets;
translated by Ratnaśānti at Ye-du during the Northern Qi dynasty. [Translated by] Dharmagupta and others during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty.
The *Mahābherī-haraka-sūtra* (大法鼓經), two fascicles, thirty-one pages, translated at Xingshan Temple;
The *Sūtra on the Essential Collection of All Buddhas* (諸佛要集經), two fascicles, thirty-three pages, translated by Guṇavarman of the Song dynasty at Yangdu;
The *Sūtra on the Adornment and Purity of Mañjuśrī’s Buddha-field* (文殊師利佛土嚴淨經), two fascicles, thirty-four pages, translated by Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin during the Yongxi era.
In the [Yuan] year, Zhu Fahu translated the *Rushou Wushang Qingjing Fenwei Jing* (The Sutra of the Supreme Pure Alms-Gathering of Nāgārjuna) in two fascicles and twenty-seven sheets;

it is also titled the *Jueliao Zhufa Ruhuansanmei Jing* (The Sutra on the Samādhi of Resolving All Dharmas as Illusory). During the Song dynasty, Master Xiang translated the *Dacheng Tongxing Jing* (The Mahāyāna Sutra of Common Nature) in two fascicles and thirty-nine sheets at Nanhai Commandery.
In the Tiānhé era of the Later Zhou, [Kumārajīva... (Note: The final character "崛" appears to be a fragment of a name, likely Kumārajīva, though the full context is missing from the provided text.)
Together with the Saṃgha, he translated the *Akṣobhyatathāgatasyavyūha-sūtra* (The Scripture on the Land of Akṣobhya Buddha) in two fascicles and thirty-eight sheets at Chang’an;
it is also titled the *Buddhakṣetra-bodhisattva-śikṣā-siddhi-sūtra*. It was translated by Zhi Chen at Luoyang during the Jianhe era of the Later Han.

He also translated the *Padmavaktra-sūtra* (The Scripture on the Lotus Face) in two fascicles and thirty-three sheets during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty; it was translated by Yaśas. Furthermore, he translated the *Mahāyāna-avadāna* (Mahāyāna Parables).
*The King Sūtra*, two fascicles, thirty-three sheets; translated at Xingshan Monastery by Jñānagupta and others during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty.
*The Kāśyapa Sūtra*, two fascicles, twenty-nine sheets; translated in Luoyang by Prince Upaśūna during the Later Wei dynasty.
*The Mahāmāyūrī Vidyārājñī Dhāraṇī Sūtra*, two fascicles, thirty-two sheets; translated by Saṃghavarman of the Liang dynasty at... [text continues].

*The Scripture on Awakening the Pure Mind*, two fascicles, twenty-seven sheets; translated at Yangdu (the capital) by Yan Yun’guan during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty by Dharmagupta and others at Xingshan Monastery.
*The Scripture on the Supreme Reliance*, two fascicles, thirty-one sheets; translated at Guangzhou by Paramārtha of the Chen dynasty.
*The Scripture on the Transference of Consciousness*, two fascicles, thirty-three sheets; translated during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty by Dharmagupta and others.
*The Sutra of Unprecedented Events*, two fascicles, forty sheets, translated by Baotou et al. at Xingshan Temple.
*The Tathāgatagarbha Sūtra* (also known as *The Mahāvaipulya Tathāgatagarbha Sūtra*), two fascicles (or three), fifty-one sheets, translated by Tanjing at Yangdu during the Southern Qi dynasty.
*The Sūtra of Inconceivable Merit*, two fascicles (or four), thirty-eight sheets. *The Sūtra of Great Auspicious Meaning and Mantras*, two fascicles.
One fascicle, or four fascicles, thirty-eight sheets: *The Sūtra on the Dreams of the Bodhisattva*, two fascicles, thirty-four sheets;
*The Sūtra of Mañjuśrī’s Questions*, two fascicles, forty-nine sheets; *The Benevolent Kings Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, two fascicles, twenty-eight sheets;
*The Sūtra on the Non-differentiation of the Essential Nature of the Dharmadhātu*, two fascicles, twenty-four sheets; *The Secret Karma* [Sūtra].
The *Vajrapāṇi-rakṣa-sūtra* in two fascicles, thirty-six sheets; the *Mahāvaipulya-tathāgata-guhya-nidhi-sūtra* in two fascicles, thirty-four sheets;
the *Subāhu-bodhisattva-paripṛcchā-sūtra* in two fascicles, twenty-six sheets; and the *Mahāśuddha-dharmaparyāya-sūtra* in one fascicle, twenty-four sheets.
These were translated by Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin dynasty; the above constitutes one set of scriptures.
Translated again by Jñānayaśas of the Sui dynasty as the *Mahāvyūha-dharmaparyāya-sūtra* in two fascicles.
The textual meaning is largely identical.

*Shunquan fangbian jing* (Sutra on Accordance with Expedient Means), three fascicles or one fascicle, twenty-seven sheets; also titled *Zhuan nushen pusa jing* (Sutra on the Bodhisattva Transforming the Female Body), translated by Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin. The above is one sutra.
During the Song dynasty, Fahai also translated it;
it is titled the *Lèyíngluòzhuāngyánfāngbiàn Jīng* (Sūtra on the Skillful Means of the Adornment of Joyful Garlands),
in one fascicle.
Wen Tong did not record it.
*The Great Cloud Wheel Sūtra for Invoking Rain*, two fascicles, twenty-eight sheets; translated by Jñānayaśas during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty. The above sūtra has three translations.
The first was translated by Zhu Fajü during the Zhou dynasty and titled the *Mahāmegha-vṛṣṭi-sūtra*.
Later, during the Sui dynasty, Jñānagupta translated it again.
The characters for *Mahāvaipulya* have been enlarged.
Because the meaning is the same, it is abbreviated here.

*The Tathāgata-alaṃkāra-jñānaprabha-buddhaviṣayapraveśa Sūtra*, one fascicle, thirty-four sheets; translated at the capital of Luoyang by Bodhiruci during the Later Wei dynasty. This is the third translation of this sūtra.
The version translated by Saṃghavarman during the Liang dynasty is titled the *Buddhaviṣayajñānālaṃkārasūtra*.
There is also a separately translated version titled the *Jñānaprabhālaṃkārasūtra*;
these are different translations of the same original text.

The *Sūtra of the Elder Guṇapāla*, two fascicles, twenty-six pages; translated at Chang’an by [Dharmayaśas] during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty. This aforementioned sūtra has three translations;
the first was produced by Zhu Fahu of the Jin dynasty.
*The Scripture on the Youth Candraprabha*,
one fascicle;
alternatively translated as *The Scripture on Śunika*.
The details are omitted here.
*The Scripture of the Good-Thought Youth*, two fascicles, twenty sheets; translated by Jñānagupta during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty. The above scripture has three translations.
Originally titled *The King of the Pinnacle of the Great Vaipulya*,
it was also known as the *Sutra on the Questions of Vimalakīrti’s Son*.
Later, it appeared again under the title *The Mahāyāna Pinnacle King Sutra*.
The textual characteristics are largely identical.
*Yugakarāyati-prcchā-bodhisattvacaryā-sūtra*, one fascicle, twenty-five sheets, translated by Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin. The above is one sutra.
There are three translations.
The first was produced during the Later Han dynasty by An Xuan and titled the *Fajing jing* (Sūtra on the Dharma Mirror).
Translated later by the monk Seng Kai of the Northern Wei dynasty;
it is titled the *Ugraparipṛcchā-sūtra*,
and its literary style and principles are largely identical [to the previous version].

The *Wúliàng qīngjìng píngděng jué jīng* (Sūtra of the Immeasurable Pure Equal Enlightenment), two fascicles, sixty sheets; translated during the Wei dynasty by Bo Yan. This aforementioned sūtra has three translations;
that which was produced by Zhi Qian during the Wu dynasty is as follows.
The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*,
in two fascicles,
translated by Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin dynasty.
It is titled the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Life*.
It consists of two fascicles;
its literary style and principles are no different [from the previous version].
Therefore, it is abbreviated.
*The Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja*, two fascicles, thirty sheets; translated by Jñānagupta during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty. The above sūtra has four translations.
The one translated by Buddhayaśas during the Later Qin period is titled the *Ākāśagarbha-mantra-sūtra*.
The one translated during the Song period by Dhamamitra is [the same].
It is titled the *Sūtra on the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha Contemplating Emptiness*,
and is also separately translated as the *Ākāśagarbha Sūtra*;
these versions differ in their extensive and abbreviated texts.
The meaning is identical.
*Pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*, two fascicles, twenty-three sheets; translated by Jñānagupta at the Shànglín Garden in the Eastern Capital during the Dàyè era of the Sui dynasty. The above is one sutra.
Translated again by Xuanzang of the Tang Dynasty;
titled the *Pratītyasamutpādādivibhaṅganirdeśa-sūtra*.
Two fascicles.
Although the language is skillful and clever, those who investigate it find it easy to turn back.
From the *Sūtra of the Tathāgata Supreme Lamp King of the East* (13 sheets) onwards, there are one hundred and forty-eight single [entries].
During the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty, Dharmagupta translated the *Sarvadharmāgrarāja-sūtra* in twenty-two sheets at Daxingshan Temple;
during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty, Dharmagupta also translated the *Saddharmaprabhāsa-samādhi-sūtra* in twenty-two sheets.
During the reign of Emperor Ling of the Later Han, Zhi Yao translated the *Sudāna-jātaka-sūtra* in sixteen sheets. [Translated during] the Western Qin...

The *Prince Mupo Jing* (Sūtra of Prince Mupo), five sheets, translated by Fajian during the time of Qifu Guoren; the *Surataparipṛcchā Sūtra* (Xulai Jing), nineteen sheets, translated by Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin;
the *Suvarṇavarṇa-avadāna Sūtra* (Jinsewang Jing), eight sheets, translated by Zhi Qian during the Huangwu era of the Wu dynasty;
and the *Ekavyūha-svayaṃprati-jñāna-samādhi Sūtra* (Duzheng Zishi Sanmei Jing), eight sheets, translated by Prajñāruci at the capital of Luoyang during the Later Wei—these constitute one [set].
The *Nāmasvayaṃpratiśrutkasamādhi-sūtra*, translated by Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin dynasty, comprising twenty-five scrolls;
the *Mahāmāyā-sūtra*, translated by Tanjing of the Southern Qi dynasty at Yangdu;
the *Mahāvaipulyatathāgatagarbha-sūtra*, nine scrolls, translated by Buddhabhadra at Yangdu during the Yixi era of the Eastern Jin; and the *Tathāgata-upāyakauśalya-mantra*.
*The Śrīmālādevī Siṃhanāda Sūtra on the Expedient Means of the One Vehicle*, translated by Guṇabhadra during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty, ten scrolls, nineteen pages;
*The Sumati Sūtra*, also known as the *Sumati Bodhisattva Sūtra*, translated by Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin dynasty, eight scrolls, eight pages;
*The Sūtra on the Rare and Comparative Measurement*, translated by Guṇabhadra at the capital of Yangdu during the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty, nineteen pages.

*Guǐdé jīng* (Sūtra on Merit), six sheets; translated by Jñānagupta during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty. *Fànnǚ shǒuyì jīng* (Sūtra of the Brahmin Woman Śrīmatī), six sheets; translated by Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin dynasty.
*Cīmóbōdì shòujì jīng* (Sūtra of the Prediction for Kṣemavatī), four sheets; translated by Bodhiruci at the capital of Luò during the Later Wei dynasty.

*Yuèmíng púsà jīng* (Sūtra of the Bodhisattva Candraprabha), three sheets; translated by Zhi Qian during the Huangwu era of the Wu dynasty. *Míshífāngmíng* (Extinction of the Darkness of the Ten Directions).
*The Sūtra of the Birth of the Bodhicitta*, six sheets; translated by Dharmarakṣa during the Yuexi era of the Western Jin dynasty.

*The Sūtra of the Universal Gate Chapter*, eleven sheets; translated by Jñānagupta at Xingshan Monastery during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty. *The Sūtra of the Heavenly Son King Śreṇika*, twelve sheets;
translated by Dharmarakṣa during the Taikang era of the Western Jin dynasty. *The Sūtra of the Heavenly Son King Śreṇika*, sixteen sheets; translated during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty.
Kumārajīva translated the *Cittavidyā-sūtra* (Heart-Clarifying Sūtra) in three fascicles at Xingshan Temple.

During the Western Jin dynasty, Dharmarakṣa translated the *Candrapradīpa-samādhi-sūtra* (Moon-Lamp Samādhi Sūtra) in ten fascicles—also known as the *Mañjuśrī-daśakriyā-sūtra* (Sūtra on the Ten Deeds of Mañjuśrī) or the *Pratibhāna-samādhi-sūtra* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of Constructing Wisdom).

During the Song dynasty, the Venerable Master [Guṇabhadra] translated the *Acintyaprabhāsa-bodhisattva-bhāṣita-sūtra* (Sūtra Spoken by the Bodhisattva Inconceivable Radiance) in twelve fascicles—also known as the [same title].
The *Aksayamati-nirdeśa Sūtra* (translated by Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin);
the *Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā-bodhisattva-vyākaraṇa Sūtra*, twenty sheets, also known as the *Vyākaraṇa Sūtra* (translated by Zhi Chen during the reign of Emperor Ling of the Later Han);
the *Candraprabha-kumāra Sūtra*, nineteen sheets, also known as the *Sūrata-paripṛcchā-candraprabha-kumāra Sūtra* (Western Jin).
Originally, during the year [of the reign of Emperor Hui] of the Later Han, Zhu Fahu translated the *Dīpadāna-puṇya-sūtra* (The Sutra on the Merit of Offering Lamps) in fourteen sheets at Chang’an.
Later, during the Qi dynasty, Saṃghayeśas translated the *Bodhisattva-rañjanā-vivarjana-sūtra* (The Sutra of the Bodhisattva’s Rebuke of Lust) in two sheets at Ye.

During the Hongshi era of the Later Qin, Kumārajīva translated the *Puruṣa-mūla-kāma-utpatti-sūtra* (The Sutra on the Origin of Human Desire) in fourteen sheets at Chang’an. Furthermore, Zhu Fahu produced the *Ren suo cong chushi jing* (The Sutra on Whom People Follow).
*The Sūtra on the Non-Increase, Non-Decrease*: Six pages; translated by An Shigao during the reign of Emperor Huan of the Later Han.
*The Sūtra of the Buddha’s Words*: Three pages; translated by Dharmaruci during the Zhengguang era of the Later Wei, produced at Luoyang.
*The Sūtra of the Jewel Casket Without Letters*: Six pages; translated by Dharmaruci of the Later Wei. *The Sūtra of the Lion’s Roar*.
*The Sūtra on the Ten Dharmas*, five sheets; translated by Bodhiruci and Buddhayaśas during the Northern Wei dynasty. *The Sūtra on the Twenty Dharmas*, twenty sheets;

translated by Saṃghavarman at the capital of Yangdu during the Putong era of the Liang dynasty. *The Sūtra on the Non-Necessity of Entering Nirvāṇa*, twenty-one sheets; translated by Bodhiruci during the Northern Wei dynasty.
*The Sūtra of the Divine Mantras of the Names of the Twelve Buddhas*, six sheets; translated during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty.
*Māraparājayasūtra*, translated by Kumārajīva, 18 sheets; translated by Dharmarakṣa during the Taikang era of the Western Jin dynasty, 14 sheets;
*Sarvabuddhaviṣayāvatārajñānālokālaṃkārasūtra*, translated by Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin dynasty, 6 sheets;
*Ratnakaraṇḍakavyūhasūtra*, 8 sheets, translated during the reign of Emperor Ling of the Later Han dynasty.

At that time, Dharmakṣema translated the *Mahāvaipulya-dhāraṇī-sūtra* in thirteen sheets; during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty, Vinītāruci translated the *Maitreya-paripṛcchā-praṇidhāna-sūtra* in eight sheets;
during the Western Jin dynasty, Dharmarakṣa translated the *Mañjuśrī-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* in twenty-two sheets;
and during the Tianjian era of the Liang dynasty, Mandaraka translated [the same] at the capital of Yangdu.
*The Sūtra of the Firm Woman*, six sheets; translated by Jñānayaśas during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty. *The Sūtra Expounding the Deeds of the Laity and the Clergy*, nine sheets;
translated by Dharmabuddhin in Henan during the Western Qin dynasty. *The Sūtra on the Birthplace of the Bodhisattva*, three sheets; also titled *The Cāmara Sūtra*;
translated by Zhi Qian during the Huangwu era of the Wu dynasty. *The Sūtra of the Private-Ha Samādhi*, eleven sheets; also titled *The Bodhisattva...* [text fragment].
*The Way-Tree Sūtra* (also known as *The Way-Tree Samādhi*), translated by Zhi Qian during the Huangwu era of the Wu Dynasty; twenty-two sheets.

*The Jewel Net Youth Sūtra* (also known as *The Jewel Net Sūtra*), translated by Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin Dynasty; six sheets. *The Sūtra of the Names of One Hundred Buddhas*, translated by Yaśas during the Kaihuang era of the Sui Dynasty;
seventeen sheets. *The Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings*, translated in the Jianyuan era of the Southern Qi Dynasty; seventeen sheets.
*Dharmayaśas* translated the *Sūtra on Contemplating Maitreya’s Ascent to Tuṣita Heaven* in eight sheets at Guangzhou;
*Jing Sheng*, Marquis of Anyang under Juqu [Mendun] of Northern Liang, translated the *Sūtra on Contemplating Immeasurable Life* in sixteen sheets;

during the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty, *Kālayaśas* translated the *Sūtra on Contemplating the Practices of Samantabhadra* in sixteen sheets at the capital of Yangdu. During the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty...
In the [Liu] Song dynasty, during the Yuanjia era, Dharmamitra translated the *Bhaiṣajyarāja-bhaiṣajyasamudgata-dvibodhisattva-sūtra* in nineteen sheets at Yangdu;
during the same Yuanjia era, Jñānayaśas translated the *Avalokiteśvara-vinipāta-parihāra-sūtra* in eleven sheets;
and during the Song dynasty, the foreign ship-owner Zhu Nanti translated the *Avalokiteśvara-vyākaraṇa-sūtra* in fourteen sheets.
At that time, Dharmarakṣa translated the *Mṛgajā-sūtra* in four sheets at the capital of Yangdu; Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin translated the *Mṛgaśīrṣa-sūtra* in three sheets;
Zhi Qian of the Jianxing era of the Wu dynasty translated the *Bhaya-vinodana-sūtra* in fifteen sheets;
Bo Yan of the Wei dynasty translated the *Jentāka-mahāsāṃghika-sūtra* in three sheets; and Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin translated [the following] four [sheets].
*The Sūtra on the Unattainable*, four sheets, translated by Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin;

*The Sūtra on the Field of Merit*, six sheets—also titled *The Sūtra on the Field of Merit for All Virtues*—translated by Dharmarakṣa and Dharmasthiti of the Western Jin; *The Sūtra on the Merit of Leaving Home*, five sheets, translated by Zhi Qian during the Wu period;
*The Sūtra on the Essential Nature of Entering the Dharma-realm*, ten sheets, translated by Jñānagupta and others during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty.
The *Maitreya-buddhābhisaṃbodhi-sūtra* in seventeen fascicles, translated at Xingshan Monastery; translated by Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin.
The above scripture has three translations.
Translated by Kumārajīva of Later Qin.
Intended for Maitreya’s descent to be born,
the prose is fluent and elegant, yet the details of the events and their meanings are somewhat deficient.
Furthermore, there is a separate translation by another person titled *The Sūtra on Maitreya’s Coming*,
consisting of approximately three sheets;
its wording and principles are incomplete.
Therefore, the original edition is preserved.
The *Amoghapāśa-mantra-sūtra* in twelve sheets, translated by Xuanzang of the Tang dynasty—
this aforementioned sūtra is the same text as the *Amoghapāśa-sūtra* previously translated by Jñānagupta of the Sui dynasty.
The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* (Five sheets), translated by Kumārajīva during the Hongshi era of the Later Qin dynasty. This aforementioned sūtra has three translations;
it is identical to that produced during the Song period by Guṇabhadra.
The *Sūtra of the Praise of the Pure Land and its Reception*, translated by Xuanzang of the Tang dynasty,
as well as the *Smaller Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*.
Since these are the same texts, they are not presented twice.

Regarding the *Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabhā-sūtra* in thirteen sheets, which many who have not extensively investigated it consider to be a spurious sūtra: this aforementioned sūtra was translated by a śramaṇa from Luyesisi Temple during the Song dynasty.
There are three translations.
This is identical to the *Bhaiṣajyaguru-vaiḍūryaprabhāsa-pūrvapraṇidhāna-sūtra* translated by Dharmagupta during the Sui dynasty,
and it does not differ from that produced by Xuanzang of the Tang dynasty.
The *Lǎomǔ jīng* (Sūtra of the Old Mother), in two fascicles, also known as the *Lǎonǚrén jīng* (Sūtra of the Old Woman), translated by Zhi Qian during the Wu period.
This aforementioned sūtra is identical to the separately translated *Lǎomǔ liùyīng jīng*.
They cannot be practiced simultaneously;
one version must be retained.
This is the standard rule for other scriptures as well.
The *Mañjuśrīcaryā-sūtra*, seven sheets long, translated by Jñānagupta during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty.
This aforementioned sūtra is the same original text as the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra* translated by Dharmaruci of the Later Wei.
The *Vajramaṇḍala-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, fourteen folios, translated by Jñānagupta during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty.
This aforementioned sūtra is identical to the *Vajrottama-rasa-sūtra* produced by Saṃghavarman of the Later Wei dynasty.
The *Sūtra on Skillful Reverence*, seven sheets; translated by Jñānagupta during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty.
The above-mentioned sūtra is identical to the *Sūtra on Right Reverence* produced by Saṃghavarman.
The *Vimaladattā-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, twenty-five sheets; translated by Gautama Dharmaruci at the capital of Ye during the Later Wei dynasty. The above-mentioned sūtra is [as follows].
Three translations.
These are identical to the *Vimaladattā-dārikā-sūtra* and the *Vimaladattā-bodhisattvāvadāna-sūtra*.
The *Abhayamati-dārikā-sūtra*, consisting of fifteen sheets, was translated by Buddhayaśas during the Yuanxiang era of the Northern Wei dynasty. This concludes the aforementioned scripture.
This is identical to the *Ajātaśatru-rāja-āśvarya-bodhisattva-sūtra* translated by Dharmarakṣa during the Western Jin dynasty.
The *Uṣṇīṣavijayā-vividha-mukha-praveśa-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, seventeen sheets, was translated at the capital of Ye by the lay devotee Wan Tianyi of the Northern Qi. This concludes the first scripture.
This is identical to the *Dharmadhātuprakṛtyasambhedanirdeśa-dharmaparyāya-sūtra* translated by Fa-jian.

The *Mahātejo’rciḥ-ṛṣiparipṛcchā-sūtra*, fourteen sheets, translated by Jñānagupta during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty; this single sūtra is identical to the *Paramārthadharmavijaya-sūtra* translated by Dharmaruci during the Later Wei dynasty.
*The Sūtra of the Eight Buddha Names*, three sheets; translated during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty by Jñānagupta.
This aforementioned sūtra is identical to the *Sūtra of the Eight Auspicious Ones* produced by Guṇabhadra during the Song dynasty.
The *Sūtra on the Past Deeds of the Bodhisattva Nāgadatta* in four sheets. The aforementioned sūtra is identical to the *Sūtra of the Daughter Nāgadatta* translated by Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin.
The *Sūtra of Śyāmaka* in five sheets, translated by Dharmakṣema of the Later Qin. The aforementioned sūtra.
It is identical to the *Śānta-bodhisattva-sūtra* translated separately.
The *Śāli-stamba-sūtra* (six sheets) on the right is identical to the version of the *Utpāda-vyaya-sūtra* produced by Zhi Qian.
The *Bodhicittālaṃkāra-sūtra*, seven sheets; translated by Kumārajīva of the Later Qin.
This aforementioned sūtra is identical to the *Mahāvaipulya-bodhisattva-daśabhūmi-sūtra* produced by Dharmarakṣa.

The *Aniṣṭhā-sūtra* (Sūtra on Having No Expectations), nineteen sheets; also known as the *Hastipada-sūtra* (Elephant’s Footprint Sūtra), translated by Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin. The above-mentioned sūtra is identical to the separately translated *Hastikakṣya-sūtra*.
The Mahāvaipulya Sūtra-rāja, two sheets, translated by Dharmaruci of the Later Wei. The above sutra is identical to another translation, the *Parivarta Sūtra*.
The *Maitreya-paripṛcchā Sūtra*, four sheets, translated by Dharmaruci of the Later Wei. The above sutra is [as follows].
This is identical to the *Mahāyāna Vaipulya Essential Wisdom Sūtra* translated separately.
The *Huiyin Samādhi Sūtra* in twenty sheets was translated by Zhi Qian during the Wu period.
This aforementioned sūtra is identical to the *Tathāgata-Jñānamudrā Sūtra* translated separately.
The *Sarvadharmagaru-rāja-sūtra* in twenty sheets, translated by [Dharmaruci] during the Xinghe era of the Northern Wei dynasty.
This aforementioned sūtra is identical to the separately translated *Sarvadharmanirbhaya-rāja-sūtra*.
*The Sūtra on the Decisive Dhāraṇī*, eight sheets; translated by Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin.
The above-mentioned sūtra is identical to the *Sūtra on Leaving Zhu and Accusing the Buddha*.
*The Sūtra of the Buddha of Milk Light*, six sheets; translated by Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin. The above-mentioned sūtra is [as follows].
This is identical to the separate translation of the *Vatsīputrīya Sūtra*.

It appears as the twenty-first fascicle of the *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*, though the translator of this separate version is lost and its date unknown. Thus, this single sūtra exists in three translations.
This is identical to the *Buddhāvatamsaka-ratnakoṭi-sūtra* and the *Mahāyāna-ratnakūṭa-sūtra* translated by Zhi Chen.

The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, consisting of thirteen sheets, was translated by Kumārajīva at Chang’an during the Hongshi era of the Later Qin dynasty; this concludes the aforementioned scripture.
There were four translations.
That produced by Liu Zhi during the Later Wei dynasty accords with the treatise;
nevertheless, those who uphold [the text] mostly prefer the Qin version.
Therefore, the other three versions of these texts were seldom used during that time.

The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (The Vinaya of the Dharmaguptakas), translated by the Elder’s Son Zhi [Fonian], consists of six fascicles; it is also known as the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Alternative Translation).
This is one sutra with three versions.
This is identical to the two types of *Sūtra on the Parinirvāṇa of the Śrāvaka and Bodhisattva* translated by Dharmarakṣa;
therefore, one version has been included here accordingly.
*Hastikṣaya-vihāra-sūtra*, nine sheets, translated by Vinītāruci during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty. This concludes the first sūtra.
Three translations exist.
This is identical to the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-bodhicitta-sūtra* and the *Gayāśīrṣa-sūtra*.
The *Dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda-sūtra*, four pages long, was translated by Guṇavidi during the Yongming era of the Southern Qi dynasty. The above constitutes one scripture.
Third, the *Sutra on the Causes and Conditions of Contemplation under the Peepal Tree*, translated by Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin,
is identical to the *Sutra on Hearing the Formation of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination* translated by An Shigao of the Han.
The *Sūtra on the Transformation of the Female Body* consists of nineteen sheets.

This single sūtra has been translated four times; it is identical to the *Sūtra on the Girl in the Womb Listening to the Dharma*, the *Womb Treasury Sūtra*, and the *Sūtra of the Stainless Noble Woman*.
The *Ekāntika-bodhisattva-utpatti-sūtra*, eleven sheets; translated by Jñānagupta at Xingshan Monastery during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty.
This aforementioned sūtra has six translations and is identical to the *Ananta-mukha-sūkṣma-rahasya-sūtra*.
The *Sūtra on Holding the Dharma through Immeasurable Gateways*,
the *Ānanda-mukha Sūtra*,
and the *Sūtra on Breaking Māra through Immeasurable Gateways*.
The *Śāriputra-dhāraṇī-sūtra* is the same [as its counterpart].
The *Ekādaśamukha-avalokiteśvara-sūtra*, ten sheets, translated by Jñānagupta during the Later Zhou dynasty—
this aforementioned sūtra is identical to the *Ekādaśamukha-avalokiteśvara-devatā-mantra-sūtra* translated by Xuanzang of the Imperial Court.
The *Sūtra on the Three Turnings of the Previous Life*, three scrolls;
the above is one sūtra, which is identical to the separately translated *Sūtra of the Silver-Colored Woman*.
The *Sūtra of Prince Śuddhodana*, four scrolls; the above is one sūtra.
It is identical to the *Sūtra on Prince Andhaka* translated separately.
The *Bodhisattva-upāya-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, six sheets;
the aforementioned sūtra is identical to the *Vajra-guhyadhāraṇī-sūtra* translated separately.
The *Aśokarāja-vyākaraṇa-sūtra* in four sheets;
this sutra is identical to the *Puṣpāhāra-rājopasaṃkramaṇa-buddha-vyākaraṇa-sūtra*.
The *Kusuma-rāja-dhāraṇī-sūtra* in three sheets; this is another sutra.
Three translations.
These are identical to the *Siṃhavikrīḍita-paripṛcchā-sūtra* and the *Puṣpakūṭa-dhāraṇī-sūtra*.

The six folios of the *Pātra-prakṣālana-sūtra* are a separate chapter of the *Suvikrāntavikrāmi-paripṛcchā-sūtra* translated differently. The *Ratnarāśi-bodhisattva-sūtra* consists of thirteen [folios].
The *Banzhou sanmei jing biepin* (Separate Chapter of the Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra), eight sheets; translated during the Xiankang era of the Eastern Jin by Śrīmitra.
The *Xukongzang pusa wen chijing fu jing* (Sūtra on the Merit of Holding the Scripture Asked by Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha), six sheets;

translator lost. Other scriptures may be known by analogy. The *Pusa xiuxing jing* (Sūtra on the Practice of Bodhisattvas), seven sheets; also titled *Weishi changzhe guan* (The Vision of the Layman of Majestic Power).
The Scripture on the Causes and Conditions of the Bodhisattva’s Sacrifice of His Body to a Starving Tiger and the Erection of a Stupa, seven pages;
The Scripture on King Sarvamdada Practicing the Dānapāramitā, four pages; The Scripture on King Bimbisāra Visiting the Buddha to Make Offerings, five pages;
The Scripture on the King of Sālā, four pages; The Scripture on the Great Meaning, five pages; and The Scripture on Pilo, the Crown Prince of the Heavenly King, three pages.
The Sūtra on the Elder Joyful Sound, five sheets; the Sūtra on the Wife of the Elder Dharma-Will, three sheets;
the Sūtra on the Rishi Sarvajñāprabha’s Compassionate Mind and Abstention from Meat, five sheets; the Mañjuśrī-parinirvāṇa Sūtra, four sheets;
the Siṃhacandra-buddha-jātaka Sūtra, seven sheets; and the Amitābha-dundubhi-nirghoṣa-dhāraṇī Sūtra, four sheets.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi Sūtra* in eleven sheets; the *Vajrasamādhi-bhāva-akṣaya-aniruddha Sūtra* in eight sheets—also known as the *Vajra-viśuddhi Sūtra*;
the *Ratnakūṭa-samādhi-mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā-dharmakāya Sūtra* in six sheets;
the *Sahasrabuddha-nidāna Sūtra* in eighteen sheets; the *Aṣṭabuddhanāma Sūtra* in two sheets; and the *Aṣṭamaṅgala-devatā-mantra Sūtra*.
The *Daśadharmanirdeśa-aṣṭamaṅgalika-mantra-sūtra*, three fascicles; the *Daśamaṅgalika-sūtra*, two fascicles;
the *Bhadramukha-sūtra* (also known as the *Bhadravargīya-bhāryā-sūtra*), three fascicles; the *Gambhīra-mahāpariṇāma-sūtra*, five fascicles;

the *Bhadrapañcaguṇa-sūtra*, two fascicles; the *Māyāśubhasattva-sūtra*, eighteen fascicles; the *Aṣṭamahāpuruṣapudgala-bodhi-sūtra*, two fascicles; the *Later Translation of the A...* [text continues].
The *Amitābha Sūtra*, one sheet; the *Extremely Rare Sūtra*, five sheets; the sixteen sūtras following these were all translated by Xuanzang of the Tang dynasty at the capital;
the *Sūtra of the Peerless One*, two sheets; the *Sūtra of the Dhāraṇī of the Heart of All Buddhas*, two sheets;

the *Sūtra on Receiving and Maintaining the Names of the Seven Buddhas*, five sheets; the *Sūtra on the Buddha’s Prophecy Concerning the Persistence of the Dharma at the Time of His Parinirvāṇa*, five sheets; the Buddha... [text ends].

The *Dìjīng* (Earth Sūtra) in ten scrolls; the *Chēngzàn Dàshèng Gōngdé Jīng* (Sūtra Praising the Merits of the Mahāyāna) in five scrolls; the *Xiǎn Wúbiān Fótǔ Jīng* (Sūtra Revealing Boundless Buddha-lands) in two scrolls;

the *Shèngdāng Bìyìn Tuóluóní Jīng* (Sūtra of the Dhāraṇī of the Victorious Banner and Arm Seal) in three scrolls; the *Jìkǔ Tuóluóní Jīng* (Sūtra of the Dhāraṇī for Relieving Suffering) in two scrolls;

the *Bāyīn Pùmì Tuóluóní Jīng* (Sūtra of the Dhāraṇī of the Eightfold Universal Secret) in two scrolls; the *Chíshì Tuóluóní Jīng* (Sūtra of the Dhāraṇī for Sustaining the World) in seven scrolls; and the *Yuánqǐ Shèng* (Noble Account of the Origins).

The *Daojing* (Scripture on the Path) in five sheets; the *Dumen tuoluoni jing* (Dhāraṇī Scripture of the Six Gates) in two sheets; the *Bore duoxin jing* (Heart Sūtra of Prajñāpāramitā) in one sheet;
the *Tianqingwen jing* (Sūtra of Questions by Devaputra) in three sheets; the Mahāyāna Vinaya in twenty sections totaling thirty-one fascicles and four hundred and twenty sheets;
and the *Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra* in six or seven fascicles totaling eighty-two sheets—these are present here.
*Jiājia púsà jì* (Bodhisattva Precepts of the Family), translated by Dharmakṣema at the Xiányù Palace in the capital of Liáng during the Northern Liáng dynasty;

four fascicles, sixty-nine sheets. *Fózàng jīng* (Sūtra of the Buddha-treasury), translated by Kumārajīva in Cháng'ān during the Later Qín dynasty; three fascicles, forty-four sheets. *Fāngguǎng sānjiè jīng* (Vaipulya Sūtra on the Threefold Precepts), three fascicles, forty-four sheets.
*Bǎoliáng jīng* (Ratnarāśi Sūtra), two fascicles, thirty sheets. *Fànwǎng jīng* (Brahmajāla Sūtra), translated by Dàogōng during the Northern Liáng dynasty.
Two fascicles, thirty-four sheets; translated by Kumārajīva of the Later Qin, the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra* (nine sheets);
translated at the capital of Yangdu during the Tianjian era of the Liang dynasty by Saṃghavarman, the *Vinayaviniścaya-sūtra* (seventeen sheets).

All catalogs state these were translated at Dunhuang, though the names of the persons and the specific period are not clearly indicated. [Also] the *Mañjuśrī-paṇḍita-deśanā-avyavakīrṇa-sūtra*, two [fascicles].
11 sheets; also titled *The Scripture on Mañjuśrī’s Five-Part Confession of Transgressions*, translated by Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin dynasty.
*The Scripture on Śāriputra’s Confession of Transgressions*, 5 sheets; also titled *The Scripture on Confession of Transgressions*, translated by Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin dynasty.

*The Scripture on the Questions of Praśāntavighuṣṭasvara*, 18 sheets, translated by Fahui during the Song dynasty. The above one scripture is identical to that produced during the Western Jin dynasty.
The *Vini-viśuddhi-vaipulya-sūtra* and the *Mañjuśrī-viśuddha-vinaya-sūtra* are identical;
therefore, only one version has been retained.
The *Mahāyāna-tri-skandha-pratideśana-sūtra*, thirteen sheets, was translated by Ratnamati and others at Xingshan Monastery during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty.
The *Bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* translated by Saṃghavarman, eighteen sheets; translated by Xuanzang at Cuiwei Palace in the twenty-first year of the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty.
The *Bodhisattva-karman* translated by Xuanzang at Cuiwei Palace in the twenty-third year of the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty, six sheets.
The *Dharmasamādhi-sūtra*, seven sheets; the *Bodhisattvāntara-śīla-sūtra*, seventeen [sheets].
*The Sutra of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra*, three scrolls; *The Sutra on the Bodhisattva Receiving the Fast*, two scrolls;
*The Sutra on Purifying Karmic Obstructions*, fourteen scrolls; *The Sutra on the Good Precepts of the Bodhisattva*, fifteen scrolls;
*The Sutra on the Fivefold Repentance of the Bodhisattva*, two scrolls; and the Mahāyāna Śāstras, totaling sixty-three works in four hundred and forty-five fascicles.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom) in one hundred fascicles consists of eight thousand one hundred and fifteen sheets;
translated by Kumārajīva at the Ximing Monastery Tower in Chang’an during the Hongshi era of the Later Qin dynasty.

The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Treatise on the Stages of Yoga Practice) in one hundred fascicles consists of one thousand eight hundred and forty-eight sheets; translated by Xuanzang in the twentieth year of the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty.

Xuanzang translated the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* (顯揚聖教論) in twenty fascicles and two hundred and twenty-six sheets at the Great Ci'en Monastery during the nineteenth year of the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty.

Xuanzang translated the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-vyākhyā* (阿毘達磨雜集論) in sixteen fascicles and three hundred and fifty-five sheets at the Hongfu Monastery during the nineteenth year of the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty. At the Hongfu Monastery... [text continues]
*Prajñāpradīpa-śāstra*, fifteen fascicles, two hundred forty-two sheets;
translated by Fú Sì at Shèngguāng Temple during the third year of the Zhēnguān era of the Táng dynasty. *Mahāvyūha-śāstra*, fifteen fascicles (or ten fascicles), two hundred ten sheets;
composed by Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa and translated by Kumārajīva of the Later Qín dynasty. *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*.
*Treatise* (Śāstra), fourteen fascicles, two hundred and seventy sheets; composed by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna, translated by Kumārajīva of the Later Qin.
*Mahāyāna-sūtrālaṃkāra*, thirteen fascicles, two hundred sheets; translated by Śīlabhadra at Shengguang Temple during the fourth year of the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty.
*Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, twelve fascicles, two hundred and forty-five sheets; [translated] during the Yongming era of the Northern Wei.
The *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-bhāṣya* in ten fascicles and one hundred and eighty sheets, translated at the Shaolin Monastery in Luoyang by Ratnamati and others;
the commentary by Vasubandhu Bodhisattva, translated during the Yonghui era of the Tang dynasty by Xuanzang at the Northern Gate and Ci'en Monastery.
The above is one treatise.
The four translations are identical to the two versions translated by Paramārtha during the Liang dynasty,
as well as the one produced by Jñānagupta during the Sui dynasty.
The meaning is no different [between these].

The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* (Ten fascicles, 220 sheets), composed by Bodhisattva Asvabhāva, was translated by Xuanzang at Ci'en Monastery during the Yonghui era of the Tang dynasty. The *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śīla-sūtra* (Ten fascicles, or eight fascicles, 181 sheets) was translated by Dharmakṣema of the Northern Liang at Guzang. The above is one treatise.
It is largely identical to the *Śīla-sūtra*.
The *Śata-śāstra-vṛtti* in ten fascicles consists of two hundred and two sheets; it was translated by Xuanzang at Cien Monastery during the Xianqing era of the Tang dynasty.
The *Mahāyāna-abhidharma-samuccaya-śāstra* in seven fascicles consists of one hundred and eight sheets; it was translated by Xuanzang during the Xianqing era of the Tang dynasty.
*Fodi jing lun* (Buddhabhūmi-sūtra-śāstra), seven fascicles, one hundred and nineteen sheets; translated by Xuanzang during the Yonghui era of the Tang dynasty.

*Bodhicaryāvatāra-prajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, six fascicles, sixty-seven sheets; translated by Jñānagupta at the Translation Hall in the Shanglin Garden of the Eastern Capital during the Daye era of the Sui dynasty.
*Maitreya-paripṛcchā-sūtra-śāstra*, five fascicles (or ten fascicles); one.
*Mahāratnakūṭa-sūtra-śāstra*, four fascicles, 125 sheets; translated by Dharmaruci of the Later Wei.
*Suvikrāntavikrāmi-paripṛcchā-sūtra-śāstra*, four fascicles, 84 sheets; translated by Dharmaruci of the Later Wei.
*Buddhadhātu-śāstra*, four fascicles, 50 sheets; translated by Dharmatāśata of the Chen. *Mūlamadhyamaka-kārikā*, four fascicles, 97 sheets.
*Mahāyānottaratantra-śāstra* (Jìngxìng lùn), four fascicles, eighty-six sheets; translated by Kumārajīva of the Later Qin at Cháng'ān.
*Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra-śāstra*, three fascicles, thirty-seven sheets; translated by Bodhiruci of the Later Wei at the capital Luò.
*Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya*, three fascicles; translated by Bodhiruci of the Later Wei at the residence of the Duke Wénxuān of Qín Tàishàng.
Volume Sixty-one, Paper [Number]. Translated by Xuanzang at the Yuhua Palace in the twenty-third year of the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty.
The above treatise was translated three times.
This is largely identical to the two versions by Paramārtha of Chen and Śānta of Wei.
The *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchābodhicittabhūmi-sūtra-śāstra* in two fascicles consists of twenty-eight pages;
it is also known as the *Gayāśīrṣa-sūtra* and was translated at the capital of Luoyang by Bodhiruci of the Later Wei. The *Mahāpuruṣa-śāstra* in two fascicles consists of thirty-four pages.
*Madhyāntavibhāga-bhāṣya* (Discrimination of the Middle and the Extremes), composed by Bodhisattva Deva; translated by Dao Tai during the Northern Liang dynasty, two fascicles, thirty-eight sheets.

*Abhidharma-avatāra-śāstra* (Introduction to the Abhidharma), translated by Paramārtha of the Chen dynasty, two fascicles, thirty-four sheets. *Madhyamaka-hṛdaya-vṛtti-tarkajvālā* (The Blaze of Reasoning:

A Commentary on the Heart of the Middle Way), translated by Paramārtha of the Chen dynasty, three fascicles, thirty-three sheets. *Śata-śāstra* (Treatise in One Hundred Verses), upper and lower volumes, translated by Bodhiruci of the Later Wei dynasty.
*Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, two fascicles, thirty-two sheets; translated by Kumārajīva of the Later Qin.

*Sāṃkhya-bodhisattva-śāstra*, two fascicles, twenty-eight sheets; composed by the Bodhisattva Sāṃkhya; translated by Dharmagupta at the Shanglin Garden in the Eastern Capital in the ninth year of the Daye era of the Sui dynasty.
*Tri-svabhāva-śāstra*, two fascicles, thirty-four sheets; translated by Paramārtha of the Chen dynasty. *Mahāyāna-samgraha-śāstra*, two fascicles... [fragmentary].
Scroll 39, Paper 1–28: *Bodhicittotpāda-śāstra* (Treatise on the Arousing of the Bodhi-mind), composed by Sthiramati Bodhisattva, translated by Dao Tai during the Northern Liang dynasty;
two scrolls, 28 papers. Translator unknown, period unknown. *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only), 19 papers;

"Consciousness-only without external objects," translated by Gautama Dharmaruci of the Later Wei dynasty. The aforementioned treatise is largely identical to that produced by Paramārtha of the Chen dynasty.
The *Cintā-mahābhūta-śāstra* (Treatise on the Object of Thought), three sheets, translated by Paramārtha.
The above treatise is identical to the separately translated *Ālambana-parīkṣā-śāstra*.

The *Mahāyāna-karmasiddhi-prakaraṇa* (Treatise on the Establishment of Karma in the Mahāyāna), seventeen sheets, translated by Xuanzang during the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty. The above treatise is [as follows].
It is largely identical to the *Karmasiddhiprakaraṇa* translated by Gautama Ratnākara during the Later Wei dynasty.
The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra-śāstra* in eleven pages was translated by Dharmaprabha in the Chen dynasty;
the *Nirvāṇa-pūrvabhava-adhunābhāva-vāda* in six pages was translated by Paramārtha in Guangzhou; the *Trisamaya-śāstra* in six pages [was translated] by Bodhi... during the Later Wei dynasty.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra-śāstra*, twenty-five sheets, translated by Bodhiruci of the Later Wei; the *Dharmacakra-pravartana-śāstra*, ten sheets, translated by Bodhiruci of the Later Wei at Ye;
the *Ratnabandhu-bodhisattva-caturdharma-sūtra-śāstra*, twelve sheets, translated by Bodhiruci of the Later Wei;
and the *Amitāyus-sūtra-śāstra*, eight sheets, [translated by] Bodhiruci of the Later Wei.

*Vigrahavyāvartanī-śāstra*, twelve sheets, translated by Bodhiruci of the Wei dynasty; *Aśraddhabodha-vyākhyāna* (Treatise on Arousing Faith), twenty-three sheets, translated by Gautama Prajñāruci of the Later Wei dynasty;
*Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* (Treatise on Establishing Reality), twenty-three sheets, translated by Paramārtha of the Chen dynasty;

*Dvādaśamukha-śāstra* (Twelve Gates Treatise), twenty-three sheets, translated by Kumārajīva of the Later Qin dynasty; *Śūnyatā-saptati-śāstra* (Treatise on the Eighteen Emptinesses), nineteen sheets.
*Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* (Treatise on the Awakening of Faith), seventeen sheets; translated by Ji Jiaye and Tan Yao during the Yanxing era of the Northern Wei.
*Muṣṭi-sūtra-vyākhyāna* (Explanation of the Fist Sūtra), two sheets; translated by Paramārtha of the Chen dynasty. *Pratītyasamutpāda-śāstra* (Treatise on Dependent Origination), ten sheets;

translated by Jñānagupta at the Shanglin Garden in the Eastern Capital during the Daye era of the Sui dynasty. *Dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda-śāstra* (Treatise on the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination), nine sheets; translated by Bodhiruci of the Northern Wei.
*Ekaslokika-śāstra*: translated by [Xuanzang], four pages; composed by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna, translated during the Later Wei by Gautama Dharmaruci.
*Śatapañcāśatka-śāstra*: eight pages; translated during the Later Wei by Bodhiruci. *Tattvasaṃgraha-śāstra*: two fascicles, thirty-two pages;
the following eight treatises were all translated by Xuanzang. *Hetuvidyānyāyamukha-śāstra*: twelve pages; *Hetuvidyā*.

*Zhengli men lun* (Treatise on Entering the Gateway of Correct Principle), six sheets; *Dacheng wuyun lun* (Treatise on the Five Aggregates of the Mahāyāna), eight sheets; *Wangfa zhengli lun* (Treatise on the Correct Principle of the King’s Law), seventeen sheets;

*Bai fa mingmen lun* (Treatise on the Illuminating Gateway of the Hundred Dharmas), two sheets; *Xianyang lun song ben* (Verses of the Manifesting [Mahāyāna] Treatise), eleven sheets; *Guangbai lun ben* (Root Text of the Extensive Hundred Treatise), twelve sheets.
A record of whether there were single or multiple translations of the sūtras, vinayas, and śāstras of the Hīnayāna, including those that exist and those that do not.

Four hundred and thirteen fascicles and six thousand seven hundred and thirteen sheets; the Vinaya comprises two hundred and seventy-four fascicles and five thousand seven hundred and eighteen sheets;
the Śāstra comprises five hundred and sixty-five fascicles and nine thousand nine hundred and ninety-seven sheets.
In total, these comprise one hundred and eighty-two works of the Hīnayāna Sūtra, Vinaya, and Śāstra.
One thousand two hundred and fifty-two fascicles and twenty-two thousand four hundred and twenty-eight sheets of Hinayana sutras;
the Hinayana sutras comprise one hundred and eighteen sections in total.

The *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna-sūtra* consists of seventy fascicles and one thousand two hundred sheets, translated in the capital of Luoyang by Bodhiruci of the Later Wei dynasty. The *Madhyama Āgama* consists of sixty [fascicles].
Volume 1,147, translated by Saṃghadeva during the Eastern Jin dynasty.
The twenty-six separate translations of this single sūtra, appearing earlier and later,
differ in their phrasing but are identical in meaning.
Therefore, the original text of this scripture has been recorded;
other scriptures are largely missing.

The *Ekottarika Āgama* (Zengyi Ahan Jing), fifty fascicles and seven hundred and ninety-five sheets, was translated at Chang’an by Dharmanandi during the Jianyuan era of the Former Qin dynasty of the Eastern Jin. This concludes the record of one scripture.
There are seventeen separate translations [of this work] from earlier and later periods;
as their wording and meaning do not differ,
they are omitted here for brevity.

The *Saṃyukta Āgama*, fifty fascicles, one thousand and thirty sheets, translated by Guṇabhadra at the capital of Yangdu during the Song dynasty. To the right, this single scripture comprises fifteen distinct translations made at various times.

The *Dàtóng* (Mahāvaipulya) version is extensive, so it is not listed again here. Furthermore, there is a separate translation of the *Zá āhán jīng* (Saṃyuktāgama) in twenty fascicles; its categories can be understood by approximating its textual meaning.

The *Cháng āhán jīng* (Dīrghāgama) consists of twenty fascicles and four hundred and twenty-six sheets; it was translated at Cháng'ān by Buddhayaśas during the Hóngshǐ era of the Later Qín dynasty under the Eastern Jin. The above constitutes one scripture.
There are eleven translations from earlier and later periods;
as they are all based on the same original text,
they are not listed again here.

The *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish*, thirteen fascicles (or sixteen fascicles), totaling three hundred and seventy-five sheets, was translated during the Song dynasty by Huìjué and Wēidé at Gāochāng Commandery.

The *Sūtra on the Origin of the World*, ten fascicles, totaling one hundred and sixty-five sheets, was translated during the Dàyè era of the Sui dynasty by Jīduō at the Shànglín Garden in the Eastern Capital.
The *Sūtra of the Storehouse of Various Jewels*, eight fascicles (or ten fascicles).
Volume 150, 147 sheets. Translated by Jikaya (Jñānagupta) together with Tanyao at Beitaishan during the Yanxing era of the Northern Wei;
the *Lalitavistara Sūtra* in eight or ten fascicles. Translated by Dharmarakṣa during the Yongjia era of the Western Jin;
the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* in seven fascicles, 94 sheets. Translated by Xuanzang during the Yonghui era of the Tang...
*Xiuxing daodi jing* (Sūtra on the Stages of Cultivating the Path), six fascicles, one hundred and thirty sheets; translated by An Shigao of the Later Han.
*Sheng jing* (Sūtra on Births), five fascicles (or four fascicles), one hundred and seven sheets; translated by Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin.
*Alanya xichan jing* (Sūtra on Practicing Dhyāna in Āraṇya), two fascicles, fifty sheets; translated by Kumārajīva at Chang’an during the Hongshi era of the Later Qin.
The above sutra is largely identical to the separately translated *Zuochan sanmei jing*.
The *Madengjia jing* consists of three fascicles—or alternatively two fascicles—comprising thirty-two sheets. The above is one sutra.

It is identical to the *Śatruñjaya-sūtra* translated by Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin dynasty; it is also titled the *Sūtra on the Twenty-eight Lunar Mansions of the Prince*, or alternatively, the *Sūtra of Prince Harisikha*.

The *Past and Present Causes and Effects Sūtra* (Guoqu xianzai yinguo jing), four fascicles, ninety-six sheets, translated at the capital of Yangdu by Guṇabhadra during the Song dynasty. This aforementioned sūtra has three translations.
The work translated by Dharmaphala during the early Later Han dynasty is titled *Xiuxing benqi* (The Origin of Practice).
It is identical in meaning to the *Ruishiying jing* (Sutra of Auspicious Responses) from the Wu period.
The *Benxiang yizhi jing* (Sutra on the Causes and Conditions of Past Manifestations), consisting of three sheets, was translated by An Shigao of the Later Han dynasty; this concludes one sutra.
This is identical to the *Bieyi yuanben zhijing* (Another Translation of the Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions).

The *Ānwen shifo jixiong jing* (Sūtra on Ānanda Asking about the Auspiciousness and Inauspiciousness of Serving the Buddha), four sheets, translated by Fa-jian during the reign of Qi-fu Ren of the Xiqin dynasty. The above is one sūtra.
This is identical to the *Ānanda-vibhaṅga-sūtra* translated separately [by others].
The *Karmavibhaṅga-sūtra*, fifteen sheets, translated by Tanfazhi during the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty; this constitutes one sutra.
This is identical to the *Sūtra on the Retribution of Sin and Merit* translated separately.
The *Sūtra of the Tathāgata’s Instruction to King Jayasena*, eight sheets, was translated by Xuanzang at Ci'en Monastery during the Yonghui era of the Tang dynasty. The above is one sūtra.
This is identical to the *Sūtra on Admonishing the King* translated by another hand.
The *Sūtra of the Five Mothers and Sons*, two sheets, is to the right;
this sūtra is identical to the *Sūtra of Śamīra* translated by another hand.
The *Yujie jing* (Sūtra of Yujie), four sheets long, also known as the *Shuo zifu wujing jing* (Sūtra on Explaining the Lack of Reverence in Sons' Wives) or the *Qifujing* (Sūtra of the Seven Wives).
This single sūtra is identical to the separately translated *Axiuda jing*.
The *Ullambana Sūtra*, one sheet, right side;
three versions.
These are identical to the *Guanla jing*, *Ba'en fengpen jing*, and *Jingtu ullambana jing*.
The *Mādreyī-vimokṣa-ṣaḍvastu-sūtra* in three sheets.
This aforementioned sūtra is identical to the separately translated *Mādrī-sūtra*.
Furthermore, although the two titles differ, the texts are in fact one and the same sūtra.
*Śarīra-skandha-āyatana-sūtra*, two fascicles, thirty-two pages; translated by An Shigao of the Later Han.
*Madhyama-āgama-sūtra*, three fascicles, forty-seven pages; translated by Kang Mengxiang together with Zhu Dalie during the Jian’an era of the Later Han.
*Xingqi xing jing* (Sūtra on the Arising of Practice), two fascicles, twenty-eight pages; translated by Kang Mengxiang of the Later Han. *Dharmatrāta-dhyāna-sūtra*...
*Jing* (Sūtra), two fascicles, fifty sheets; translated by Buddhabhadra of the Later Qin. *Yizu jing* (Sūtra on the Fulfillment of Meaning), two fascicles, forty-one sheets;
translated by Zhi Qian during the Huangwu era of the Wu dynasty. *Piyeshawen jing* (Sūtra of the Questions of Viśvāmitra), two fascicles, thirty sheets;
translated by Bodhiruci of the Northern Wei. *Daban shouyi jing* (Sūtra on Guarding the Mind through Great Ānāpāna), two fascicles—or one fascicle—thirty [sheets].
Paper [count]: The *Upāsikā-śīla-sūtra* (The Scripture on the Pure Conduct of Laywomen), translated by An Shigao of the Later Han, two fascicles, thirty sheets;

the *Nāgasena-bhikṣu-sūtra* (The Scripture of the Bhikṣu Nāgasena), two fascicles or one fascicle, thirty sheets; the *Mahānāpāna-sūtra* (The Great Scripture on Ānāpāna), two fascicles or one fascicle, twenty sheets;
the *Parinirvāṇa-sūtra*, translated by An Shigao of the Later Han, one fascicle, twenty-two sheets. Total: [as above].
The following one hundred and two fascicles were all translated individually by Guṇabhadra at the capital of Yangdu during the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty:
*The Sūtra on Future Transformations*, two sheets; translated by Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin. *The Sūtra on the Past Buddha’s Almsround*, two sheets;
translated by Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin. *The Sūtra of the Maiden Nai and Jīvaka*, nineteen sheets; translated by Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin.
*The Sūtra on the Parinirvāṇa of King Śuddhodana*, six sheets, translated by Juqu Jingsheng, Marquis of Anyang, during the Northern Liang dynasty;
*The Sūtra of the Eight Teachers*, three sheets, translated by Zhi Qian during the Wu dynasty; *The Mahākāśyapa-mūla-sūtra*, five sheets, translated by Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin dynasty;
*The Sūtra of the Four Vows*, two sheets, translated by Zhi Qian during the Huangwu era of the Wu dynasty; *The Sūtra of the Woman Meeting with Misfortune*, two sheets.
*The Sūtra on the Elder’s Son Bianyi Questioning [the Buddha]* (one fascicle), translated by Dharmayānas in the Western Qin; nine sheets.
Also known as *The Sūtra on the Elder’s Inquiry into the Meaning*, translated by Dharmarakṣa during the Later Wei.

*The Sūtra on the Womb* (fifteen sheets), also known as *The Sūtra on Receiving a Body in the Womb*, translated by Dharmarakṣa in the Taian era of the Western Jin. *The Sūtra on the Four Self-Inflicted Injuries* (four sheets). West.
*The Sutra on the Past Deeds of the Five Hundred Disciples*, translated by Zhu Fahu of the Jin Dynasty, twenty sheets; translated by Zhu Fahu of the Taikang era of the Western Jin, seven sheets.
*The Sutra of the Seven Daughters*, translated by Zhi Qian of the Huangwu era of the Wu Dynasty, three sheets.

*The Sutra on the Four Matters Concerning Ānanda*, translated by Zhi Qian of the Wu Dynasty, two sheets. *The Sutra on the Sufferings Brought About by Desires*, translated by Zhu Fahu of the Western Jin Dynasty, two sheets.

*Fashouchen jing* (Sūtra on the Translation of Dharmas Receiving Sensory Objects), two sheets; translated by An Shigao of the Later Han. *Canyingfaxiang jing* (Sūtra on the Dhyāna Practice of Mental Conception of Dharmas), two sheets; translated by An Shigao of the Later Han.
*Sijianwang jing* (Sūtra of the Four Heavenly Kings), two sheets; translated by Zhiyan and Baoyun et al. at the capital of Yang during the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty.
*Folinieban luejie jing* (Sūtra of the Brief Admonition as the Buddha Approached Nirvāṇa), six sheets; also titled *Yijiao jing* (Sūtra of the Bequeathed Teaching); translated during the Later Qin.
The *Śāriputramaudgalyāyanacatvaraṃcarita-sūtra* translated by Kumārajīva at Cháng'ān; the *Nandika-sūtra* translated by Zhú Fǎhù of the Western Jìn;
four pages and below of sūtras with lost translations; the *Vimalā-upāsikā-paripṛcchā-sūtra* in three pages;
the *Pratimā-pratiṣṭhā-puṇyavipāka-sūtra* in two pages; the *Dharmasthititā-sūtra* in two pages; and the *Kusīda-karṣaka-sūtra*.
The *Sūtra on the Two Sheets*; the *Udayana-rāja-sūtra* in five sheets, also titled the *Udayana-rāja-buddha-pratimā-karaṇa-sūtra*;
the *Ānanda-sapta-svapna-sūtra* in two sheets (some say "eight dreams," which is an error); the *Guhyapāda-vajrapāṇi-paridevana-sūtra*;
the *Kāśyapa-gamana-nirvāṇa-sūtra* in two sheets; and the *Dharma-sūtra on the Funeral Rites after the Buddha’s Parinirvāṇa*.

Three sheets: one titled *The Sūtra on the Teacher of Bhikṣus*, and the *Mahāsthāmaprāpta Sūtra* (four sheets). One titled *The Sūtra on Washing the Buddha*, and the *Rāhula’s Sūtra on Forbearance* (three sheets).
One titled *The Sūtra on Forbearance* and the *Sūtra on the Circumstances of Leaving Home* (two sheets). Three sections:
the *Sūtra on the Disciples* (three sheets), and the *Sūtra on the Disciples Learning in Three Grades* and the *Sūtra on the Four Grades* (three sheets). [End of] the "Seeing" section.
The Seven-Paper Sutra on the Transformation of Consciousness in Birth and Death; the Two-Paper Sutra on the *Arhat* (A-na) named *Hediao*;
the Three-Paper Sutra on the Five Non-Returners (*Anāgāmin*) named *Youfanfu*;
the Four-Paper Sutra on Right Practice named *Zhengyi*; the Two-Paper Sutra on Fear named *Wukongbu*; and the Sutra on the Matter of the Great Fish.
Two sheets: *The Sūtra of Āṭavaka*; two sheets: *The Sūtra of King Brahmadatta*; two sheets:
*The Sūtra of Mahākāśyapa Saving the Poor Mother*; five sheets: *The Central Heart Sūtra*; three sheets: *The Sūtra of the Brotherly Nāga Kings*, also known as *The Sūtra on Subduing the Dragon*;
two sheets: *The Sūtra on the Merits of the Bhikṣu Śakra*; [two sheets]: *The Sūtra of the Elder Jyotiṣka*.
The Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of the Elder Rudrāyaṇa, five sheets; the Sūtra of the Elder Sumati, nine sheets; the Sūtra of the Five Kings, eight sheets;
the Sūtra of the Twelve Classes of Birth and Death, four sheets; the Sūtra of King Mada, two sheets; the Sūtra of King Malla, two sheets;
the Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of the Lamp-Finger, eight sheets; the Sūtra of King Pūrṇabhadra, three sheets; [and] the Kingdom of Gandhāra.
The *Rājan-sūtra*, two sheets; the *Dṛḍhamati-sūtra*, two sheets; the *Buddha-mahāsāṃghika-sūtra*, six sheets; the *Cīvara-sūtra*, two sheets;
the *Dvādaśa-dhūta-sūtra* (also known as the *Śramaṇa-dhūta-sūtra*), five sheets; the *Śuci-rakṣā-sūtra*, two sheets; the *Kāṣṭhapuṭaka-sūtra*, one sheet;
the *Kāla-akāla-sūtra*, two sheets; the *Mārga-labdha-sopāna-sūtra*, two sheets; the *Candana... [sūtra]*.
The *Candana-vṛkṣa-sūtra*, three sheets; the *Navavarṣa-sūtra*, five sheets—also known as the *Bhāvara-sūtra*;
the *Daridra-vṛddha-puruṣa-sūtra*, three sheets—also known as the *Daridra-vṛddha-sūtra*; the *Dāraka-putra-tri-sthāna-paritāpa-sūtra*, four sheets;
the *Buddhabhāṣita-vyatīta-nara-sūtra*, two sheets; the *Candana-vyaya-rāja-sūtra*, three sheets; the *Ātmavatsala-sūtra*, four sheets—also known as the [Ātma-]sūtra.
The *Buzi'ai jing* (Sūtra on Not Loving Oneself), spoken by the Buddha; the *Chuchu jing* (Sūtra on Various Places) in ten sheets; the *Wushangchu jing* (Sūtra on the Unsurpassed Place) in one sheet;

the *Zhuanlun wudao zui fu jing* (Sūtra on the Five Realms of Transmigration, Sins, and Merits) in four sheets; the *Weishengyuan jing* (Sūtra on Ajātaśatru) in three sheets; the *Shiba nili jing* (Sūtra on the Eighteen Hells) in five sheets;

and the *Nili jing* (Sūtra on the Hells), also known as the *Qinku nili zuoye baoying jiaohua diyu jing* (Sūtra on Teaching and Transforming the Hell of the Retribution for Karmic Deeds in the Painful Hells), in twelve sheets.

The *Senghu jing* (Saṃgharakṣita-sūtra), six fascicles; the *Weichengyou jing* (Adbhuta-dharma-sūtra), twenty fascicles; the *Jiayan shuofa mu jie* (Kātyāyanīputra-bhāṣita-dharmapada-gāthā), three fascicles;
the *Fowei shaobiqu shuo zhengshi jing* (Buddhabhāṣita-śrāmaṇera-vastu-sūtra), three fascicles; the *Sipin xuefa jing* (Catuṣparivarta-dharmaparyāya-sūtra), one fascicle;
and the *Xiaoshenglü* (Hīnayāna Vinaya), totaling thirty-five sections and two hundred seventy-four fascicles, comprising five thousand seven [hundred] characters.
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Four-Part Vinaya) in sixty fascicles consists of one hundred and eighteen sheets, totaling one thousand two hundred and ten characters;
it was translated at Chang’an by Buddhayaśas during the Hongshi era of the Later Qin.

The *Sarvāstivāda-saṃghabhedavastu* (Ten Recitation Vinaya) in sixty fascicles consists of one thousand three hundred and ninety-one characters; it was [translated] by Puṇyatāra during the Hongshi era of the Later Qin.
The first two divisions were translated together with Kumārajīva; the subsequent portions were continued by Mahāyāna and completed by Vimalākṣa.

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* in forty fascicles and nine hundred seventy-three pages was translated at the capital of Yangdu by Buddhabhadra together with Faxian during the Eastern Jin dynasty. The *Mahīśāsaka-pañcavargika-vinaya* in thirty fascicles and five hundred ninety-seven pages was translated at the capital of Yangdu by Buddhajīva together with Daosheng and Zhisheng during the Jingping era of the Song dynasty. The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā-vinaya* in eighteen fascicles and three hundred sixty-eight pages was translated in Guangzhou by Saṃghabhadra during the Yongming era of the Southern Qi dynasty. The *Vinayamātṛkā* in ten fascicles and one hundred fifty-five pages was translated in Chang’an by Zhu Fonian together with Dao’an and others during the Former Qin dynasty.
*Samayabhedoparacanacakra* (Sa-p'o-to-mo-t'e-le-ka), ten fascicles, one hundred and ninety-five sheets;
translated at Yangdu during the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty by Saṃghavarman. *Sarvāstivādavinayavibhāṣā*, nine fascicles, one hundred and eighty-two sheets;
translator lost, dating from an unknown period. *Mahābhikṣu-trisahasra-vidhi* (Da-bi-qiu-san-qian-wei-yi), two fascicles, thirty-two sheets.
*Vinayamātṛkā* (The Mother of the Vinaya), eight fascicles, 153 sheets; *Mahāprajāpatī Bhikṣuṇī Sūtra*, two fascicles, 41 sheets;
*Dharmaguptaka-vinaya Bhikṣu Prātimokṣa*, twenty-three sheets; translated by Buddhayaśas of the Later Qin at Chang’an;
*Dharmaguptaka-vinaya Bhikṣuṇī Prātimokṣa*, twenty-one sheets; *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya Bhikṣu [Prātimokṣa]*.
The *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* consists of twenty sheets; the *Bhikṣuṇī-prātimokṣa-sūtra* of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* consists of twenty-six sheets;
and the *Bhikṣu-prātimokṣa-sūtra* of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* consists of twenty sheets. These were translated at Xuchang by Dharmakāla during the Former Wei dynasty.

The *Mahāsāṃghika Bhikṣuṇī Prātimokṣa Sūtra*, twenty-four sheets; the *Mahīśāsaka Pañcavargika Prātimokṣa Sūtra*, nineteen sheets, translated at the capital of Yang by Buddhayaśas during the Jingping era of the Song dynasty; the *Vimukti Prātimokṣa Sūtra*, twenty-one sheets, extracted from the *Kāśyapīya Vinaya* and translated by Gautama Dharmaruci during the Later Wei; and the *Dharmaguptaka Karmavācanā*, forty-one sheets, translated by Tandi at Luoyang in the first year of the Zhengyuan era of the Former Wei.

The *Caturvargika Bhikṣuṇī Karmavācanā*, fifteen sheets; translated by Guṇavarman during the Yuanjia era of the Song dynasty. The *Daśabhāṇavāra Karmavācanā*, twenty-three sheets. The *Śramaṇa Ekottara-karmavācanā*, twenty-two sheets.

The *Śrāmaṇera-daśa-śīla with Dignity and Deportment*, twenty-one sheets. The *Śrāmaṇerī-daśa-śīla*, four sheets. The *Śrāmaṇera-vinirbhoga-śīla*, four sheets. The *Śrāmaṇera-dignity and deportment*, nine sheets.
The *Upāsaka-pañca-śīla-lakṣaṇa*, fifteen sheets; translated by Guṇavarman of the Song dynasty. The *Śāriputra-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, eleven sheets; translated by Zhen [Dharmarakṣa].

*The Sūtra on False Śramaṇas*, three sheets; also known as *The Mahābhikṣu Sūtra*. *The Sūtra on Precepts for the Elimination of Calamities*, four sheets. *The Kāśyapa Prohibitory Precepts Sūtra*, three sheets.

*The Sūtra on the Lightness or Heaviness of the Retribution for Violating Precepts*, two sheets; also known as *The Sūtra on Committing Offenses*. *The Upāsaka Pañcaśīla Vinaya-vidhi*, twenty-three sheets.

*Upāli’s Questions on the Vinaya*, twenty-three sheets. *The Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra*, twenty-four sheets; also known as *The Vinaya-viṃśati-prakaraṇa-śāstra*. Translated by Paramārtha of the Chen dynasty at Linchuan Commandery. Treatises on the Hīnayāna. Treatises on the Hīnayāna.
In total, there are twenty-nine sections comprising five hundred and sixty-five fascicles and nine thousand nine hundred and ninety-seven sheets.

The two hundred fascicles of the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, totaling three thousand one hundred and nine sheets, were translated by Xuanzang at the capital during the Yonghui era of the Tang dynasty;
they correspond to the sixty fascicles of the *Aṣṭagrantha-vibhāṣā* (Abhidharma-aṣṭagrantha-vibhāṣā) produced by Daoyan of the Northern Liang.

However, they differ now in their extent. The *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* (Treatise in Accordance with Correct Reasoning) consists of eighty fascicles and one thousand four hundred and twenty sheets; translated by Xuanzang during the Yonghui era of the Tang dynasty. The *Abhidharmakośa-prakaraṇa-śāstra* (Treatise on the Manifestation of the Abhidharma) consists of forty fascicles and six hundred and forty-four sheets; translated by Xuanzang during the Yonghui era of the Tang dynasty. The *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* (Treatise on the Foundation of Knowledge) consists of twenty fascicles and three hundred and sixty-four sheets; translated by Xuanzang during the Yonghui era of the Tang dynasty. The aforementioned treatises are identical to the old *Kātyāyanīputra-śāstra* (*Aṣṭagrantha*) in thirty fascicles.
The Abhidharmakośa-śāstra, thirty fascicles, four hundred and seventy sheets; translated by Xuanzang during the Xianqing era of the Tang dynasty.
This treatise is identical to the twenty-two fascicle version produced by Paramārtha.
*Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra*, twenty-two fascicles, five hundred and ninety-nine sheets; translated at Chang’an by Dharmagupta during the Hongshi era of the Later Qin dynasty.

*Abhidharmadīpa-śāstra*, twenty fascicles, four hundred and eighty-seven sheets; translated at Chang’an by Zhu Fonian during the Former Qin dynasty. *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, four fascicles, four hundred sheets;

twenty fascicles (or ten) translated by Kumārajīva of the Later Qin dynasty. *Vijñānakāya-pāda-śāstra*, sixteen fascicles, two hundred and seventy-one sheets; translated by Xuanzang during the Xianqing era of the Tang dynasty. *Vibhāṣā-śāstra*... [text truncated]
*Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra*, fourteen fascicles, three hundred and forty-seven sheets; translated at Luoyang by Saṃghadeva during the Jiànyuán era of the Former Qín dynasty.

*Dharmaskandha-pāda-śāstra*, twelve fascicles, one hundred and ninety-two sheets; translated by Xuánzàng during the Xiǎnqìng era of the Táng dynasty. *Vimuktimārga-śāstra*, twelve fascicles, one hundred and ninety-eight sheets;

translated by Saṃghavarman at the Zhānyún Hall in the capital of Yáng during the Liáng dynasty. *Saṅgītiparyāya-abhidharma*, twelve fascicles, two hundred and nine sheets. *Sāṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*.

Catalogue of Extant and Missing Titles of Scriptures Throughout the Successive Dynasties, Part Five. The Preface states:
Since the Buddhist scriptures first circulated in the Eastern Lands,
more than six hundred years have passed;
yet they have been suppressed and eradicated three times.
When one encounters a protector of the Dharma, they observe the capacities of beings and act accordingly;
first, they remain hidden in mountain caves, firmly guarding the ultimate truth.
Even when drenched by clouds and mist, they are further submerged and decayed.
Later, when the Dharma was revived, matters were undertaken to recover what had been lost;
yet not one in a hundred remained.
For now, only the essential framework has been preserved.
Fortunately, during the Five Dynasties period in the region south of the Yangtze River, faith remained unimpaired;
thus, the transmission of the Dharma was able to spread throughout the world.
However, at the end of the Western Jin dynasty, the empire fell into fragmentation.
The translator encountered peril and had no place to lay his dying body;
yet he ensured that the text of the sutra alone remained safe and secure.
Furthermore, Emperor Ling of the Han dynasty traveled in haste from east to west to visit it.
Buddhist scriptures and secular classics have perished therein;
consequently, there are not a few instances where both the titles and the texts themselves have been lost.
I have now compiled these from various records and gathered them together here.
It was absent from the collated manuscript,
yet it appears in the catalog;
I fear that future finders will rely on the current record and assume it was missing.
Consequently, they cast it aside as something dubious and spurious;
for this reason, I have examined the various catalogs of past and present,
collating and verifying the existence or non-existence of the scriptural texts.
If there is [a copy], one shall rely upon it and enter the collection;
if not, one shall draft a title and seek it out,
hoping that there may be fellow travelers on the same boat.
Huaisi gathered them extensively, remarking:
"In searching through various records, I found that many texts were missing and their categories were numerous.
I have now attempted to collate them against extant scriptures to establish a definitive catalog."
Truly, these manifest wonders.
Now, I wish to list their names and demonstrate them extensively;
however, they have already been fully set forth in the preceding chapter.
Since paper and ink would become overly cumbersome, it would ultimately result in a waste of words;
therefore, I have omitted them and shall not record them here.
Even if one were to search for and obtain the original texts, it would be impossible to distinguish between the authentic and the spurious.
If there are those for whom the era is not yet clear,
they may consult the records and examine the chronology;
thus, the names and titles will become manifest, and right and wrong will be settled.
Therefore, there is no need for the labor of recording them all;
furthermore, the later catalogs of successive dynasties all list them consecutively,
making them easy to consult.

From the end of the Han dynasty through the beginning of the Jin,
the military and civil administrations vied with one another, alternating between division and unification; thus,
while the teachings were not yet fully integrated, although there were those who composed treatises, they remained incomplete.
Since the previously prepared substitute records are already largely based on these texts,
they have not been reproduced here.
From the Eastern Jin dynasty until the present, the poetic compositions have become numerous and abundant.
If one does not manifest [the teachings] through successive stages, how could one present their traces?
Therefore, they emerge in accordance with the times;
this shall be prepared in detail hereafter.
However, the titles within the *Xùfǎ lùn* (Treatise on the Continuation of the Dharma) were composed in the vernacular;
upon examining various catalogs, I found there were not a few omissions.
Therefore, I have compiled them here in sequence.
Furthermore, the original texts are rarely complete, making them difficult to consult;
I have thus recorded the titles of those I have correctly obtained here.
Alas, that these writings have been neglected and allowed to fall into ruin!
