excerpts from the "Chapter on the Original Vows and Practices of Bodhisattvas"; excerpts from the essential enumerations of the *Catuḥsatya Sūtra*; excerpts from the *Samantabhadra-bhadracaryā-praṇidhāna-pūjā-vidhi*;
excerpts from the *Abhidharma-pañcadharma-caryā Sūtra*; excerpts from the *Vibhaṅga Sūtra*; [excerpts from the] *Māra*...

The *Bianhua biqiu jing* (Sutra on the Transformation of a Bhikṣu), the *Youposai shoujie pin* (Chapter on the Upāsaka Precepts), the *Youposai shoujie fa* (Method for Receiving the Upāsaka Precepts),
and the *Tannü wei guowang furen jing* (Sutra on a Greedy Woman Becoming a King’s Consort)— these twenty-three works [are included].
It consists of twenty-nine fascicles and was all excerpted by Prince Jingling of the Qi dynasty;
as it differs from the original scriptures, it constitutes a distinct version.
The headings and excerpts clarify the distinctions,
enabling later seekers to know their sources;
yet the flavor and style are broad and pervasive, while the principles and meanings are perfectly coherent.
Encountering the profusion and diversity of the mundane world,
and examining the divergent paths of human dispositions and desires,
there exists therein the Way.
The meaning is neither doubtful nor false;
yet, in the catalogs of Sengyou and Baochang,
they all annotate it as a "doubtful scripture."
There was no one who did not fear that, by venturing into the lingering waves of superficiality, they would lose the original essence.
Yet, in their sentiments they sought harmonious understanding, and in their affairs they sought brevity and essentials;
among the various translations and transmissions made earlier and later, there was not a single complete version.
It is still able to illuminate the semblance and the true, and to guide and instruct the ignorant masses.
The analogy of the precious gem in the half-verse and the full hymn is clearly evident;
in these four characters and eight words, the method for calming and overturning [delusion] is entrusted.
Based on this account,
how can you treat all things as identical?
Are there not those capable of discerning between jade and stone?
Regarding the *Sarvajñatā-parivāra-vyūha-sūtra* (The Sūtra on the Adornments of the Retinue of Omniscience) mentioned above:
according to an examination of Sengyou’s catalogue,
it was [translated] in the ninth year of the Tianjian era of the Liang dynasty.
These were produced by the monk Miaoguang of Yingzhou.
After the imperial court had completed the formal proscription,
the Vinaya Master Jiangbi’s daughter, the Bhikṣuṇī Sengfa, recited and brought forth three scriptures, including the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra*.

The fifteen volumes have already been prepared; upon consulting the *Dailu* (Record of Substitutes), they were not found among the translated works, and thus all are entered into the "Doubtful" category:

the *Brahmadeva-śakuna-sūtra*, the *Tianhuang-fanmo-jing*, the *Anmu-jing*, the *Anzhong-jing*, the *Anzhai-jing*, the *Weicui-jing*, the *Anzhai-shenzhou-jing*, the *Tiangong-jing*, the *Du-shengsi-hai-shenchuan-jing*, the *Dufahujing*, and the *Juyi-jing*.
The *Śrāmaṇera Sūtra*, the *Sūtra on Bowing to the Buddha and Making Vows in the North*, the *Sūtra on Reverencing Merit*, the *Sūtra of King Arahada*,

the *Sūtra of the Five Hundred Brahmans* (also known as the *Sūtra of Being Both and Not Being*), the *Sūtra on the Expedient Means of Practice*, the *Geyarāja Sūtra*, the *Sūtra on Transcending the World and Immortality*,
the *Sūtra on the Purity of the Fasting Rite*, the *Buddha-spoken Sūtra on the Right Fasting*, and the *Buddha-spoken Sūtra on the Dharma Society*.

I have searched through ancient records and further consulted other original copies of the following scriptures: the *Zhumei jing* (Scripture on Exorcising Demons), the *Shidulin jing* (Scripture on the Śītavana Forest), the *Zhaohunpo jing* (Scripture on Summoning Souls), the *Taizi zan jing* (Scripture on the Praise of the Prince),

the *Biqiu fazang jian diyu bian jing* (Scripture on the Bhikṣu Dharmakośa Witnessing the Transformations of Hell), the *Renmin qiuyuan jing* (Scripture on the People’s Petitions for Vows), the *Yanluowang dong taishan jing* (Scripture of King Yama and Mount Tai in the East),

the *Qibao jing* (Scripture of the Seven Jewels), the *Zilun jing* (Scripture on the Theory of Characters), the *Jiuhu zhongsheng eji jing* (Scripture on Saving and Protecting Sentient Beings from Malignant Diseases), and the *Jiuhushen* (Scripture on Saving and Protecting the Body).

The *Jīvitapraśna-sūtra*, the *Dṛṣṭānta-sūtra*, the *Sarvabhūta-paritrāṇa-sūtra* (also known as the *Śālisambhava-sūtra*), the *Ekapiṇḍaka-dārakadārikā-sūtra*, and the *Rājan-paurajanaparitrāṇa-śīlasamādāna-samyagdarśana-kudṛṣṭinirghātana-sūtra*. These constitute twenty-eight sections.
Regarding the *Dān jīng* (Single Sūtra):
upon examining the *Fǎshī lù* (Record of Dharma Master [Jìng]yǒu) of the Sui Dynasty,
it is classified among the spurious and false works.
*The Scripture on the Descent of All Buddhas as Great Dharma Kings*, sixty fascicles; I personally saw this text in the Fen region.

*The Scripture on the Extensive Elimination of Sins and the Attainment of Buddhahood*, three fascicles; *The Scripture on the Divination of Contemplation*, two fascicles—the first fascicle contains one hundred and eighty methods of divination;

*The Scripture on the Verses of the Dharma*, two fascicles—the second fascicle contains the *Sūtra of the Precious Radiance Bodhisattva’s Final Exhortation at the Golden Coffin* concerning sins and blessings.

The *Jueyi jing* (Sutra on Resolving Doubts), the *Wuxin jing* (Sutra on the Five Pungent Herbs), the *Chujiao jing* (Sutra on Initial Teaching), and the *Zuibao jing* (Sutra on Karmic Retribution for Offenses) differ entirely from the authentic scriptures regarding the gravity of karmic retribution.

The *Riyun gongyang jing* (Sutra on Offering the Solar Wheel) and the *Ruguang jing* (Sutra of the Milk-Light) have texts that are entirely different from the authentic scriptures, stating that one incurs sin if they consume milk.

The *Futian baoying jing* (Sutra on the Retribution of Merit Fields), the *Baoyin jing* (Sutra of the Precious Seal), and the three-fascicle *Jujing dabei jing* (Sutra of Ultimate Great Compassion) concern the Pratyekabuddhas.
The *Vinayaviniścaya-sūtra-śāstra*, the *Upāli-paripṛcchā-śāstra*, the *Sarvaviniścaya-śāstra* (one version adds the word "Vijñaptimātra"),
the *Ānanda-paripṛcchā-vinaya-śāstra*, the *Kāśyapa-paripṛcchā-śāstra*, the *Mahā-ācāra-paripṛcchā-śāstra*, the *Ratnamālā-śāstra*, the *Śāsanoddhāra-śāstra*,
and the *Śrāmaṇera-śāstra-mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā-prakaraṇa*: these are the aforementioned spurious sūtras and śāstras.
Humanity Sūtras (Puruṣasūtra) are frequently found;
their original texts are still numerous.
I shall record them further upon seeing them.
9. Catalogues of the Various Scriptures Produced in Successive Dynasties, Part Nine. Preface:
The establishment of the positions of the Name-teachings (Confucianism) serves to rescue those who have sunk into ruin.
This will cause the true and the false to flow in separate streams and the heterodox and the orthodox to follow divergent paths.
For this reason, throughout successive dynasties, both monastics and laypeople have revered the Dharma-gate;
they have all diligently compiled and arranged [the teachings], maintaining them without interruption through the ages.
I have collated and verified over thirty extant and lost sources;
in determining the chronology of individuals, I have followed the *Anlu* (Records of An).
Yet, as for [Dao’an], the Sublime Sage under Heaven, his Way permeates both the realms of the hidden and the manifest.
Moved by the divine monk, he was shown the Compassionate Heaven;
having received the seal of approval, he clarified the commentaries.
Thus, he was able to verify and examine the essential tenets of the teachings.
They lightly chisel away at the profound style while valuing the pure wind;
they deliberate upon the meaning of phrases,
prioritizing substance over ornament while rejecting the rustic.
Consequently, his surviving writings and deeds have become ever more fresh through successive generations;
his virtue was so profoundly brilliant that it is difficult to fully describe or approximate.
All subsequent compositions are designated as "family names" (mingjia).
Their terminology is so varied—ranging from prolix to concise—that it is difficult to provide a universal simplification.
Nevertheless, through successive multiplication and placement within positions, they continue to produce new scriptures.
Both monastics and laypeople have praised [this work] at all times.
Lately, however, many have been indolent in their studies and lacked the leisure for broad observation;
they vied with one another to excerpt from the original scriptures, resulting in few who possess comprehensive mastery.
Therefore, the transmission and exposition of this text are largely deficient. Nevertheless,
in opening the way for faith and leading others toward the Path, employing skillful means as a guide to reach the source of transformation,
its principles encompass both worldly scriptures and sacred doctrine.
Thus, Huiyuan resolved the doubts of Huan Xuan;
Daolin opened the faith of Xi Chao;
and Senghui dispelled the delusions of the King of Wu.
Next, Dao Hong [discussed] the mind of the Song sovereign;
following that precedent down to the present day,
there have been instances where he did not fail to elegantly cite matters spanning the three periods of time.
He reported the workings of retribution as clearly as if pointing at one's palm;
he synthesized the Six Classics and elucidated how calamities and blessings alternate and lie in wait.
Incorporating the annals and histories from the periphery, he provides detailed analogies;
by using the near to verify the distant, he employs the mundane to awaken one to the Way.
To know the subtle signs with such spiritual acuity is achieved in this single stroke.
How could one allow their names to be buried and their traces erased, failing to include those who stand out as eminent?

What I have now compiled and recorded encompasses the works of various masters; I have scrutinized them to distinguish the authentic from the spurious and researched to recover what was lost, ensuring that nothing false has been included.
Without relying on the eyes, one cannot determine the names of these lost writings;
what I seek is for them to be arranged in scrolls so that they may be clearly recorded.
I venture to recount their origins in order to present this as a testament to my aspirations.
I have further compiled and arranged these for the consideration of all who come to examine them.
One scroll of the *Gujinglu* (Record of Ancient Scriptures): according to various ancient catalogs, this is most commonly referred to as the *Gulü* (Ancient Record).
This resembles the catalogues of scriptures brought by Śilabhadra and others during the Qin dynasty.
It consists of one scroll from the old records;
upon examination, it appears to be the work of Liu Xiang of the Former Han, who collated the books in the celestial archives.
These are frequently seen in many Buddhist scriptures;
they are precisely what were recorded in ancient catalogs of the Tripitaka as being hidden within the walls of the Confucian temple.
Alternatively, it may have been among those books preserved by people during the time of the Qin Emperor’s book-burning;
this single scroll of the *Buddhist Sūtra Catalogue* from the Han period, which I have examined,
appears to be the *Sūtra in Forty-two Sections* and other texts translated by Kāśyapa Mātanga.
I have therefore compiled and recorded them.
The one volume of the Han Catalogue by the Śramaṇa Zhu Shixing of the Wei period— right, according to my verification—
he was originally a śramaṇa from Yingchuan.
While lecturing on the *Daoxing jing* (Aṣṭasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra) in Luoyang, he consequently composed its catalog.
One scroll of the *Zhongjing lu* (Catalogue of Various Scriptures) by the Western Jin śramaṇa Dharmarakṣa. The above is verified according to the original.
This is a śramaṇa from a great monastery outside the Qing Gate of Chang’an during the reign of Emperor Wu of the Jin dynasty.
He translated a vast number of scriptures, and consequently, this catalog was produced.
One scroll of the *Zhòngjīnglù* (Catalogue of All Scriptures) by the lay follower of the Western Jin, Nie Dàozhēn. The above is verified according to the original source.
During the Yongjia era of the Jin dynasty’s Emperor Hui,
he was a disciple who received the teachings from Master Hu.
Later, he translated scriptures himself.
The *Yin chut lu* (Record of Excerpts) states:
"One fascicle of the *Catalogue of the Two Zhao Canons* (Erzhao jinglu). Right: This was verified [by me].
It appears to be a remote annotation of various catalogues from the period of the two Shi-Vaoshis."
The clan name is unknown.
One scroll of the *Zhongli zhongjing mulu* (Catalogue of the Scriptures Compiled by the Community) by the Śramaṇa Shi Dao’an of Former Qin. The above is verified according to the records.
During the Taiyuan era of Emperor Xiaowu of Eastern Jin.
He was a śramaṇa of the Former Qin dynasty.
In the various catalogs prior to this one,
they merely listed the titles of the scriptures along with their categories and the scale of their size.
As human generations have passed, there is no longer any record;
those born later who seek to trace them cannot fathom their origins.
Dao’an, therefore, has compiled these titles to indicate their respective eras.
The new and old versions were collated and their production standardized;
thus, the various scriptures gained clarity through these evidentiary sources.
Subsequently, the numerous catalogs drew upon them to expand and broaden the collection.
Thus we know that this auspicious destiny of the age has given rise to a sovereign of transcendent wisdom;
how could one fail to take this as a mirror?
The text is found in Sengyou’s *Lu*.
One fascicle of the *Lü* (Record) of Shi Sengrui, a Śramaṇa of Later Qin. [This entry] is verified based on the right-hand source.
He was a Śramaṇa of Chang’an during the Hongshi era of Yao Xing of Later Qin.
He was a disciple of the aforementioned Dao’an;
his spiritual faculties were clear and penetrating, and his intellectual power was preeminent.
He participated in the translation work at the school of Kumārajīva and compiled many of the texts.

The *Catalogue of the Four Collections of Scriptures* by the Eastern Jin śramaṇa Zhu Daozu consists of four parts: one scroll of the *Catalogue of Scriptures from the Wei Period*, one scroll of the *Catalogue of Scriptures from the Wu Period*, one scroll of the *Miscellaneous Catalogue of the Jin Period*, and one scroll of the *Catalogue of Scriptures from Hexi*. These are the four catalogues mentioned above.
According to an investigation, this was originally composed by the monk Shi Daoliu, a disciple of Master Huiyuan of Donglin Monastery on Mount Lu during the Eastern Jin dynasty;
he passed away before completing it,
and his fellow student Daozu finished it for him.
One fascicle of the *Zhī Míndù Jīnglùn Dūlù* (General Catalogue of Sūtras and Śāstras by the Eastern Jin Monk Zhī Míndù). The above is verified according to records.
He was a monk of Mount Yúzhāng during the reign of Emperor Chéng of the Jin dynasty.
This individual collated and edited the various sūtras of both ancient and modern times.
Therefore, he compiled the *Dulu* (General Catalog).
Mindu also compiled a separate catalog in one fascicle.
The two-fascicle record by the former Qi śramaṇa Shi Wangzong is listed above for verification.
He was a śramaṇa during the reign of Emperor Wu of the Qi dynasty.
This catalogue was produced by him,
as recorded in the *Biographies of the Tripiṭaka Masters of the Liang Dynasty*.

The *Qi Lu* (Record of Qi) by the former Qi śramaṇa Shi Daohui; the *Lu* (Record) of the Later Wei śramaṇa Bodhiruci; the *Lu* of the Later Qi śramaṇa Shi Daoping; the *Shixing Lu* (Record of Shixing), author unknown; the *Lushan Lu* (Record of Mount Lu), author unknown; the *Lu* of Shi Zhengdu; the *Lu* of General Wang; the *Lu* of Cen Hao; the *Lu* of Shi Hongchong; the four-fascicle *Hualin Fodian Lu* (Record of the Huilin Monastery Buddha Hall) by a resident of Yangdu during the Southern Qi, compiled by imperial decree in the Tianjian era of the Liang by the śramaṇa Sengshao; and the eight-fascicle *Zhongjing Dulu* (General Record of All Scriptures) translated by the Sui śramaṇa Shi Lingyu—these aforementioned records appear to have been compiled by collating various schools of thought, yet their authors remain uncertain.
There are twenty-four families.
I have verified their existence through the *Ji* and *Zhuan*,
though I have not yet seen the original texts themselves.

Therefore, I have merely listed their names. The *Zhongjing bielu* (Separate Record of Various Scriptures) in two volumes, whose author is unknown, appears to have been compiled during the Song dynasty. The upper volume contains three catalogs: first, the Catalog of Mahāyāna Scriptures; second, the Catalog of Teachings Common to the Three Vehicles; third, the Catalog of Mahāyāna within the Three Vehicles. The lower volume contains seven catalogs: fourth, the Catalog of Hīnayāna Scriptures; fifth, the Catalog of Missing Titles; sixth, the Catalog of Scriptures Not Classified as Mahāyāna or Hīnayāna; seventh, the Catalog of Doubtful Scriptures; eighth, the Catalog of Vinaya; ninth, the Numerical Catalog; tenth, the Catalog of Śāstras. In total, there are one thousand eighty-nine works comprising two thousand five hundred and ninety-three fascicles.

The *Collected Records of the Tripitaka Translated during the Liang Dynasty*, compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Sengyou at the end of the Qi and beginning of the Liang dynasties, consists of twelve sections: 1. A New Collection of Records of Scriptures and Treatises Newly Compiled and Translated; 2. A New Collection of Records of Scriptures and Treatises of Diverse Origins; 3. A New Collection of Records of the Fourfold Vinaya with Prefaces; 4. A New Collection of An Gong’s Records of Ancient and Variant Scriptures; 5. A New Collection of An Gong’s Records of Lost Translations; 6. A New Collection of An Gong’s Records of Variant Scriptures from the Liang Region; 7. A New Collection of An Gong’s Records of Variant Scriptures from Guanzhong; 8. A New Collection of Continued Compilations of Lost Translations; 9. A New Collection of Records of Excerpts from Scriptures; 10. A New Collection of An Gong’s Records of Doubtful Scriptures; 11. A New Collection of Records of Doubtful Scriptures and Apocryphal Compositions; 12. A New Collection of An Gong’s Commentaries and Miscellaneous Notes. Altogether, these twelve sections comprise two thousand one hundred and sixty-two works in four thousand three hundred and twenty-eight fascicles.

The Catalogue of Various Scriptures of the Northern Wei Dynasty, compiled by Imperial Edict during the Yongxi era under the direction of the Palace Attendant Li Kuò, comprises ten sections: 1. Catalogue of Mahāyāna Sūtras; 2. Catalogue of Mahāyāna Śāstras; 3. Catalogue of Commentaries on Mahāyāna Sūtras; 4. Catalogue of Untranslated Mahāyāna Sūtras and Śāstras; 5. Catalogue of Hīnayāna Sūtras and Vinaya; 6. Catalogue of Hīnayāna Śāstras; 7. Catalogue of Works for Which the Texts are Missing despite the Existence of a Title; 8. Catalogue of Non-Genuine Sūtras; 9. Catalogue of Non-Genuine Śāstras; 10. Catalogue of Entirely Spurious Works Composed by Ignorant Persons. In total, these comprise ten sections, totaling four hundred twenty-seven works in two thousand fifty-three fascicles.

The *Catalogue of All Scriptures of the Liang Dynasty*, compiled by the śramaṇa Baochang by imperial decree in the seventeenth year of the Tianjian era, consists of four volumes: Volume One, Mahāyāna; Volume Two, Hīnayāna; Volume Three, previously translated scriptures, dhyāna scriptures, vinaya, doubtful scriptures, annotated scriptures, numerical treatises, commentaries on meaning, and records; and Volume Four, titles categorized by subject matter, titles with lost names, parables, names of Buddhas, and divine mantras. These four volumes comprise twenty sections, totaling one thousand four hundred thirty-three works in three thousand seven hundred forty-one fascicles.

The Catalogue of All Scriptures from the Qi Dynasty, compiled by the śramaṇa Fashang during the Wuping era, consists of eight sections: the *Zaxang lu* (Catalogue of the Miscellaneous Piṭaka), the *Xiuduo lu* (Sūtra Catalogue), the *Bini lu* (Vinaya Catalogue), the *Abidun lu* (Abhidharma Catalogue), the *Bielu* (Separate Catalogue), the *Zhongjing chao lu* (Catalogue of Excerpts from Various Scriptures), and the *Jilu renzhuazuo lu* (Catalogue of Works Compiled by Individuals). Altogether, these eight categories comprise seven hundred and eighty-seven works in two thousand three hundred and thirty-four fascicles, containing both authentic and spurious sūtras, vinayas, and śāstras.

The *Great Sui Catalogue of All Scriptures* in seven fascicles was compiled by twenty great virtuous monks, including the śramaṇa Fajing and others, at the Bureau for Translating Scriptures by imperial decree in the fourteenth year of the Kaihuang era, according to the official inspection.
The catalog is organized into nine sections and divided into forty-two categories.
The first six categories provide a brief overview of the distinctions between the three baskets of Sūtra, Vinaya, and Abhidharma, as well as the Great and Small Vehicles.
The first [of these] is a general catalog of translations, distinguishing between the authentic and the spurious.
The latter three catalogs are all collections of biographies and commentaries.
These are known as the practices cultivated by both the clergy and the laity.
Although they were not composed in the Western Regions (India),
they all serve to glorify and support the orthodox scriptures, elucidate the religious teachings, and inspire the advancement of future students.
The above nine catalogs comprise a total of two thousand two hundred and fifty-seven works in five thousand three hundred and ten fascicles.

Compiled by Fei Changfang, a *bānzhōu xuéshì* (translation scholar) at Dàxīngshàn Temple in the seventeenth year of the Kaihuang era, the *Kāiyuáng Sānbǎo Lù* consists of fifteen volumes in total: one volume for the general table of contents, two volumes on the inclusion in the canon (*rùzàng*), three volumes on imperial reign dates, and nine volumes on the records of successive dynasties.
The scriptures, vinayas, śāstras, and biographies produced above total two thousand one hundred and forty-six works in six thousand two hundred and thirty-five fascicles.

According to the *Neidian lu* (Record of Inner Scriptures) in five fascicles compiled during the Renshou era of the Sui dynasty, the biography of the monk Shi Xuanyuan of Yanxing Temple in the capital states that Emperor Wen issued an edict to the Virtuous Masters of Daxingshan Temple and the śramaṇa-translators and scholars to examine the Dharma-treasury and meticulously determine this catalogue. It consists of five categories: first, single-text editions; second, works translated more than once; third, collections of the biographies of worthies and sages; fourth, separately produced works; and fifth, those of doubtful or spurious origin. These are the five items.
At present, the transcription and circulation of these works throughout the capital are widespread;
yet, while the titles of the scriptures are listed directly and their translations are cataloged,
more than half have been omitted, making them insufficient for consultation.
The preface briefly states:
"Those [texts] separately classified as spurious need not be transcribed;
the remaining three parts have been included in the Tripitaka."
As for works such as the *Fǎbǎo jí* (Collection of Dharma Treasures) and those like the *Jìngzhù zǐ* (Son of Pure Abiding),
they are essentially nothing more than abbreviated compilations.
Examples include the *Biesheng* (Separate Biographies) and other monastic biographies (*sengzhuan*),
as well as collections of prose and literary works (*wenci*).
Its substance is not pure or correct;
whom can one seek for its facts?
Its meaning is not worth recording.
Thus it is said, as recorded above.

The collection of the King’s translations of sutras, vinayas, śāstras, and commentaries, transcribed at Ximing Monastery in the capital of the Great Tang, was officially entered into the canon in the third year of the Xianqing era. It comprised a total of seven hundred and ninety-nine works, consisting of three thousand three hundred and sixty-one fascicles and fifty-six thousand one hundred and seventy-five sheets of paper.

The *Dàtáng nèidiǎn lù* (Record of the Inner Scriptures of the Great Tang), one bundle in ten volumes, consists of the following: the *Lìdài zhòngjīng chuányì lù* (Record of the Translation of Various Scriptures Throughout the Successive Dynasties) in five volumes; the *Lìdài fānjīng dānchóng réndài cūnwáng lù* (Record of the Single or Multiple Translators and Their Existence or Extinction by Dynasty) in one volume; the *Lìdài zhòngjīng fēnshèng rùzàng lù* (Record of the Classification of Various Scriptures into Vehicles and their Inclusion in the Canon) in two volumes; the *Lìdài zhòngjīng jǔyào zhuǎndú lù* (Record of the Essential Recitation of Various Scriptures Throughout the Successive Dynasties) in one volume; the *Lìdài zhòngjīng yǒumù quēběn lù* (Record of Various Scriptures with Catalogs but Missing Texts); the *Lìdài dàosú shùzuò zhùjiě lù* (Record of Works and Commentaries Composed by Monastics and Laypeople Throughout the Successive Dynasties); the *Lìdài zhòngjīng zhīliú chénhuà lù* (Record of the Branch Streams and Dissemination of Various Scriptures Throughout the Successive Dynasties); the *Lìdài suochū yíwěi jīnglùn lù* (Record of Suspected and Spurious Scriptures and Treatises Produced Throughout the Successive Dynasties); and the *Lìdài zhòngjīng lùmù suó cóng xù* (Preface to the Sources of the Catalogs of Various Scriptures Throughout the Successive Dynasties) and the *Lìdài zhòngjīng yìnggǎn xìngjìng lù* (Record of Responses and Veneration Regarding Various Scriptures Throughout the Successive Dynasties). These last six records together constitute one volume.

The above totals eighteen generations of translated scriptures, numbering two thousand two hundred and sixty-two works in over seven thousand fascicles; one may calculate this for oneself and realize that the authors were exhausted by the task.
I have been bathed in the stream of the Dharma since my youth for over fifty years;
the patriarchs have perfected the teachings, and the masters have upheld the models with wisdom.
Whenever I encountered the scriptures and treatises, there were none whose virtues and capacities I did not examine personally or visit in person.
As for the great records of the Sūtra-piṭaka, I gained much joy and awakening from them;
regardless of whether they were authentic or spurious, I reflected upon their differences.
Since Zhang Fangshuo beheld the ashes of Kunming and Liu Xiang collated the Buddhist scriptures in the celestial library,
we know that the Zhou and Han dynasties had long heard of them.
It was not until later that the *Abhidharmakośa* (Xianzong) was introduced to this land;
thus, Dharmaratna first produced the draft of the chapters,
while An Shigao extensively translated various scriptures.
In other schools, there are no paths that do not follow one another;
thus, from the Wei and Jin dynasties onward, translations have flourished like a steaming heat.
The catalogues and discussions regarding them are manifestly not uniform.
Either by enumerating numbers,
or by seeking through names,
or by relying on historical periods.
Some were invited to participate in the translation;
each recorded their own perspective, striving to preserve their insights.
These individuals were all of that time renowned for their erudition, discernment, and cultivated understanding of antiquity.
As for why my compilation and editorial revisions have not reached the level of detailed precision,
it is not because my talent is insufficient or my wisdom incomplete;
it is simply because the world in which I dwell has fallen into fragmentation and collapse.
The borders and frontier passes were so difficult to traverse that one could not even read through the Sūtra sections;
